default.q.n2-11-q28-28.why.1: Correct: 「微妙に違っている」 is the standard expression for a very small, subtle difference that is not immediately noticeable to the naked eye.
default.q.n2-11-q28-28.why.2: Incorrect. For a person whose secretive and suspicious behavior causes fear, use 「怪しい人（あやしいひと）」 or 「不審な人」, not 「微妙な人」.
default.q.n2-11-q28-28.why.3: Incorrect: For being slightly older, use 「わずかに年上」 or 「少し年上」, not 「微妙に年上」, because an age difference is a specific, measurable number.
default.q.n2-11-q29-29.explanation: 「あかり（明かり・灯り）」refers to light from a lamp, candle, streetlight, or similar source that drives away darkness. It is commonly used in expressions such as 「あかりをつける／消す」(to turn the light on/off) and 「あかりを灯す」(to light a lamp). Example: 窓から街のあかりが見える。(You can see the city lights from the window.)
default.q.n2-11-q29-29.why.0: Incorrect: A clue or lead that results in the arrest of a criminal must be expressed with「手がかり（てがかり）」, not「あかり」.
default.q.n2-11-q29-29.why.1: Incorrect: To boil water using the heat or fire of a heater, use 「熱（ねつ）」 or 「火（ひ）」. 「あかり」 means light for illumination and cannot boil water.
default.q.n2-11-q29-29.why.2: Correct: 「暗いからあかりをつけてください」 is completely appropriate. 「あかりをつける」 means to turn on a light or illuminate a room when it is dark.
default.q.n2-11-q29-29.why.3: Incorrect because glaring summer sunlight should be expressed with 「（太陽の）光（ひかり）」or「日差し（ひざし）」, not 「太陽のあかり」.
default.q.n2-11-q30-30.explanation:
「むかい（向かい）」means opposite or across from something, such as across a street, courtyard, or passageway. Common expressions include 「〜の向かい」(opposite/across from...), and 「向かいの部屋／家／席」(the room/house/seat opposite).
Example: 駅の向かいに新しいカフェがオープンした。(A new café opened across from the station.)
default.q.n2-11-q30-30.why.0: Incorrect: When seeing a boat far offshore, use 「沖（おき）」or 「海の向こう」; the vast open sea is not expressed with 「海のむかい」.
default.q.n2-11-q30-30.why.1: Incorrect. For a room facing south, use「南向き（みなみむき）」; 「南むかい」is not used.
default.q.n2-11-q30-30.why.2: Incorrect: When returning to one's country and referring to someone or somewhere on the other side, in one's hometown or destination, use 「向こう（むこう）」 or 「現地」, not 「むかい」.
default.q.n2-11-q30-30.why.3: Correct: 「うちのむかい」 indicates a house directly across the road, which is accurate in both meaning and context.
default.q.n2-11-q31-31.explanation: 「わずか（僅か）」is an adverb/noun indicating an extremely small amount, degree, distance, or length of time; only, merely, a scant amount (often placed before a counter). Example: 残りはわずか100円しかない。(Only 100 yen remains.)
default.q.n2-11-q31-31.why.0: Correct: 「わずか5分」 means “only five minutes” or “a mere five minutes,” emphasizing an extremely short duration and sounding completely natural.
default.q.n2-11-q31-31.why.1: Incorrect: being left completely alone after one’s parents die is expressed with 「たった一人」or 「ひとりぼっち」, not 「わずか一人」in this exclamatory structure.
default.q.n2-11-q31-31.why.2: Incorrect. For something that can be done with a little thought, use 「少し」 or 「ちょっと」, not 「わずかに考えれば」.
default.q.n2-11-q31-31.why.3: Incorrect: When a teacher's voice is too quiet to hear, use 「小さすぎて（声が小さい）」, not 「わずかすぎて」for voice volume.
default.q.n2-11-q32-32.explanation:
「実施（じっし）」means to implement, apply, or carry out plans, policies, regulations, examinations, or surveys in practice. It is commonly used in phrases such as 「〜を実施する／が実施される」.
Example: 来週、避難訓練を実施します。(An evacuation drill will be conducted next week.)
default.q.n2-11-q32-32.why.0: Incorrect: when a dream becomes a reality, use 「実現した（じつげんした）」 or 「かなった」. 「実施」 is used for plans or rules carried out intentionally by a person or organization.
default.q.n2-11-q32-32.why.1: Incorrect. When an ideal differs from reality, use「現実（げんじつ）」or「実際（じっさい）」, not「実施」.
default.q.n2-11-q32-32.why.2: Incorrect. For something practical or realistic, use 「現実的（げんじつてき）」 or 「実際的」. The word 「実施的」 does not exist in Japanese.
default.q.n2-11-q32-32.why.3: Correct: 「新制度が実施される」 (the new system is implemented) is a grammatically correct and natural Japanese structure.
default.q.n2-11-q1-1.verdict: The correct answer is 3 (まんいち).
default.q.n2-11-q1-1.explanation:
- Sentence meaning: "Airlines always have rescue procedures ready in case an accident should occur."
- Kanji:
  + 万 (VẠN): on-readings まん (as in 万一: まんいち, 万国: まんこく) and ばん (as in 万全: ばんぜん, 万能: ばんのう).
  + 一 (NHẤT): on-reading いち (or いつ).
- Another example: 万一雨が降ったら、イベントは延期になります。 (If it should happen to rain, the event will be postponed.)
default.q.n2-11-q1-1.why.0: (a) 「まいち」is an incorrect reading of 「万一」.
default.q.n2-11-q1-1.why.1: (b) 「ばいち」 is an incorrect reading of 「万一」 (even when 万 is read as ばん, it does not combine to form ばいち).
default.q.n2-11-q1-1.why.2: (c) 「まんいち」 is the correct reading of 「万一」, meaning “if by any chance,” “in the unlikely event,” or “should something happen.”
default.q.n2-11-q1-1.why.3: (d) 「ばんいち」is an incorrect reading of 「万一」.
default.q.n2-11-q2-2.verdict: The correct answer is 3 (こうかん).
default.q.n2-11-q2-2.explanation:
- Sentence meaning: “A great many international students took part in the gathering and exchanged opinions.”
- Kanji:
  + 交 (GIAO): the on-reading is こう (as in 交流: こうりゅう, 交通: こうつう, 交渉: こうしょう).
  + 換 (HOÁN): the on-reading is かん (as in 変換: へんかん, 換気: かんき; verbs 換える / 換わる: かえる / かわる).
- Additional example: 会議の前に名刺を交換しましょう。 (Let’s exchange business cards before the meeting.)
default.q.n2-11-q2-2.why.0: (a) 「こうたい」 is the reading of 「交代」 (taking turns, changing shifts) or 「後退」 (retreat, decline), not 交換.
default.q.n2-11-q2-2.why.1: (b) 「こうだい」 is the reading of 「広大」 (vast, expansive), not 交換.
default.q.n2-11-q2-2.why.2: (c) 「こうかん」 is the correct reading of 「交換」 (exchange, swapping).
default.q.n2-11-q2-2.why.3: (d) 「こうがん」 is an incorrect reading in this context. Although 厚顔 (shamelessness) is read こうがん, it does not fit the context.
default.q.n2-11-q3-3.verdict: The correct answer is 4 (めずらしい).
default.q.n2-11-q3-3.explanation:
- Meaning: “If you find a rare plant species, please investigate it in detail and record your findings.”
- Kanji:
  + 珍 (rare): kun-reading めずら・しい; on-reading ちん, as in 珍味 (ちんみ — a rare delicacy) and 珍重 (ちんちょう — to value highly).
- Another example: 日本では珍しい果物を食べた。 (I ate a fruit that is rare in Japan.)
default.q.n2-11-q3-3.why.0: (a) 「あやしい」is the reading of「怪しい」(suspicious, dubious).
default.q.n2-11-q3-3.why.1: (b) 「ひとしい」 is the reading of 「等しい」 (equal, equivalent).
default.q.n2-11-q3-3.why.2: (c) 「なつかしい」 is the reading of 「懐かしい」 (nostalgic, fondly remembered).
default.q.n2-11-q3-3.why.3: (d) 「めずらしい」 is the correct reading of 「珍しい」, meaning "rare, precious, unusual."
default.q.n2-11-q4-4.verdict: The correct answer is 4 (せっしょく).
default.q.n2-11-q4-4.explanation:
- Sentence meaning: "An elderly man on a bicycle collided with a bus, fell, and broke his leg."
- Kanji:
  + 接 (TIẾP): on-reading せつ, as in 接続 (せつぞく) and 直接 (ちょくせつ). When followed by a sound from the さ/しゃ row, it becomes the geminate sound せっ.
  + 触 (XÚC): on-reading しょく, as in 感触 (かんしょく); kun-readings さわ・る and ふ・れる.
- Another example: 車とバイクが接触する事故が発生した。 (A traffic accident involving a car and a motorcycle occurred.)
default.q.n2-11-q4-4.why.0: (a) 「せつぞく」 is the reading of 「接続」 (connection, linking).
default.q.n2-11-q4-4.why.1: (b) 「ぜつじょく」 is an incorrect reading; 「雪辱」 is read せつじょく and means to restore one's honor or avenge a defeat.
default.q.n2-11-q4-4.why.2: (c) 「せっそく」 is the reading of 「拙速」, meaning fast but clumsy, or it omits the “sh” sound in the reading of 触.
default.q.n2-11-q4-4.why.3: (d) 「せっしょく」 is the correct reading of 「接触」. The sokuon sound change occurs before しょく (せつ → せっ), and the word means “contact” or “collision.”
default.q.n2-11-q5-5.explanation:
- Meaning: “Residents who are concerned about environmental pollution are opposing the development/extraction of a new ore mine.”
- Kanji:
  + 汚: On-reading お, as in 汚染 (おせん) and 汚職 (おしょく); kun-readings きたな・い, よご・れる/よご・す, and けが・れる/けが・す.
  + 染: On-reading せん, as in 感染 (かんせん) and 伝染 (でんせん); kun-readings そ・める/そ・まる, し・みる/し・まらせる.
- Another example: 工場からの排煙が大気汚染の原因となっている。 (Smoke emitted from factories is causing air pollution.)
default.q.n2-11-q5-5.why.0: (a) 「おせん」 is the correct reading of 「汚染」, meaning “pollution” or “contamination.”
default.q.n2-11-q5-5.why.1: (b) 「かせん」 is the reading of 「河川」 (rivers and streams) or 「下線」 (underline), not 汚染.
default.q.n2-11-q5-5.why.2: (c) 「かんせん」 is the reading of 「感染」, meaning infection, or 「幹線」, meaning a main line or trunk route.
default.q.n2-11-q5-5.why.3: (d) 「でんせん」 is the reading of 「伝染」 (the spread of disease) or 「電線」 (electric wire).
default.q.n2-11-q6-6.verdict: The correct answer is 3. 階 (2階: second floor).
default.q.n2-11-q6-6.explanation:
- Meaning: I found a wallet near the escalator leading to the second floor of the hall.
- Sino-Japanese reading: 階 (KAI - floor, stair/step).
- Example: 私の部屋はアパートの3階にあります。(My room is on the third floor of the apartment building.)
default.q.n2-11-q6-6.why.0: (a) 「皆」 (GAKAI, on-reading: かい, kun-reading: みな) means "everyone, all"; it is not used as a counter for building floors.
default.q.n2-11-q6-6.why.1: (b) 「偕」 (on-reading: かい) means “together,” as in 偕老同穴; it is not used to indicate a floor or story.
default.q.n2-11-q6-6.why.2: (c) 「階」 (GIAI, on-reading: かい) means “floor” or “stairs.” 「2階」 (にかい) means “the second floor,” which fits the context perfectly.
default.q.n2-11-q6-6.why.3: (d) 「諧」 (かい) means harmony, accord, or humor, as in 諧謔; it is not used to count floors.
default.q.n2-11-q7-7.verdict: The correct answer is 1. 永遠 (永遠: forever, eternity).
default.q.n2-11-q7-7.explanation:
- Meaning: Do you think the universe will exist forever?
- Sino-Japanese reading: 永遠 (えいえん: forever, eternity).
- Example: 二人の愛が永遠に続くことを祈っています。(I pray that the love between the two of you will last forever.)
default.q.n2-11-q7-7.why.0: (a) 「永遠」 (えいえん) combines 永 (eternity) and 遠 (long-lasting, distant) and means “eternal, forever,” so it is completely correct.
default.q.n2-11-q7-7.why.1: (b) 「永延」 uses the wrong second kanji; 「延」 has the on-reading えん but means to prolong or postpone, as in 延長 and 延期, and does not form the word えいえん.
default.q.n2-11-q7-7.why.2: (c) 「氷遠」 has the wrong first kanji; 「氷」 (ice) has an extra dot and looks similar to 「永」 (eternity), but the kanji and meaning are incorrect.
default.q.n2-11-q7-7.why.3: (d) 「氷延」 uses the wrong kanji for both characters: 「氷」 is confused with 「永」, and 「延」 with 「遠」.
default.q.n2-11-q8-8.verdict: The correct answer is 4. 移動 (移動: moving to another position, relocating).
default.q.n2-11-q8-8.explanation:
- Translation: Move the car to the designated location.
- Sino-Japanese note: 移動 (いどう: to move, relocate). It should be distinguished from 異動 (いどう: a personnel transfer).
- Example: バスで次の目的地へ移動した。(We traveled to the next destination by bus.)
default.q.n2-11-q8-8.why.0: (a)「異道」is not a standard Japanese vocabulary word for moving a vehicle or changing position.
default.q.n2-11-q8-8.why.1: (b) 「異動」 (TRANSFER, pronounced いどう) refers to a change or transfer in one's work position or personnel assignment (such as 人事異動); it is not used for the physical movement of vehicles or objects.
default.q.n2-11-q8-8.why.2: (c) 「移道」is an nonexistent kanji compound for expressing the act of moving.
default.q.n2-11-q8-8.why.3: (d) 「移動」 (いどう) means moving or changing location from one place to another physically, so it is entirely suitable for moving a car.
default.q.n2-11-q9-9.verdict: The correct answer is 4. 予算 (予算: budget, projected expenses).
default.q.n2-11-q9-9.explanation:
- Meaning: It is said that next fiscal year's budget will exceed 200 million yen.
- Sino-Japanese reading: 予算 (YOSAN - budget, planned expenditure).
- Example: 今年の予算案を立てる。(Draw up this year's draft budget.)
default.q.n2-11-q9-9.why.0: (a) 「要算」uses the wrong first kanji; 「要」has the on-reading よう, as in 必要, and does not combine to form よさん meaning “budget.”
default.q.n2-11-q9-9.why.1: (b) 「余算」uses the wrong first kanji; 「余」means excess or surplus and is read よ in on-reading, but it does not combine with 算 to mean a reserve budget.
default.q.n2-11-q9-9.why.2: (c) The first kanji in 「与算」 is incorrect; 「与」 (to give, on-reading: よ) does not combine to form a word meaning budget or expenses.
default.q.n2-11-q9-9.why.3: (d) 「予算」(read よさん) combines 「予」(anticipation) and 「算」(calculation), meaning “budget, projected expenses.” It is completely correct.
default.q.n2-11-q10-10.verdict: The correct answer is 3. 楽器 (楽器: musical instrument).
default.q.n2-11-q10-10.explanation:
- Meaning: I withdrew all my savings to buy a musical instrument.
- Kanji note: 楽器 means musical instrument.
- Example: 彼はピアノやギターなど、色々な楽器が演奏できる。(He can play various musical instruments, such as the piano and guitar.)
default.q.n2-11-q10-10.why.0: (a) 「楽机」has the wrong second kanji; 「机」(kun-reading: つくえ, on-reading: き) means “desk” and does not form a word for a musical instrument.
default.q.n2-11-q10-10.why.1: (b) 「楽歳」 has the second kanji wrong; 「歳」 (on-readings: さい/せい) means age or years, and has nothing to do with musical instruments.
default.q.n2-11-q10-10.why.2: (c) 「楽器」, read がっき, consists of 「楽」, meaning music, and 「器」, meaning instrument or tool; it correctly means “musical instrument.”
default.q.n2-11-q10-10.why.3: (d) 「楽機」 uses the wrong second kanji; 「機」 (on-reading: き) generally refers to machinery or opportunity, as in 機械 and 機会, and is not used for musical instruments.
default.q.n2-12-q33-33.verdict: The correct answer is 4. 買い物をしてきた.
default.q.n2-12-q33-33.explanation:
Sentence meaning: “While seeing a guest off to the station, Mother went shopping and then came home.”
N2 grammar:「V-る / V-た / Nの + ついでに」(while doing A, take the opportunity to do B). The second clause describes an intentional action performed during the same trip or occasion.
Example: 散歩のついでに、この手紙を出してきてくれない？ (While you’re out for a walk, could you mail this letter for me?)
default.q.n2-12-q33-33.why.0: (a) Incorrect because “your friend coming over” is an event caused by someone else, not an intentional action by the mother when she goes out.
default.q.n2-12-q33-33.why.1: (b) Incorrect because traveling is a major activity and is not something one would do “while one is at it” when seeing a guest off at the station.
default.q.n2-12-q33-33.why.2: (c) Incorrect because “hearing music” is a naturally occurring perception, not a deliberate action.
default.q.n2-12-q33-33.why.3: (d) Correct because shopping is an intentional action, so it is natural to combine it with stopping by the station to see someone off and then shopping while already there.
default.q.n2-12-q34-34.verdict: The correct answer is 1. ことで.
default.q.n2-12-q34-34.explanation:
Meaning: "It was winning the international violin competition last year that made Mr. Nakada known to the public for the first time."
N2 grammar:「V-た / V-る / Nの + ことで」(by / through doing something, resulting in...).
Example: 留学したことで、視野が広がった。(Studying abroad broadened my horizons.)
default.q.n2-12-q34-34.why.0: (a) Correct because 「〜たことで」 indicates the cause or reason leading to the result or change in the following clause: becoming known after winning an award.
default.q.n2-12-q34-34.why.1: (b) Incorrect because「ことなら」means “if it is a matter of...,” and is not used to explain the cause of an outcome that has already occurred.
default.q.n2-12-q34-34.why.2: (c) Incorrect because「ことには」is generally used in the pattern「〜ないことには〜ない」(unless..., ... cannot happen).
default.q.n2-12-q34-34.why.3: (d) Incorrect because 「〜ことだから」 is used to make a supposition based on someone's personality or habits, commonly with 「Nのことだから」.
default.q.n2-12-q35-35.verdict: The correct answer is 2. 見てもつまらない.
default.q.n2-12-q35-35.explanation:
Sentence meaning: “This movie is intended for adults, so even if children watch it, they will find it boring.”
N2 grammar: 「N + 向け」 means “intended for N.” Since the first clause clearly states that the movie is for adults, the logical result is that children will not find it interesting even if they watch it.
Example: この本は初心者向けに書かれている。(This book is written for beginners.)
default.q.n2-12-q35-35.why.0: (a) Incorrect because “it is enjoyable even when watched” logically contradicts the preceding phrase “a film intended for adults.”
default.q.n2-12-q35-35.why.1: (b) Correct because “even watching it would be boring” fits the cause-and-effect logic of its being “a film intended for adults.”
default.q.n2-12-q35-35.why.2: (c) Incorrect because「V-る + ところだ」means “be about to do something,” which does not fit the meaning of the sentence.
default.q.n2-12-q35-35.why.3: (d) Incorrect because 「〜ところではない」 means “it is not the time to...” or “one is in no state to...,” and does not form a natural complete sentence here.
default.q.n2-12-q36-36.verdict: The correct answer is 3. 無理だった.
default.q.n2-12-q36-36.explanation:
Sentence translation: “I heard that this game is popular among young people, so I tried playing it, but it was too much for me.”
N2 grammar: 「V-た + ものの」(although... but...) and 「〜には無理だ」(too difficult or demanding for someone).
Kanji reading: 無理 (too demanding, impossible).
Example: 車を買ったものの、あまり乗る機会がない。(Although I bought a car, I do not have many opportunities to drive it.)
default.q.n2-12-q36-36.why.0: (a) Incorrect because 「ものの」 connects contrasting clauses (“although I tried playing, I could not enjoy it”). Using 「楽しめた」would contradict both the logic and the unnatural grammar of 「わたしには楽しめた」.
default.q.n2-12-q36-36.why.1: (b) Incorrect because 「わたしには若すぎた」 (too young for me) does not fit the meaning in this context.
default.q.n2-12-q36-36.why.2: (c) Correct because 「わたしには無理だった」 (it was too much for me; I couldn't manage it) provides a perfect contrast with 「やってはみたものの」.
default.q.n2-12-q36-36.why.3: (d) Incorrect because「年を取ってい」is grammatically incomplete as the ending of a sentence.
default.q.n2-12-q37-37.verdict: The correct answer is 4. からして.
default.q.n2-12-q37-37.explanation:
Meaning: "Mr. Tanaka's plan was highly original from the very idea itself."
N2 grammar: 「N + からして」 means "right from / judging from..." It presents a representative, specific example and uses it to evaluate the whole.
Kanji-based terms: 発想 (idea), 独特 (distinctive, original).
Example: 彼は話し方からして生意気だ。(He seems conceited from the way he talks alone.)
default.q.n2-12-q37-37.why.0: (a) Incorrect because 「〜をして〜しめる」 is an archaic causative structure and is not appropriate here.
default.q.n2-12-q37-37.why.1: (b) Incorrect because「からは」indicates a starting point; it does not give a representative example for evaluation as「からして」does.
default.q.n2-12-q37-37.why.2: (c) Incorrect because「〜を待って」means "after waiting for... / while waiting for..." and is unrelated.
default.q.n2-12-q37-37.why.3: (d) Correct because 「発想からして独特だ」 (“the idea itself is unique from the outset”) accurately demonstrates the grammar pattern 「〜からして」.
default.q.n2-12-q38-38.verdict: The correct answer is 2. もとに.
default.q.n2-12-q38-38.explanation:
Sentence translation: “I intend to decide our future policy based on Mr. Yamakawa’s survey results.”
N2 grammar: 「N + をもとに (をもとにして)」(based on N; using N as the foundation or basis).
Kanji vocabulary: 調査 (CHOU-SA - survey, investigation), 方針 (HOU-SHIN - policy, course of action).
Example: この小説は事実をもとにして書かれた。(This novel was written based on actual events.)
default.q.n2-12-q38-38.why.0: (a) This is incorrect because 「〜をこめて」(putting one's feelings or devotion into something) is used with emotional nouns such as 愛、心、 and 祈り.
default.q.n2-12-q38-38.why.1: (b) Correct because「〜をもとに」(based on) is used with data, documents, and investigation results.
default.q.n2-12-q38-38.why.2: (c) Incorrect because 「〜をはじめ (として)」means “foremost among them is…” or “starting with…,” and is used for listing examples.

default.q.n2-12-q39-39.verdict: The correct answer is 1. 拝見いたしました.
default.q.n2-12-q39-39.explanation:
Translation: “A moment ago, I read the essay that Professor Ueda wrote for the magazine.”
N2 honorific grammar: 「拝見する / 拝見いたします」 is the humble form (謙譲語) of 「見る / 読む」, used when the speaker humbly refers to viewing or reading something written by a superior, here Professor Ueda.
Kanji: 拝見.
Example: 先生の新しいご著書を拝見いたしました。(I have read your new book, Professor.)
default.q.n2-12-q39-39.why.0: (a) Correct because 「拝見いたしました」is the humble form of 「見る/読む」, used for one's own act of reading a professor's materials.
default.q.n2-12-q39-39.why.1: (b) Incorrect because 「お読みになりました」 is respectful language (尊敬語), used for the professor’s action, not for my own action.
default.q.n2-12-q39-39.why.2: (c) 「お目にかかる」is the humble form of「会う」(to meet a person), so it is not used for reading books or newspapers.
default.q.n2-12-q39-39.why.3: (d) Incorrect because 「承る (うけたまわる)」is the humble form of「聞く / 引き受ける」(to hear / accept or undertake), not a word meaning to read a dissertation.
default.q.n2-12-q40-40.verdict: The correct answer is 1. する.
default.q.n2-12-q40-40.explanation:
Translation: "The voting results determined that Mr. Yamada would be appointed chairperson."
N2 grammar:「A を B とする」(to choose, decide on, or regard A as B). When used with the particle「〜を」, it takes the transitive verb「する」.
Kanji vocabulary: 投票 (voting), 会長 (chairperson), 決定 (decision).
Example: 来年度から彼をリーダーとすることになった。(It was decided that he would become the leader starting next fiscal year.)
default.q.n2-12-q40-40.why.0: (a) Correct because the pattern 「〜を〜とする」 means to appoint or choose someone for a particular position.
default.q.n2-12-q40-40.why.1: (b) Incorrect because「なる」is an intransitive verb and takes the particle「が」(山田氏が会長になる); it does not form the pattern「山田氏を会長と...」.
default.q.n2-12-q40-40.why.2: (c) Incorrect because 「〜ととる」 does not form a grammar pattern meaning “to appoint someone to a position.”
default.q.n2-12-q40-40.why.3: (d) Incorrect because 「〜とえる」 does not form a meaningful grammar pattern.
default.q.n2-12-q41-41.verdict: The correct answer is 3. おそれがある.
default.q.n2-12-q41-41.explanation:
Sentence translation: “The business run by someone I know seems to be in quite a difficult situation; at this rate, there is a risk that it will go bankrupt.”
N2 grammar: 「V-る / Nの + おそれがある (恐れがある)」(there is a fear or risk that something bad will happen).
Kanji note: 恐れ (fear, risk).
Example: この台風により、大雨になる恐れがあります。(Because of this typhoon, there is a risk of heavy rain.)
default.q.n2-12-q41-41.why.0: (a) Incorrect because 「〜わけがある」means “there is a reason/cause that ...,” and is not used to warn of a future danger.
default.q.n2-12-q41-41.why.1: (b) Incorrect because 「〜ことがある」 means “there are times when...” or “have sometimes...,” and does not convey concern about risk.
default.q.n2-12-q41-41.why.2: (c) Correct because 「〜おそれがある」 expresses concern about the possibility of a negative event, such as bankruptcy, occurring.
default.q.n2-12-q41-41.why.3: (d) Incorrect: the combination 「つぶれるしだいがある」 does not exist with the meaning of predicting a risk.
default.q.n2-12-q42-42.verdict: The correct answer is 1. ないだろう.
default.q.n2-12-q42-42.explanation:
Translation: "The population in this area is gradually declining, and unless measures are taken, it is unlikely to increase in the future."
N2 grammar:「〜ない限り、〜ない」(unless..., ...not...). The clause following「ない限り」must have a negative meaning.
Example: 一生懸命練習しない限り、試合には勝てない。(Unless you practice hard, you cannot win the match.)
default.q.n2-12-q42-42.why.0: (a) Correct because the clause following 「〜ない限り」 requires a clause with a negative meaning, 「増えることはないだろう」 (“it probably will not increase”).
default.q.n2-12-q42-42.why.1: (b) Incorrect because 「あるだろう」 is an affirmative assertion, which conflicts logically with the negative condition 「〜ない限り」.
default.q.n2-12-q42-42.why.2: (c) Incorrect because「あるかもしれない」(there may be) expresses possibility, contradicting the logic of the preceding clause.
default.q.n2-12-q42-42.why.3: (d) Incorrect because the grammatical combination is wrong. It would have to be 「〜ことにはならない」, but even that would be less appropriate in meaning than 「ないだろう」 here.
default.q.n2-12-q43-43.verdict: The correct answer is 4. できなく はない.

Sentence translation: "Yamamoto suddenly quit his job one day, surprising everyone around him, but considering his personality, it is not impossible to understand."
N2 grammar: 「V-ない + ことはない / なくはない」means 'it is not that...not' or 'it is somewhat possible to...'. The potential form 「理解できる」is changed into the double negative 「理解できなくはない」to express that the situation can be understood or sympathized with to some extent.

default.q.n2-12-q43-43.why.1: (b) Incorrect because with verbs of perception or understanding, the potential form 「できなくはない」 is more natural and accurate than 「しなくはない」.
default.q.n2-12-q43-43.why.2: (c) Incorrect because 「できそうもない」(seems completely impossible) means that something probably cannot be done or understood, which conflicts with the conjunction 「が」and the phrase 「あの人の性格を考えると」.
default.q.n2-12-q43-43.why.3: (d) Correct because 「理解できなくはない」 (it is not that it cannot be understood) expresses partial understanding and fits the context perfectly.
default.q.n2-12-q44-44.verdict: The correct answer is 2. つつある.
default.q.n2-12-q44-44.explanation:
Translation: “In many countries, environmental pollution is becoming increasingly serious, while on the other hand, the number of countries cooperating technically to eliminate pollution is also gradually increasing.”
N2 grammar: 「V-stem + つつある」 (be gradually / steadily becoming...). It is commonly used with verbs describing changes or developments, such as 増える、減る、変化する.
Kanji readings and meanings: 公害 (environmental pollution), 協力 (cooperation).
Example: 景気は回復しつつある。(The economy is gradually recovering.)
default.q.n2-12-q44-44.why.0: (a) Incorrect because 「V-stem + がたい」means “difficult to do” emotionally or psychologically, as in 信じがたい; it does not combine with 増える.
default.q.n2-12-q44-44.why.1: (b) Correct. 「増えつつある」 expresses a gradual change in progress (“steadily increasing”), which is grammatically appropriate for JLPT N2.
default.q.n2-12-q44-44.why.2: (c) Incorrect because V-stem + きれない means “cannot completely ...” or “too much to ...,” which does not fit the meaning.
default.q.n2-12-q44-44.why.3: (d) Incorrect because V-stem + がち generally indicates a negative tendency or something that often happens undesirably (such as 遅れがち or 忘れがち), so it does not fit the positive meaning here.

default.q.n2-12-q50-50.verdict: The correct answer is 1. というのは.
default.q.n2-12-q50-50.explanation: This conjunction begins a sentence explaining the underlying reason why the husband often buys gifts for his wife, as indicated by the explanatory sentence ending 〜からである. In Japanese, 「というのは」(the reason is that / this is because...) is specifically used to introduce an explanation for the matter just mentioned. Therefore, choice 1 is the correct answer.
default.q.n2-12-q50-50.why.0: (a) Correct. 「というのは」is used at the beginning of a sentence to introduce an explanation of the reason or cause for something mentioned in the previous sentence, often ending with 〜からだ or 〜のである.
default.q.n2-12-q50-50.why.1: (b) Incorrect. 「すると」means “then; immediately afterward” (successive development) or “if so, then” (logical inference); it is not used to explain a reason.
default.q.n2-12-q50-50.why.2: (c) Incorrect. 「しかも」 means "moreover" or "in addition," adding further information, so it does not fit the logic of explaining a cause.
default.q.n2-12-q50-50.why.3: (d) Incorrect. 「さて」 is a conjunction used to shift to a new topic (“now then / next”), not to continue explaining the cause of the previous sentence.
default.q.n2-12-q51-51.verdict: The correct answer is 2. 置いたきり.
default.q.n2-12-q51-51.explanation: The structure 「V-たきり」 (N2) means that after doing V, one remains in that state without taking any further action that would normally be expected. In this sentence, the adverb 「ぽんと」 (plop something down) combined with 「置いたきり」 vividly depicts the wife accepting the gift, plopping it on top of the refrigerator, and leaving it there without showing any excitement or opening it. This expresses her indifference and her husband's disappointment. Therefore, choice 2 is the correct answer.
default.q.n2-12-q51-51.why.0: (a) Incorrect. 「〜たところ」 describes discovering an unexpected result after performing an action; it does not describe leaving an object unattended after putting it down.
default.q.n2-12-q51-51.why.1: (b) Correct. The grammar pattern 「V-たきり」means that after doing V, the resulting state remains unchanged without any subsequent action. It accurately describes the wife plopping the gift on top of the refrigerator and leaving it there without giving it any further thought.
default.q.n2-12-q51-51.why.2: (c) Incorrect. 「置けば」is the hypothetical conditional form “if one places,” which does not fit a declarative sentence describing an actual sequence of events.
default.q.n2-12-q51-51.why.3: (d) Incorrect. 「〜たからといって」 means “just because…” or “even if…,” and is typically followed by a negative or qualifying clause such as “that does not necessarily mean…,” so it does not fit the flow of the sentence.
default.q.n2-12-q52-52.verdict: The correct answer is 3. がっかりさせられる.
default.q.n2-12-q52-52.explanation: The adverb 「いたく」 (甚く: extremely, intensely) is often used with verbs expressing strong emotions. When an event or another person's actions naturally cause an involuntary emotional response, Japanese uses the psychological passive / causative-passive form 「〜させられる」 (here, がっかりさせられる: to be made disappointed / to feel extremely disappointed). Therefore, choice 3 is correct.
default.q.n2-12-q52-52.why.0: (a) Incorrect. 「がっかりさせてしまった」 is the causative form, meaning “caused someone to be disappointed” (the subject must be the person causing the disappointment), which is the opposite of the subject being the person experiencing disappointment here.
default.q.n2-12-q52-52.why.1: (b) Incorrect. 「がっかりするだろうか」 is a rhetorical question or speculation (“I wonder if they will be disappointed”), which does not fit a narrative sentence asserting strong emotion with the adverb いたく (“extremely”).
default.q.n2-12-q52-52.why.2: (c) Correct. The passive-causative or emotional passive form 「がっかりさせられる」describes a natural emotional response caused by another person's actions ('to be deeply disappointed' or 'to feel extremely let down').
default.q.n2-12-q52-52.why.3: (d) Incorrect. 「がっかりしそうにない」 means “does not seem disappointed at all,” which completely contradicts the strongly emphatic adverb いたく (“extremely,” “deeply”).
default.q.n2-12-q53-53.verdict: The correct answer is 4. 言ってくれなくていい.

Rather than having the other person say such things to him, he would prefer a sincere expression of gratitude. The structure 「V-てくれなくていい」 expresses the wish that someone does not need to do something for the speaker. Therefore, choice 4 is correct.

default.q.n2-12-q53-53.why.1: (b) Incorrect. 「言ってもらえたらうれしい」 means "I would be happy if you said it for me," which completely contradicts the context describing disappointing, mechanical phrases.
default.q.n2-12-q53-53.why.2: (c) Incorrect. 「言いそうにない」 means “does not seem likely to say,” expressing an outsider's prediction; it does not express the speaker's wish concerning the other person's wording.
default.q.n2-12-q53-53.why.3: (d) Correct. 「〜てくれなくていい」 means 'you do not need to do that for me,' expressing exasperation with mechanical, impersonal procedural questions.
default.q.n2-12-q54-54.verdict: The correct answer is 1. 言ってあげる.

Therefore, choice 1 is correct.
default.q.n2-12-q54-54.why.0: (a) Correct. 「〜てあげる」expresses doing something for another person, so it fits the wife’s or author’s words about intentionally giving her husband the words “Thank you.”

default.q.n2-12-q56-56.verdict: The correct answer is 1: The author’s main point is that mothers today scold their children more often.
default.q.n2-12-q56-56.explanation:
**1. Summary and main point of the passage:**
A child psychologist observed children's drawings of their mothers at the same kindergarten for 20 years and noticed two recent changes: the outer corners of the eyes were drawn slanting upward, and the mouths were drawn larger. The author remarks that children are very honest; through their drawings, mothers appear to have lost their smiles and instead glare at their children with their mouths wide open, shouting and nagging. The author's main point is that mothers today scold their children more often.

**2. Translation of the question and answer choices:**
- **Question:** What is the author's main point in this passage?
- **Choice 1:** Mothers have been scolding their children more often in recent years. (Correct)
- **Choice 2:** Mothers have larger mouths than they used to. (Incorrect)
- **Choice 3:** Children have become better at drawing their mothers' faces in recent years. (Incorrect)
- **Choice 4:** Children have become more honest than they used to be. (Incorrect)
default.q.n2-12-q56-56.why.0: (a) Correct. The author points to changes in the children's drawings, such as slanted eyes and a larger mouth, and states: 「子供は正直です。母親の顔から笑顔が消えて、子供を睨みつけ、大きな口を開けてがみがみと怒鳴りつける母親の顔が見えてくるようです。」 Children are honest. We can see a mother whose smile has disappeared, who glares at her child, opens her mouth wide, and harshly scolds the child. This expresses the author's view that mothers today scold their children more often.
default.q.n2-12-q56-56.why.1: (b) Incorrect. The "mouth becoming larger" (口が大きくなってきた) is a feature in the child's drawing showing the mother opening her mouth wide to scold the child (大きな口を開けてがみがみと怒鳴りつける), not an actual increase in the mother's mouth size.
default.q.n2-12-q56-56.why.2: (c) Incorrect: The passage mentions only two changes in the way the mother's face was drawn and says nothing at all about the child's drawing skills becoming better or more skillful (絵が上手になった).
default.q.n2-12-q56-56.why.3: (d) Correct. The author writes 「子供は正直です」(Children are honest) to explain that the drawing accurately reflects the mother often scolding her child, not to compare children today with those in the past (以前に比べて正直になった).
default.q.n2-12-q57-57.verdict: The correct answer is 4 (A: 家庭生活, B: 社会通念 · 慣習 · しきたり, C: ぐ律や制度上).
default.q.n2-12-q57-57.explanation:
■ Summary of the passage's main ideas:
The passage presents survey results on how people aged 20 and over perceive gender equality in three areas:
1. Law and institutions (「法律や制度上」—mistakenly written in the passage as 「ぐ律や制度上」): About 55% of women believe that men receive preferential treatment (either considerably or to some extent), while only 30.8% of women believe that the situation is equal.
2. Family life (「家庭生活」): The percentage of women who feel that men receive preferential treatment is higher than in the area of law and institutions (>55%), and about half of men (50%) feel similarly.
3. Social norms, customs, and traditions (「社会通念・慣習・しきたり」): Very high percentages of both men and women—between 70% and 80%—believe that men receive preferential treatment.

■ Translation of the question:
"The following graphs A, B, and C illustrate perceptions of gender equality in the areas of [law and institutions], [family life], and [social norms · customs · traditions], respectively. Choose the answer choice that correctly matches each graph A, B, and C with its corresponding area."

■ Translation of the answer choices:
1. A: Law and institutions | B: Social norms · customs · traditions | C: Family life
2. A: Family life | B: Law and institutions | C: Social norms · customs · traditions
3. A: Social norms · customs · traditions | B: Family life | C: Law and institutions
4. A: Family life | B: Social norms · customs · traditions | C: Law and institutions
default.q.n2-12-q57-57.why.0: (a) Incorrect because this combination assigns A to「規律や制度上」and C to「家庭生活」, which do not correspond to the data characteristics of charts A and C in the passage.
default.q.n2-12-q57-57.why.1: (b) Incorrect because the positions of B and C have been reversed: B is assigned 「ぐ律や制度上」and C is assigned 「社会通念 · 慣習 · しきたり」.
default.q.n2-12-q57-57.why.2: (c) Incorrect because this combination assigns the wrong labels to the charts: A as 「社会通念 · 慣習 · しきたり」 and C as 「ぐ律や制度上」.
default.q.n2-12-q57-57.why.3: (d) Correct. Based on the following sentences in the passage: (1) A (Family life): «［家庭生活］においては男性のほうが優伝されていると感じる女性が［ぐ律や制度上］より増加するが、同様に感じる男性は全体のほぼ半数である» (In family life, the proportion of women who feel that men are favored is higher than in the area of laws and institutions, while nearly half of all men feel the same); (2) B (Social norms, customs, and conventions): «［社会通念 · 慣習 · しきたり］においては、「男性のほうが非常に優伝されている」または「どちらかといえ消男性の方が優伝されている」という意見が男女とも 70～80％を占めている» (For both men and women, 70–80% believe that men are favored either “to a great extent” or “to some extent”); (3) C (Laws and institutions): «［ぐ律や制度上］は女性の約 55 ％が「男性の 方が非常に優伝されている」または「どちらかといえ消男性のほうが優伝されている」と考えており、「平等である」と考える女性は 30．8 ％にとどまる». Therefore, the corresponding order is exactly A: 家庭生活, B: 社会通念 · 慣習 · しきたり, C: ぐ律や制度上.
default.q.n2-12-q58-58.verdict: The correct answer is 3: それぞれに偏っていても、集まり全体としてみればバランスがとれている (Even if each individual is biased in their own way, the group as a whole is balanced.)
default.q.n2-12-q58-58.explanation:
- Main point: The author argues that a good group is one that achieves a harmonious balance overall (全体としてのバランスの程のよさが好ましい). In contrast, if every individual tries to become the same kind of "balanced person," the group as viewed from the outside becomes abnormal and one-sided (異様な偏った集団). The author doubts whether a truly "balanced person" even exists. Therefore, the ideal (むしろ...そのほうが理想だろう) is for each individual to have a distinct personal bias or character, while the group as a whole achieves balance.

- Question:
What should be inserted in the [ ] in this passage?

- Answer choices:
1. Even if each individual is balanced, the group as a whole is biased in one direction.
2. Each individual is balanced, and the group as a whole is balanced as well.
3. Even if each individual is biased in their own way, the group as a whole achieves balance.
4. Each individual is biased in their own way, and the group as a whole is biased in one direction.
default.q.n2-12-q58-58.why.0: (a) This choice describes the negative condition criticized by the author in the preceding sentence (“一人一人が「バランスのとれた人間」になろうと...外からは異様な偏った集団に見えてくる”), so it cannot be the ideal state (理想) introduced by “rather” or “on the contrary” (むしろ).
default.q.n2-12-q58-58.why.1: (b) This choice is inappropriate because the author questions whether a “balanced person” really exists (「バランスのとれた人間」なんてものが、本当にあるものかどうか、疑わしくもある), and trying to make everyone balanced can backfire. Therefore, the author is not aiming for every individual to achieve balance.
default.q.n2-12-q58-58.why.2: (c) The quotation provides the evidence: "いろいろあっても、全体としてのバランスの程のよさが好ましい" (Even if there is variety, an overall balance is preferable). Together with the conjunction "むしろ" (rather), which follows the rejection of everyone trying to become a "balanced person," the author asserts that the ideal is for each individual to retain their own distinctive bias (それぞれに偏っていても), while complementing one another so that the group as a whole achieves balance (集まり全体としてみればバランスがとれている).
default.q.n2-12-q58-58.why.3: (d) This choice is incorrect because a group leaning in one direction is described by the author in the opening sentence as ominous or unsettling (「人間の集まりが、一つの方向に偏っているのは不吉だ」), which is completely contrary to an “ideal” (理想).
default.q.n2-12-q59-59.verdict: The correct answer is 2: 元の大きさを思い浮かべるから (Because they picture or recall the original size in their minds).
default.q.n2-12-q59-59.explanation:
**Main point of the related passage:** Even when a distant person appears so small that they seem to fit through a 5-yen coin's hole, our brain still perceives the distance and automatically imagines the person's actual height, converting the image back to its original size rather than thinking that the person has literally shrunk.

**Question translation:**
The passage says, "We do not think that the person has shrunk enough to fit through a 5-yen coin's hole." [Why is that?]

**Answer choices:**
1. Because we view the person from multiple angles.
2. Because we imagine the person's original size (actual height).
3. Because the person is someone we know well.
4. Because we do not know the person's original size.
default.q.n2-12-q59-59.why.0: (a) Inaccurate. Viewing things from different angles is mentioned only at the end of the passage, when extending the discussion to other objects such as the width of a road, circles, and squares; it is not the reason given for not thinking that the person had been shrunk.
default.q.n2-12-q59-59.why.1: (b) Correct. The passage states: 「頭の中では身長を活ゃんと思い浮かべているのである。五円⋢の穴の中に収まるくらい小注くなってしまったとは思わないのである。小注く見えるということが距離を感じ、頭の中でもとの大きさに活かづけて解釈しているのである」 (The person still clearly imagines the actual height and interprets the apparently small image by relating it to its original size).
default.q.n2-12-q59-59.why.2: (c) Incorrect. The familiar person is only a hypothetical example at the beginning of the passage (「よく知っている人が遠くに見えたとする」). The following text expands the rule to apply to all objects (「人に限らず...」), so the reason is not that the person is familiar.
default.q.n2-12-q59-59.why.3: (d) Incorrect. The passage states that people have developed the habit of perceiving and sensing the original size and shape of things (「元の大きさ、カタチを感じとるという習慣がついている」), not that they are unaware of them.
default.q.n2-12-q60-60.verdict: The correct answer is choice 3: 山田さんは、今日用事がある とか で、早く帰りました。
default.q.n2-12-q60-60.explanation:
Summary and grammar analysis:
The opening sentence of the passage is: "巨大な石像群だけが砂の上に残る太平洋の島イースター島、ここもかつては大きな木の生い茂る島だった とか。" The particle 「とか」 at the end of the sentence indicates hearsay: information the speaker has heard but cannot confirm with complete certainty. Of the four choices, only choice 3 uses 「〜とかで」 to give a reason based on hearsay (“apparently,” “I hear that…”).

Translation of the question and answer choices:
- Question: Which use of 「とか」 below has the same meaning as its use in the passage?
- 1. On my days off, I usually go to the movies, for example. (とか lists examples.)
- 2. How about something like jewelry as a gift? (とか offers a suggestion.)
- 3. Yamada apparently went home early because he had something to do today. (とか indicates hearsay.)
- 4. Things like computers and printers are very cheap today. (とか lists items in parallel.)
default.q.n2-12-q60-60.why.0: (a) Incorrect because 「とか」 here introduces representative examples of actions in a non-exhaustive list; it does not indicate hearsay as it does in the passage.
default.q.n2-12-q60-60.why.1: (b) Incorrect because 「とか」 here is used to make a gentle suggestion or propose an option to the other person, not to report something heard.
default.q.n2-12-q60-60.why.2: (c) Correct because in the passage, 「大きな木の生い茂る島だったとか」uses 「とか」to indicate information heard or passed down by hearsay. Similarly, choice 3 uses 「用事があるとかで」to express a rumored or vaguely reported reason that someone had other business.
default.q.n2-12-q60-60.why.3: (d) Incorrect because 「とか」 is used here as a pair to list equivalent nouns, such as computers and printers.
default.q.n2-12-q61-61.verdict: The correct answer is choice 4: 巨大な石像を海岸まで運ぶには木を切り倒す必要があった。
default.q.n2-12-q61-61.explanation:
Summary of the main idea:
The passage describes how the people of Easter Island carved enormous stone statues to display their power. To drag or transport these statues to the coast, they repeatedly cut down trees without waiting for new growth to mature.

Question and answer choices:
- Question: Which of the following is consistent with the content of the passage?
- 1. On Easter Island, people cut down trees to build houses and boats.
- 2. On Easter Island, people cut down trees to make enormous stone statues.
- 3. The islanders waited for the next generation of trees to grow before cutting them down.
- 4. Trees had to be cut down in order to transport the enormous stone statues to the coast.
default.q.n2-12-q61-61.why.0: (a) Incorrect because the original purpose of cutting down the trees was to transport the stone statue; the inability to build houses or boats was a consequence after all the trees had been cut down ("木がなくては、住民は家も建てられず、船も造れない").
default.q.n2-12-q61-61.why.1: (b) Incorrect because the statues carved from stone and wood were used only to transport the stone statues to the seashore, not to make the statues ("大きな石像を造って、それを海岸まで運ぶために木をどんどん切り倒した").
default.q.n2-12-q61-61.why.2: (c) Incorrect because the text clearly states that the islanders continually cut down trees without waiting for young trees to grow: 「若い木が育つのも待たずに」.
default.q.n2-12-q61-61.why.3: (d) Correct because the passage clearly states: "島民は自分たちの勢力を誇示するため大きな石像を造って、それを海岸まで運ぶために木をどんどん切り倒した" (The islanders made large stone statues to demonstrate their power, and repeatedly cut down trees to transport them to the coast).
default.q.n2-12-q62-62.verdict: The correct answer is choice 1: イースター島の例を挙げて資源を大切にしようといっている。
default.q.n2-12-q62-62.explanation:
Main point:
The author uses the historical story of the decline and destruction of the inhabitants of Easter Island, caused by the exhaustion of its forest resources, to warn modern human society: resources are not unlimited, and if people fail to preserve and value them, modern society may also reach the brink of extinction.

Question and answer choices:
- Question: What does the author want to say in this passage?
- 1. The author gives Easter Island as an example to advise people to value resources.
- 2. The author describes the history of Easter Island by using its huge stone statues as an example.
- 3. The author says that conflicts arise among residents when resources are exhausted.
- 4. The author says that trees are very useful for transporting heavy, large objects such as huge stone statues.
default.q.n2-12-q62-62.why.0: (a) Correct because the author states the message directly at the end: "この話は過去の話ではない。現在にも通じるものがある。今のままでは、我々の社会もやがて滅亡へと向かうだろう。過去の失敗を繰り返してはならない。資源は無尽蔵ではないのだ" (This story is relevant to the present; we must not repeat the mistakes of the past; resources are not infinite.) The author uses the lesson of Easter Island to call for the protection and responsible use of resources.
default.q.n2-12-q62-62.why.1: (b) The story of Easter Island is merely an illustrative example supporting the argument, not the main purpose of the article.
default.q.n2-12-q62-62.why.2: (c) Incorrect because the conflict over resources is only one detail in the story of Easter Island; it does not represent the central message directed toward present-day society.
default.q.n2-12-q62-62.why.3: (d) Incorrect because using trees to transport stone statues is merely a supplementary detail explaining the cause of deforestation in the past.
default.q.n2-12-q63-63.verdict: The correct answer is 1: Because he did not want his wife to find out about his lottery win (妻に知られたくないから).
default.q.n2-12-q63-63.explanation:
- Main idea: A man, A, won 8 million yen in the lottery and planned to use the money to buy the imported car he had always wanted. However, he was afraid that if his wife found out, she would make him use all the money to repay the home loan instead of buying the car. Therefore, he secretly brought the money home, wrapped it in a bedsheet, and hid it in a built-in closet (押し入れ).
- Question translation: The passage says that he "hid it." Why did he do so?
- Translation of the answer choices:
  1. Because he did not want his wife to find out.
  2. Because he was afraid his daughter would find it and throw it away.
  3. So that a thief would not find it.
  4. Because he would not use it until he bought the car.
default.q.n2-12-q63-63.why.0: (a) Correct. The passage states: 「『しかし、妻に知られたら、『そんなものは買山ないで、家のローンの返済にあてて活ょうだい』と言われるに活がいない』と考えた A 氏は、 100 万円ずつ束にしたその現金を、そっと家に持ち帰り、シーツに包んで押し入れに ① かくしておいたのである。」 Mr. A thought that if his wife found out, she would certainly tell him not to buy such a thing and to use the money to repay the home loan, so he secretly took the cash home and hid it in the closet wrapped in a sheet.
default.q.n2-12-q63-63.why.1: (b) Incorrect. The detail about the mischievous two-year-old daughter throwing things into the street occurs later, after the money had been left to dry on the balcony; it was not the reason A hid the money in the built-in cabinet in the first place.
default.q.n2-12-q63-63.why.2: (c) Incorrect. The passage does not mention hiding money to prevent theft by どろぼう.
default.q.n2-12-q63-63.why.3: (d) Incorrect. A hid the money to conceal it from his wife, not because he would not use it until buying a car.
default.q.n2-12-q64-64.verdict: The correct answer is 4: Hiding bundles of cash in the built-in closet (札束を押入れにかくしておいたこと).
default.q.n2-12-q64-64.explanation:
- Main point: The demonstrative pronoun 「これ」 refers to the entire action described in the immediately preceding sentence: A brought a bundle of cash home and hid it inside the bedsheets in a built-in closet. It was this act of hiding the money (これ) that led to the unexpected result (思わぬ結果) of his wife accidentally taking all the bedsheets from the closet to be washed the next day.
- Question translation: What does “this” refer to?
- Answer choices:
  1. The fact that the weather was nice.
  2. The fact that the wife washed the bedsheets.
  3. The act of laying out the bundles of cash on the balcony.
  4. The act of hiding the bundles of cash in the built-in closet.
default.q.n2-12-q64-64.why.0: (a) Incorrect. 「天気がとてもいい」 is the objective factor that causes the wife to decide to wash the bed linens the next day; it is not something indicated by 「これ」.
default.q.n2-12-q64-64.why.1: (b) Incorrect. The wife washing the bed sheets is an unintended result that occurred afterward (思わぬ結果), rather than the thing referred to by the pronoun「これ」.
default.q.n2-12-q64-64.why.2: (c) Incorrect. Hanging the bundles of money out on the balcony happened after the wife had finished washing the sheets and discovered the money.
default.q.n2-12-q64-64.why.3: (d) Correct. The passage says: 「100 万円ずつ束にしたその現金を、そっと家に持ち帰り、シーツに包んで押し入れに ① かくしておいたのである。ところが、告 これが思わぬ結果をまねいた。」 The pronoun 「これ」 directly refers to the act of hiding the money wrapped in a sheet inside the closet in the preceding sentence.
default.q.n2-12-q65-65.verdict: The correct answer is 3: Because they thought their daughter had dropped the money on the road (娘が道路に落としたと思ったから).
default.q.n2-12-q65-65.explanation:
- Main idea: Person A's two-year-old daughter is at an energetic age and loves throwing things from the balcony down into the street. When his wife told him that the bundles of cash drying on the balcony had disappeared, Person A hurried downstairs to look for them because he thought his daughter had mischievously thrown the money into the street.
- Question translation: Why does the phrase "look for it in the street" appear?
- Answer choices:
  1. Because he thought a thief had thrown it into the street.
  2. Because he heard his wife say that she had thrown it into the street.
  3. Because he thought his daughter had dropped or thrown it into the street.
  4. Because he thought the wind had blown it into the street.
default.q.n2-12-q65-65.why.0: (a) Incorrect. The passage only speculates that someone who happened to pass along the road picked it up and took it away (おそらく道路を通りかかっただれかが拾って持ち去ったのであろう); A does not think that a thief threw it into the street.
default.q.n2-12-q65-65.why.1: (b) Incorrect. The wife only discovered that the money being dried on the balcony was missing; she never said that she had thrown it into the street.
default.q.n2-12-q65-65.why.2: (c) Correct. The passage states: 「A 氏の娘は 2 歳のいたずらざかり。ベランダからいろいろなものを道路に落として遊ぶのが大好きだ。夕方になり、妻はベランダの現金がなくなっていることに気づいた。そこへ、 A 氏が仕事から帰ってきた。妻から話を聞いてあ山てて ③ 道路を注がした（探した）が後の祭り…」 (The daughter loved throwing various objects from the balcony onto the street, so after hearing that the money on the balcony had disappeared, A hurriedly searched the street, assuming that she had thrown it down.)
default.q.n2-12-q65-65.why.3: (d) Incorrect. The passage contains no information about the wind blowing money away.
default.q.n2-12-q66-66.verdict: The correct answer is 4: The author had never been asked a question like this in class before.
default.q.n2-12-q66-66.explanation:
- Main point: The author imagines that if a student asked 「日本人はだれかがくしゃみをしても、何も言わないんですか。」 (“When someone sneezes, do Japanese people not say anything?”) in a Japanese class, the author would probably blurt out that there is no such custom. The hypothetical structure 「もし～ていたら」 shows that the author has never actually received this question in class.
- Question translation: Which of the following statements about underlined question ① is correct?
- Answer choices:
  1. This is one of the questions that foreigners often ask Japanese people.
  2. This is a question the author was once asked in a Japanese language school class.
  3. In response to this question, the author answered, “There is no such custom, is there?”
  4. The author has never been asked such a question in class.
default.q.n2-12-q66-66.why.0: (a) Incorrect. The passage does not mention that this is one of the questions that foreigners often ask Japanese people (外国人が日本人によくする質問の一つ).
default.q.n2-12-q66-66.why.1: (b) Incorrect. The author uses the counterfactual 「もし、こんな質問を教室でされていたら...」 (“If I had been asked this question in class...”), showing that they had never actually been asked this question in class.
default.q.n2-12-q66-66.why.2: (c) Incorrect. The author writes 「～と簡単に答えてしまっていただろう」 (I probably would have answered easily that...), which is only the author's speculation about how they would have answered if asked. It does not mean that the author actually gave that answer.
default.q.n2-12-q66-66.why.3: (d) Correct. The hypothetical sentence is: 「もし、こんな質問を教室でされていたら、なんと答えていただろう。」 (If I had been asked a question like this in class, I wonder how I would have answered.) The hypothetical pattern 「もし～ていたら」 describes a situation that did not actually occur, showing that the author had never been asked this question in class.
default.q.n2-12-q67-67.verdict: The correct answer is 3: 「く注めく注め」and 「クスクェー」are expressions equivalent to “Bless you!” in English.
default.q.n2-12-q67-67.explanation:
- Summary of the main point: In English-speaking cultures, people say “Bless you!” when someone sneezes. The author investigated this and discovered that Japanese culture also had a similar custom in the past: the old expression 「くさめくさめ」 was recorded in the 14th-century work 『Tsurezuregusa』, and in Okinawa today people still say 「クスクェー」 when a child sneezes. Both expressions are equivalent to “Bless you!” in English.
- Translation of the question: Which of the following is consistent with the content of the passage?
- Translation of the answer choices:
  1. Because English was once used in Okinawa, Okinawan has an expression similar to English.
  2. Studying the Okinawan language would give us a thorough understanding of 14th-century Old Japanese.
  3. “Kusame kusame” and “Kusukue” are expressions equivalent to “Bless you!” in English.
  4. In the past, Japanese people recited “Kusame kusame” as a prayer when they encountered illness or natural disasters.
default.q.n2-12-q67-67.why.0: (a) Incorrect. The article explains that Okinawa’s custom of saying 「クスクェー」 originates from the folk belief that children who do not speak will be taken away by ghosts (言山ない子供が幽霊に連れていかれるという言い伝えによるもの), not from Okinawa having once spoken English.
default.q.n2-12-q67-67.why.1: (b) Incorrect. The passage only says that, when researching the author, a similar record was found in 『Tsurezuregusa』 (around 1330); it does not say that studying the Okinawan language would help people understand fourteenth-century Japanese more clearly.
default.q.n2-12-q67-67.why.2: (c) Correct. The passage provides the following evidence: 「つまり、英語の “ Bless you ！ ” に当たるようなものがないのか次という質問だ。日本にも活ゃんとそういう習慣が過去にあり、さらに現在でも沖⦖に残っている... 沖⦖では...「クスクェー」と言うらしい。...『徒然草』...にも、くしゃみが出たときに「く注めく注 め」と訪えないと【んでしまうという記述がある」. Both expressions are Japanese blessings or protective phrases said after someone sneezes, equivalent to “Bless you!” in English.
default.q.n2-12-q67-67.why.3: (d) Incorrect. In the passage, 「く注めく注 め」 (Kusame kusame) is a chant recited when sneezing to ward off misfortune or death (くしゃみが出たときに「く注めく注 め」と訪えないと【んでしまう), not a prayer used generally when facing illness or natural disasters.
default.q.n2-12-q68-68.verdict: The correct answer is 1: Being Japanese does not necessarily mean that a person fully understands the Japanese language.
default.q.n2-12-q68-68.explanation:
- Main point: The author is Japanese and teaches Japanese to foreigners, but does not know about the Okinawan dialect or the archaic Japanese word related to the custom of responding to a sneeze. The author feels embarrassed and reminds themselves that being Japanese does not automatically mean knowing everything about the Japanese language.
- Question: With what feelings or thoughts did the author say the underlined sentence ②?
- Choices:
  1. One cannot say that simply being Japanese means one understands Japanese well.
  2. If one is not Japanese, it is difficult to understand the nuances of Japanese.
  3. Teaching Japanese without knowing archaic words or dialects is impossible.
  4. Japanese people actually do not know Japanese, so they need to be careful.
default.q.n2-12-q68-68.why.0: (a) Correct. The preceding sentence states: 「日本人であり、日本語を外国人に教える自分が、沖⦖の言葉も知らず、日本語の古語も知らないことを恥ずかしく思った。 告 日本人の日本語知らずには要注意だ 。」 The author realizes that, despite being a native Japanese person who teaches Japanese, he lacks knowledge of dialects and classical Japanese, and concludes that being Japanese does not necessarily mean having a thorough knowledge of the language.
default.q.n2-12-q68-68.why.1: (b) Incorrect. The author is reflecting on themself and Japanese people in general, not discussing foreigners’ difficulty understanding the nuances (ニ画アンス) of Japanese.
default.q.n2-12-q68-68.why.2: (c) Incorrect. The author feels embarrassed and does not claim that teaching Japanese is impossible (教えることは不可能である) without knowing archaic words or dialects.
default.q.n2-12-q68-68.why.3: (d) Incorrect. This choice makes the extreme, sweeping claim that “Japanese people actually do not know Japanese” (日本人は実は日本語を知らない), whereas the author only says that native speakers should not assume they know everything, accurately expressed in choice 1 through the structure ～とは限らない.
default.q.n2-12-q69-69.verdict: The correct answer is 2. Both A and B state that it is completely normal for the person being asked not to know what they want to do.
default.q.n2-12-q69-69.explanation:
- Summary: The questioner is a high school student worried because they do not yet know what they want to do in the future and wonder whether they are immature or inadequate. Both answers A and B reassure them and affirm that, at this age, not yet having a future goal is completely normal (普通).
- Question translation: What do answers A and B have in common?
- Answer choices:
1. Both say that they cannot understand the questioner's worries.
2. Both say that the questioner's worries are normal.
3. Both say that the questioner should try doing something.
4. Both say that there is nothing the questioner needs to do now and nothing to worry about.
default.q.n2-12-q69-69.why.0: (a) Incorrect because both A and B understand the questioner’s concerns and provide specific explanations and analysis; they do not say that they “do not understand the questioner’s concerns.”
default.q.n2-12-q69-69.why.1: (b) Correct. Both answers state that this is normal. A says 「あなたの年齢で将来したいことがわからないのは、普通です。」 (It is normal not to know what you want to do in the future at your age), while B says 「そんなあなたは、幼いのでもなく、だめなのでもなく、普通なのです。」 (You are neither immature nor inadequate; you are normal).
default.q.n2-12-q69-69.why.2: (c) Incorrect because only B recommends trying something more expressive of oneself (「スポーツとか、より自己表現的な何かをしてみたらどうでしょうか」), while A believes that one should simply start working naturally and gradually come to understand.
default.q.n2-12-q69-69.why.3: (d) Incorrect because only A says not to worry (「何も心配いりません」), whereas B recommends trying something new.
default.q.n2-12-q70-70.verdict: The correct answer is 3. A says that it is fine for the questioner to remain as they are and that they will understand later once they start working, whereas B advises them to try doing something proactive that expresses themselves.
default.q.n2-12-q70-70.explanation:
- Summary: When giving advice, A says there is no need to worry and that if things are left as they are, the person will gradually discover what they like or are suited to after starting work. B, in contrast, says the person’s current interests are somewhat passive and recommends trying something more active and self-expressive, such as sports, to find a direction.
- Question: Which statement correctly describes A and B’s responses to the person seeking advice?
- Answer choices:
1. A says that once the person joins a company, they will come to like their job, while B says that playing sports will help them make an effort.
2. A recommends getting a job, while B recommends pursuing a hobby.
3. A says it is fine to leave things as they are, while B says the person should try doing something.
4. A says that being indecisive is bad, while B says that being passive is bad.
default.q.n2-12-q70-70.why.0: (a) Incorrect. A does not say that one will like one’s job as soon as one joins a company; it says that through working, one gradually comes to understand what one likes or is suited for: 「仕事をしているうちに、だんだん何が好きなのか...わかってくる」. B gives sports as an example of an activity through which people express themselves; it does not say that playing sports will make someone able to persevere.
default.q.n2-12-q70-70.why.1: (b) Incorrect because A does not advise starting work immediately (it discusses the natural process of entering the workforce later), while B suggests trying activities that reveal one's strengths and interests to discover what one wants to do, not pursuing a hobby.
default.q.n2-12-q70-70.why.2: (c) Correct. A says that it is fine to leave things as they are and that the person will understand after starting work (「みんな、あなたのようにはっきりしないまま... とりあえず、どこかの会社に入ることになるでしょう... 何も心配いりません」), while B advises trying something proactive and self-expressive (「スポーツとか、より自己表現的な何かをしてみたらどうでしょうか」).
default.q.n2-12-q70-70.why.3: (d) Incorrect because A does not say that being undecided is bad; on the contrary, it states that everyone feels this way and that there is no need to worry. B merely observes that one's current preferences are somewhat passive and suggests trying something new; it does not say that passivity is bad.
default.q.n2-12-q71-71.verdict: The correct answer is 4: The passage is about how to convey information clearly to listeners.
default.q.n2-12-q71-71.explanation:
Main point: The author begins with a university-class communication game in which students describe a drawing for someone else to reproduce, but the success rate is only about 10%. The author analyzes the reasons for this and presents two core principles for effective communication: (1) speak from the whole first (全体から話す), and (2) speak specifically (具体的に話す). The purpose of the passage is to explain how to convey information clearly and accurately to listeners.

Question translation: What is this passage about?
Answer choices:
1. A method for measuring the intellectual level of university students today.
2. A method for organizing an interesting class.
3. A method for conducting a psychological test using drawings.
4. A method for communicating clearly to listeners.
default.q.n2-12-q71-71.why.0: (a) Incorrect because the passage does not mention checking or measuring university students’ level of understanding or intellectual ability.
default.q.n2-12-q71-71.why.1: (b) Incorrect because the classroom game at a university is merely an introductory example illustrating the topic of communication, not instructions for organizing an interesting class.
default.q.n2-12-q71-71.why.2: (c) Incorrect. The statement 「心理テストにでも使ったらおもしろそうだ」 (“It might be interesting to use it as a psychological test”) is merely the author’s humorous association, not the subject of the article.
default.q.n2-12-q71-71.why.3: (d) Correct because the author analyzes key points so that listeners can clearly understand the speaker’s message. Evidence: 「そう、わかりやすく話すための第 1 のポイントは全体から話すことである。」, 「2 番目のポイントは「具体的に話すこと」である。この第 2 のポイント、何事も具体的に話す習慣をつけると、コミュニケーション上手な人に一歩近づける。」 and 「自分の意図をできるだけブレの少ない形で伝えたいと思うなら、やはり具体的に話すことが重要になる。」
default.q.n2-12-q72-72.verdict: The correct answer is 4: The low success rate is due to the speaker’s poor explanation and lack of consideration for the listener.
default.q.n2-12-q72-72.explanation:
Main point: The game’s success rate is only about 10% (very low), even though the drawing is not particularly complicated. The reason is that the explainer hurriedly said, “Draw a circle,” before the listener had grasped either the overall picture or the details of its size, leaving the listener confused. The author concludes that this happened because the speaker lacked presentation skills and did not explain things from the listener’s perspective—in other words, the explanation was poor.

Question: Why is the rate “very low”?
Answer choices:
1. Because it is not a particularly complicated drawing.
2. Because drawing the figure is difficult.
3. Because the listener’s psychological level is low.
4. Because the explanation is poor.
default.q.n2-12-q72-72.why.0: (a) Incorrect. “The drawing was not particularly complex” is a contrasting fact presented by the author to emphasize how difficult the failure is to understand, not the reason for the low rate.
default.q.n2-12-q72-72.why.1: (b) Incorrect because the passage clearly states that the figure is not very complicated (「それほど複雑な図形でもない」); therefore, the reason is not that drawing the figure is difficult.
default.q.n2-12-q72-72.why.2: (c) Incorrect because the passage contains no concept or mention of the “psychological level of the listener” (聞き手の心理度).
default.q.n2-12-q72-72.why.3: (d) Correct because the explanation was poorly presented and did not provide an overall picture, leaving the listener confused. Evidence: 「いきなり、ただ「丸を描け」と言われても、全体像が見えていないのだから、聞き手は戸惑うばかりだ。話し手のプレゼンテーション・マインドが欠けていて、聞き手本位の話し方ができていないといえる。」
default.q.n2-12-q73-73.verdict: The correct answer is 2: Position A expresses that each person will picture a different specific type of dog.
default.q.n2-12-q73-73.explanation:
Main point: The author uses the word “dog” (犬) as an example. When people hear this word, everyone who understands the Japanese convention associates it with “an animal that barks woof woof”; this is the common element shared by everyone. However (しかし), the specific dog that appears in each person's mind—a large dog, a small dog, a particular breed, and so on—differs from person to person. Therefore, to communicate exactly what kind of dog is meant, we need to add a specific explanation. Thus, the sentence in [A] after the conjunction “However” must express the idea that each person imagines a different kind of dog.

Translation of the question: What content should be inserted in section A of the passage?
Translation of the answer choices:
1. Everyone has the same association when they think of “a dog.”
2. What kind of “dog” people associate with differs from person to person.
3. There are cases in which people associate it with something other than “a dog.”
4. It is possible not to understand the word “dog.”
default.q.n2-12-q73-73.why.0: (a) Incorrect because the preceding sentence has already stated that everyone shares the same idea of an animal barking "bow-wow" (「ここまでは皆いっしょだ」), so after the contrastive conjunction 「しかし」(however), the same idea cannot be repeated.
default.q.n2-12-q73-73.why.1: (b) Correct. Once everyone shares a general concept of a “dog,” the specific image of a dog in each person’s mind differs. That is why the following sentence requires a more detailed explanation to communicate the meaning accurately. The evidence flows continuously: 「「犬」と聞けば、あるいは読めば、日本語の約束を知っている人なら誰でも「ワンワン鳴く動物」を思い浮かべる。ここまでは皆いっしょだ。しかし、[どのような「犬」を思い浮かべるかは人によって違う]。そこで、こんな犬だということを正確に伝えるために、私たちはより具体的に説明を加えるであろう。」
default.q.n2-12-q73-73.why.2: (c) Incorrect because according to the passage, people who know the Japanese word for “dog” all associate it with a barking animal when they hear the word “dog,” rather than associating it with something that is not a dog.
default.q.n2-12-q73-73.why.3: (d) Incorrect because the passage states the premise that readers/recipients understand the common symbol system called Japanese (「日本語という共通の記号を理解している」), so there is no possibility that they would fail to understand the word “dog.”
default.q.n2-12-q74-74.verdict: The correct answer is 1 (A と B), because type A is for people with tired eyes, while type B is for people who have difficulty concentrating.
default.q.n2-12-q74-74.explanation:
- **Question translation**: What type of supplement is recommended for someone who has recently been unable to concentrate and has tired eyes?
- **Choice translations**:
  1. A and B
  2. B and C
  3. D and E
  4. E and A because of insufficient exercise
- **Main point and explanation**:
  + Type A contains vitamin A, which is good for the eyes and especially recommended for people whose eyes become tired from using a computer frequently (目が疲れている方).
  + Type B contains cardamom, which may improve concentration and is recommended for people who have trouble concentrating on one thing (一つのことに集中できなくて困っている方).
  + Because the symptoms are tired eyes and difficulty concentrating, the correct answer is A and B (Answer 1).
default.q.n2-12-q74-74.why.0: (a) Correct. Passage A clearly states: 「パソコンを長時間使って目が疲れている方などには特にお勧めです」, and passage B states: 「これは集中力を高めるのに非常に泊果的、なかなか一つのことに集中できなくて困っている方、ぜひ一度おためしください」. Therefore, A and B correspond to the two symptoms: tired eyes and difficulty concentrating.
default.q.n2-12-q74-74.why.1: (b) Incorrect. Type B improves concentration, whereas type C contains fat-burning ingredients for people who eat a lot of sweets, enjoy meat, or lack exercise and want to lose weight (「脂肪を燃やす成分... 運動不足だなと思っている方、ダイエットしたい方に最彙です」). It is unrelated to eye fatigue.
default.q.n2-12-q74-74.why.2: (c) Incorrect. Type D is for people with allergies or hay fever (「抗アレルギーの成分が配合されています... 花協症などのアレルギーにお悩みの方」), while Type E is for people who feel tired or are concerned about aging (「体がだるい、どうも最近疲れやすいなどという方」). Neither matches tired eyes and difficulty concentrating.
default.q.n2-12-q74-74.why.3: (d) Incorrect. Type E is intended for fatigue and aging, while Type A is good for the eyes but does not address difficulty concentrating because it lacks Type B; the added explanation is also inappropriate.
default.q.n2-12-q75-75.verdict: The correct answer is 4 (C and E) because type C supports people who feel physically heavy and lack exercise, while type E supports people who are tired and have reduced physical strength.
default.q.n2-12-q75-75.explanation:
- Translation of the question: What type of supplement is good for someone with symptoms such as feeling physically heavy, having low energy, and becoming tired easily?
- Translation of the choices:
  1. A and E
  2. B and C
  3. E and A
  4. C and E
- Main idea and explanation:
  + The symptom “feeling physically heavy” (体が重い) is associated with feeling overweight and lacking exercise, indicating a need to burn fat → type C contains ingredients that burn fat for people who feel they do not get enough exercise (運動不足だなと思っている方).
  + The symptoms “becoming tired easily and feeling sluggish” (疲れやすい、体がだるい) correspond to type E, a multivitamin recommended for people who feel sluggish, tire easily, or are concerned about aging (体がだるい、どうも最近疲れやすいなどという方).
  + Therefore, the combination of C and E is the most appropriate (correct answer: 4).
default.q.n2-12-q75-75.why.0: (a) Incorrect. Option A contains vitamin A, which is good for the eyes and skin (「ビタ田ン A が配合されていて目にいいのはも活ろん、肌にも泊果があります」), so it is unrelated to physical heaviness or loss of energy.
default.q.n2-12-q75-75.why.1: (b) Incorrect. Type B contains cardamom, which improves concentration (「集中力を高めるのに非常に泊果的」); it does not relieve physical heaviness or fatigue.
default.q.n2-12-q75-75.why.2: (c) Incorrect. This choice combines types E and A; type A is beneficial only for the eyes and skin and does not help with a heavy physical condition or lack of exercise.
default.q.n2-12-q75-75.why.3: (d) Correct. Type C contains fat-burning ingredients and is suitable for people with heavy bodies or insufficient exercise (「脂肪を燃やす成分が配合されています... 運動不足だなと思っている方」). Type E is suitable for people who often feel tired or have reduced physical strength (「体がだるい、どうも最近疲れやすいなどという方... ま注にマルチビタ田ンとも言えます」).
default.q.n2-12-q11-11.verdict: The correct answer is 3. いよいよ, meaning “finally” or “at long last,” and indicating that an eagerly awaited important moment has arrived.
default.q.n2-12-q11-11.explanation:
- Translation: “At last, the time to depart for Japan has arrived.”
- Vocabulary and kanji-related note:
  + いよいよ: at last, finally (used when an anticipated or important moment is about to begin).
  + 出発【XUẤT PHÁT】(しゅっぱつ): departure, setting off.
- Example: いよいよ明日から新しい仕事が始まる。(Finally, my new job begins tomorrow.)
default.q.n2-12-q11-11.why.0: (a) 「いきいき」 means lively, energetic, or full of life; it is not used to refer to an important moment that is about to occur.
default.q.n2-12-q11-11.why.1: (b) 「いろいろ」 means “various, diverse, or plentiful” and is not suitable for modifying a departure time.
default.q.n2-12-q11-11.why.2: (c) 「いよいよ」 (at last, finally) expresses that an important or long-awaited moment has finally arrived, making it a very good fit with 「～時が来た」.
default.q.n2-12-q11-11.why.3: (d) 「い活い活」 is an incorrect spelling and has no meaning. The correct expression is 「生き生き」, or 「いきいき」 in hiragana.
default.q.n2-12-q12-12.verdict: The correct answer is 4. けずられて is the passive form of 「削られる」, meaning “to be cut,” and naturally forms 「予算が削られる」 (the budget is cut).
default.q.n2-12-q12-12.explanation:
- Sentence translation: "The plan was canceled because the budget had been cut."
- Related vocabulary and kanji:
  + 削る(けずる): to shave; plane; cut (a budget, costs, time, etc.). The passive form is 削られる (けずられる).
  + 予算(よさん): budget; estimate.
  + 中止(ちゅうし): suspension; cancellation.
- Example: 睡眠時間を削って試験勉強をした。(I cut back on my sleeping time to study for the exam.)
default.q.n2-12-q12-12.why.0: (a) 「とじられて」is the passive form of 「閉じる / 綴じる」(to close / bind documents), and it does not go with 「予算」(budget).
default.q.n2-12-q12-12.why.1: (b) 「こすらてて」 is misspelled. The correct form is 「こすられて」, from the verb 「擦る・こする」 (to rub or scrub), and it does not fit the meaning as written.
default.q.n2-12-q12-12.why.2: (c) 「にげられて」 is the passive form of 「逃げる」 (to run away, evade), and it does not combine with 「予算」.
default.q.n2-12-q12-12.why.3: (d) 「けずられて」 is the passive form of 「削る」 (けずる: shave, cut back, reduce). Combined with 「予算」, it forms 「予算が削られる」 (the budget is cut), leading to the cancellation of the plan.
default.q.n2-12-q13-13.verdict: The correct answer is 3. 有効な because it means “effective” or “効acious,” forming the phrase 「有効な使い方」(an effective way to use something).
default.q.n2-12-q13-13.explanation:
- Sentence translation: “Consider how to use the donations sent from all over the country effectively.”
- Related vocabulary and kanji:
  + 有効【有効】: effective, valid, useful. Antonym: 無効【無効】(invalid, ineffective).
  + 寄付金【寄付金】(きふきん): donations, donated funds.
  + 検討【検討】(けんとう): consideration, examination, deliberation.
- Example: 限られた時間を有効に使うべきだ。(You should use the limited time effectively.)
default.q.n2-12-q13-13.why.0: (a) 「退客な」is a meaningless compound and does not exist in Japanese.
default.q.n2-12-q13-13.why.1: (b) 「無中な」 is a misspelling and has no meaning. It may be confused with 「夢中 - むちゅう」, but 夢中 also cannot be used in this context.
default.q.n2-12-q13-13.why.2: (c) 「有効な」(ゆうこうな: effective, useful) modifies「使い方」to form「有効な使い方」(an effective way to use the donated money), so it is completely appropriate.
default.q.n2-12-q13-13.why.3: (d) 「粗末な」 (そまつな: crude, shabby, wasteful, or treating something carelessly) has a negative nuance and does not fit a discussion about how donated money should be used.
default.q.n2-12-q14-14.verdict: The correct answer is 2. いきなり is an adverb meaning “suddenly” or “unexpectedly,” and it naturally combines with the action 「飛び出してきた」 (came rushing out).
default.q.n2-12-q14-14.explanation:
- Translation: “A child suddenly ran out, so I slammed on the brakes.”
- Vocabulary and adverb:
  + いきなり: suddenly, unexpectedly (= 突然 / 急に).
  + 飛び出す (とびだす): to rush out, dart out.
  + ブレーキをかける: to apply the brakes / brake (急ブレーキ: sudden braking).
- Example: 後ろからいきなり肩をたたかれて驚いた。(I was startled when someone suddenly tapped me on the shoulder from behind.)
default.q.n2-12-q14-14.why.0: (a) 「おそらく」 means “probably” or “presumably” and is an adverb of conjecture, commonly used with 「～だろう」 or 「～かもしれない」 at the end of the sentence; it is not used to describe a sudden action.
default.q.n2-12-q14-14.why.1: (b) 「いきなり」 (suddenly, all of a sudden) describes an action that occurs unexpectedly without warning, fitting 「飛び出してきた」 perfectly.
default.q.n2-12-q14-14.why.2: (c) 「ぜひとも」(by all means, earnestly) is commonly used with expressions of desire or requests such as 「～たい / ～てください」.
default.q.n2-12-q14-14.why.3: (d) 「めっきり」 means noticeably or markedly. It describes a clear change in state over time (e.g., めっきり寒くなった: it has become noticeably colder).
default.q.n2-12-q15-15.verdict: The correct answer is 4. ドラマ because the Katakana word 「ドラマ」 means “television drama,” which fits the context of a program shown on television featuring a famous actor.
default.q.n2-12-q15-15.explanation:
- Sentence translation: "The new television drama that recently aired features a famous actor."
- Related vocabulary & katakana:
  + ドラマ (drama): television drama.
  + 俳優【】(はいゆう): actor.
- Example: 毎週楽しみに見ているドラマが今夜最終回を迎える。(The drama I look forward to watching every week will air its final episode tonight.)
default.q.n2-12-q15-15.why.0: (a) 「レベル」 (level: degree, proficiency) is not used to refer to a television program.
default.q.n2-12-q15-15.why.1: (b) 「モデル」 (model: fashion model, model) is not a television program that can follow 「テレビで新しく始まった」.
default.q.n2-12-q15-15.why.2: (c) 「テンポ」 (tempo: rhythm, pace) does not mean a broadcast program.
default.q.n2-12-q15-15.why.3: (d) 「ドラマ」(television drama) combines to form「新しく始まったドラマ」(a newly started television drama), in which a famous actor (俳優) appears.
default.q.n2-12-q16-16.verdict: The correct answer is 2. 不満.
default.q.n2-12-q16-16.explanation:
Meaning: "The pay is low and the work is boring, so I have many complaints about this company."
- Kanji meaning: 不満 (dissatisfaction, discontent).
- Common expressions: 不満を抱く (to harbor dissatisfaction), 不満を漏らす (to voice complaints, express dissatisfaction).
- Example: 待遇に対する不満が高まっている。(Dissatisfaction with the working conditions is growing.)
default.q.n2-12-q16-16.why.0: (a) 期待 (expectation, anticipation): Has a positive meaning, expressing hope for something good; it does not fit the preceding list of negative factors (low pay, boring work).
