default.q.n2-19-q33-33.verdict: The correct answer is 2 (あいだは).
default.q.n2-19-q33-33.explanation:
- Sentence translation: Please keep quiet throughout the examination.
- Grammar: 「N + の間（は）」: throughout the period during which N takes place; the following clause describes a state or action continuing for the entire period. This differs from 「〜の間に」, where the following action occurs at some point during that period.
- Example: 夏休みの間は、毎日プールで泳いでいた。(Throughout summer vacation, I swam in the pool every day.)
default.q.n2-19-q33-33.why.0: (a) 「う活」: This is not a meaningful Japanese grammar form; it is an OCR error for うち or うちは.
default.q.n2-19-q33-33.why.1: (b) 「あいだは」(間は): The pattern「N の間は」means “throughout the period of N,” fitting the requirement to maintain the state continuously in「静かにしてください」.
default.q.n2-19-q33-33.why.2: (c) 「まに」(間に): 「〜の間に」describes a short action or moment occurring within a period of time. It cannot express maintaining a state throughout the entire exam, and the spelling is also incomplete.
default.q.n2-19-q33-33.why.3: (d) 「うちに」(内に) describes doing something before a condition changes, so it is unsuitable for requesting that order be maintained continuously throughout the exam.
default.q.n2-19-q34-34.explanation:
- Sentence translation: As for this apartment, I want to decide whether to rent it only after seeing the inside.
- Grammar: 「V-た + 上で（うえで）」: after doing V, then take the next action; the first action serves as an important prerequisite or basis for the second.
- Related kanji readings: 部屋: room; 決める: to decide.
- Example: 専門家に相談した上で、決めるつもりです。(I intend to make a decision after consulting an expert.)
default.q.n2-19-q34-34.why.0: (a) 「うえに」(上に) means "in addition" or "not only... but also..."; it does not express the sequence of finishing one task before doing another.
default.q.n2-19-q34-34.why.1: (b) 「うえから」(上から) means “from above,” and does not form a grammar pattern expressing a condition or premise.
default.q.n2-19-q34-34.why.2: (c) 「うえにも」(上にも) does not form a grammatically appropriate pattern in this sentence.
default.q.n2-19-q34-34.why.3: (d) 「うえで」(上で): The structure 「V-た + 上で」 means “after doing V, then...,” which perfectly fits the context of viewing the room before deciding whether to rent it.
default.q.n2-19-q35-35.verdict: The provided answer is 1 (読まれて), but grammatically the accurate answer is 3 (読ませて - 読ませていただきました).
default.q.n2-19-q35-35.explanation:
- Sentence translation: I read the book I had borrowed with great enjoyment / enthusiasm.
- Grammar: The humble form 「V-(さ)せていただく」indicates that the speaker was allowed or given the opportunity by someone else to perform an action, expressing gratitude for that favor. The correct form is 「読ませていただきました」.
- Kanji readings: 読 (reading), 借 (borrowing).
- Example: 先輩にいただいた資料を読ませていただきました。(I was allowed to read the materials my senior gave me.)
default.q.n2-19-q35-35.why.0: (a) 「読まれて」: The passive/honorific form of 読む cannot be combined with 「〜いただきました」 as 「読まれていただきました」 because the honorific grammar is incorrect.
default.q.n2-19-q35-35.why.1: (b) 「お読みに」 is normally used in the honorific form 「お読みになる」 or the humble form 「お読みする」; it cannot be combined as 「お読みにいただきました」.
default.q.n2-19-q35-35.why.2: (c) 「読ませて」: The causative form combines with いただく in 「読ませていただきました」, a humble expression meaning “I was permitted to read” or “I read the book.” This is the most grammatically accurate answer.
default.q.n2-19-q35-35.why.3: (d) 「読まされて」 is the causative-passive form, meaning being forced to read. This conflicts with the meaning of 「楽しく」 (enjoyably) and the benefactive auxiliary 「いただきました」.
default.q.n2-19-q36-36.verdict: The correct answer is 1 (かか山らず / かかわらず).
default.q.n2-19-q36-36.explanation:
- Meaning: Regardless of the weather, the match will be held from 2 p.m. tomorrow.
- Grammar: 「N + にかかわらず / に拘わらず」: regardless of, irrespective of, without regard to N.
- Vocabulary: 天候 (weather conditions), 試合 (match), 行う (hold, conduct).
- Example: 参加の有無にかかわらず、ご連絡ください。(Please contact us regardless of whether you will participate.)
default.q.n2-19-q36-36.why.0: (a) 「かか山らず」: An OCR error for 「かかわらず」(関わらず/拘わらず). The pattern 「N + にかかわらず」 means “regardless of N,” fitting “regardless of the weather” perfectly.
default.q.n2-19-q36-36.why.1: (b) 「よると」: The pattern 「〜によると」 means “according to (a source),” so the following clause must convey reported information (〜そうだ / 〜ということだ); it does not combine with a direct action such as 「試合を行います」.
default.q.n2-19-q36-36.why.2: (c) 「よれ消」 is an OCR error for 「よれば」 (〜によれば, “according to” or “based on”), similar to によると, and does not fit this sentence.
default.q.n2-19-q36-36.why.3: (d) 「かか山り」 is an OCR error for 「かかわり」(関わり, “involvement” or “relation”); standing alone after に, it does not form a grammar pattern meaning “regardless of.”
default.q.n2-19-q37-37.explanation:
- Meaning: After checking the telephone directory, I found that there was no company with that name.
- Grammar: 「V-た + ところ」: After trying an action, one obtains a result or discovers the actual situation, often something newly learned or unexpected.
- Kanji notes: 電話帳 (telephone directory), 調べる (to look up, investigate), 会社 (company).
- Example: 病院で検査してもらったところ、異常はなかった。(After being examined at the hospital, I found that there was nothing abnormal.)
default.q.n2-19-q37-37.why.0: (a) 「ところ」: The pattern 「V-た + ところ」means “after doing V, I found that...,” fitting the context of checking the directory and discovering that the company did not exist.
default.q.n2-19-q37-37.why.1: (b) 「だけに」 means "precisely because..., naturally..." and indicates a cause leading to an inevitable result, so it does not fit the sentence logically.
default.q.n2-19-q37-37.why.2: (c) 「からに」: 「からに」by itself does not form a valid grammar pattern here; the pattern expressing a reason is「からには」.
default.q.n2-19-q37-37.why.3: (d) 「ばかりでは」 means “if it is nothing but ...” and does not fit the grammar or meaning of expressing the result after looking something up.
default.q.n2-19-q38-38.verdict: The correct answer is 3 (むかって).
default.q.n2-19-q38-38.explanation:
- Translation: The happiest moment is when I am heading straight toward my goal.
- Grammar: 「N + に向かって / にむかって」: toward N, indicating a spatial direction or an abstract goal or destination.
- Kanji: 目的 (purpose, goal), 進む (to advance), 幸せ (happiness).
- Example: 夢に向かって、一歩一歩進んでいく。(I move forward step by step toward my dream.)
default.q.n2-19-q38-38.why.0: (a) 「あたって」(当たって): The pattern 「〜にあたって」 means “on the occasion of” or “when preparing to undertake a major event”; it does not mean moving straight toward something.
default.q.n2-19-q38-38.why.1: (b) 「のって」(乗って): 「〜にのって」 means "based on / by riding," and does not combine with 目的 to indicate the direction of progress.
default.q.n2-19-q38-38.why.2: (c) 「むかって」(向かって): The pattern「N + に向かって」means “toward N” or “in the direction of N,” and fits「まっすぐに進んでいる」perfectly.
default.q.n2-19-q38-38.why.3: (d) 「あって」(合って/会って): Means “to suit/match” or “to meet”; it does not fit a structure expressing direction toward a goal.
default.q.n2-19-q39-39.explanation:
- Meaning: Stop joking around and think seriously!
- Grammar: 「N + 抜きで / 抜きにして（ぬきで）」 means without N, leaving N out, or setting N aside. A very common fixed expression is 「冗談抜きで」(seriously, no kidding).
- Kanji compounds: 冗談 (joke), 抜 (pull out, leave out).
- Example: 冗談は抜きにして、本題に入りましょう。(Let’s stop joking and get to the main topic.)
default.q.n2-19-q39-39.why.0: (a) 「ぬいて」(抜いて): the te-form of the transitive verb 抜く; it does not directly follow a noun to form an adverbial exclusion phrase such as 「N抜きで」.
default.q.n2-19-q39-39.why.1: (b) 「しないで」 requires an object particle, such as in 「冗談をしないで」, and is not the natural standard expression in this context.
default.q.n2-19-q39-39.why.2: (c) 「しても」 means “even if one jokes ...,” which is completely illogical in this sentence.
default.q.n2-19-q39-39.why.3: (d) 「ぬきで」 (抜きで): The pattern 「N + 抜きで」 means “leaving N out” or “setting N aside.” The fixed expression 「冗談抜きで」 means “seriously” or “no kidding.”
default.q.n2-19-q40-40.verdict: The correct answer is 3 (じゃないか).
default.q.n2-19-q40-40.explanation:
- Sentence translation: Don't just stay at home all the time—let's go see a movie together!
- Grammar: 「V-（よ）う + じゃないか / ではないか」: Used to make an enthusiastic proposal, invitation, or appeal for everyone to do something together.
- Sino-Japanese readings: 映画 (— films), 見る (— see/watch).
- Example: みんなで力を合わせて、この困難を乗り越えようじゃないか。(Let's join forces and overcome this difficulty together!)
default.q.n2-19-q40-40.why.0: (a) 「まいか」: The pattern 「V-ようか V-るまいか」 means “whether to do something or not,” while 「V-まい」 means “will probably not / be determined not to.” It does not follow the volitional form 「見に行こう」 to make an invitation.
default.q.n2-19-q40-40.why.1: (b) 「ともしない」: The structure 「〜ようともしない」 means “to have absolutely no intention of doing something”; it is not used to invite the other person to do something.
default.q.n2-19-q40-40.why.2: (c) 「じゃないか」: The pattern 「V-(よ)う + じゃないか」 expresses an invitation or appeal to do something together ("Let's...!"), so it fits the sentence very well.
default.q.n2-19-q40-40.why.3: (d) 「ともする」: 「〜ようともする」 expresses trying or intending to do something, so it is not used at the end of a sentence functioning as a call to action.
default.q.n2-19-q41-41.explanation:
- Sentence translation: Today is my graduation ceremony, so I will wear the scarf my younger sister bought for me when I go to the ceremony.
- Grammar: 「A が 私に V-てくれる / くださる」: A performs action V for me. Because A is the younger sister (妹 - a family member or someone junior), the ordinary form 「〜てくれた」 is used.
- Vocabulary: 卒業式 (graduation ceremony), 妹 (younger sister), 買う (to buy).
- Example: 誕生日に友だちが作ってくれたケーキを食べた。(I ate the cake my friend made for me on my birthday.)
default.q.n2-19-q41-41.why.0: (a) 「いただいた」: The structure 「（私が）〜に V-ていただく」 means “I receive an action from someone,” so the subject must be the recipient (私). Here, however, the subject marked by が is 「妹が」.
default.q.n2-19-q41-41.why.1: (b) 「くだ注った」: An OCR error for 「くださった」(the honorific form of くれた, used for someone of higher status); くださった is not used for a younger sister (妹).
default.q.n2-19-q41-41.why.2: (c) 「もらった」: The structure 「（私が）〜に V-てもらう」 means “I receive an action from someone.” The subject is the recipient (私), so it cannot follow 「妹が私に」.
default.q.n2-19-q41-41.why.3: (d) 「くれた」: The structure 「[Someone else] が [me] に V-てくれる」 means that someone does something for me. Since the subject is the younger sister (妹) and the beneficiary is me (私), 「買ってくれた」 is the correct form.
default.q.n2-19-q42-42.verdict: The correct answer is 1 (になって).
default.q.n2-19-q42-42.explanation:
- Sentence translation: Please wait here.
- Grammar: The honorific request pattern 「お + V-stem + になってください」 is a formal version of 「お + V-stem + ください」. It must be distinguished from the humble form 「お + V-stem + する」, which is used only for the speaker's own actions.
- 待つ: to wait.
- Example: 少々こちらでお待ちになってください。(Please wait here for a moment.)
default.q.n2-19-q42-42.why.0: (a) 「になって」: The honorific pattern「お + V (stem) + になる」combines with「〜てください」to form「お〜になってください」(please...), creating the polite honorific sentence: 「ここでお待ちになってください」.
default.q.n2-19-q42-42.why.1: (b) 「して」: 「お + V(stem) + する」 is humble language used for one’s own actions. It cannot be combined with 「〜ください」 to ask someone else to act; 「お待ちしてください」 is incorrect.
default.q.n2-19-q42-42.why.2: (c) 「にな注って」 is an OCR error for another word, not a standard grammatical form.
default.q.n2-19-q42-42.why.3: (d) 「注せて」 is an OCR error for 「させて」 and does not form an appropriate honorific expression in this context.
default.q.n2-19-q43-43.verdict: The correct answer is 2 (からには).
default.q.n2-19-q43-43.explanation:
- Sentence translation: Now that we have accepted this job, let's do our very best together!
- Grammar: 「V-る / V-た + からには」: Once one has..., one naturally must or is determined to see it through to the end. The following clause commonly expresses intention, determination, or obligation, such as 〜よう, 〜たい, or 〜べきだ.
- Kanji-based vocabulary: 引受 (acceptance, undertaking), 全力 (full effort).
- Example: 約束したからには、最後まで守らなければならない。(Once you have made a promise, you must keep it to the end.)
default.q.n2-19-q43-43.why.0: (a) 「からに」is not a complete grammar pattern expressing a cause-and-effect condition or determination; it should be 「からには」.
default.q.n2-19-q43-43.why.1: (b) 「からには」: The pattern 「V + からには」 means “now that..., one must...” or “once..., definitely...”. The following clause expresses determination: 「全力でやろう」, so this choice is correct.
default.q.n2-19-q43-43.why.2: (c) 「かぎりに」: The pattern 「〜を限りに」 means “until the end of” or “as far as possible,” and does not directly follow a verb in dictionary form to mean “once.”
default.q.n2-19-q43-43.why.3: (d) 「かぎりで」: The pattern 「〜かぎりでは」 means “within the scope of what one knows or sees,” so it does not fit a following clause expressing determination.
default.q.n2-19-q44-44.explanation:
- Translation: The water bill costs about 3,000 yen per month.
- Grammar: 「Number + につき」 means per each or for every, expressing a corresponding rate of quantity or cost per unit. (Note: 「水道答」 in the question is an OCR error for 「水道代」, meaning water bill.)
- Vocabulary: 水道代: water bill; 月: month.
- Example: この部屋の家賃は、1か月につき8万円です。(The rent for this room is 80,000 yen per month.)
default.q.n2-19-q44-44.why.0: (a) 「つき」(につき): The structure 「quantity + につき」 means “per / for each unit.” Here, 「一か月につき」 means “3,000 yen per month,” so it is completely correct.
default.q.n2-19-q44-44.why.1: (b) 「とって」(にとって): The pattern 「〜にとって」means “for” or “from the standpoint of,” and is not used after a unit of quantity to indicate a unit price or periodic rate.
default.q.n2-19-q44-44.why.2: (c) 「わたり」(にわたり): the pattern 「〜にわたり / にわたって」 means “throughout / over the entire period,” and is not used to express a recurring monthly unit price.
default.q.n2-19-q44-44.why.3: (d) 「かけ」(にかけ): The pattern 「〜から〜にかけて」 means “from... to...,” and 「一か月にかけ」 cannot stand alone.

default.q.n2-19-q55-55.verdict: The correct answer is 4: Until around the age of 9 or 10, children should have plenty of opportunities to play outdoors.
default.q.n2-19-q55-55.explanation:
**Main point of the passage:**
Sports originally developed from adult culture. For children to enjoy sports, they need plenty of outdoor play from early childhood through the elementary-school years so that their minds and bodies can develop in ways similar to those of adults. The appropriate age for children to begin sports is around 9–10, when their competitive feelings, ability to understand rules and techniques, and physical strength have developed. If children do not get enough outdoor play before that age or are forced to begin sports too early, they are likely to suffer psychological, developmental, and physical harm or disorders.

**Translation of the question and choices:**
- **Question:** Which of the following is closest to the author's view?
- **1.** Children should not play outdoors very much.
- **2.** Children should not play sports until they become adults.
- **3.** Children should start playing sports as early as possible.
- **4.** Children should play outdoors sufficiently until they are 9 or 10 years old.
default.q.n2-19-q55-55.why.0: (a) Incorrect because the author says that during early childhood and the elementary-school years, children need sufficient experience playing outdoors (「外遊びをじゅんぶんに体験し」), which is the exact opposite of the claim that they should not play outdoors much.
default.q.n2-19-q55-55.why.1: (b) Incorrect because the author says that children can begin becoming familiar with and enjoying sports at around age 9 or 10 (「子どもがスポーツを楽しめるようになるのは、およそ 9、10歳のころといわれている。スポーツとの出会いの時期だ」), not that they must wait until adulthood to play.

default.q.n2-19-q55-55.why.3: (d) Correct because the author emphasizes that children need sufficient outdoor play before the age of 9 or 10: 「子どもがスポーツを楽しむのには幼児から児童にかけての段階で外遊びをじゅんぶんに体験し... 子どもがスポーツを楽しめるようになるのは、およそ 9、10歳のころといわれている。...もし、それ以前の外遊びがじゅんぶんでなかったり、それより早い時期にスポーツを無理やり教えこまれると、心や体の障害を起こしやすくなる。」

- Answer choices:
1. Because turning in an ordinary key would be a nuisance.
2. Because he thought he might be able to use the key someday.
3. Because the key had a very unusual shape.
4. Because he thought he had found something very valuable.
default.q.n2-19-q60-60.why.0: (a) Correct. This matches the passage: 「男は手にとり、ただの鍵と知流て、ちょっとが流かりした。...しかし、拾ってしまうと捨てるのもめんどうく注く、それをポケットに入れた。したがって、①山ざ山ざ交番へとどける気にならなかったのは、いうまでもない。」 (The man realized that it was just an ordinary key and, thinking that throwing it away or turning it in would be troublesome, put it in his pocket.)
default.q.n2-19-q60-60.why.1: (b) Incorrect. When the man first picked up the key, he thought it was just an ordinary key (ただの鍵) and felt disappointed. It was only several days later that he came up with the idea of using it to commit a theft.
default.q.n2-19-q60-60.why.2: (c) Incorrect. At first, the man regarded it as an ordinary key (ただの鍵). Only later, when he looked at it again in a bright place, did he notice its unusual shape (明るいところで見ると...形が大いに違っていた).
default.q.n2-19-q60-60.why.3: (d) Incorrect. When he first picked it up, the man knew it was just an ordinary key and felt disappointed (ただの鍵と知流て、ちょっとが流かりした); he did not think it was an expensive item.
default.q.n2-19-q61-61.explanation:
- Main point: The man thinks that if he uses this key to break into an empty house and steal valuables, he will gain something valuable if he succeeds, while if he happens to be discovered, he can claim that he was returning a key he had found. In other words, “if it works, the reward is great, and even if it fails, the risk is small.”
- Question: What does ② “if it works, the reward is great, and even if it fails, the risk is small” mean?
- Answer choices:
1. If it works, he can enter an empty house, and if he cannot get in, it does not matter.
2. If it works, he can return the key to its owner, and if he is mistaken, he can make an excuse.
3. If it works, he can steal highly valuable items, while if he is discovered, the chance of being considered a criminal is very low.
4. If it works, he can hand over the key, while if he is discovered, the chance of being arrested is very low.
default.q.n2-19-q61-61.why.0: (a) Incorrect. “A big haul” here does not merely mean getting into the house; it means stealing valuables (金目のものを持ち出す).
default.q.n2-19-q61-61.why.1: (b) Incorrect. The man’s actual purpose was theft, not returning the key to the person who dropped it; “returning the key” was merely an excuse after he was discovered.
default.q.n2-19-q61-61.why.2: (c) Correct. This matches the content of the passage: 「これを使え消、留守宅に忍びこんで、金目のものを持ち出すことができるかもしれないな。...侵入した時に見とがめられたとしても、拾った鍵をおとどけに来たのだと言え消、い活おうの言い訳にはなる。...うまくいけ消収穫は大きく、失敗しても危険は少ない。」 (If things went well, they could steal valuables; even if they were spotted entering, they could claim that they had come to return a key they had found, giving them an excuse and reducing the risk of being charged with a crime.)
default.q.n2-19-q61-61.why.3: (d) Incorrect. The man's purpose was not to “deliver the key” (鍵をとどける); that was merely an excuse to justify breaking in.
default.q.n2-19-q62-62.explanation:
- Main idea: Believing that this special key belonged to a wealthy person's mansion, the man began carrying out his burglary plan by approaching luxurious mansions and secretly trying the key in their doors, starting in the area where he had found it.
- Question translation: What did "begin to carry out that plan" mean he did?
- Answer choices:
1. To return the key, he tried it in the doors of houses around the area where he had found it.
2. To commit burglary, he tried it in the doors of all the houses around the area where he had found it.
3. To find the key's owner, he tried it in the doors of houses around the area where he had found it.
4. To commit burglary, he tried it in the doors of houses that appeared to belong to wealthy people.
default.q.n2-19-q62-62.why.0: (a) Incorrect. The man’s real purpose was to sneak in and steal valuables (泥棒), not to return the key.
default.q.n2-19-q62-62.why.1: (b) Incorrect. The passage says that the man approached several luxurious villas (いくつもの立派な邸宅), not that he tried to enter “all the houses” (すべて).
default.q.n2-19-q62-62.why.2: (c) Incorrect. He has no intention of finding the owner of the key; this is merely a prepared excuse to use if he is discovered.
default.q.n2-19-q62-62.why.3: (d) Correct. The passage states: 「どこか金持ちの邸の鍵かもしれない。...男は③その計画を実行に移しはじめた。鍵を拾ったあたりの家々を手はじめに、いくつもの立派な邸宅の玄関に近より、ひそかに試みた。」 (He thought it might be the key to a rich person's house, so he secretly tried it in the doors of several grand residences in order to steal from them.)
default.q.n2-19-q63-63.verdict: The correct answer is 2: The author likes maps because of the way colors are combined and used on them.
default.q.n2-19-q63-63.explanation:
- Main point: The author says that they have loved maps since childhood and once wondered why they were so fascinated by them. The author concludes that the harmonious combination, variation, and balance of colors on maps—the brown of mountains, the green of plains, and the red of urban areas—creates a pleasant and enjoyable feeling.

- Question: Why does the author say they like maps?
- Choices:
1. Because looking at a map prevents them from getting lost.
2. Because they like the use of colors on maps.
3. Because they like memorizing place names.
4. Because they find it interesting that maps differ from actual scenery.
default.q.n2-19-q63-63.why.0: (a) Incorrect because in paragraph 3 the author writes:「地図を見るのが好きだといっても、知らない土地では道に迷う」(Even if you like looking at maps, you can still get lost in an unfamiliar place), not that looking at a map prevents you from getting lost.
default.q.n2-19-q63-63.why.1: (b) Correct because the second paragraph clearly states the author's conclusion: 「地図に使われている色、たとえ消山の茶色、平野の緑、都市の赤などの変化や理ランスが心地よいのだろう次という結論になった」 (I reached the conclusion that the changes and balance among the colors used on maps—such as brown for mountains, green for plains, and red for cities—probably create a pleasant feeling.)
default.q.n2-19-q63-63.why.2: (c) Incorrect because the passage does not say that the author likes maps because they enjoy memorizing place names. Paragraph 1 only says that, by often looking at maps, they remembered the locations and shapes of the prefectures from the age of seven.
default.q.n2-19-q63-63.why.3: (d) Incorrect because paragraph 3 says that the difference between the actual scenery and the map naturally causes people to get lost (「地図と実際の風景はまったく違うから、迷うもの当然なのだ」). The author does not say that this is interesting or why they like maps.
default.q.n2-19-q64-64.verdict: The correct answer is 2: The author avoids the route that goes uphill because they really hate having to climb hills.
default.q.n2-19-q64-64.explanation:
- Main point: When going from Sakashita (the bottom of the slope) to Sakaue (the top of the slope), the author actually had to climb a slope. At that time, the author was not used to it and strongly disliked climbing slopes. Because of this dislike, the author has avoided routes going from the bottom of a slope to the top ever since.

- Question: Why does the author say, “Ever since then, I have avoided routes going from the bottom of a slope to the top”?
- Answer choices:
1. Because there was a steep slope.
2. Because the author disliked climbing slopes.
3. Because maps were often inaccurate.
4. Because the author felt uneasy when unfamiliar with the place name. (Includes the beginning of the next question.)
default.q.n2-19-q64-64.why.0: (a) Incorrect because the presence of steep slopes is merely an actual condition encountered along the route; the direct reason the author deliberately avoids it is that the author dislikes climbing slopes.
default.q.n2-19-q64-64.why.1: (b) Correct because paragraph 4 clearly states: 「しかし、実際に行ってみたらᆏを上らなければならなかったのだ。当時、私はᆏに慣れていなくて嫌いだった」 (However, when I actually went there, I had to climb a slope. At the time, I was not used to climbing ᆏ and disliked it.) This led to the result: 「① それ以来、ᆏ下からᆏ上に行くコースは避けている」 (Since then, I have avoided routes that go from the bottom of ᆏ to the top of ᆏ).
default.q.n2-19-q64-64.why.2: (c) Incorrect because the map itself is not wrong (the place names correctly reflect their positions uphill and downhill: 「ᆏ上は本当にᆏの上、ᆏ下は本当にᆏの下」); it is simply a flat map that cannot visually represent the slope.
default.q.n2-19-q64-64.why.3: (d) Incorrect because the passage does not mention feeling anxious because one does not know place names. The author only reminds himself that he should have paid more attention to place names (「地名にもっと注意しなければならなかった」).
default.q.n2-19-q65-65.verdict: The correct answer is 4: Looking only at a flat map does not reveal how strenuous walking actually is, such as having to climb steep slopes.
default.q.n2-19-q65-65.explanation:
- Main point: The author realizes that a map is only a two-dimensional plane (「地図は平面である」), and that simply looking at a map cannot reveal how steep or difficult the terrain will be when walking in reality. Therefore, map readers need to understand that a flat map cannot show the full difficulty of traveling in the real world.

- Question: What does the author say one needs to keep in mind when looking at a map?
- Choices:
1. Even after looking at a map, one may get lost in an unfamiliar area.
2. The balance between mountains and plains cannot be understood from colors alone.
3. In many cases, a place that looks far away on a map is actually close when walking.
4. A map showing only a flat surface cannot reveal how difficult walking there will be in reality.
default.q.n2-19-q65-65.why.0: (a) Incorrect because the author regards getting lost in an unfamiliar place as natural (「迷うもの当然なのだ。そのことは何とも思っていなかった」), not as an important lesson or point to remember.
default.q.n2-19-q65-65.why.1: (b) Incorrect because color is the factor that made the author like maps in paragraph 2. The passage does not mention “being unable to recognize the balance between mountains and plains through color.”
default.q.n2-19-q65-65.why.2: (c) Incorrect because the author searched for the shortest route on a map but encountered difficult slopes in reality. The passage does not mention the situation of “a place looking far away on the map but being close in reality.”
default.q.n2-19-q65-65.why.3: (d) Correct, because the author emphasizes the shock of realizing 「地図は平面である」 (A map is flat) and concludes that 「地図で見ているだけでは、急なᆏがあってもわからない」 (Simply looking at a map will not tell you that there is a steep slope), showing that a flat map cannot convey how difficult the actual walk will be.
default.q.n2-19-q66-66.verdict: The correct answer is 1 (次々に): After looking at the most important person (the keyman), the speaker needs to shift their gaze successively to the other participants.
default.q.n2-19-q66-66.explanation:
- Main idea: The passage explains how to speak during a meeting: the important thing is to speak confidently and look directly at the listeners. When speaking, one should first look at the key person (for example, the department manager), then gradually shift one's gaze from person to person, speaking to each one as if having a direct, personal conversation.
- Question translation: Which word best fits ( ① )?
- Answer choices:
  1. 次々に: one after another, successively.
  2. 徐々に: gradually, little by little (indicating a change in degree or state over time).
  3. どんどん: rapidly, continuously, in quick succession.
  4. 一気に: all at once, in one go, without stopping.
default.q.n2-19-q66-66.why.0: (a) Correct. The passage states: 「まずはキーマン...の顔を見て、それから（次々に）視線を移していき、一人一人の顔を見つめつつ、語りかけるように話していきます」 (First look at the key person's face... then shift your gaze from one person to the next and speak while looking at each person's face, as if talking directly to them). The adverb 「次々に」 describes shifting one's gaze successively from one person to another.
default.q.n2-19-q66-66.why.1: (b) Incorrect. 「徐々に」(gradually, little by little) describes a gradual change in degree, state, or speed over time; it is not suitable for describing people shifting their gaze back and forth among individuals in a meeting room.
default.q.n2-19-q66-66.why.2: (c) Incorrect. 「どんどん」 describes rapid speed or an intense pace, so it does not fit calmly shifting one’s gaze to look at and talk with each person.
default.q.n2-19-q66-66.why.3: (d) Incorrect. 「一気に」 describes decisively completing an action all at once, so it cannot be used for shifting one’s gaze from one person to the next.
default.q.n2-19-q67-67.verdict: The correct answer is 4: Explaining where the content appears in a document is merely an exceptional case that should be kept to a minimum; it is not one of the positive presentation skills referred to by “these things” (こうしたこと).
default.q.n2-19-q67-67.explanation:
- Main point: The phrase ② 「こうしたこと」 (“things like these”) summarizes the presentation skills requested in the preceding paragraph: speaking confidently, looking around at each participant’s face while talking, and minimizing the need to look at the material. Looking at the material to explain where something is written is merely an exceptional situation in which looking is permitted, not a core behavior the speaker needs to practice.
- Translation of the question: Which of the following is NOT included in ② “things like these”?
- Translation of the choices:
  1. 自信を持って落ち着いて話すこと: Speaking calmly and confidently.
  2. 出席者の顔を見渡しながら語りかけるように話をすること: Speaking as if conversing while looking around at the faces of the attendees.
  3. あまり書面を見ずに話をすること: Speaking without looking at the written material too much.
  4. 話している内容がどこに書いてあるか説明すること: Explaining where the content being discussed is written in the material.
default.q.n2-19-q67-67.why.0: (a) Incorrect because this content IS included in 「こうしたこと」. The passage emphasizes: 「まず大切なのは自信を持つこと」 (The first important thing is to have confidence).
default.q.n2-19-q67-67.why.1: (b) Incorrect because this content is included in 「こうしたこと」. The passage states: 「一人一人の顔を見つめつつ、語りかけるように話していきます」 (speaking while looking at each person's face, as if talking to them personally).
default.q.n2-19-q67-67.why.2: (c) Incorrect because this content IS included in 「こうしたこと」. The passage states: 「出席者の顔を見渡すのですから、当然、書面に目を落としてばかりはいられません」 (Since you must look around at the faces of the attendees, naturally you cannot keep your eyes fixed on the document).
default.q.n2-19-q67-67.why.3: (d) Correct because it is not included in 「こうしたこと」. The passage states: 「むしろ書面を見るのは、内容を確認したり、話している内容が書面のどこに書いてあるか説明したりするときぐらいにとどめたいものです」. Looking at the document to explain where something is written is merely a minimal activity that should be limited; it is not a core presentation skill or behavior summarized by 「こうしたこと」.
default.q.n2-19-q68-68.verdict: The correct answer is 4 (準備を怠らないで、十分練ってから会議に臨むこと): the author asserts that thorough preparation and careful refinement of the plan in advance are the most essential prerequisites for presenting with confidence.
default.q.n2-19-q68-68.explanation:
- Main idea: The author argues that a presentation does not begin only when one enters the meeting room; it begins when the plan is first conceived. To present confidently without becoming flustered, the most important prerequisite is to prepare thoroughly and refine the plan's content carefully before attending the meeting.
- Question translation: What does the author consider most important when giving a presentation?
- Answer choices:
  1. Speak properly and confidently without fear or confusion.
  2. Look over the faces of the participants in order, starting with the key people, and make eye contact while speaking.
  3. Occasionally check the material and speak cautiously.
  4. Prepare thoroughly without neglecting the planning stage, then attend the meeting.
default.q.n2-19-q68-68.why.0: (a) Incorrect. Although the passage mentions that one should not speak timidly or nervously (「声が小さく、オドオド、あるいはモジモジしながら発表するようでは...」), the author identifies thorough preparation beforehand as the essential factor, rather than merely forcing oneself to act confidently in the meeting room.
default.q.n2-19-q68-68.why.1: (b) Incorrect. Looking at the key person and then scanning each person is merely an eye-contact skill used when giving a presentation, not the most important prerequisite.
default.q.n2-19-q68-68.why.2: (c) Incorrect. The passage recommends limiting the act of looking at the materials as much as possible (「～ぐらいにとどめたいものです」); it does not encourage occasionally checking the materials in order to speak carefully.
default.q.n2-19-q68-68.why.3: (d) Correct. The author states: 「事前の準備が重要になります」 (Advance preparation is important) and 「自信を持って発表するには、企画自体をしっかり練って自分のものにしておくことが大前提」 (To give a presentation confidently, the essential prerequisite is to thoroughly develop the plan itself and make it truly one's own.)
default.q.n2-19-q69-69.verdict: The correct answer is 2: 自分を守るためのスペースを確保する (to secure or create space to protect oneself).
default.q.n2-19-q69-69.explanation:
**Main point:**
The passage begins by describing a common psychological tendency: when space permits, people unconsciously maintain a certain distance from strangers to create a separating barrier. Passage A further explains that this barrier comes from the need to protect one's "personal space" or territory as a form of self-defense (自己防衛).

**Question and answer choices:**
- Question: Which meaning is closest to 「空間的に他者とのしきり（注 2 ）を無意識につくっている」(unconsciously creating a spatial barrier between oneself and others)?
- 1. Separating the current situation by various methods.
- 2. Securing or creating space to protect oneself.
- 3. Closing one's eyes and thinking.
- 4. Escaping stress on a crowded train.
default.q.n2-19-q69-69.why.0: (a) Choice 1 is incorrect because cutting off the current situation in various ways is a response to being forced into a situation where physical distance cannot be created, such as closing one's eyes on a crowded train. It is not the essence of unconsciously creating a natural spatial barrier under ordinary conditions.
default.q.n2-19-q69-69.why.1: (b) Choice 2 is correct because the text explains the motive for creating a barrier or spatial distance through the words of a psychology professor: 「これは、『パーソナルスペース』つまり、自分のテリトリー（注 4 ）を守りたいという心理が働いているようで、自己防衛のためのスペースを確保しているのだそうです」 (This seems to result from the psychological desire to protect one's “personal space,” that is, one's own territory, thereby securing space for self-defense.)
default.q.n2-19-q69-69.why.2: (c) Choice 3 is incorrect because “closing one’s eyes” is merely an example of a nonphysical coping method when it is impossible to maintain distance on a crowded train (「たとえば目をつぶることで、視覚的に現状を消し去ろうとする」), not the central meaning of creating a spatial barrier.
default.q.n2-19-q69-69.why.3: (d) Incorrect because it contradicts the argument in the passage. “Escaping the stress of a crowded train” is the purpose of creating a nonphysical distance in section B by becoming absorbed in reading or listening to music, not the meaning of creating a physical spatial barrier.
default.q.n2-19-q70-70.verdict: The correct answer is 3: A は他人との物理的距離、 B は非物理的距離について話している (A discusses physical distance, whereas B discusses nonphysical distance from other people).
default.q.n2-19-q70-70.explanation:
**Main point:**
- Story A: It describes choosing a seat at the end of a long train bench so that only one stranger sits beside you, rather than being squeezed between two people. This creates and maintains physical distance (物理的距離).
- Story B: It describes how, on a crowded train where physical distance cannot be created, people immerse themselves in reading or listening to music to create personal space in their minds. This creates non-physical distance (非物理的距離).

**Question and answer choices:**
- Question: Which of the following is correct regarding the stories of A and B?
- 1. Both A and B discuss physical distance from other people.
- 2. Both A and B discuss non-physical distance from other people.
- 3. A discusses physical distance, while B discusses non-physical distance from other people.
- 4. A discusses non-physical distance, while B discusses physical distance from other people.
default.q.n2-19-q70-70.why.0: (a) Choice 1 is incorrect because B's story is not about physical distance. It describes creating nonphysical distance (非物理的な「パーソナルスペース」) by immersing oneself in books or music when physical distance cannot be maintained.
default.q.n2-19-q70-70.why.1: (b) Choice 2 is incorrect because Story A describes choosing a seat at the edge or corner (端の席) to reduce contact with people nearby. This is behavior that creates physical distance (物理的距離).
default.q.n2-19-q70-70.why.2:
(c) Choice 3 is correct because it is directly supported by the passage:
- Paragraph A discusses physical distance: 「隣にいる他人が一人だけなのと、両側から挟まれているのとでは、居心地の点でかなりの違いがある…自己防衛のためのスペースを確保している」 (There is a considerable difference in comfort between having only one stranger next to you and being surrounded on both sides… people secure space for self-protection).
- Paragraph B discusses nonphysical distance: 「満員電車のような物理的な『パーソナルスペース』を確保できない状態では、読書、携帯のメール、音楽などに没頭することにより、非物理的な『パーソナルスペース』を確保し…」 (When it is impossible to secure physical “personal space,” as on a crowded train, immersing oneself in reading, mobile-phone messages, or music helps secure nonphysical “personal space”).
default.q.n2-19-q70-70.why.3: (d) Choice 4 is incorrect because it reverses the content of Story A (physical distance) and Story B (nonphysical distance).
default.q.n2-19-q71-71.verdict: The correct answer is 4: You do not need to try to draw it realistically or make it look proper.
default.q.n2-19-q71-71.explanation:
- Summary: The author explains that many people think they "cannot draw" or "do not want to draw" because they are overly concerned with drawing something that looks "proper" or realistic. In reality, art does not require absolute accuracy; it allows a wide range of acceptable expression. Each person only needs to express things in their own form and according to their own perception, without trying to make the drawing look realistic.
- Question translation: What does the author advise people who say, "I am not good at drawing, so I do not want to draw"?
- Answer choices:
  1. It is fine to draw a dog as a cow and an apple as a tangerine.
  2. It is fine to draw the dog or apple that you own.
  3. If you want to draw something realistically, copying it is enough.
  4. You do not need to try to make your drawings look proper or realistic.
default.q.n2-19-q71-71.why.0: (a) Incorrect because drawing a dog as a cow or an apple as a tangerine is merely an example the author gives of an artist's inferiority complex when their drawing does not resemble the model; the author is not recommending that people draw this way intentionally.
default.q.n2-19-q71-71.why.1: (b) Incorrect because the phrase “my dog, my apple” (自分の犬、自分のりんご) refers to drawing in one’s own style and according to one’s personal perception, not to drawing animals or objects one owns in real life.
default.q.n2-19-q71-71.why.2: (c) Incorrect because the author says that drawing something realistically is essentially copying it (写す), rather than drawing it in the true creative sense (描く). The author does not advise people who want to draw realistically to copy.
default.q.n2-19-q71-71.why.3: (d) Correct. QUOTE: 「でも描けないというのは、「それらしく」描かなくてはならないという気持ちがあるからだ。……でも、絵は正確注を要求されるものではない。自分の㤿、自分のりんごを描け消いい。……描くということは自分なりの形でいいのだ。」 (The reason people cannot draw is that they feel they must draw something “convincingly” or realistically. Pictures do not require accuracy; one only needs to draw them in one’s own way, without forcing oneself to make them look realistic.)
default.q.n2-19-q72-72.verdict: The correct answer is 3: The author began coloring the paper personally.
default.q.n2-19-q72-72.explanation:
- Main point: When the atmosphere of the meeting with the children with disabilities seemed awkward, tense, and hesitant, the author decided to act first to break down the barrier by spreading a large sheet of white paper on the table and coloring it decisively, energetically, and quickly.
- Question translation: The phrase “act first” appears. Who did what?
- Answer choices:
  1. The children spread a sheet of white paper on the table.
  2. The children began coloring.
  3. The author began coloring.
  4. The author began making the children draw pictures.
default.q.n2-19-q72-72.why.0: (a) Incorrect because the author, not the children, spread the large blank sheet of paper on the table in preparation for drawing.
default.q.n2-19-q72-72.why.1: (b) Incorrect because the author initially took the initiative and began coloring decisively. Only afterward did the children become interested by watching and join in drawing.
default.q.n2-19-q72-72.why.2: (c) Correct. QUOTE: 「そこで、大きな白い紙を机の上に広げて、 告 とりあえずアクシ自ンを起こす 。 まず採で塗る。とにかく、勢いよく塗り始めた。」 (The author spread a large white sheet of paper on the desk and immediately took action by energetically painting it red.)
default.q.n2-19-q72-72.why.3: (d) Incorrect because the author did not force or ask the children to draw pictures, but colored first to attract their attention and inspire them naturally.
default.q.n2-19-q73-73.verdict: The correct answer is 4: In painting, the joy of painting is more important than using technique to make the picture look realistic.

default.q.n2-19-q28-28.verdict: The correct answer is 1 (the base word being examined is 錆びる: to become rusty, to rust).
default.q.n2-19-q28-28.explanation:

default.q.n2-19-q29-29.explanation:
見下ろす (みおろす): to look down from above at scenery, streets, the sea, and so on, from a mountain summit, tall building, airplane, and so forth.
Example: 展望台から街の夜景を見下ろす。(Look down from the observation deck at the city's nighttime view.)
default.q.n2-19-q29-29.why.0: Used incorrectly: To unload baggage or cargo from a truck, use 降ろす (トラックから降ろす / 荷下ろしをする), not 見下ろす.
default.q.n2-19-q29-29.why.1: Incorrect usage: When you happen to see someone at a supermarket, use 見かける (“happen to see”), 会う, or 出くわす, not 見下ろす.

default.q.n2-19-q29-29.why.3: Correct in context: 見下ろす (みおろす) means to look down from a higher position (山の上から見下ろす: to look down from the mountaintop).
default.q.n2-19-q30-30.explanation:
抱える (かかえる):
1. To hold, carry in one's arms, or carry under one's arm (荷物・頭を抱える).
2. To bear or have problems, responsibilities, burdens, debts, illnesses, or family members (問題・借金・重病・家族を抱える).

default.q.n2-19-q30-30.why.0: The word choice is incorrect. To add or sprinkle salt into a dish, use 加える (くわえる, “add”), 振る, or 入れる, not 抱える (“hold in one's arms”).
default.q.n2-19-q30-30.why.1: Used appropriately: 抱える (かかえる) means to shoulder, have, or face difficulties or problems (問題を抱える: to have or face many problems).
default.q.n2-19-q30-30.why.2: Used incorrectly: When referring to an event that is remembered in history or changes history, use 歴史に残る事件 or 歴史を変える事件, not かかえる.

default.q.n2-19-q31-31.explanation:
膨らむ (ふくらむ): to swell, expand, or become inflated, literally as with a balloon, air bag, or stomach, or figuratively as with dreams, hopes, a budget, or a deficit: 夢・期待・予算・赤字が膨らむ.

default.q.n2-19-q31-31.why.0: Correct in this context: 膨らむ (ふくらむ) means to swell, expand, or become inflated when air or another substance fills the inside, as in 「風船が膨らむ」.
default.q.n2-19-q31-31.why.1: Incorrect usage: To describe someone sulking or pouting, use 拗ねる (すねる), むくれる, or 「ほおを膨らませる」/「膨れる」. Do not use the construction “person + 膨らむ” directly.
default.q.n2-19-q31-31.why.2: Incorrect usage: When a train is about to depart or has just left, use 電車が出る / 発車する / 行ってしまう, not 膨らむ.
default.q.n2-19-q31-31.why.3: Incorrect: When a pencil tip has been sharpened to a point, use 尖っている (とがっている: pointed), not 膨らむ.
default.q.n2-19-q32-32.explanation:
逆らう (さからう):
1. To go against the direction of a natural flow (流れ・風・波に逆らう: to swim against the current or go against the wind or waves).
2. To oppose, disobey, or act contrary to someone’s wishes, an order, or a rule (親・上司・命令・時代の流れに逆らう: to disobey one’s parents, defy one’s superior’s orders, or go against the tide of the times).

default.q.n2-19-q32-32.why.1: This fits the context: 逆らう (さからう) combines with 流れ (current) in the standard collocation 流れに逆らう, meaning to swim or move against the current.
default.q.n2-19-q32-32.why.2: Incorrect: When the order between two people is reversed, use 順番が逆になる or 狂う, not 逆らう.
default.q.n2-19-q32-32.why.3: Incorrect usage: When the upper and lower positions are reversed, use 上と下が逆になる / ひっくり返る, not 逆らう.

default.q.n2-2-q64-64.why.3: (d) This is unsuitable because explaining rules in a dogmatic way, such as "you must do this" or "you must not do that," does not make children understand and agree as effectively as allowing them to experience being praised by others.
default.q.n2-2-q65-65.verdict: The correct answer is choice 1: When children eat alone, it is difficult for them to develop and acquire proper table manners.
default.q.n2-2-q65-65.explanation:
• Main point: Good table manners develop through one's "relationship with other people" (the desire to present a good image in front of others). Therefore, when eating alone, people pay less attention to table manners. The modern phenomenon of children eating alone ("solitary eating") is a serious issue because it makes it difficult for them to learn appropriate table manners.
• Question: What does the author think about children eating meals alone ("solitary eating")?
• Answer choices:
1. It is difficult to develop proper table manners when eating alone.
2. By eating alone, children will gradually develop appropriate table manners.
3. People tend to try harder to eat properly when eating alone.
4. Even when eating alone, people are required to eat with proper table manners.
default.q.n2-2-q65-65.why.0: (a) The passage states: "人は人前で食事をするとき、一人で食べるよりもそれなりに整った食べ方をしようとするものです。... 一方、一人で食事をとるときは、食事のマナーを感ずることが少ないのではないでしょうか。近頃の家庭の多く見られる“子供の独食”は、子供に彙切なマナーを身につけ注せるという意味においても考慮すべき問題であるといえるのです。" Because manners arise from the need to interact with others ("他者との関係"), eating alone reduces awareness of proper manners and makes it difficult for children to learn appropriate conduct.
default.q.n2-2-q65-65.why.1: (b) It is inappropriate because it completely contradicts the passage, which states that eating alone is an obstacle to learning manners.
default.q.n2-2-q65-65.why.2: (c) This is unsuitable because the passage states that when people eat in front of others, they try to eat more properly than when eating alone (“人は人前で食事をするとき、一人で食べるよりもそれなりに整った食べ方をしようとするものです”).
default.q.n2-2-q65-65.why.3: (d) Does not fit because the author only analyzes the natural tendency to be less self-conscious when eating alone and warns about the reality of “solo eating.” The author does not give a moral instruction or rule that people must maintain proper manners even when eating alone.
default.q.n2-2-q66-66.verdict: The correct answer is 4. 実験をした人 (the person who conducted the experiment).
default.q.n2-2-q66-66.explanation:
- Main point: To investigate the relationship between the amount of food consumed and changes in body weight, an Italian scientist about 380 years ago used his own body for an experiment. He had a special large scale made that could hold a person, sat on it continuously for several days, ate and drank, urinated and defecated, and carefully measured his weight each time.
- Question: The passage says that someone "ate and drank, defecated, and urinated." Who did those things?
- Answer choices:
  1. The person asked to conduct the experiment.
  2. The person who assisted with the experiment.
  3. The person who observed the experiment.
  4. The person who conducted the experiment.
default.q.n2-2-q66-66.why.0: (a) Incorrect because the passage does not mention having someone else do it; the scholar personally carried it out using their own body (「自分の体を使って」).
default.q.n2-2-q66-66.why.1: (b) Incorrect because the person who directly sat on the scale, ate, and excreted for the measurements was the scholar conducting the experiment, not an “assistant.”
default.q.n2-2-q66-66.why.2: (c) Incorrect because the person who sat on the scale for days and carried out those activities was not a “spectator” or “observer.”
default.q.n2-2-q66-66.why.3: (d) Correct because the passage states: 「あるイタリアの学者が、食べ物の重注と体重の関係を知るために、自分の体を使って体重の変化をこまかく調べた。まず、人間が乗ることのできる大きなはかりを特別に作り、その上に何日間もす山りつづけて、 ① 食べたり飲んだり、大便や小便をしたりした。」 (An Italian scholar used his own body to study changes in weight in detail. First, he specially made a large scale that a person could stand on, remained on it for several days, and ① ate, drank, and urinated and defecated.) Therefore, the person who carried out these activities was the experimenter.
default.q.n2-2-q67-67.verdict: The correct answer is 2. 期待どおりの結果が出なかったから。 (Because the expected result was not achieved.)
default.q.n2-2-q67-67.explanation:
- Main point: At first, the scholar thought that his body weight would increase by exactly the weight of the food and drink he consumed minus the weight of the feces and urine he excreted. However, the actual results showed that his weight did not increase as much as he had expected. Thinking there must be an error, he repeated the experiment several times, but the results remained unchanged, leaving him extremely confused and at an impasse.
- Question translation: It says that he became confused and reached an impasse. Why did he become confused?
- Answer choices:
  1. Because the calculations were too difficult.
  2. Because the results did not turn out as he had initially expected or predicted.
  3. Because there were too many errors in the experiment.
  4. Because he was unable to move for many days.
default.q.n2-2-q67-67.why.0: (a) Incorrect because the scholar performed only a simple subtraction (「単純に引き算した」); that was not the reason he became confused.
default.q.n2-2-q67-67.why.1: (b) Correct, because the passage clearly states: 「最初、その学者が考えたのは、食べたり飲んだりした物の重さから、外に出した大便や小便の重注を単純に引き算した分だけ体重はふえるだろう次ということだった。ところが、実験をしてみた結果、彼が考えていたほど体重はふえなかったのである。彼は実験に間違いがあったのかもしてないと思って何回もやりなおしてみたが、結果はやはり同じだった。彼は 告 困ってしまった。」 (The scholar expected body weight to increase by the amount consumed minus the amount excreted, but in reality it did not increase as much as he expected, even after he repeated the experiment several times.)
default.q.n2-2-q67-67.why.2: (c) Incorrect because the experiment had no error; the result remained unchanged even after he repeated it several times (“結果はやはり同じだった”).
default.q.n2-2-q67-67.why.3: (d) Incorrect because sitting on the scale for several days was a method the man devised for his own experiment, not the cause of his confusion after obtaining the results.
default.q.n2-2-q68-68.verdict: The correct answer is 1. 彼が考えたこと (what he had guessed/thought about).
default.q.n2-2-q68-68.explanation:
- Summary of the main point: After repeatedly verifying that the increase in weight was smaller than expected, the scholar hypothesized that some of the food and drink had been transformed into something invisible and escaped from the body. His conclusion was completely correct, because later research showed that the missing mass consisted of sweat and CO2 released through respiration.
- Question translation: The passage says that "it was not wrong at all." What was not wrong?
- Answer choices:
  1. What he thought or hypothesized.
  2. The fact that he became confused or stuck.
  3. The fact that he became angry.
  4. What he failed to realize.
default.q.n2-2-q68-68.why.0: (a) Correct because the passage states: 「おそらく、食べ物や飲み物の一部は、何か目には見えない物となって体の外へ出て行ってしまったのだろう、結局、彼はそう考えた。そう、彼は ③ 間違っていなかった。」 (He eventually concluded that some of the food and drink had probably become something invisible and left his body. He was not wrong, because the author later clarifies that the invisible substances were sweat and CO2).
default.q.n2-2-q68-68.why.1: (b) Incorrect because “being troubled” (困ってしまった) describes the man’s feelings when the result was not what he expected; it is not what is asserted to be true or false at position ③.
default.q.n2-2-q68-68.why.2: (c) Incorrect because the word “怒る” appears in paragraph 1 only to warn readers not to become impatient with an obvious answer (“あたり前じゃないかと怒ってはいけない”); it is unrelated to the scholar.
default.q.n2-2-q68-68.why.3: (d) Incorrect because what he failed to recognize (that CO2 is released through respiration, since gases were not understood at the time) reflects a historical limitation, contradicting the question's statement that he was "not wrong."
default.q.n2-2-q69-69.verdict: The correct answer is choice 3: The number of days they are open remains the same as before, but their opening hours have been shortened.
default.q.n2-2-q69-69.explanation:
- The library began opening on the second and fourth Saturdays of each month, but in return it closes the following Monday (Paragraph A: "その代わりに開館した土曜日の次の月曜日は休館になりました", "結局開館日が増えたわけではありません" → the total number of days open per month or week has not increased). Regarding opening hours, weekdays remain 9:00 to 18:00 (9 hours), while Saturdays are only 9:00 to 15:00 (6 hours) (Paragraph B: "平日の開館時間は以前の通り9時から 6 時までなのに、土曜日はどうして9時から3時までなのでしょうか") → total opening hours have become shorter than before.
- Question translation: How have the number of opening days and the opening hours of this library changed?
- Answer choices:
1. Compared with before, the number of opening days has increased and the opening hours are also longer.
2. The number of opening days is unchanged, but the opening hours are longer.
3. The number of opening days is unchanged, but the opening hours are shorter.
4. Compared with before, the number of opening days has increased, but the opening hours are shorter.
default.q.n2-2-q69-69.why.0: (a) Choice 1 is incorrect because the number of days open did not increase (Saturday was added, but Monday became a closing day), and the opening hours did not become longer; Saturday closes at 3 p.m. instead of Monday's 6 p.m.
default.q.n2-2-q69-69.why.1: (b) Choice 2 is incorrect in saying that the opening hours became longer (長くなった). In reality, the facility is open for only 6 hours on Saturdays (9:00–15:00), which is shorter than the 9-hour weekday schedule (9:00–18:00).
default.q.n2-2-q69-69.why.2: (c) Choice 3 is correct. Passage A clearly states「次の月曜が休館なので、結局開館日が増えたわけではありません」(the number of days the library is open has not increased), while Passage B states「平日の開館時間は以前の通り9時から 6 時までなのに、土曜日はどうして9時から3時までなのでしょうか」(although weekday hours remain 9 a.m. to 6 p.m., Saturday hours are only 9 a.m. to 3 p.m.), meaning that Monday’s 9 a.m.–6 p.m. opening has merely been replaced by shorter Saturday hours.
default.q.n2-2-q69-69.why.3: (d) Answer choice 4 is incorrect because the number of days open does not increase (増えた): Although the library opens on Saturday, it closes the following Monday as a compensatory day off, so the total number of open days remains unchanged.
default.q.n2-2-q70-70.verdict: The correct answer is choice 3: Person A feels dissatisfied, while Person B views the change as positive.
default.q.n2-2-q70-70.explanation:
- Main ideas:
+ User A, who is preparing for university entrance exams, needs a quiet space and a regular study seat. When the library is crowded on Saturdays, it is difficult to find a seat, and the Monday closure is inconvenient, so A wants the library to reconsider its opening days.
+ User B, a working adult, used to find the library closed after work on weekdays. B is now very pleased that it is open on weekends and considers it a new source of weekend enjoyment, although B suggests that the library open every week and stay open later.
- Question translation: What do users "A" and "B" think about the change in the library’s opening days?
- Answer choices:
1. Both "A" and "B" are satisfied.
2. Neither "A" nor "B" has a particular opinion.
3. "A" is dissatisfied, but "B" is pleased.
4. "A" is pleased, but "B" is dissatisfied.
default.q.n2-2-q70-70.why.0: (a) Choice 1 is incorrect because person A is not satisfied (満足している) at all; instead, they ask the library to reconsider its opening day because it is crowded and they lose Monday as a study day.
default.q.n2-2-q70-70.why.1: (b) Answer choice 2 is incorrect because both people clearly state their opinions, requests, and wishes to the library.
default.q.n2-2-q70-70.why.2: (c) Choice 3 is correct. Evidence from the passage: Person A is dissatisfied: 「土曜は朝から利用者が多く、席が取れないこともあります。私の勝手な希望かもしれませんが、もう一度開館日を考え直していた だけませんか」, while Person B is pleased to be able to use the library on weekends: 「先日から週末にも利用できるようになり、週末の楽しみが一つ増えました」.
default.q.n2-2-q70-70.why.3: (d) Choice 4 is incorrect because it completely reverses the two people’s attitudes: in reality, A is dissatisfied while B feels positive.
default.q.n2-2-q71-71.verdict: The correct answer is 3 (正しい - correct / accurate).
default.q.n2-2-q71-71.explanation:
Summary: The author quotes the saying, “If you formulate a question accurately, you have already found half the answer,” and completely agrees with this view (まったく正しい). The author extends this idea by saying that in an interview, knowing exactly what you need to ask means that you have already obtained half the information.

Question translation: What is the appropriate word to fill position ①?
Answer choices:
1. 不思議である: Strange / puzzling
2. おかしい: Odd / funny
3. 正しい: Correct / accurate
4. 同じである: The same
default.q.n2-2-q71-71.why.0: (a) 「不思議である」 (strange / puzzling) does not fit because the author fully agrees with and affirms the validity of the proverb, rather than finding it strange or difficult to understand.
default.q.n2-2-q71-71.why.1: (b) 「おかしい」(strange, absurd, laughable) is incorrect because the author acknowledges the value of the statement rather than regarding it as unreasonable or laughable.
default.q.n2-2-q71-71.why.2: (c) Quotation: 「『問題を正しくたてられたら、答えを半分見い出したも同然。』とよくいわれる。これはまったく①（正しい）。同様に、聞き取りに際しても、聞くべきことがわかっていれば、半分聞き出したも同然なのである。」— The author states that the saying is completely correct, establishing an equivalent comparison with interviewing.
default.q.n2-2-q71-71.why.3: (d) 「同じである」 (“to be the same”) is grammatically and semantically unsuitable with the adverb 「まったく」 in the context of evaluating the statement above.
default.q.n2-2-q72-72.verdict: The correct answer is 2 (人に取材されて — being interviewed by someone).
default.q.n2-2-q72-72.explanation:
Summary: The author clearly states that recently, in addition to interviewing other people, they themselves have also been interviewed frequently. It was through being interviewed by others (人から取材されて) that the author realized many interviewers do not clearly understand what they need to ask.

Question translation: If ②『それで』 (therefore/that is how) were expressed differently, which option would be closest in meaning here?
Choice translations:
1. 人に取材して: Interviewing other people
2. 人に取材されて: Being interviewed by other people
3. 人に取材できて: Being able to interview other people
4. 人に取材注: (Ungrammatical phrase / meaningless)
default.q.n2-2-q72-72.why.0: (a) 「人に取材して」(interviewing other people) is incorrect because the new experience that helped the author recognize reporters' shortcomings was being in the position of the person interviewed: the author increasingly came to be interviewed by others (人から取材されることも結構多くなった).
default.q.n2-2-q72-72.why.1: (b) The passage states: 「最近私は、人に取材するばかりでなく、人から取材されることも結構多くなった。②それでわかったことは、自分で何を聞くべきかが充分わかっていないで人にものを聞く人間がいかに多いかである。」 “それで” (as a result / through that experience) directly refers to the fact that the author had recently often been interviewed by others (人から取材されて).
default.q.n2-2-q72-72.why.2: (c) 「人に取材できて」(being able to interview other people) is incorrect because it emphasizes the ability to go and interview others, rather than reflecting the interviewee's role in this context.
default.q.n2-2-q72-72.why.3: (d) 「人に取材注」is grammatically and semantically incorrect (a printing error) and cannot replace a conjunction expressing a cause-and-effect relationship based on experience.
default.q.n2-2-q73-73.verdict: The correct answer is 4: During an interview, the most important thing is to prepare carefully and clearly understand what you need to ask the other person.
default.q.n2-2-q73-73.explanation:
Summary: The entire passage emphasizes that the most important and fundamental aspect of an interview is for the interviewer to clearly understand and keep in mind what they need to ask the other person (聞くべきこと・問うべきもの), rather than relying only on superficial prompts or shallow interviewing techniques.

Question translation: What does the author most want to say in this passage?
Answer choices:
1. (Choice 1)
2. (Choice 2)
3. (Choice 3)
4. (Choice 4 - Correct answer): In an interview, the most important thing is to prepare thoroughly and have a firm grasp of what you need to ask the other person.
default.q.n2-2-q73-73.why.0: (a) Choice 1 does not reflect the central idea of the passage; it is merely a minor detail or an interpretation that does not match the main focus on the interviewer's preparation.
default.q.n2-2-q73-73.why.1: (b) Choice 2 is not what the author primarily wants to emphasize; the discussion of the phenomenon on television is merely an example illustrating the naivety and dependence of journalists who are unprepared.
default.q.n2-2-q73-73.why.2: (c) Choice 3 is incorrect because the author strongly criticizes superficial, easy questions and regards outward techniques merely as 「粗末なテクニック論」 rather than the essence.
default.q.n2-2-q73-73.why.3: (d) The passage states: 「最も大切なことは、自分がその相手から聞くべきことを知っておくことである。（中略）私にいわせれば、これ以上に本質的に大切なことは何もなく、あとは大部分が粗末なテクニック論である。」 and 「自分の中に問うべきものをしっかり持っている人は、質問を返されたときすぐにきちんとした質問で切り返すことができるものである。しかし、それを持たない人はまともな質問がついにできない。」 The author asserts that the essential point in an interview is knowing what one needs to ask.
default.q.n2-2-q74-74.verdict: The provided answer is 2; however, according to the passage, the correct answer is 4 because a foreigner who attended school in Fujiyama City and stayed in Japan for three years satisfies all the participation requirements.
default.q.n2-2-q74-74.explanation:
**Summary of the relevant passage:**
The 10th Japanese Speech Contest for Foreign Nationals sets three mandatory eligibility requirements (failing to meet even one means disqualification):
1. The participant must be at least 18 years old (a high school student may participate if they are 18 or older).
2. The participant must be a foreign national living in Fujiyama City or working or studying there.
3. The participant must have lived in Japan for no more than five years.

**Translation of the question and choices:**
- *Question:* Who among the following people is eligible to participate in this speech contest?
- 1. A foreign national who is a 12th-grade student living in Fujiyama City.
- 2. A foreign national studying at a university in Fujiyama City who has been in Japan for six years.
- 3. A Japanese national who has been in Japan for two years, lives outside Fujiyama City, and works in Fujiyama City.
- 4. A foreign national who has been in Japan for three years, lives outside Fujiyama City, and studies in Fujiyama City.
default.q.n2-2-q74-74.why.0: (a) Incorrect. This choice does not clearly state the required length of stay in Japan (it must be five years or less: 「日本滞在期間が 5 年以内の方」) or whether the applicant is at least 18 years old (「年齢 18 歳以上（高校生可）」).
default.q.n2-2-q74-74.why.1: (b) According to the provided answer key, this is choice 2, but in reality the choice is incorrect because the person has already been in Japan for six years, violating 「日本滞在期間が 5 年以内の方」 and the rule 「上の条件が1つでもあてはまらない人は応募できません」.
default.q.n2-2-q74-74.why.2: (c) Incorrect. The rules require applicants to be foreign nationals (「ふじやま市内在住、または、ふじやま市に通勤･通学している外国人」), so Japanese nationals (日本人) are not eligible to participate.
default.q.n2-2-q74-74.why.3: (d) Correct according to the passage. The eligibility requirements include 「ふじやま市内在住、または、ふじやま市に通勤･通学している外国人」, meaning that foreigners who live outside the city but commute to school in Fujiyama City are eligible, and 「日本滞在期間が 5 年以内の方」, meaning that someone in their third year in Japan meets the requirement of having stayed for less than 5 years. This is the most accurate answer.
default.q.n2-2-q75-75.verdict: The correct answer is 3: Mail a recording of a speech about yourself, approximately 2 minutes long, before October 1.
default.q.n2-2-q75-75.explanation:
**Relevant passage summary:**
The competition's selection process consists of two rounds:
- Round 1 (1次審査, deadline: September 1): Submit an 800-character summary of the speech on two manuscript sheets by post or email.
- Round 2 (2次審査, deadline: October 1): The 20 applicants who pass Round 1 are selected to submit a video recording of themselves giving a speech of about 2 minutes (on a DVD or cassette tape) by post.
- The final selection results will be announced to all applicants by October 10.

**Question and answer choice translations:**
- *Question:* What should someone who has passed the preliminary selection in Round 1 do?
- 1. Summarize the speech in 800 characters and send it by post before October 10.
- 2. Summarize the speech on one manuscript sheet and send it by post before September 1.
- 3. Send a video recording of yourself giving a speech of about 2 minutes by post before October 1.
- 4. Record the entire speech and send it by post before October 10.
default.q.n2-2-q75-75.why.0: (a) Incorrect. Summarizing the speech in 800 characters is a requirement for the first round (「1、審査：発表内容を原稿用紙2枚（800字）以内に要約して」). October 10 is the deadline for notifying all applicants of the final results (「選考結果は、10月10日までに、応募者全員に通知します」).
default.q.n2-2-q75-75.why.1: (b) Incorrect. The content summary is required in round 1 and must be within two manuscript sheets (800 characters), not one sheet (「原稿用紙2枚（800字）以内」). September 1 is the submission deadline for round 1 (「1、審査：9月1日」).
default.q.n2-2-q75-75.why.2: (c) Correct. The evidence in the text states in Round 2: 「☆ 2、審査：応募者の中から、20名の方を選び、本人のスピーチの録画を送っていただきます。2分程度の録画を DVD またはテープで郵送してください。」 This is combined with the Round 2 deadline: 「「応募締切」... 2、審査：10月1日」.
default.q.n2-2-q75-75.why.3: (d) Incorrect. The text requests a video approximately 2 minutes long (「2分程度の録画」), not the entire speech, which lasts up to 7 minutes. In addition, the submission deadline is October 1, not October 10.
default.q.n2-2-q11-11.verdict: The correct answer is 1 (諸): a prefix forming the noun 諸問題 (various problems, numerous problems).
default.q.n2-2-q11-11.explanation:
Sentence meaning: Today’s speech is about various issues in education.
- Kanji note: 諸 means various or numerous, as in 諸問題 (various issues).
- Example: 環境に関する諸問題を解決するために、国際的な協力が不可欠だ。(International cooperation is essential for solving various environmental issues.)
default.q.n2-2-q11-11.why.0: (a) 諸 (しょ): a prefix meaning “many,” “various,” or “the various...”; it commonly combines with nouns to refer to a group of multiple items in formal writing, forming 諸問題 (しょもんだい: various problems).
default.q.n2-2-q11-11.why.1: (b) 複 (ふく - FUKU): means “multiple, complex,” and is used in 複数 (plural) and 複雑 (complex); it does not function as a prefix before 問題 to form *複問題.
default.q.n2-2-q11-11.why.2: (c) 雑 (ざつ): means “mixed” or “miscellaneous,” commonly used in 雑音 (noise) and 雑誌 (magazine), and cannot precede 問題 to mean “problems.”
default.q.n2-2-q11-11.why.3: (d) 類 (るい—type, category): usually functions as a suffix, as in 書類 and 人類; it does not function as a prefix before 問題 to form *類問題.
default.q.n2-2-q12-12.verdict: The correct answer is 3 (街): a suffix forming the noun 商店街 (shopping district, shopping street).
default.q.n2-2-q12-12.explanation:
Meaning: Let’s do some shopping in the shopping district in front of the station before going home.
- Kanji-based vocabulary: 商店街 (shopping district, commercial street).

Distinction: 「せめて」expresses the speaker's subjective wish, whereas「少なくとも」is used for objective estimates of quantity or facts.
