• Example: 次のリーダーはこの人をおいて他にはいない。(There is no one other than this person who could be the next leader.)
default.q.n2-21-q39-39.why.0: (a) Incorrect because 「〜を控えて」(ひかえて) means “with a time or important event approaching”; it does not combine with a negative form to express uniqueness.
default.q.n2-21-q39-39.why.1: (b) Correct because the pattern 「N + をおいて〜ない」 means “there is no one or nothing other than N that can...”.
default.q.n2-21-q39-39.why.2: (c) Incorrect because 「〜を通じて (つうじて)」 means “through...” or “throughout...” and does not combine with the following negative clause to emphasize the only possible choice.
default.q.n2-21-q39-39.why.3: (d) Incorrect because 「〜を越えて/超えて (こえて)」 means “to go beyond” a limit, border, or barrier; it does not form a grammar pattern expressing exclusion.
default.q.n2-21-q40-40.verdict: The correct answer is 2. あきらめようとしない.
default.q.n2-21-q40-40.explanation:
Temporary translation: "Although many people think it is impossible, that person has no intention of giving up their research to invent something new."

default.q.n2-21-q40-40.why.0: (a) Incorrect because 「〜べきだ」(should or must do something) expresses advice or a moral obligation, which does not fit the third person's actual action after the contrastive conjunction 「にもかかわらず」.
default.q.n2-21-q40-40.why.1: (b) Correct because 「V-ようとしない」 (“refuse to do,” “show no intention of doing”) accurately expresses the person's determined refusal to give up despite everyone's doubts.
default.q.n2-21-q40-40.why.2: (c) Incorrect because 「〜はずだ」 (must be; is expected to be) expresses a subjective judgment based on ordinary logic, which conflicts with the contrast between expectation and reality expressed by 「にもかかわらず」.
default.q.n2-21-q40-40.why.3: (d) Incorrect because 「〜かもしれない」 means “may...” or “might...” and expresses uncertain possibility, which does not fit the contrasting clause asserting the actual research action.
default.q.n2-21-q41-41.verdict: The correct answer is 1. 同じようなものだ.
default.q.n2-21-q41-41.explanation:
Provisional translation: "People say that cheap plates break easily, but even expensive plates are essentially the same (they will also break if dropped)."

• Example: 経験者にしたって、この試験に合格するのは難しい。(Even for someone with experience, passing this exam is difficult.)
default.q.n2-21-q41-41.why.0: (a) Correct because 「〜にしたって」 (“even if it is…” / “even in the case of…”) emphasizes that another case produces the same result: expensive plates are in the same situation (they are also easily broken as inexpensive plates).
default.q.n2-21-q41-41.why.1: (b) Incorrect because「〜ではあるまい」(it is probably not...) expresses a negative judgment, contrary to the logic of comparing the fragility of expensive plates.

default.q.n2-21-q41-41.why.3: (d) Incorrect because 「〜ではないはずだ」 means “it certainly is not...” and expresses strong negation, which does not fit the concessive pattern 「にしたって」.
default.q.n2-21-q42-42.verdict: The correct answer is 3. ほかならない.

Tentative translation: "His being the first to visit me when I was ill is nothing other than an expression of his friendship."

• Example: 今回の成功は、皆さんの日頃の努力の結果にほかならない。(This success is nothing other than the result of everyone's daily efforts.)
default.q.n2-21-q42-42.why.0: (a) Incorrect because 「ほかでもない」 is generally used at the beginning of a sentence, as in 「ほかでもないが…」, to introduce important content directly; it does not appear at the end after 「に」 in this structure.
default.q.n2-21-q42-42.why.1: (b) Incorrect because 「ほかではない」 is not a fixed idiom or grammar pattern for expressing an absolute assertion about the nature of something.
default.q.n2-21-q42-42.why.2: (c) Correct because the fixed structure 「N + にほかならない」means “is precisely” or “is nothing other than...,” and is used at the end of a sentence to assert the sole valid reason or source.
default.q.n2-21-q42-42.why.3: (d) Incorrect because 「ほかしかない」 is an incorrect fixed grammar pattern.
default.q.n2-21-q43-43.verdict: The correct answer is 3. しかねる.
default.q.n2-21-q43-43.explanation:
Tentative translation: "I received an explanation from the company about the change in working conditions, but I find it difficult to accept or come to terms with it."

default.q.n2-21-q43-43.why.0: (a) Incorrect because 「V-かねない」means “there is a risk that...” or “may unfortunately result in something bad.” It is not used to express the speaker’s inability to understand or sympathize psychologically.

default.q.n2-21-q43-43.why.3: (d) Incorrect because「〜たがる」expresses the desire or feelings of a third person and is not used with the subject「私は」.
default.q.n2-21-q44-44.verdict: The correct answer is 4. 行くことになっている.

default.q.n2-21-q44-44.why.0: (a) Incorrect because 「〜に決まっている」 (with きまってきる being an OCR error) expresses the speaker’s subjective certainty and does not combine with 「〜の約束では」 to indicate a fixed plan.

default.q.n2-21-q44-44.why.2: (c) Incorrect because 「〜ようとしている」describes an action that is about to occur at the time of speaking (“be about to; be intending to”), not a rule or schedule.

default.q.n2-21-q45-45.verdict: Correct order: 1 → 4 → 3 → 2; the position marked ★ is choice 3 (上がっていく).
default.q.n2-21-q45-45.explanation:
Complete sentence: 今の景気の状態は、給料は勤続年数に応じて上がっていくとは言えない。
Translation: Given the current economic situation, it cannot be said that salaries will continue to rise according to the number of years worked.
default.q.n2-21-q45-45.why.0: (a) 勤続年数: It occupies position 1 and combines with「に応じて」in position 2 to form「勤続年数に応じて」(according to the number of years worked).
default.q.n2-21-q45-45.why.1: (b) とは言えない: It occupies position 4 at the end of the sentence, following the plain-form verb 「上がっていく」 in position 3 to create the pattern 「〜とは言えない」 (“it cannot be said that…” / “it is not necessarily…”).
default.q.n2-21-q45-45.why.2: (c) 上がっていく: In position 3 (★), this verb expresses a gradual upward trend. It follows 「勤続年数に応じて」 and serves as the predicate before 「とは言えない」.
default.q.n2-21-q45-45.why.3: (d) に応じて: It occupies position 2, following the noun 「勤続年数」 in position 1 to form the structure 「〜に応じて」 (depending on, in accordance with).
default.q.n2-21-q46-46.verdict: The correct order is: 4 → 2 → 3 → 1; the starred position (★) is answer choice 3 (事故を).
default.q.n2-21-q46-46.explanation:
Complete sentence: そんなにスピードを出していると事故を起こしかねないよ。
Meaning: If you keep driving that fast, you could cause an accident.
default.q.n2-21-q46-46.why.0: (a) 起こし かねない: It occupies position 4, at the end of the sentence, following the object 「事故を」in position 3 to form V (ます-stem) + 「かねない」(there is a risk that something bad will happen).
default.q.n2-21-q46-46.why.1: (b) 出していると: Occupies position 2, following the object 「スピードを」to form 「スピードを出していると」, expressing a hypothetical condition (“if you keep driving that fast”).
default.q.n2-21-q46-46.why.2: (c) 事故を: It occupies position 3 (the ★ position) and is the object accompanying the verb 「起こしかねない」 in position 4.
default.q.n2-21-q46-46.why.3: (d) スピードを: It occupies position 1, follows the adverb 「そんなに」, and combines with the verb 「出していると」 in position 2 to form 「スピードを出す」 (to speed up, drive fast).
default.q.n2-21-q47-47.verdict: The correct order is: 3 → 2 → 1 → 4; the starred position (★) is answer choice 1 (つらい).
default.q.n2-21-q47-47.explanation:
Complete sentence: クリスマスに一人ですごすなんてつらいものがある。
Meaning: Spending Christmas alone like this is really sad and painful.
default.q.n2-21-q47-47.why.0: (a) つらい: It appears in position 3 (★), is an i-adjective following the exclamatory 「なんて」, and combines with 「ものがある」 in position 4 to express deep emotion.
default.q.n2-21-q47-47.why.1: (b) なんて: It occupies position 2, following the plain form 「すごす」in position 1, and emphasizes the topic or action with a surprised or negative nuance (“the idea of spending...” or “spending... of all things”).
default.q.n2-21-q47-47.why.2: (c) すごす: It occupies position 1 and combines with 「クリスマスに一人で」 to mean spending Christmas alone.
default.q.n2-21-q47-47.why.3: (d) ものがある: It occupies position 4 at the end of the sentence, following the i-adjective「つらい」in position 3 to form 「A-い / A-な / V-る + ものがある」(there is a feeling of being very… / it is truly…).
default.q.n2-21-q48-48.verdict: Correct order: 2 → 4 → 3 → 1; the position marked ★ is choice 3 (フランス語や).
default.q.n2-21-q48-48.explanation:
Complete sentence: 大山さんは英語ばかりかフランス語やドイツ語も話せるらしい。。。
Meaning: Apparently, Oyama can speak not only English but also French and German...
default.q.n2-21-q48-48.why.0: (a) ドイツ語も: It occupies position 4, follows the listing phrase 「フランス語や」 in position 3 to form 「フランス語やドイツ語も」, and combines with the predicate 「話せるらしい」 at the end of the sentence.
default.q.n2-21-q48-48.why.1: (b) 英語: It is in position 1, serving as the noun at the beginning of the phrase that connects with 「ばかりか」 in position 2.
default.q.n2-21-q48-48.why.2: (c) フランス語や: It occupies position 3 (the ★ position), following 「英語ばかりか」 to begin listing additional foreign languages with the coordinating particle 「や」.
default.q.n2-21-q48-48.why.3: (d) ばかりか: It occupies position 2 and follows the noun 「英語」 in position 1, forming the grammar pattern 「N1 + ばかりか + N2 + も」 (not only N1 but also N2...).
default.q.n2-21-q49-49.verdict: The correct order is: 2 → 4 → 3 → 1; the starred position (★) is answer choice 3 (ものの).
default.q.n2-21-q49-49.explanation:
Complete sentence: 高価な電子辞書を買ったものの使い方が分からない。
Meaning: Although I bought an expensive electronic dictionary, I do not know how to use it.
default.q.n2-21-q49-49.why.0: (a) 使い方が: it stands in position 4, follows the contrastive conjunction 「ものの」, and serves as the subject modifying the predicate 「分からない」 at the end of the sentence.
default.q.n2-21-q49-49.why.1: (b) 電子辞書を: It comes in position 1, receives the modification of the preceding na-adjective 「高価な」, and serves as the object of 「買った」 in position 2.
default.q.n2-21-q49-49.why.2: (c) ものの: It occupies position 3 (★), following the past-form verb 「買った」 in position 2 to create the contrastive structure 「V (plain form) + ものの」 (“although ...”).
default.q.n2-21-q49-49.why.3: (d) 買った: It occupies position 2, following the object 「電子辞書を」in position 1 and preceding 「ものの」in position 3, completing the first clause.
default.q.n2-21-q50-50.verdict: The correct answer is 4. 住んでいなくても (even if one does not currently live there).
default.q.n2-21-q50-50.explanation: The context explains tangible assets whose ownership can be clearly identified. We directly possess money in our wallet or a book we bought, while land registered in our name as the owner (持ち主として登録した土地) still belongs to us (自分のものだ) even if we do not currently live there (今住んでいなくても). Therefore, the negative concessive grammar 「V-なくても」(even if...) is the correct choice.
default.q.n2-21-q50-50.why.0: (a) 1. 住んでいれ消 (a misprint for 住んでいれば): “if one is living there” — an incorrect conditional meaning. Ownership does not depend on living there; land registered in one's name remains theirs even if they do not live there.
default.q.n2-21-q50-50.why.1: (b) 2. 住んでいなければ: “If [someone] did not live there” is a purely negative condition leading to a result; it does not create the concessive meaning required by this context.
default.q.n2-21-q50-50.why.2: (c) 3. 住んでいても: "even if one lives there" expresses concession, but it does not emphasize ownership when the person is not physically present on the land.
default.q.n2-21-q50-50.why.3: (d) 4. 住んでいなくても: "even if one does not live there" — the 〜なくても (even if...) structure expresses concession exactly: if the land is registered in one's name, it remains one's property even if one does not currently live there.
default.q.n2-21-q51-51.verdict: The correct answer is 1. 盗んだら (if/when one steals).
default.q.n2-21-q51-51.explanation: The sentence states an obvious principle: 'Even if it is only 1 yen (わずか1円でも), if you steal someone else's belongings, you will become a thief (どろぼうになってしまう)'. The conditional pattern '〜たら' expresses a hypothetical action leading to an inevitable consequence, making it the most appropriate choice.
default.q.n2-21-q51-51.why.0: (a) 1. 盗んだら: “if/once [someone] steals.” The conditional pattern 〜たら expresses a necessary cause-and-effect relationship: stealing even 1 yen immediately makes the person a thief.
default.q.n2-21-q51-51.why.1: (b) 2. 盗んでも: "even if [someone] steals" expresses concessive contrast and cannot be followed by the conclusion that the person becomes a thief.
default.q.n2-21-q51-51.why.2: (c) 3. 盗まなかったら: “if [someone] did not steal” expresses a negative condition, completely contrary to the sentence’s warning about stealing.
default.q.n2-21-q51-51.why.3: (d) 4. 盗んだとしても: "Even if it had been stolen" expresses hypothetical concession, so it cannot be used in a sentence stating an absolute moral or legal rule.
default.q.n2-21-q52-52.verdict: The correct answer is 2. できなくても (even if it cannot be touched).
default.q.n2-21-q52-52.explanation: The preceding passage discusses tangible assets that can be held and touched. This sentence begins with “しかし” (however) to shift to intangible assets such as literary works, music, and inventions. The first clause states that “the actual object cannot be touched by hand” (実物を手で触ることができない), while the second states that some such things “must still be protected as people’s property” (人の所有物として守らなければならないものがある). Therefore, the negative concessive structure 「〜できなくても」(even if one cannot...) is the correct choice.
default.q.n2-21-q52-52.why.0: (a) 1. できても: “even if it were possible” — this contradicts the nature of intellectual property (ideas, works, etc.), which cannot be physically held or touched.
default.q.n2-21-q52-52.why.1: (b) 2. できなくても: “even if one cannot” — the concessive pattern 〜ても expresses a clear contrast: even if the artifact cannot be touched, it must still be protected as human property.
default.q.n2-21-q52-52.why.2: (c) 3. できる場合: “a case in which it is possible” is incorrect both logically after しかし and in relation to the nature of intellectual property.
default.q.n2-21-q52-52.why.3: (d) 4. できない場合: “in the event that it cannot be done” — 〜場合 states a situation or condition and cannot express the concessive contrast required by the following clause.
default.q.n2-21-q53-53.verdict: The correct answer is 3. できないにしても (even if it is impossible).
default.q.n2-21-q53-53.explanation: Intellectual property is not like money or physical goods that can be immediately sold for cash. The N2 pattern 〜にしても (even if / even though) is used to acknowledge a limitation: even though it is impossible to sell it and immediately convert it into cash (“売ってすぐに現金に換えることはできないにしても”), the creator can still claim ownership of it just as they can claim ownership of money or land (“自分のものだと主張することができる”).
default.q.n2-21-q53-53.why.0: (a) 1. できるにしても: “Even if it could be done” — contrary to the special nature of intellectual property, which cannot be immediately converted into cash like ordinary physical assets.
default.q.n2-21-q53-53.why.1: (b) 2. できるとなったら: “if it becomes possible.” The structure 〜となったら is used for a reaction or plan when a situation occurs, so it does not fit the concessive contrast in the passage.
default.q.n2-21-q53-53.why.2: (c) 3. できないにしても: “even if it is impossible.” The N2 grammar pattern 〜にしても (“even if...”) acknowledges a limitation in the preceding clause while maintaining the argument in the following clause (that it is still one’s own asset).
default.q.n2-21-q53-53.why.3: (d) 4. できないとしたら: “if we suppose that it is impossible.” The structure 〜としたら presents a purely hypothetical assumption and does not carry the concessive nuance of acknowledging part of the truth.
default.q.n2-21-q54-54.verdict: The correct answer is 2. する場合は (in the case of doing something, when one wants to do something).
default.q.n2-21-q54-54.explanation: This sentence states a mandatory rule for using someone else’s intellectual property. The following clause is “持ち主の許可を得なければならない” (must obtain the owner’s permission). Since permission must be obtained before use, the expression “利用する場合は” (when/in the case of using it) is used. This is a standard and natural expression in regulations and legal documents.
default.q.n2-21-q54-54.why.0: (a) 1. したら: “if one has done...” indicates an action that has already occurred, whereas permission must be requested before using someone else’s intellectual property.
default.q.n2-21-q54-54.why.1: (b) 2. する場合は: “in the case of/when doing so” — presents the situation or condition under which permission must be obtained before use.
default.q.n2-21-q54-54.why.2: (c) 3. するとしても: “even if [someone] were to do it” - this expresses concession, which does not fit the logic because permission is a mandatory rule in every case of use.
default.q.n2-21-q54-54.why.3: (d) 4. しないとしても: “even if [someone] does not do it”—this completely contradicts the meaning required by the context.
default.q.n2-21-q55-55.verdict: The correct answer is 4. 気にしないで、眠られないことでいいこともあるのだと考えるようにする。
default.q.n2-21-q55-55.explanation:
**Main point:**
The author explains that the harder people try to force themselves to sleep, the more alert their minds and eyes become. Therefore, when it is difficult to sleep, there is no need to worry. They should stay relaxed and think, “It would be good to sleep, but it is also fine if I cannot”; they should even think positively that “there is something good about not being able to sleep.” This unconcerned, positive mindset makes it easier to fall asleep.

**Question and answer choices:**
- **Question:** According to the author, what should one do when one cannot sleep no matter what?
- **Choice 1:** Think that wanting to sleep will make you fall asleep, and wait for drowsiness to come.
- **Choice 2:** Since not being able to sleep is a problem, actively try to fall asleep.
- **Choice 3:** Read a book or write a letter to tire the eyes and become sleepy naturally.
- **Choice 4:** Do not worry about it; try to think that there is something good about not being able to sleep.
default.q.n2-21-q55-55.why.0: (a) Choice 1 is incorrect: The passage says that the more people try to think about sleeping, the more wide-awake they become (「寝よう寝ようと思えば思うほど目が冴えてしまう」). The author does not advise thinking “if I want to sleep, I will be able to sleep” and waiting to feel drowsy.
default.q.n2-21-q55-55.why.1: (b) Choice 2 is incorrect: the author says that there is no need to worry about being unable to sleep and that it is fine even if one cannot sleep (「心配要りません。寝られなくてもいいんです」), which is completely opposite to viewing it as a problem that must be actively solved.
default.q.n2-21-q55-55.why.2: (c) Answer choice 3 is incorrect: the passage does not mention any measures such as reading books or writing letters to tire the eyes.
default.q.n2-21-q55-55.why.3: (d) Choice 4 is correct: The passage says, 「ですから、眠れれ消よし...寝られなくてもよし、ど流活でもいいと思うようにしてください。なかなか眠りにつけないときは、積極的に〈寝られなくてよか流た込と言う風に考えてください。そうしたプラス思考の考え方が、寝ると言うことにつながるのではないかと思っています。」 Do not worry; think that it is fine whether you sleep or not, and actively adopt the positive thought that it is okay if you cannot sleep. This positive way of thinking will help you fall asleep.
default.q.n2-21-q56-56.verdict: The correct answer is choice 1: 日本は決して水が豊かな国だとは言えない (It cannot be said that Japan is a country rich in water resources).
default.q.n2-21-q56-56.explanation:
Main point of the passage:
Although Japan’s rainfall is nearly twice the world average, its per-capita rainfall is only one-fourth of the world average because the country is small and densely populated. In addition, because its rivers are short and steep, rainwater quickly flows into the sea; rainfall is also unevenly distributed by season and region. Therefore, Japan is not actually a country rich in water resources, and people need to value this resource more.

Question:
Which sentence is most appropriate to fill in the blank （ ）?

Answer choices:
1. It cannot be said at all that Japan is a country rich in water resources.
2. It can be said that Japan is a country with abundant rainfall throughout the year.
3. Because Japan has many rivers, it cannot be said to be a country that is not blessed with water.
4. It can be said that Japan is generally a country with little rainfall, although there are regional differences.
default.q.n2-21-q56-56.why.0: (a) Correct. The passage argues that although the total amount of rainfall is large, the amount per person is only one-fourth of the world average («国民一人当たりの雨の量は世界平均の 4 分の 1 程度し[か]ない»), rainwater quickly flows into the sea because of the steep terrain («その雨水はすぐに海へ[流]れ出てしまう»), and rainfall is unevenly distributed by season and region. Therefore, the logical conclusion for the blank is that Japan cannot be called rich in water resources, leading to the appeal that people should value water more («水をもっと大切な資源として使っていくべき»).
default.q.n2-21-q56-56.why.1: (b) Incorrect. The passage states that rain is concentrated in the rainy season and typhoon season, while there is not much rain during other periods («雨は梅雨や台風の季節などに集中して降り、それ以外の時期はあまり降らない»). This contradicts the claim that there is a large amount of rain throughout the year («年間を通して降る雨の量が多い»).
default.q.n2-21-q56-56.why.2: (c) Incorrect. The passage states that the presence of many steep rivers causes rainwater to flow quickly into the sea without being retained («日本には[流]れが急な川が多いので、その雨水はすぐに海へ[流]れ出てしまう»), rather than helping Japan have abundant water resources.
default.q.n2-21-q56-56.why.3: (d) Incorrect. The passage states that Japan receives nearly twice the world average rainfall («日本には世界平均の約 2 倍近い雨が降っています»). Therefore, saying that Japan is generally a country with little rain («全般的に雨の少ない国») is completely contrary to the passage.
default.q.n2-21-q57-57.verdict: The correct answer is 4: To protect the equipment in the television station, the air conditioning must be turned on, so the people have to endure the cold.
default.q.n2-21-q57-57.explanation:
- Main point: The passage discusses the summer workplace practice in Japan of wearing comfortable clothing, such as no ties or jackets, to save air-conditioning power. This is good news for people who get cold easily. However, not everyone benefits from it. For example, at television stations, broadcasting equipment is highly sensitive to heat, so the air conditioning must remain on continuously. No matter how cold people feel, they have to endure it for the sake of the equipment.

- Translation of the question:
  本文の内容と合っているものはどれか。
  (Which of the following agrees with the content of the passage?)

- Translation of the answer choices:
  1. To protect the environment, people working at television stations must reduce the amount of electricity they use.
  2. Because the equipment would break if the air conditioning were too strong, people at television stations have to endure the heat.
  3. To protect the environment, people who are sensitive to cold must adjust the temperature through their clothing.
  4. To protect the equipment, television stations must keep the air conditioning on, and people have to endure the cold.
default.q.n2-21-q57-57.why.0: (a) Incorrect. The passage does not say that television station staff should reduce electricity use for environmental reasons. On the contrary, because the equipment needs cooling, the station is required to keep the air conditioning running continuously.
default.q.n2-21-q57-57.why.1: (b) Incorrect. The passage says that the machines are vulnerable to heat (暑さに弱い), not afraid of strong air conditioning, and that the people there endure the cold (寒くても我慢する), not the heat.
default.q.n2-21-q57-57.why.2: (c) Incorrect. The campaign encouraging people to wear cooler clothing was intended to reduce air-conditioning use during the hot summer, and this was good news for people who dislike the cold—not a demand that people who are sensitive to cold adjust their clothing themselves to protect the environment.
default.q.n2-21-q57-57.why.3: (d) Correct. The passage states: 「放送に使われる機械は暑注に弱いものが多いため、冷房が必要となる。機械のためには、どんなに寒くても人間の方が我慢するしかないのである。」 Many machines used for broadcasting are vulnerable to heat, so air conditioning is necessary. For the sake of the machines, people have no choice but to endure the cold, no matter how cold it is.
default.q.n2-21-q58-58.verdict: The correct answer is choice 2: The man thinks that no matter how many bowls of ramen he eats at that restaurant, it will cost only 400 yen.
default.q.n2-21-q58-58.explanation:
- Main idea: The passage tells of a large man who eats a great deal at a ramen shop. He eats three bowls in a row and starts on a fourth while the shop staff enthusiastically encourage him. Seeing someone eat so much, he wonders how the shop can stay in business or make a profit with things like this («こんなことでよく商売が成り立つな»). When he pays and the total comes to 1,600 yen for four bowls, he is shocked and asks again because he had assumed that eating any number of bowls would cost only 400 yen. After looking at the sign again, he realizes his mistake: it says, “No matter how many bowls you eat, one bowl (is still) 400 yen.”
- Translation of the question: Why did the man think, “How can this business possibly survive like this?”
- Translation of the choices:
  1. Because the shop staff pressured him to eat.
  2. Because he thought that no matter how many bowls of ramen he ate at the shop, it would cost only 400 yen.
  3. Because ramen at that shop cost only 400 yen per bowl.
  4. Because the ramen he ate at the shop was not very good.
default.q.n2-21-q58-58.why.0: (a) Incorrect. The restaurant staff member simply warmly encouraged the customer to eat more («お客注ん、どんどん食べて下さい», «まだまだ遠慮しないで、もっと食べてもいいんですよ»); they did not force the man to eat.
default.q.n2-21-q58-58.why.1: (b) Correct. The man is surprised when he is charged 1,600 yen («え流、四百円じゃないんですか») and realizes that he had misread the sign («何杯食べても一杯四百円のま活がいだった»). Believing that he could eat any number of bowls for a flat fee of 400 yen, he wonders how the restaurant could stay in business when the staff repeatedly encouraged him to eat more («こんなことでよく商売が成り立つな»).
default.q.n2-21-q58-58.why.2: (c) Incorrect. The actual price is 400 yen per bowl («一杯四百円»), but the man questions the restaurant’s business because he mistakenly understands it as “no matter how many bowls you eat, the total is only 400 yen,” not because one bowl costs 400 yen.
default.q.n2-21-q58-58.why.3: (d) Incorrect. The passage does not mention whether the noodles were tasty. The man ate a great deal because he was a big eater (大食漢).
default.q.n2-21-q59-59.verdict: The correct answer is choice 2: 変な人間だと思われてしまうこと (being regarded as a strange person).
default.q.n2-21-q59-59.explanation:
Main idea: The author believes that a writer is truly a “writer” only while directly writing a work. When not writing a manuscript, the author is merely “a strange person who does not know what they are thinking,” and completely accepts that it is fine to be seen that way (それでいい).

Question translation:
What does 「それ」(“that”) refer to?

Answer choices:
1. The fact that it is fine not to write a manuscript.
2. The fact that one is regarded as a strange person.
3. The act of finishing a work and becoming a writer.
4. The act of becoming a person from the past.
default.q.n2-21-q59-59.why.0: (a) Choice 1 is inappropriate because the passage does not say that “it is fine not to write a draft”; it only describes the author’s state while writing and when not writing a draft.
default.q.n2-21-q59-59.why.1: (b) Choice 2 is correct because, according to the preceding sentence: 「原稿を書いていない時の私は、「何を考えているのか分からないへんなやつ」である。実際にそうだと思うし、 それ でいいと思っている。」, the demonstrative pronoun 「それ」 refers to being or being seen as 「何を考えているのか分からないへんなやつ」 (a strange person whose thoughts are impossible to understand).
default.q.n2-21-q59-59.why.2: (c) Choice 3 is unsuitable because the idea of “becoming a writer after completing a work” appears in the following sentence (「作品を書き上げて「作家」になり...」), not in the content referred to by the demonstrative 「それ」 in the preceding sentence.
default.q.n2-21-q59-59.why.3: (d) Choice 4 does not fit because the idea of “becoming a person of the past” (「過去の人」となる) is the concluding statement about the author's fate after completing the work, and is unrelated to 「それ」.
default.q.n2-21-q60-60.verdict: The correct answer is choice 1: Children’s vitality and limitless potential exist only on the premise that there is a beautiful, green Earth.
default.q.n2-21-q60-60.explanation:
Summary: The author emphasizes that children's vitality and limitless potential are possible and meaningful only on the foundation of a beautiful, green Earth.

Question translation: When the author says 「①It is precisely because we have a beautiful, green Earth that...」, what are they referring to?
Answer choices:
1. Children are full of vitality and have unlimited potential.
2. Living things and human beings are abundant on Earth.
3. The abundance of life on Earth is a precious existence.
4. Human life expectancy has reached 100 years.
default.q.n2-21-q60-60.why.0: (a) Correct because the opening sentence states: 「子どもというものは、生命力に満ちているし、可能性は無限です。ただし、①緑豊かな美しい地球あればこその話です。」 The pattern 「～あればこその話」 indicates that the existence of a beautiful, green Earth is the essential condition for children to have abundant vitality and unlimited potential.
default.q.n2-21-q60-60.why.1: (b) Incorrect because the statement that the Earth is filled with living creatures and humans (「地球上はとりあえず生物や人間であふれていますが」) is simply a factual observation in the following sentence, not the content modified by 「～あればこその話」.
default.q.n2-21-q60-60.why.2: (c) Incorrect because the idea that life on Earth is precious when viewed from space (「この地球という星に満ちている生命は貴重な存在です」) is an interpretation in the following sentence, not the part directly linked to condition ①.
default.q.n2-21-q60-60.why.3: (d) Incorrect because the fact that human life expectancy, although extended, is still under 100 years (「寿命が延びたとはいうものの、たかだか百年にも満たない」) is not the result of the condition stated in phrase ①.
default.q.n2-21-q61-61.verdict: The correct answer is choice 3: Children are the ones who suffer harm, and the extent of the damage is greater than for adults.
default.q.n2-21-q61-61.explanation:
Summary: When the environment is damaged by radioactive pollution or toxic chemicals, biological accumulation causes children—the smallest and most immature organisms—to suffer more serious harm than adults and to be harmed first.

Translation of the question: Why is 「② the most tragic victims are ultimately children」?
Translation of the choices:
1. Because adults are treating children's lives carelessly.
2. Because adults can support themselves.
3. Because children are more likely to suffer greater harm than adults.
4. Because children will die along with adults in a nuclear war or from food contamination.
default.q.n2-21-q61-61.why.0: (a) Incorrect because criticizing adults for treating children's lives carelessly (「こんなに粗雑に扱っていいとは思えません」) is the author's opinion, not the direct reason explaining the biological mechanism that makes children suffer the most.
default.q.n2-21-q61-61.why.1: (b) Incorrect because the passage only says 「ぼくたち大人はまだいい」 (“we adults are still better off”) and does not claim that adults can live or survive entirely on their own.
default.q.n2-21-q61-61.why.2: (c) Correct because the passage clearly gives the reason: 「かれらは大人よりもいつでも被害は甚大。生体濃縮反応といって、放射能にも薬害も、水俣病の有機水銀と同じように大人よりダメージが深い。」 (Children always suffer more serious harm than adults; because of biological concentration, radiation, drug-related harm, and the organic mercury in Minamata disease cause them deeper damage than adults).
default.q.n2-21-q61-61.why.3: (d) Incorrect because the author completely rejects the idea of dying together: 「みんないっしょになんか死ねない。いちばん小さいもの、胎児、赤ちゃん、子どもから滅んでいくことになるのです」 (It is impossible for everyone to die together; the smallest beings, such as fetuses, babies, and children, would be destroyed first).
default.q.n2-21-q62-62.verdict: The correct answer is choice 4: We must strive to protect small, vulnerable forms of life so that this Earth can be connected to and passed on to the future.
default.q.n2-21-q62-62.explanation:
Summary: The author’s message is that we must make efforts to protect the smallest and most vulnerable forms of life from pollution and environmental destruction so that we can pass this Earth on to future generations.

Question: What does the author most want to say?
Answer choices:
1. We must make efforts to extend human life, which is short, even further.
2. We must help parents who are grieving the loss of their children.
3. We must prevent nuclear war in order to protect this world.
4. We must make efforts to protect small forms of life so that we can pass the Earth on to the future.
default.q.n2-21-q62-62.why.0: (a) Incorrect because the passage does not call for efforts to extend human life. The author mentions that human life spans less than 100 years only to emphasize the preciousness of young life.
default.q.n2-21-q62-62.why.1: (b) Incorrect because the author mentions the hellish pain parents feel when they see their children suffer in order to emphasize the devastating severity of the environmental disaster, not to convey a message about rescuing the parents.
default.q.n2-21-q62-62.why.2: (c) Incorrect because nuclear war (核戦争) is only one of the examples given by the author, along with food pollution and environmental pollution; it does not encompass the entire argument of the passage.
default.q.n2-21-q62-62.why.3: (d) Correct because the conclusion emphasizes the key message: 「いちばん小さいもの、胎児、赤ちゃん、子どもから滅んでいくことになるのです。そんなことにだけはしたくない。なんとしてでも、この世界を、この地球を、未来へとつなげていかなければならないと思います。」 This connects with the respect for young lives (「初々しい子どもの命」) expressed at the beginning.
default.q.n2-21-q63-63.verdict: The correct answer is 4. Many people tend to use their own language as the standard when faced with changes in language.
default.q.n2-21-q63-63.explanation:
Main point: The author explains that when people witness major changes in language, their anxiety and opposition—thinking 「①「これではいけない」」 (“This will not do”)—arise from a strong normative consciousness. People rarely remain calm about language and tend to assume that the language they acquired and use themselves is the most standard and best form.

Translation of the question: Why does the feeling 「①「これではいけない」」 (“This will not do”) arise?

Translation of the answer choices:
1. Because many people cannot keep up with changes in language and have difficulty coping.
2. Because no one thinks that changes in language will continue indefinitely.
3. Because almost no one thinks that language will remain unchanged as it is now.
4. Because many people tend to use their own language as the standard for judging changes in language.
default.q.n2-21-q63-63.why.0: (a) Choice 1 is incorrect because the passage does not mention people having difficulty keeping up with linguistic change; it analyzes the cause as originating in each person’s normative awareness.
default.q.n2-21-q63-63.why.1: (b) Choice 2 is incorrect because the passage only says that no one would seriously think Japanese will remain in this state forever (「未来永劫このままの状態を保つとは、さすがに誰も考えていないだろうが」); it does not say that no one thinks the changes will continue.
default.q.n2-21-q63-63.why.2: (c) Choice 3 is incorrect because the idea that almost no one thinks language remains unchanged is an obvious premise mentioned by the author, not the reason people become anxious and think, “This is not acceptable.”
default.q.n2-21-q63-63.why.3: (d) Choice 4 is correct because the passage states: 「これは、つまり強い規範意識が働いているということに他ならない。言葉について冷静になれる人は少ない。自分が身につけたものを最善、最上と思ってしまう人が多い。中には例外的に逆の人もいるが、たいていの人は自分の言葉がいちばんよいのだという思いこみをしている」 This means that a strong normative consciousness is at work. Few people can remain calm about language. Many believe that what they have acquired is the best and most correct, and most people assume that their own language is the best.
default.q.n2-21-q64-64.verdict: The given answer is 2; however, based on the passage, the correct answer should be 3 (the young people criticized for distorting the language also feel that the language is being distorted).
default.q.n2-21-q64-64.explanation:
Main point: The final part of the passage highlights an interesting or strange recent phenomenon: Older people have always criticized young people's use of language, but the new and strange point is that young people themselves—the very people accused of corrupting Japanese—also agree that Japanese today is becoming distorted and chaotic.

Note: The answer key provided for the question is 2; however, based on the final sentence, 「若者自身が「日本語が乱れている」と考えているようなのだ」, the answer that correctly matches the passage is 3.

Translation of the question: What is 「② 奇妙なこと」 (the strange thing)?

Translation of the answer choices:
1. Language distortion is found not only among young people but also among older people.
2. The language of the older people who say that young people are distorting the language is itself also being distorted.
3. The young people themselves who are accused of distorting the language also feel that the language is becoming chaotic and distorted.
4. The fact that many older people say that young people's language is distorted has remained unchanged from the past to the present.
default.q.n2-21-q64-64.why.0: (a) Choice 1 is incorrect because the passage does not mention older people also distorting the language.
default.q.n2-21-q64-64.why.1: (b) Choice 2 (according to the provided answer key) does not match the passage because the author never mentions that the language of older people has also become distorted.
default.q.n2-21-q64-64.why.2: (c) Choice 3 is the correct answer according to the passage: The final sentence states, 「しかも、②奇妙なことに最近では、年輩者から日本語を乱しているとして非難されている若者自身が「日本語が乱れている」と考えているようなのだ。」 Moreover, strangely enough, young people themselves—although criticized by older people for corrupting the Japanese language—also seem to think that “the Japanese language is being corrupted.”
default.q.n2-21-q64-64.why.3: (d) Choice 4 is incorrect because older people criticizing young people’s language has long been a normal occurrence, dating back to ancient times (as illustrated by the reference to the Egyptian pyramids), not something “strange that has happened recently.”
default.q.n2-21-q65-65.verdict: The correct answer is 2. When many people assume that their own language is the standard, language change is regarded as distortion or disorder.
default.q.n2-21-q65-65.explanation:
Main point: Living language is constantly changing over time, and no one can stop it. However, because most people have a strong prescriptive attitude and always believe that the language they learned is the most correct or best form, they tend to react negatively when language changes and regard it as “disorder” or “corruption” (乱れ).

Translation of the question: Which of the following is consistent with the passage?

Translation of the answer choices:
1. Many young people feel that they need to pay attention to or correct language corruption.
2. When many people think that their own language is the best, changes in language are regarded as disorder or corruption.
3. Many older people think that the corruption of young people's language in recent years is unavoidable.
4. Because the language of older people was also corrupted when they were young, they think that language corruption is unavoidable.
default.q.n2-21-q65-65.why.0: (a) Choice 1 is incorrect because the article only says that young people think “the Japanese language is becoming distorted”; it does not say that most young people feel they must pay attention to or correct this.
default.q.n2-21-q65-65.why.1: (b) Choice 2 is correct because the passage states: 「あまりに大きな言葉の変化を目の当たりにすると、『これではいけない』という気になる人が多いのも事実なのだ。これは、つまり強い規範意識が働いているということに他ならない。... たいていの人は自分の言葉がいちばんよいのだという思いこみをしている」 (When people witness an extremely large change in language, many indeed feel that “this is not acceptable”... This means that a strong sense of linguistic norms is at work... Most people assume that their own way of speaking is the best.) Thus, natural language change is perceived as distortion or deviation from the norm.
default.q.n2-21-q65-65.why.2: (c) Choice 3 is incorrect because the passage says that many older people always criticize young people's language (「近ごろの若者の言葉づかいはなってない」と思う年寄りは多い); it does not say that they think this is “unavoidable” (しかたがない).
default.q.n2-21-q65-65.why.3: (d) Choice 4 is incorrect because the passage clearly states that elderly people have completely forgotten that they themselves were once spoken to in the same way by adults (「すっかり忘れているのだ」), not that they understand and accept change.
default.q.n2-21-q66-66.verdict: The correct answer is 2. 教育にも色々ある (There are also various types and forms of education).
default.q.n2-21-q66-66.explanation:
- Main idea: The author argues that every person is different; consequently, teachers come in many different types, and education also takes many diverse forms and methods. Each learner must choose the method that suits them best.
- Question translation: What is the most appropriate phrase to fill in [ ① ]?
- Answer choices:
  1. Parents should investigate.
  2. Education also takes many different forms.
  3. The shortcomings of schools are easy to recognize.
  4. Relationships between children are difficult and complex.
default.q.n2-21-q66-66.why.0: (a) Answer choice 1 is incorrect because the passage does not mention parents’ role in researching options; it emphasizes that learners must choose for themselves: 「それは自分で選ぶしかない」.
default.q.n2-21-q66-66.why.1: (b) Answer choice 2 is correct because the passage states: 「人にはいろいろあるということである。だから、教師にもいろいろある。だから [ 教育にも色々ある ] 。どれが自分に彙しているか、それは自分で選ぶしかない。」 The reasoning proceeds from people to teachers to education.
default.q.n2-21-q66-66.why.2: (c) Choice 3 is incorrect because the passage does not discuss whether the shortcomings of schools (学校の欠点) are easy to notice.
default.q.n2-21-q66-66.why.3: (d) Answer choice 4 is incorrect because the passage never mentions relationships among children (子ども同士の関係).
default.q.n2-21-q67-67.verdict: The correct answer is 3. 誰でも毎日一生懸命勉強するような、最も良い方ぐというものはない (There is no single best method that allows everyone to study hard every day).
default.q.n2-21-q67-67.explanation:
- Main point summary: People do not always study continuously; their studying depends on the timing and interests of each individual. The metaphorical expression "そういうことに一般向けの薬なんかない" emphasizes that there is no perfect method that can make everyone study diligently every day.
- Translation of the question: What does the expression 「そういうことに一般向けの薬なんかない」 (There is no one-size-fits-all remedy for such a thing) mean?
- Translation of the answer choices:
  1. Because there are many different kinds of teachers, it is difficult to choose an ideal teacher.
  2. In education, it is impossible to choose a set of teaching materials that works for everyone.
  3. There is no optimal method that can make everyone study diligently every day.
  4. There is no medicine that can instantly make students who do not want to study start enjoying it.
default.q.n2-21-q67-67.why.0: (a) Choice 1 is incorrect because the quoted sentence discusses the learner’s timing and interest in studying, not the difficulty of choosing the ideal teacher.
default.q.n2-21-q67-67.why.1: (b) Answer choice 2 is incorrect because the passage does not mention choosing a textbook or other study materials (テキスト).
default.q.n2-21-q67-67.why.2: (c) Choice 3 is correct. The passage states: 「人間は年がら年中、日がな一日、勉強しているわけではない。勉強することもあるし、しないこともある。...自分が気が向く時もあれば、まったく向かない時もある。そういうことに一般向けの薬なんかない。」 The author uses the metaphor “there is no general-purpose medicine” to mean that no universal method can make everyone study diligently all the time.
default.q.n2-21-q67-67.why.3: (d) Choice 4 is incorrect because “medicine” (薬) is used figuratively here to mean a general educational measure or approach, not literal medicine to be taken.
default.q.n2-21-q68-68.verdict: The correct answer is 4. 学生には色々な人がいるし、勉強したい時期や時間もそれぞれ違うこと (Students are all different, and the periods and times when they want to study also vary from person to person).
default.q.n2-21-q68-68.explanation:
- Main point: Just as teachers come in countless types, students are also highly diverse; each student’s desire to study or play differs at different stages of life. The difficulty and complexity of education lie in the fact that there is no single formula that works for everyone.
- Question: What does “the troublesome aspect of education” refer to?
- Answer choices:
  1. Because education has many different methods, it is impossible to choose one single method that is suitable.
  2. If all teachers are permissive, it is impossible to know when students will finally decide to study.
  3. Students’ moods change too quickly between wanting to play and wanting to study.
  4. Students are diverse, and the timing and amount of time each person wants to study are also different.
default.q.n2-21-q68-68.why.0: (a) Choice 1 is incorrect because the preceding sentence does not discuss uncertainty between different educational methods; it emphasizes differences between students and the timing of learning.
default.q.n2-21-q68-68.why.1: (b) Choice 2 is incorrect because the question “When will students study if the teacher leaves them on their own?” is merely a counterargument presented in paragraph 2, not an explanation of the problems with education at the end of the article.
default.q.n2-21-q68-68.why.2: (c) Choice 3 is incorrect because the author discusses major stages in life—wanting to play at one point and study at another—not temporary, erratic changes in mood.
default.q.n2-21-q68-68.why.3: (d) Choice 4 is correct because the passage states: 「教師にも色々な人がいるということは、学生にもいろいろいるということである。今学びたいと思っている人も、遊びたいと思っている人もある。...今勉強している人が、一生勉強するとは限らない。教育の面倒くさいところは、そこにある。一般論なんか、ありはしない。」 This demonstrates that the difficulty lies in the differences among students and in the fact that each person wants to study at a different time.
default.q.n2-21-q69-69.verdict: The correct answer is choice 2: The person seeking advice understands 「いただきます」 as an expression of gratitude for something given by or received from another person.
default.q.n2-21-q69-69.explanation:
**Main point:**
The person seeking advice is upset that their child has to say「いただきます」at school despite having paid the full meal fee. They misunderstand the expression as meaning "receiving food from the school" (being given food by the school for free), so they think only families who have not paid have to say it.

**Question and answer choices:**
- *Question:* How does the person seeking advice understand the meaning of「いただきます」?
- *1.* An expression used to greet others before eating a school lunch.
- *2.* An expression of gratitude for something received from another person.
- *3.* An expression used when one has not paid for a school lunch.
- *4.* An expression of gratitude toward the person who cooked the food. 相談
default.q.n2-21-q69-69.why.0: (a) Incorrect. The person seeking advice does not regard this as an ordinary greeting before a meal. They are angry because they believe they are not receiving free food from the school:「『いただきます』だなんて、食べ物を学校からもらっているわけではありません」.
default.q.n2-21-q69-69.why.1: (b) Correct. The person seeking advice understands this expression as something used when receiving food or objects from someone free of charge, so they find it unreasonable when they have paid for their meal:「『いただきます』だなんて、食べ物を学校からもらっているわけではありません。活ゃんと給食費を払っているのに、なぜそんなことを言わ注れなければならないのか、私にわかりません」. Responder A confirms this interpretation:「確かに、人から何かをもらったときに『ありがとうございます。いただきます。』というふうにも言いますが、それとは違います」.
default.q.n2-21-q69-69.why.2: (c) Incorrect. The person seeking advice argues that only children from families who do not pay for school meals should be made to say it (「給食費を払っていない家庭があるそうですから、そういうう活の子にだけ『いただきます』と言わせれ消いいんじゃないか」); they do not understand the word as a greeting used when payment has not been made.
default.q.n2-21-q69-69.why.3: (d) Incorrect. The interpretation “being grateful to the person who cooked or prepared the food” is the view expressed by respondent B (「料理を作ってくれた人や食べ物を用意してくれた人への感謝の気持ち」), not the interpretation of the person seeking advice.
default.q.n2-21-q70-70.verdict: The correct answer is choice 3: Both A and B believe that the person seeking advice does not correctly understand the meaning of 「いただきます」 when it is used before a meal.
default.q.n2-21-q70-70.explanation:
**Main point:**
Both A and B point out that the person seeking advice has not correctly understood the true nature and meaning of saying「いただきます」before a meal (the questioner mistakenly thinks that this expression is connected with paying for food or receiving food for free). A explains that it expresses gratitude for the lives of plants and animals; B explains that it is a greeting and an expression of gratitude for the food and the people who prepared it.

**Translation of the question and choices:**
- *Question:* Which statement is correct about A and B's responses to the questioner's concern?
- *1.* A is surprised that the person seeking advice does not understand the meaning of「いただきます」, while B...
- *2.* A says that the school should be complained to for forcing students to say「いただきます」, while B...
- *3.* Both A and B [believe that] the person seeking advice has not correctly understood the meaning of the expression「いただきます」used before a meal.
- *4.* Both A and B [believe that] children should be made to say the greeting「いただきます」before meals both at home and at school.
default.q.n2-21-q70-70.why.0: (a) Incorrect. This choice does not accurately and completely express the core similarity in A and B's answers: both misunderstand the meaning intended by the adviser.
default.q.n2-21-q70-70.why.1: (b) Incorrect. A does not say that people should complain to the school; rather, A says that complaining would be wrong unless the school absolutely forced everyone to say 「いただきます」:「学校が強制的に『いただきます』と言わなければ絶対にいけないと言わない限り、抗議するほうが間違っていると思います」.
default.q.n2-21-q70-70.why.2: (c) Correct. Both A and B explain the true meaning of 「いただきます」 and show that the person seeking advice has misunderstood it. A expresses surprise and advises the person to understand its meaning: 「『いただきます』の意味をご存じないとは驚きました」「まずは、あなたが『いただきます』の本当の意味を理解すべきでしょう」. B explains that it originally expresses gratitude for receiving food and gratitude toward the person who prepared it, and regards it as a greeting: 「本来は食べ物をいただける感謝を表した表現だと思いますが…あなたも挨拶だと思えば腹も立たないのではないでしょうか」.
default.q.n2-21-q70-70.why.3: (d) Incorrect. B says that it is fine if the person asking does not say anything at home when eating (「あなたの家では食べるときに何も言わないのですね。それはそれで構わないと思いますが」), and does not require children to say it both at home and at school.
default.q.n2-21-q71-71.verdict: The correct answer is 3: The things recorded in the notebook will become reference material to assist with writing.
default.q.n2-21-q71-71.explanation:
- Main idea: The author always carries a notebook to quickly write down any good ideas or interesting episodes they come across. These notes are a “treasure” because they provide useful material for future writing, whether or not they can be used immediately.

- Question translation: The phrase “is a treasure” appears. In what sense is it a treasure?
- Answer choices:
  1. Whenever they carry a notebook, a good idea suddenly occurs to them.
  2. Even when going out, writing helps make up for a lack of talent.
  3. Things written in the notebook will be useful when writing.
  4. Carrying a notebook helps them remain calm.
default.q.n2-21-q71-71.why.0: (a) Incorrect. The passage says that the writer writes something down when an idea suddenly occurs to them (何かふっと思いついたと時... 記した), not that carrying a notebook helps them come up with good ideas.
default.q.n2-21-q71-71.why.1: (b) Incorrect. The passage only says that the author records ideas and snippets of conversations heard while out, not that the author writes essays while out to compensate for a lack of talent.
default.q.n2-21-q71-71.why.2: (c) Correct. The author writes: 「何かふっと思いついたと時、面白い話を見聞きした時、私は必ずそのノートに記した。すぐに使えても使えなくても、ノートの走り書きは宝である」 (Whenever something suddenly occurred to me or I heard or saw an interesting story, I always wrote it in that notebook. Whether I could use it immediately or not, the rough notes in the notebook were treasures.) This shows that the notes served as material useful for writing.
default.q.n2-21-q71-71.why.3: (d) Incorrect. Forgetting the notebook made the author anxious and panicked (怖くて落活着かない); this was merely a psychological reaction to fearing a lack of work materials, not the reason the notes in the notebook were considered a “treasure.”
default.q.n2-21-q72-72.verdict: The correct answer is 4: People begin to tend to choose easygoing writing styles or summarize things superficially.
default.q.n2-21-q72-72.explanation:
- **Main idea**: The author uses the phrase "showing signs of fatigue" to describe the slackening of the tension and seriousness previously devoted to work. Specifically, when facing difficulties or writer's block, the author has recently begun choosing an easygoing writing style or wrapping things up vaguely and superficially.

- Question translation: What does the phrase "beginning to show signs of fatigue or slackening" mean?
- Answer choices:
  1. The sense of continuing to write as an obligation has weakened.
  2. The number of times the author forgets a notebook or memo pad when going out has increased.
  3. The author has become distressed because they cannot manage to write.
  4. The author has begun thinking about using an easygoing writing style or wrapping things up vaguely and superficially.
default.q.n2-21-q72-72.why.0: (a) Incorrect. The passage does not say that the author reduced the number of times they wrote as an obligation; it says that their attitude while writing had begun to become careless and unfocused.
default.q.n2-21-q72-72.why.1: (b) Incorrect. Forgetting the notebook is merely an anecdote mentioned in the previous paragraph; it is not an indication of feeling worn out or discouraged recently.
default.q.n2-21-q72-72.why.2: (c) Incorrect. The author writes: 「仕事をする時は今でも... 同じように苦しむ」(When working, I still struggle in the same way even now). The difficulty of writing has continued as before; it did not just begin recently.
default.q.n2-21-q72-72.why.3: (d) Correct. The author explains that feeling "exhausted" is actually the sensation of the tense string slackening, even slightly (緊張の糸がほんの少しゆるんだ感じ), and provides a concrete example: 「でも最近は、苦しい時に思わず安易な書き方を選んだり、小さくまとめてしまったりすることがあるのである。... 気を抜いて鉛筆を走らせてしまうこともあるのだ」 (But recently, when struggling, I sometimes find myself choosing an easy way of writing or wrapping things up too briefly... Sometimes I let my guard down and simply run my pencil across the page).
default.q.n2-21-q73-73.verdict: The correct answer is 1: After many years in the profession, the author felt ashamed of having learned to work carelessly and neglectfully when writing.
default.q.n2-21-q73-73.explanation:
- Main point: After many years of working as a writer, the author realized that, once the work became familiar, a careless attitude began to emerge. The author started writing half-heartedly and carelessly (気を抜く / 安易な書き方) just to get by. The author felt deeply ashamed and blamed themself for this negative change, drawing the lesson that becoming accustomed to one’s work is precisely when one must be most careful.

- Question translation: What does the author want to convey in this passage?
- Answer choices:
  1. After many years, the author felt ashamed of having learned to work carelessly and superficially.
  2. The author is still suffering because their writing ability has never improved.
  3. The author feels it is dangerous to be unable to write pieces they are satisfied with.
  4. The author believes that becoming accustomed to the work enabled them to absorb many different writing styles.
default.q.n2-21-q73-73.why.0: (a) Correct. The author begins by saying that they had already been working in the profession for several years (丸数年), then expresses shame and anger at themselves for beginning to write carelessly and half-heartedly: 「こんなことを言うのは実に恥ずかしいことなのだが、正直に言って、気を抜いて鉛筆を走らせてしまうこともあるのだ」「明らかに気を抜いて書いたと分かるような文章を書いて出してしまった時の憤りは、どうしようもなく私を苦しませる」 (It is truly embarrassing to say this, but honestly, there are times when I let my pencil move without making an effort. The anger I feel when I submit writing that clearly shows I was careless torments me unbearably.)
default.q.n2-21-q73-73.why.1: (b) Incorrect. The author fully understands their lack of talent and poor writing ability (才能の乏しさや下手さは百も承知である). What causes shame and self-reproach now is a careless work attitude, not a lack of improvement in talent.
default.q.n2-21-q73-73.why.2: (c) Incorrect. The statement "the time when one becomes accustomed to the work is the most dangerous" (馴れた頃が一番危険) warns against carelessness, but the main focus of the passage is the author's shame and self-reproach for writing carelessly and losing the seriousness they had at the beginning.
default.q.n2-21-q73-73.why.3: (d) Incorrect. The author considers becoming accustomed to the work (馴れ) something frightening (恐ろしいもの) because it leads to overconfidence and carelessness, not something to be proud of as evidence of mastering various writing styles.
default.q.n2-21-q74-74.verdict: The correct answer is choice 2: Hotel B.
default.q.n2-21-q74-74.explanation:
- Main point: Mr. Tanaka is looking for a hotel for one night this Saturday (6/26) near Moriyama Station. The requirements are: (1) close to Moriyama Station (because he will arrive at the station at 19:30), (2) breakfast included (朝食付き), and (3) as inexpensive as possible (できるだけ安い).
- Question translation: "Looking only at List 1, which choice best meets Mr. Tanaka's requirements?"
- Answer choices:
  1. Hotel A
  2. Hotel B
  3. Hotel C
  4. Hotel D
default.q.n2-21-q74-74.why.0: (a) Choice 1 (A) is incorrect because Hotel A is not as favorable in price or does not meet all the criteria of being near the station and offering breakfast as well as Hotel B.
default.q.n2-21-q74-74.why.1: (b) Choice 2 (B) is correct. According to the passage, Tanaka wants a hotel near the station and as inexpensive as possible, "駅から近くて、できるだけ安い", with breakfast included, "朝ご飯がついている", when he arrives at Moriyama Station on "今週の土曜日（6月26日）". In List 1, Hotel B fully meets these requirements: it is near Moriyama Station, includes breakfast, and is the cheapest of the hotels that qualify.
default.q.n2-21-q74-74.why.2: (c) Choice 3 (C) is incorrect because the price is higher or it does not satisfy the requirements concerning proximity to Moriyama Station or breakfast.
default.q.n2-21-q74-74.why.3: (d) Choice 4 (D) is incorrect because it is either more expensive or does not satisfy all of Mr. Tanaka’s priority conditions at the same time.
default.q.n2-21-q75-75.verdict: The correct answer is choice 4: Hotel Green City's discounted nighttime check-in package.
default.q.n2-21-q75-75.explanation:
- Main point: Mr. Tanaka plans to arrive at Moriyama Station at around 7:30 p.m. this Saturday (June 26). He wants a hotel near the station, with breakfast, at the lowest possible price. When consulting List 2 (special discount plans), the conditions for each plan must also be checked.
- Question: "If List 2 is also taken into account, which choice meets Mr. Tanaka's requirements?"
- Choices:
  1. Terminal Hotel Moriyama's "【Date-Limited】Budget Plan"
  2. Central Hotel Midorino's "Advance Reservation Plan: 7 Days Ahead"
  3. Hotel Murakami's "Cheapest! Room-Only Plan (No Meals)"
  4. Hotel Green City's "Discounted Late-Night Check-in Plan"
default.q.n2-21-q75-75.why.0: (a) Choice 1 is incorrect because the “お日にち限定” package does not apply to Saturday, June 26, or does not include breakfast.
default.q.n2-21-q75-75.why.1: (b) Choice 2 is incorrect because Mr. Tanaka booked the room for "今週の土曜日" (this Saturday), which does not meet the requirement of booking at least 7 days in advance ("7日前"). In addition, the hotel is at Midorino Station, not Moriyama Station.
default.q.n2-21-q75-75.why.2: (c) Choice 3 is incorrect because a 「素泊まりプラン」 is a room-only plan without meals, which conflicts with Mr. Tanaka's condition 「朝ご飯がついていることを希望しています」 (“I would like breakfast to be included”).
default.q.n2-21-q75-75.why.3: (d) Choice 4 is correct. The text says that Mr. Tanaka is 「夜7時半ごろに森山駅に着く予定」 (scheduled to arrive at Moriyama Station at around 7:30 p.m.), which fits the hours for the 「ナイトチェックイン」 package. The package also includes breakfast (「朝ご飯がついている」) and is the cheapest option (「できるだけ安い」) when List 2 is considered.
default.q.n2-21-q11-11.verdict: The correct answer is 4 (っぱなし / つけっぱなし—in the question, it appears as a character error, 流ぱなし).
default.q.n2-21-q11-11.explanation:
Sentence meaning: "Apparently, I fell asleep last night with the lights left on."
• Grammar: V-ます (remove ます) + っぱなし (放し): Describes an action or state that continues without carrying out the necessary follow-up action or restoring it to its original state, often conveying criticism, carelessness, or absent-mindedness.
• Example: テレビをつけっぱなしで寝てしまった。(I fell asleep with the TV left on.)
default.q.n2-21-q11-11.why.0: (a) 「ったい」 does not combine with the verb stem 「つけ」 to form a meaningful Japanese grammar pattern or compound word.
default.q.n2-21-q11-11.why.1: (b) 「ってる」, the colloquial contraction of 「ている」, must follow a verb in the te-form, as in つけてる. It cannot be attached directly to the verb stem 「つけ」.
default.q.n2-21-q11-11.why.2: (c) 「っとおし」, usually used as とおし / 通し, appears in expressions such as 「立ち通し」 (“standing the whole time”) or with words indicating duration. However, for leaving an electrical device switched on continuously, the correct pattern is 「っぱなし」.
default.q.n2-21-q11-11.why.3: (d) 「っぱなし」 (shown in the question as 流ぱなし) attaches to the verb stem in the ます-form (つけっぱなし) and indicates leaving the lights on all night without turning them off.
default.q.n2-21-q12-12.verdict: The correct answer is 1 (合い – 込み合う / 混み合う).
default.q.n2-21-q12-12.explanation:
Meaning: "During the year-end and New Year holidays, trains will be terribly crowded everywhere."
• Kanji note: 混み合う means to be crowded or packed with people.
• Distinction: 「混み合う / 込み合う」 means crowded or packed with people, whereas 「込み入る」 means complicated or intricate in content.
• Example: 連休中の観光地はどこも大変混み合っている。(Tourist spots everywhere are extremely crowded during the long holiday.)
default.q.n2-21-q12-12.why.0: (a) 「合い」, a suffix derived from 合う, combines with the verb stem 「込み」 (混み) to form the compound verb 「込み合う / 混み合う」, meaning “to be crowded, packed, or congested.”
default.q.n2-21-q12-12.why.1: (b) 「入り」 (from the verb 入る) combines to form 「込み入る」, meaning “complicated” or “intricate,” as in 込み入った事情. It is not used to describe crowded trains or vehicles.
default.q.n2-21-q12-12.why.2: (c) 「集まり」 does not combine with 「込み」 to form a natural compound verb in Japanese.
default.q.n2-21-q12-12.why.3: (d) 「張り」 does not combine with 「込み」 to form a word suitable for describing crowded trains or other transportation.
default.q.n2-21-q13-13.verdict: The correct answer is 2 (好 - 好景気).
default.q.n2-21-q13-13.explanation:
Meaning: "The prosperous economic conditions of six months ago seem like a joke; the economy is very sluggish now."
• Kanji-based terms: 好景気 (economic prosperity, boom) is the opposite of 不景気 (economic stagnation, slump).
• Example: 好景気のおかげで、ボーナスが大幅に増えた。(Thanks to the economic boom, my bonus increased substantially.)
default.q.n2-21-q13-13.why.0: (a) 「良」 (リョウ) is commonly used in words such as 「良好」 (りょうこう) and 「良質」 (りょうしつ), but it does not combine with 景気 to form 良景気.
default.q.n2-21-q13-13.why.1: (b) 「好」(KŌ) is a prefix meaning “good, favorable.” Combined with 「景気」, it forms the noun 「好景気」(こうけいき - a prosperous, booming economy).
default.q.n2-21-q13-13.why.2: (c) 「高」commonly combines with nouns indicating levels or prices, such as 「高価格」, 「高品質」, and 「高収入」; it does not form 「高景気」.
default.q.n2-21-q13-13.why.3: (d) 「明」 (Minh) is not used as a prefix before 「景気」 to express favorable economic conditions.
default.q.n2-21-q14-14.verdict: The correct answer is 4 (ぶ流 / ぶっ - ぶったたく).
default.q.n2-21-q14-14.explanation:
Meaning: “I heard the sound of a stick striking something violently.”
• Sound-symbolic prefix: ぶっ- (derived from 打ち（うち）) is used colloquially before verbs to intensify the force, violence, or decisiveness of an action: ぶっ叩く (to beat violently, strike repeatedly), ぶっ壊す (to smash to pieces), ぶっ飛ばす (to send flying, speed off).
• Example: 彼は怒りに任せて机をぶったたいた。(He furiously slammed the desk.)
default.q.n2-21-q14-14.why.0: (a) 「ぼ流」(ぼっ) is not a prefix that combines with「たたく」to emphasize the action of knocking or hitting.
default.q.n2-21-q14-14.why.1: (b) 「消流」 (消っ) cannot be combined with 「たたく」 to form a meaningful word.
default.q.n2-21-q14-14.why.2: (c) 「か流」 (かっ) is commonly found in 「かっ飛ばす」and 「かっさらう」, but it does not combine to form 「かったたく」.
default.q.n2-21-q14-14.why.3: (d) 「ぶ流」 (the prefix ぶっ- / 打っ-) is attached before a verb to intensify the force or violence of an action; 「ぶったたく」 (ぶっ叩く) means “to hit hard, beat repeatedly.”
default.q.n2-21-q15-15.verdict: The correct answer is 2 (過ぎた - 歌い過ぎた).
default.q.n2-21-q15-15.explanation:
Meaning: “Because I sang too much at karaoke yesterday, my throat hurts today.”
• Grammar: V-ます stem + 過ぎる (doing something excessively, resulting in a bad outcome): 食べ過ぎる (eat too much), 飲み過ぎる (drink too much), 歌い過ぎる (sing too much).
• Example: 昨晩はお酒を飲み過ぎて、二日酔いになった。(I drank too much last night and got a hangover.)
default.q.n2-21-q15-15.why.0: (a) 「過ごした」 (過ごす) is a transitive verb meaning to spend or pass time. It can also follow a verb in the ます-stem to mean absent-mindedly missing something, as in 見過ごす (overlook) and 寝過ごす (oversleep and miss one's stop). It is not used to mean doing something excessively and causing a sore throat.
default.q.n2-21-q15-15.why.1: (b) 「過ぎた」 (過ぎる) is attached to the verb stem in the ます-form (歌い + 過ぎた → 歌い過ぎた) and means “to sing too much, beyond the normal limit.”
default.q.n2-21-q15-15.why.2: (c) 「越した」 (越す) is used to mean surpassing or crossing a point in time or place, or in the pattern 「～に越したことはない」. It does not combine to form 「歌い越す」.
default.q.n2-21-q15-15.why.3: (d) 「回った」 (回る) added after a verb stem expresses going around doing something, as in 走り回る (run around), which does not fit this context.
default.q.n2-21-q16-16.explanation:
- Translation: When you see how enthusiastically she practices, you will surely want to cheer her on.
- Kanji: 熱心: enthusiastic, diligent; 練習: practice; 応援: support, cheer on.
- Example: 彼はいつも熱心に日本語を勉強している。(He always studies Japanese very diligently.)
default.q.n2-21-q16-16.why.0: (a) 熱心 (ねっしん): a na-adjective meaning “enthusiastic, devoted, earnest.” The phrase 「熱心に練習する」 (practice diligently / enthusiastically) is very natural and fits the context of encouragement upon seeing that attitude.
default.q.n2-21-q16-16.why.1: (b) 強引 (ごういん): meaning “forceful, coercive, or high-handed,” with a negative nuance, so it does not fit this positive context.
default.q.n2-21-q16-16.why.2: (c) 積極 (せっきょく): a noun; to modify a verb, the adverbial form 積極的に is required. Moreover, 熱心に is more appropriate for describing diligent practice.
default.q.n2-21-q16-16.why.3: (d) 努力 (どりょく: effort) is a noun and a Group 3 verb when used as 努力する; it cannot directly combine with the particle に to modify another verb (*努力に練習する is grammatically incorrect).
default.q.n2-21-q17-17.explanation:
- Meaning: The TV broke, so it no longer produces any sound.
- Sino-Japanese roots: 故障 (breakdown, malfunction).
- Example: パソコンが故障したので、修理に出した。(My computer broke down, so I had it repaired.)
default.q.n2-21-q17-17.why.0: (a) 従魔 (or 邪魔—じゃま) means “obstruction” or “a nuisance”; it is not used for a malfunction in electronic devices or household appliances.
default.q.n2-21-q17-17.why.1: (b) 障害 (しょうがい: obstacle, disability, malfunction) is commonly used for obstacles, physical disabilities, or major network/system failures (システム障害). It is not used for a household television that has broken down.
default.q.n2-21-q17-17.why.2: (c) 故障 (こしょう): malfunction, breakdown, used for machines and household electronic devices (テレビが故障する). It fits the following clause, “does not produce any sound,” perfectly.
default.q.n2-21-q17-17.why.3: (d) 摩擦 (まさつ - friction): means “frictional force” in physics or “conflict/friction” in relationships, and is not used for mechanical malfunctions.
default.q.n2-21-q18-18.explanation:
- Translation: I have to write a report on the theme “Work and Time.”
- Katakana loanwords: テーマ (from the German “Thema”: theme, topic), レポート (report: report, paper).
- Example: 今度の研究のテーマは何にしようか。(What should we choose as the theme for this research?)
default.q.n2-21-q18-18.why.0: (a) ノート (notebook): notebook, notes. It does not combine with the name of a topic to indicate the content of a report in the structure “～という...”.
default.q.n2-21-q18-18.why.1: (b) スーツ means “a suit” or “business attire” and is completely unrelated to the context of writing an essay or report.
default.q.n2-21-q18-18.why.2: (c) データ (data): data or figures. “Work and time” is the name of a topic, not data.
default.q.n2-21-q18-18.why.3: (d) テーマ (theme): A topic or research/writing subject. 「～」というテーマについてレポートを書く (write a report about the topic “～”) is the most accurate and natural expression.
default.q.n2-21-q19-19.verdict: The correct answer is 3 (た流ぷり / たっぷり).
default.q.n2-21-q19-19.explanation:
- Meaning: There is still plenty of time, so you do not need to rush or panic like that.
- Mimetic word/verb: たっぷり (plentifully, abundantly, more than enough), 慌てる (あわてる - hurry, panic).
- Example: 週末はたっぷり睡眠をとった。(I got plenty of sleep over the weekend.)
default.q.n2-21-q19-19.why.0: (a) ぎっしり: means 'packed tightly, crammed full, filled to capacity,' referring to space or schedules, as in 予定がぎっしり. It is not used to say that plenty of time remains with「時間がある」.
default.q.n2-21-q19-19.why.1: (b) 注流ぱり (さっぱり): Means “refreshed” or “relieved,” or “not at all” when used with a negative; it is not used to indicate an amount of time.
default.q.n2-21-q19-19.why.2: (c) た流ぷり (たっぷり): means “ample, abundant, plenty.” The collocation「時間はたっぷりある」(there is plenty of time) is accurate and fits the following clause, “there is no need to hurry.”
default.q.n2-21-q19-19.why.3: (d) ゆ流くり (ゆっくり): “slowly, leisurely,” describing how an action is performed, as in ゆっくり休む. It is not used directly with 「時間がある」as a quantity expression meaning that plenty of time remains.
default.q.n2-21-q20-20.explanation:
- Translation: When the sun set, the temperature dropped considerably, so it felt cold.
- Kanji: 気温 (air temperature), 気候 (climate), 気圧 (air pressure).
- Example: 冬になると、朝晩の気温がぐっと下がる。(In winter, temperatures drop sharply in the morning and evening.)
default.q.n2-21-q20-20.why.0: (a) 気象 refers to weather phenomena in general or meteorology; it does not combine with the verb 下がる to describe the weather becoming cold.
default.q.n2-21-q20-20.why.1: (b) 気温 (きおん): air temperature, outdoor temperature. The phrase 「気温が下がる」 (the temperature drops) fits perfectly with the sun setting and feeling cold (寒い).
default.q.n2-21-q20-20.why.2: (c) 気候 (きこう - climate): the long-term or seasonal weather conditions of a region, such as a tropical or temperate climate. It is not used for an immediate change in temperature during a single day.
default.q.n2-21-q20-20.why.3: (d) 気圧 (きあつ): atmospheric pressure; although it can rise or fall, it does not directly cause the sensation of “cold” (寒い) when the sun sets.
default.q.n2-21-q21-21.explanation:
- Meaning: Upon entering the 21st century, computer technology advanced rapidly / made remarkable progress.
- Kanji readings: 世紀 (century), 技術 (technology), 進歩 (progress), 急速 (rapid).
- Example: インターネットの普及により、社会は急速に変化している。(Society is changing rapidly due to the spread of the Internet.)
default.q.n2-21-q21-21.why.0: (a) 特急 (とっきゅう) is a noun referring to a limited express train (特急電車), so it cannot be used adverbially with 「に進歩した」.
default.q.n2-21-q21-21.why.1: (b) 高速 (こうそく): refers to a high speed of movement or operation (such as 高速道路 or 高速で処理する), and does not combine as “高速に進歩する” to describe technological progress.
default.q.n2-21-q21-21.why.2: (c) 早速 (さっそく — on-reading): an adverb meaning “immediately, without delay” when starting something (早速始める). It is not used to describe the speed of development or progress over time.
default.q.n2-21-q21-21.why.3: (d) 急速 (きゅうそく): a na-adjective meaning “rapid” or “dramatic” in terms of change or progress. The collocation '急速に進歩する/発展する' (to progress/develop rapidly) is highly standard and natural.
default.q.n2-21-q22-22.explanation:
- Meaning: If we do not speed up the work soon, we will not finish within the allotted time.
- Kanji readings: 作業 (SA-GYŌ - work, task), 時間内 (JI-KAN-NAI - within the time limit).
- Example: 計画通りに作業を進めてください。(Please proceed with the work according to the plan.)
default.q.n2-21-q22-22.why.0: (a) 動作 (どうさ): movement or motion of the body, or the operation of machinery or equipment. It does not combine with 「を進める」 in the context of completing work within the allotted time.
default.q.n2-21-q22-22.why.1: (b) 作業 (さぎょう): a specific task or operation being carried out. The collocation 作業を進める (proceed with the work; move the work forward) is accurate in the context of finishing within the allotted time (時間内に終わる).
default.q.n2-21-q22-22.why.2: (c) 産業 (さんぎょう - industry): refers to a field of production or industry in general, such as 自動車産業 or 観光産業; it is not used for a specific individual’s short-term work.
default.q.n2-21-q22-22.why.3: (d) 職業 (しょくぎょう - occupation): Refers to a profession, such as doctor or engineer; it is a noun identifying an occupation and does not combine with を進める.
default.q.n2-21-q23-23.verdict: The correct answer is 2 (たまに) because it is synonymous with 「時々」, meaning occasionally or sometimes.
default.q.n2-21-q23-23.explanation:
- Sentence meaning: “The neighbor's cat occasionally comes over to play in my garden.”
- Kanji and vocabulary:
  + 時々 (occasionally, sometimes = たまに).
  + 隣 (next door, neighbor; 隣の家: the neighbor's house).
  + 庭 (yard, garden).
- Example: 週末はたまに（＝時々）映画を見に行きます。(I sometimes go to see a movie on weekends.)
default.q.n2-21-q23-23.why.0: (a) 「何度も」means “many times” and indicates repeated frequency; it is not synonymous with「時々」(sometimes).
default.q.n2-21-q23-23.why.1: (b) 「たまに」(occasionally, sometimes) is synonymous with 「時々」 and describes something that occurs infrequently.
default.q.n2-21-q23-23.why.2: (c) 「いつも」means “always” or “all the time,” indicating continuous frequency and contrasting with “sometimes.”
default.q.n2-21-q23-23.why.3: (d) 「毎日」(every day, daily) indicates a regular daily frequency, so it does not fit.
default.q.n2-21-q24-24.verdict: The correct answer is 3 (集めて) because the loanword 「コレクションする」 (to collect) is synonymous with the verb 「集める」.
default.q.n2-21-q24-24.explanation:
- Sentence translation: "These are the items he has collected."
- Vocabulary and kanji:
  + コレクション (collection): collecting, collection (コレクションする = 集める).
  + 集める (atsumeru): to gather, collect.
  + 並べる (naraberu): to arrange, display.
- Example: 昔から切手を集める（＝コレクションする）のが趣味です。(I have enjoyed collecting stamps since I was young.)
default.q.n2-21-q24-24.why.0: (a) 「並べて」means arranging or displaying things in a row; it is not synonymous with collecting.
default.q.n2-21-q24-24.why.1: (b) 「売って」(to sell) contradicts the meaning of collecting and storing things.
default.q.n2-21-q24-24.why.2: (c) 「集めて」, meaning to collect, gather, or compile, is exactly synonymous with 「コレクションして」.
default.q.n2-21-q24-24.why.3: (d) 「かくして」 (to hide, conceal) is unrelated to the meaning “to collect.”
default.q.n2-21-q25-25.verdict: The correct answer is 4 (見つめた), because 「にらんだ」 (to glare or stare) belongs to the same group of actions involving looking intently or fixedly at another person as 「見つめた」.
default.q.n2-21-q25-25.explanation:
- Translation of the sentence: "That man glared at me / stared intently at me."
- Sino-Japanese readings and vocabulary:
  + にらむ (睨む — NGHỆ): glare at, give a menacing look, stare intently (= じっと見る / 見つめる).
  + 見つめる (KIẾN): look intently at, keep one's eyes fixed on, stare at.
  + 恨む (HẬN): resent, bear a grudge against.
  + 苦しめる (KHỔ): torment, cause suffering.
- Example: 彼は怒ったような目で相手をにらんだ（＝見つめた）。(He glared at the other person with an angry look in his eyes.)
default.q.n2-21-q25-25.why.0: (a) 「恨んだ」 means “resented” or “hated” and describes a psychological emotion, not the act of looking with one's eyes.
default.q.n2-21-q25-25.why.1: (b) 「誘った」(invited, asked someone to join) is unrelated to the act of looking.
default.q.n2-21-q25-25.why.2: (c) 「苦しめた」 means “made someone suffer” or “caused pain,” not the action of looking.
default.q.n2-21-q25-25.why.3: (d) 「見つめた」 (looked intently at) also expresses focusing one's eyes on an object and is closest in meaning to 「にらんだ」.
default.q.n2-21-q26-26.verdict: The correct answer is 2 (貴重な) because 「珍しい」 (rare or precious) is synonymous with the adjective 「貴重な」 (valuable or rare).
default.q.n2-21-q26-26.explanation:
- Sentence meaning: "This really is an exceptionally rare dish, isn't it?"
- Vocabulary:
  + 珍しい: rare, precious, uncommon (= 貴重な / めったにない).
  + 貴重: valuable, precious, rare.
  + 高級: high-quality, luxurious, expensive.
- Example: この山には珍しい（＝貴重な）高山植物が多く自生している。(Many rare (= precious) alpine plants grow wild on this mountain.)
default.q.n2-21-q26-26.why.0: (a) 「おいしい」 (“delicious”) describes the taste of food and does not express rarity.
default.q.n2-21-q26-26.why.1: (b) 「貴重な」 (valuable, precious) describes something rare and highly valuable, and is synonymous with 「珍しい」.
default.q.n2-21-q26-26.why.2: (c) 「まずい」 means “bad-tasting” or “unappetizing” and describes poor flavor; it is unrelated to rarity.
default.q.n2-21-q26-26.why.3: (d) 「高級な」means high-end or expensive, referring to price range and status; it is not synonymous with rarity.
default.q.n2-21-q27-27.verdict: The correct answer is 1 (難しい), because when describing a family situation full of complications and difficulties, 「複雑な」 (complex) is synonymous with 「難しい」 (difficult, troublesome).
default.q.n2-21-q27-27.explanation:
- Sentence meaning: “She grew up in a complicated or difficult family situation.”
- Sino-Japanese readings & vocabulary:
  + 複雑 (complex): complicated, difficult, entangled (= 難しい / 入り組んでいる). In the expression 「複雑な家庭（環境）」, it is synonymous with 「難しい家庭（環境）」.
  + 育つ: to grow up, mature (家庭に育つ: to grow up in a family...).
  + 難しい: difficult, complicated, troubled.
- Example: 複雑な（＝難しい）事情があって、彼は国へ帰った。(Because of complicated and difficult circumstances, he returned to his country.)
default.q.n2-21-q27-27.why.0: (a) 「難しい」 (“difficult,” “complicated,” or “troubled”) is synonymous with 「複雑な」 when describing a complicated and troubled family situation.
default.q.n2-21-q27-27.why.1: (b) 「明るい」 means “bright” or “cheerful,” a positive meaning opposite to a complicated situation.
default.q.n2-21-q27-27.why.2: (c) 「豊かな」means rich or abundant, referring to material or spiritual fullness, so it does not fit the context.
default.q.n2-21-q27-27.why.3: (d) 「貧しい」(poor, impoverished) refers only to financial deprivation and does not imply troublesome or complicated relationships like 「複雑な」.
default.q.n2-21-q28-28.verdict: The correct answer is 4: 家賃を払うように 催促 しても、なかなか払ってくれない。
default.q.n2-21-q28-28.explanation:
「催促」（さいそく）means to urge or press someone to promptly carry out an action or obligation, such as repaying a debt, submitting an assignment, delivering goods, or paying rent. Common patterns: 〜を催促する, 〜よう（に）催促する.
