Meaning: “My older sister always looks down on me because I’m bad at math. I’ll definitely get a high score on the next test and show her!”
On-readings: 数学 (mathematics), 絶対に (definitely, without fail).
Structure: V-てみせる (to do something to show someone; expressing determination to prove oneself).
Example: 今度こそ絶対に勝ってみせる。(This time, I will definitely win!)
default.q.n2-26-q44-44.why.0: (a) Incorrect because 「〜てみよう」 is the volitional form of 「〜てみる」 (“let's try doing it”), and does not express a strong determination to retaliate against someone.
default.q.n2-26-q44-44.why.1: (b) Incorrect because「〜てごらん」is used by someone senior to tell or advise someone junior to try doing something, equivalent to「〜てみなさい」.
default.q.n2-26-q44-44.why.2: (c) Incorrect because 「〜てしまう」 expresses completion, regret, or an unfortunate outcome, and does not fit the determined intention “will definitely...” in the sentence.
default.q.n2-26-q44-44.why.3: (d) Correct because 「V-てみせる」 expresses determination to accomplish something no matter what, often to prove it to someone else (“I will definitely get a high score and show my sister”).
default.q.n2-26-q45-45.verdict: Correct order: 3 → 1 → 4 → 2; choice 4 is placed at ★ (ほめる).
default.q.n2-26-q45-45.explanation: あの先生は厳しくしかる一方でほめることもわすれない。 (That teacher scolds students harshly, but at the same time never forgets to praise them.)
default.q.n2-26-q45-45.why.0: (a) It follows the dictionary form of the verb 「しかる」 to create the sentence pattern 「〜一方で」 (on the one hand ..., on the other hand ...).
default.q.n2-26-q45-45.why.1: (b) It follows the verb 「ほめる」 to form a nominalized phrase, combined with the particle 「も」 before the predicate 「わすれない」 (“not forget ... either”).
default.q.n2-26-q45-45.why.2: (c) The dictionary-form verb follows the adverb 「厳しく」 in blank 1 (scold harshly).
default.q.n2-26-q45-45.why.3: (d) The verb follows 「一方で」 and modifies 「こともわすれない」, so it belongs in the ★ position (slot 3).
default.q.n2-26-q46-46.verdict: Correct order: 4 → 1 → 3 → 2; choice 3 is placed at ★ (最新の).
default.q.n2-26-q46-46.explanation: 新製品の開発にともなって最新の技術もまた開発されてきた。 (Along with the development of new products, the latest technologies have also been developed.)
default.q.n2-26-q46-46.why.0: (a) Following 「開発に」, it forms the grammar pattern 「〜に伴って / にともなって」(along with, accompanying...).
default.q.n2-26-q46-46.why.1: (b) It follows the modifier 「最新の」 and serves as the subject of the predicate 「開発されてきた」 at the end of the sentence.
default.q.n2-26-q46-46.why.2: (c) The adjective/noun phrase modifies the noun 「技術」 that follows and therefore belongs in the ★ position (slot 3).
default.q.n2-26-q46-46.why.3: (d) It follows 「新製品の」 to form 「新製品の開発に」, which connects with 「ともなって」.
default.q.n2-26-q47-47.verdict: Correct order: 3 → 2 → 1 → 4; the ★ position is answer choice 1 (この辺りは).
default.q.n2-26-q47-47.explanation: サクラの季節はもとより休みの日ともなるとこの辺りは若い人たちでいっぱいになる。 (Not only during cherry blossom season, but whenever a day off comes around, this area becomes packed with young people.)
default.q.n2-26-q47-47.why.0: (a) It serves as the subject introducing the location for the following clause (“as for this area ...”) and belongs in the ★ position (slot 3).
default.q.n2-26-q47-47.why.1: (b) It follows the clause 「〜はもとより」 in the pattern 「〜ともなると」 (when it comes to, whenever it is the occasion of).
default.q.n2-26-q47-47.why.2: (c) It follows the noun「サクラの季節」to form the structure「〜はもとより」(not only...; needless to say...).
default.q.n2-26-q47-47.why.3: (d) It comes directly before 「になる」 at the end of the sentence to form 「若い人たちでいっぱいになる」, meaning “become filled with young people.”
default.q.n2-26-q48-48.verdict: The correct order is: 2 → 4 → 1 → 3; the ★ position is answer choice 1 (思ったとおりに).
default.q.n2-26-q48-48.explanation: 人がなんと言おうと思ったとおりにやることにしました。 (No matter what people say, I decided to do exactly what I believe is right.)
default.q.n2-26-q48-48.why.0: (a) It modifies the action 「やることに」, meaning “to do it exactly as intended,” and belongs in the ★ blank (blank 3).
default.q.n2-26-q48-48.why.1: (b) It comes immediately after 「人が」and before 「言おうと」to form 「何と言おうと」(no matter what one says).
default.q.n2-26-q48-48.why.2: (c) Used with 「しました」 at the end of the sentence, it forms 「〜ことにする / ことにしました」 (to decide to do something).
default.q.n2-26-q48-48.why.3: (d) The volitional form combines with 「と」 to create the concessive conditional pattern 「〜（よ）うと」 (no matter how much... / even if...).
default.q.n2-26-q49-49.verdict: The correct order is: 2 → 4 → 1 → 3; the ★ position is answer choice 1 (見られる).
default.q.n2-26-q49-49.explanation: この辺りは四季を通して美しい草花が見られることで有名だ。 (This area is famous for its beautiful plants and flowers, which can be enjoyed throughout all four seasons.)
default.q.n2-26-q49-49.why.0: (a) The potential-form verb follows the subject 「美しい草花が」 and modifies 「こと」, so it belongs in the ★ position (slot 3).
default.q.n2-26-q49-49.why.1: (b) The time adverbial phrase 「〜を通して」 (throughout the four seasons) comes directly after 「この辺りは」.
default.q.n2-26-q49-49.why.2: (c) Following the verb 「見られる」, it forms the pattern 「〜ことで有名だ」, meaning “famous for doing something.”
default.q.n2-26-q49-49.why.3: (d) The noun phrase with the particle 「が」 serves as the subject of the potential verb 「見られる」.
default.q.n2-26-q50-50.verdict: The correct answer is 2. 可能性があるので (because there is a possibility...).
default.q.n2-26-q50-50.explanation:
The passage begins by describing how a railway company refused to display posters promoting a thousand-year-old traditional festival at its stations. The company’s reason was that the image of a shirtless man showing his chest hair might make female passengers uncomfortable and “could constitute sexual harassment” (セクシャルハラスメントにあたる).
The following clause is the decisive action 「掲示を断った」, so the blank requires a conjunction expressing an objective reason or cause for that action. The pattern 「〜可能性があるので」(because there is a possibility that...) is grammatically correct and fits the logical flow of the passage.
default.q.n2-26-q50-50.why.0: (a) Incorrect because 「〜ないなら」 means “if there is no...” and is a negative conditional, which is the exact opposite of the railway company’s actual reason for refusing.
default.q.n2-26-q50-50.why.1: (b) Correct because 「〜可能性があるので」 (because there is a possibility that …) gives an objective reason for the decision in the following clause to refuse to put up the poster.
default.q.n2-26-q50-50.why.2: (c) Incorrect because「〜あろうか」is a rhetorical question expressing doubt or a negative challenge ("could that possibly be the case?"), and it cannot serve as a reason clause for an actual action.
default.q.n2-26-q50-50.why.3: (d) Incorrect because 「〜ないからには」 means “once it is not possible to...,” expressing determination or obligation based on a negative condition, which does not fit the context.
default.q.n2-26-q51-51.verdict: The correct answer is 1. 考えなかった (did not think of it at all / did not expect it).
default.q.n2-26-q51-51.explanation:
The author is analyzing the organizers’ mindset when they made the promotional poster for the festival. To them, it was a photograph that truthfully captured the traditional appearance of festival participants over the years. Therefore, at the time it was created in the past, they "did not think at all / never imagined" (考えなかった) that it would later be regarded as sexual harassment.
Because the event occurred in the past and the sentence describes failing to anticipate the problem, the past negative form 「考えなかった」, with its unexpected-result nuance, is the most appropriate choice.
default.q.n2-26-q51-51.why.0: (a) Correct because 「考えなかった」is in the negative past tense, expressing that when the poster was made earlier, the person had never thought of or expected this situation.
default.q.n2-26-q51-51.why.1: (b) Incorrect because 「考えた」, “thought,” is affirmative and contradicts the surprise and shock at the public reaction.
default.q.n2-26-q51-51.why.2: (c) Incorrect because 「考えられる」 is the passive/potential form (“is thought to be / can be regarded as”), and does not express the poster-maker’s subjective, unforeseen state of mind.
default.q.n2-26-q51-51.why.3: (d) Incorrect because 「考えていない」(the negative progressive form) describes a present state, whereas the failure to anticipate it occurred when the poster was designed in the past.
default.q.n2-26-q52-52.verdict: The correct answer is 4. なったのなら (if it has become... then).
default.q.n2-26-q52-52.explanation:
The sentence directly quotes the man's own words in the photograph: 「親からもらった大切な体だし、人より少し毛が濃かっただけ。でも、このことで今まであまり知られていなかった祭りが有名に＿＿、自分はそれでもかまわない」.
The man believes that although his photo was rejected and he was subjected to gossip, “if this commotion makes a festival that was previously little known become famous (祭りが有名になったのなら), then he does not mind enduring it.”
The pattern [V-ta + のなら] takes an event or result as a premise and expresses an attitude or course of action in the following clause, including a willingness to make a personal sacrifice.
default.q.n2-26-q52-52.why.0: (a) Incorrect because 「〜たかったら」 expresses a desire (“if you want to become ...”) and is not used with a subject referring to an object or event, such as a festival (祭り).
default.q.n2-26-q52-52.why.1: (b) Incorrect because 「〜までは」 means “until...”; it does not create a conditional structure that fits the following result, “I am fine too.”
default.q.n2-26-q52-52.why.2: (c) Incorrect because 「〜てみると」 describes discovering a new result after trying something, so it does not appropriately connect to the concessive attitude that follows.
default.q.n2-26-q52-52.why.3: (d) This is correct because 「〜たのなら」 (“if things have turned out that way...”) presents an assumption based on a situation or result that has already occurred, which serves as the basis for the acceptance expressed in the following clause.
default.q.n2-26-q53-53.verdict: The correct answer is 3. こそ (it is precisely ... / ... is what truly ...).
default.q.n2-26-q53-53.explanation:
After quoting the heartfelt and generous words of the man participating in the festival, the author expresses admiration for his devotion to the traditions of his hometown.
The particle 「こそ」 means “precisely” or “it is ... that,” emphasizing the noun or noun phrase before it and asserting that this willingness to sacrifice for the community, both in thought and action, is truly the genuine expression of pride in one’s hometown.
default.q.n2-26-q53-53.why.0: (a) Incorrect because 「のだと」 is used to quote an indirect statement or belief ("that..."), not to emphasize the person being praised.
default.q.n2-26-q53-53.why.1: (b) Incorrect because 「ね消」 is a misspelled, meaningless choice that does not exist in Japanese grammar.
default.q.n2-26-q53-53.why.2: (c) Correct because the particle 「こそ」 emphasizes a particular object or quality: “it is precisely this spirit that truly is ...”
default.q.n2-26-q53-53.why.3: (d) Incorrect because 「ほど」expresses degree (“to the extent that...”) or comparison; it is not used to identify and emphasize a quality.
default.q.n2-26-q54-54.verdict: The correct answer is 1. セクハラというなら (if this is considered sexual harassment...).
default.q.n2-26-q54-54.explanation:
In the conclusion of the passage, the author discusses in greater depth the excessiveness of modern social standards, which readily label every form of cultural expression as harassment.
The pattern [N + というなら] (if one says or regards N as...) is used to present a counterargument: If even the authentic appearance of a thousand-year-old traditional festival is labeled "sexual harassment" (セクハラというなら), society will become excessively strict, and most other forms of cultural and artistic expression will also become difficult to sustain. Therefore, choice 1 is entirely appropriate.
default.q.n2-26-q54-54.why.0: (a) Correct because 「セクハラというなら」 (“if this is called sexual harassment...”) presents the key premise for the author's argument that society is being excessively strict.
default.q.n2-26-q54-54.why.1: (b) Incorrect because「おどろくというなら」(if you say it is surprising...) does not reflect the central issue of the debate concerning social stereotypes.
default.q.n2-26-q54-54.why.2: (c) Incorrect because 「困ったというなら」(“if you say it was troublesome”) does not highlight the key issue debated in the article: “sexual harassment.”
default.q.n2-26-q54-54.why.3: (d) Incorrect because 「ポスターというなら」('if we call it a poster...') misses the point. The issue being debated here is labeling that poster as harassment.
default.q.n2-26-q55-55.verdict: The correct answer is 3: 自動販売機が使う電力 when it contains both cold and hot drinks.
default.q.n2-26-q55-55.explanation:
- Relevant main point: The passage discusses the large amount of electricity consumed by vending machines in Japan. The author gives the example of a vending machine that sells both hot and cold drinks, consuming about 350–450 kWh of electricity per month. This amount of electricity (「これ」) is equivalent to the consumption of an entire household.
- Question translation: What does 「これ」 (“this”) refer to?
- Answer choices:
1. The amount of electricity consumed by one vending machine in one month.
2. The amount of electricity consumed by electrical appliances in an ordinary household.
3. The amount of electricity consumed by a vending machine that sells both cold and hot drinks.
4. The amount of electricity generated by solar panels on a house’s roof.
default.q.n2-26-q55-55.why.0: (a) Incorrect because the passage gives only the specific example of a vending machine that sells both cold and hot drinks (冷たい飲物と温かい飲物の両方が買える販売機を例にとると...). It does not discuss the electricity consumption of all different kinds of vending machines (各種の自動販売機).
default.q.n2-26-q55-55.why.1: (b) Incorrect because the amount of electricity used by one household (1 家族が使う電気消費量) is what 「これ」 is compared with in 「これは 1 家族が使う電気消費量とほぼ同じになります」; 「これ」 itself does not refer specifically to that amount of electricity.
default.q.n2-26-q55-55.why.2: (c) Correct. The passage states: 「冷たい飲物と温かい飲物の両方が買える販売機を例にとると、 1 ヶ月に消費する電力は 350 ～ 450 キロワット時で、これは 1 家族が使う電気消費量とほぼ同じになります。」 The demonstrative 「これ」 directly refers to the monthly electricity consumption of 350～450 kWh for a vending machine that sells both hot and cold drinks, mentioned immediately beforehand.
default.q.n2-26-q55-55.why.3: (d) Incorrect because the solar panel on the roof is mentioned in the following sentence as a comparison to illustrate the area of panel required, not as the object referred to by 「これ」.
default.q.n2-26-q56-56.verdict: The correct answer is 1: 「いまの自分」を肯定できないということは.
default.q.n2-26-q56-56.explanation:
- Main point: The author argues that it is perfectly natural for people to show different “faces” (ways of behaving) depending on whom they are talking to. All of these are one’s “true self,” so they should not be rigidly divided into real and false. If we become preoccupied with separating the real from the false, we will be unable to accept or affirm our “present self” and our “present friends.” Being unable to affirm the present self also means being unable to affirm the self of the past or the future.

- Question translation:
  Fill in the appropriate content at （ ★ ）.

- Answer choices:
  1. Being unable to affirm the “present self” means
  2. Being unable to make friends with a “true friend” means
  3. Being unable to understand the “true self” means
  4. The “false self” being discovered by others means
default.q.n2-26-q56-56.why.0: (a) Correct. Immediately before the blank, the author writes: 「真か偽かを考えているうちは、いつまでも『いまの自分』も『いまの友人』肯定できません。」 (As long as we keep considering whether something is true or false, we can never affirm “the present self” or “the present friends.”) The expression 「『いまの自分』を肯定できないということは」 (The inability to affirm “the present self” means that...) provides a perfectly logical transition to the following consequence: the inability to affirm one’s past and future selves as well.
default.q.n2-26-q56-56.why.1: (b) Incorrect. This choice concerns “being unable to make genuine friends,” which does not fit the preceding sentence, which is about being unable to assert “the present self.”
default.q.n2-26-q56-56.why.2: (c) Incorrect. The passage considers all of them to be one's “true self”; it does not discuss “not understanding one's real self,” so it does not fit the line of reasoning at position ( ★ ).
default.q.n2-26-q56-56.why.3: (d) Incorrect. The passage never mentions “the fake self being discovered by others”; this is an unsupported inference.
default.q.n2-26-q57-57.verdict: The correct answer is 3: In reality, there are cases in which the program recognizes adult male voices well but does not recognize the voices of other groups as well.
default.q.n2-26-q57-57.explanation:
**Main point of the passage:**
Many speech-recognition programs are currently advertised as being able to "recognize anyone’s voice," but this should not be taken completely literally. In practice, "anyone’s voice" often only means that the program can distinguish adult male voices; in some cases, it may not recognize women’s voices, elderly people’s voices, or children’s voices well.

**Question translation:**
Why does the passage say, "Perhaps this should not be taken literally"?

**Answer choices:**
1. Because in some cases, the program can recognize only elderly people’s voices.
2. Because in some cases, the program can recognize only women’s voices.
3. Because in some cases, the program can recognize only men’s voices.
4. Because in some cases, the program can recognize only children’s voices.
default.q.n2-26-q57-57.why.0: (a) Choice 1 is incorrect because, according to the passage, an elderly person’s hoarse voice is an example of a voice that the program may fail to recognize accurately (「老人のし山がれた声…についてはうまく認識できないという場合がある」), not a voice that it “can recognize only when spoken by an elderly person.”
default.q.n2-26-q57-57.why.1: (b) Choice 2 is incorrect because female voices may also be among the voices that are not recognized well (「女の子の声…についてはうまく認識できないという場合がある」), rather than being the only voices that can be recognized.
default.q.n2-26-q57-57.why.2: (c) Choice 3 is correct. The passage states: 「『どの人の声でも』といったとき男の大人の声ならほとんど聞き分けられるということを意味していることが多く次女の子の声や老人のし山がれた声、子供の声（中略）についてはうまく認識できないという場合がある。」 This explains why “being able to recognize anyone’s voice” should not be taken literally: in reality, it may only mean recognizing most adult male voices.
default.q.n2-26-q57-57.why.3: (d) Choice 4 is incorrect because children's voices are among the types of audio that may be difficult to recognize accurately (「子供の声（中略）についてはうまく認識できないという場合がある」), which contradicts the choice.
default.q.n2-26-q58-58.verdict: The correct answer is 3: The author used to keep wrapping paper, but shopping now produces so much packaging waste that the author feels excessive packaging should be reduced.
default.q.n2-26-q58-58.explanation:
**Main point:** As a child, the author loved beautifully wrapped gifts and always carefully kept the wrapping paper after taking out what was inside. However, after seeing the excessive layers of packaging used when buying confectionery at department stores today—each piece wrapped in an attractively illustrated bag, placed in a box, wrapped in paper, tied with a bow, and then put into a shopping bag—the author feels troubled by the amount of waste. The author believes that although the traditional culture of wrapping should be preserved, excessive packaging (過剰包装) should be reduced.

**Translation of the question:**
What does the sentence 「最近は子供のころと違って、包むことの対する考えが変わってきた」 mean?

**Translation of the answer choices:**
1. Japan has had a gift-giving culture since ancient times, and the custom of wrapping things in beautiful paper or cloth...
2. Although this is an age in which resources should be valued, Japan’s traditional custom of wrapping things has changed...
3. In the past, people kept the wrapping paper, but nowadays the many layers of packaging that come with every purchase become waste, so...
4. Wrapping used to be very beautiful, but nowadays people no longer use attractive paper to wrap products...
default.q.n2-26-q58-58.why.0: (a) Choice 1 is inaccurate because it merely repeats part of the background about the traditional Japanese practice of wrapping gifts or purchased items in paper or cloth, 「日本には、昔から贈り物や買った物を紙や布で包む習慣があった」. It does not clarify the author's change in perception from the past to the present.
default.q.n2-26-q58-58.why.1: (b) Choice 2 is incorrect because the passage does not discuss how traditional Japanese habits have changed in an age that requires resource conservation. Its main point is that excessive layers of packaging when shopping today create too much waste.
default.q.n2-26-q58-58.why.2: (c) Choice 3 is correct. The author once carefully kept wrapping paper after taking out its contents (「中のものを取り出してからもその紙が捨てられなかった。一枚一枚ていねいにたたんで、しばらく大切に持っていた」), but now feels that excessive packaging should be reduced because shopping produces too much packaging waste (「食べ終わるとたくさんのゴ田が出 る。 1 回の買い物でこんなにゴ田を出してしまっていいのだろうかと考えてしまう。...過剰な 包装は減らしていった方がいいと思う」).
default.q.n2-26-q58-58.why.3: (d) Choice 4 is incorrect because it contradicts the passage. The passage clearly states that stores still use attractive packaging and wrapping paper: 「一つ一つのお菓子はきれいな絵の描かれた袋に入っている。それを箱にき活んと入れて、箱をまた紙で包んでリボンをかけたりする」. It is not true that attractive paper is no longer used.
default.q.n2-26-q59-59.verdict: The correct answer is 2: When taking photos or recording videos, one should pay attention to eye level / the camera angle (目線).
default.q.n2-26-q59-59.explanation:
■ Main point:
Taking photos and videos is the most common and convenient way to preserve travel memories, but if the photos turn out poorly—out of focus, with monotonous angles, or unclear subjects—you will be very disappointed when you look back at them at home. To avoid disappointment and prevent beautiful memories from being wasted, the author’s key advice is to pay attention to the "目線" (eye level / the angle at which the camera is directed at the subject).

■ Question translation:
What does the author think you should do to avoid being "disappointed"?

■ Answer choices:
1. You should not use photos or videos to preserve memories of your trip.
2. When taking photos or videos, you should pay attention to eye level / the camera angle.
3. It is enough to be careful to avoid blur and focus properly.
4. It is best not to look back at the photos or videos taken during the trip.
default.q.n2-26-q59-59.why.0: (a) Choice 1 is incorrect because the author states that taking photos and videos is the most standard way to preserve travel memories (そんな旅の想い出づくりで一番スタンダードなのが写真やビデオ), rather than advising people not to use them.
default.q.n2-26-q59-59.why.1: (b) Choice 2 is correct because the concluding sentence clearly states the solution: 「写真やビデオで大切なのは目線です。これは被写体にどの角度からレンズを向けるかということ。カメラをかまえたときに立っているか座っているかだけでも、出来上がりはまったく違った印象になります。」 (What matters in photographs and videos is eye level—the angle from which the lens is pointed at the subject.)
default.q.n2-26-q59-59.why.2: (c) Answer choice 3 is incorrect because an out-of-focus image (ぼけたピント) is merely one example of a common failure listed by the author. The author does not recommend simply paying attention to focusing; the key point is the viewing angle / eye level (目線).
default.q.n2-26-q59-59.why.3: (d) Choice 4 is incorrect because the author says it would be unfortunate and wasteful if a precious memory ended up becoming something one “never wanted to look at a second time” (せっかくの想い出のはずが、2度と見たくないということになったのではもったいないです), rather than advising people not to look back at photos or videos.
default.q.n2-26-q60-60.verdict: The correct answer is 3: The Shinkansen has become indispensable to modern society.
default.q.n2-26-q60-60.explanation:
- Main point summary: During the 40 years since its opening, the Tokaido Shinkansen increased its speed, increased the number of services, and became an essential means of transportation in modern life.
- Question translation: How did the Shinkansen change during the 40 years after its opening?
- Answer choices:
  1. The average delay per train became 10 seconds.
  2. Damage to nearby residents disappeared completely.
  3. It became indispensable to modern society.
  4. Accidents such as collisions completely disappeared.
default.q.n2-26-q60-60.why.0: (a) Incorrect because the passage says「1 列車あたりの平均の遅れは、 10 秒にまで 短 縮 された」(the average delay per train was shortened to just 10 seconds), not that the train was delayed by 10 seconds.
default.q.n2-26-q60-60.why.1: (b) Incorrect because the article states 「周辺住所の被害も忘れてはなるまい」(we must not forget the damage or effects on nearby residents), showing that these issues still need attention rather than having disappeared.
default.q.n2-26-q60-60.why.2: (c) Correct because the final paragraph states: “40 年で速度は上がり、本数は増えた。現答には欠かせないものになったからこそ...” (“Over 40 years, the speed increased and the number of services grew. Precisely because it has become indispensable to modern life...”)
default.q.n2-26-q60-60.why.3: (d) Incorrect because the passage says "この間、 衝 突 のような事故が全く無かった" (there had been no accidents such as collisions at all during that period), meaning none had occurred up to that point, not that they had "stopped occurring" after 40 years.
default.q.n2-26-q61-61.verdict: The correct answer is 2: The sentence describes the Shinkansen speeding along with extremely intense speed and force.
default.q.n2-26-q61-61.explanation:
- Main point: When standing at a station and watching a Shinkansen rush past, people can clearly sense its terrifying, almost airborne speed. The Chinese visitor's metaphor, “as if it were being whipped from behind and chased,” vividly describes the train's extraordinary speed and fierce momentum.
- Question: What does “as if it were being whipped from behind and chased” mean?
- Answer choices:
  1. The sound of the passing Shinkansen is frightening.
  2. The Shinkansen rushes forward with tremendous force.
  3. The Shinkansen is like a horse from the past that works very hard.
  4. It is pitiful to see the Shinkansen being forced to run so fast.
default.q.n2-26-q61-61.why.0: (a) Incorrect. The simile is not intended to describe a frightening sound as a train passes through a station.
default.q.n2-26-q61-61.why.1: (b) Correct because the author previously describes: "新幹線の駅のホー由で次のぞみ が通過するのを見る時、その爆走ぶりを実感する。走るというより飛んでゆく感じがある" (when you watch the train pass, you truly feel how it speeds along as if flying), a quotation used to convey the Shinkansen's forceful, whirlwind-like speed.
default.q.n2-26-q61-61.why.2: (c) Incorrect because the passage uses a whip for horses as a metaphor for the speed of being pursued, not to compare the train’s diligence with a horse’s.
default.q.n2-26-q61-61.why.3: (d) Incorrect because this is an exclamatory metaphor describing extremely fast movement; it does not imply sympathy or pity for a train being forced to run quickly.
default.q.n2-26-q62-62.verdict: The correct answer is 1: The author believes that what the Shinkansen should continue pursuing and improving in the future is world-leading safety.
default.q.n2-26-q62-62.explanation:
- Main point: The passage concludes that, rather than simply continuing the race to achieve the world's highest speed, what is more important and necessary for the Shinkansen in the future is to maintain and further improve its position as the world's safest railway.
- Question translation: What does the author think will be even more necessary for the Shinkansen in the future?
- Answer choices:
  1. Improve safety.
  2. Increase speed.
  3. Maintain punctuality.
  4. Increase the number of train services.
default.q.n2-26-q62-62.why.0: (a) Correct because the concluding sentence clearly states: 「世界一の速度を競うより、世界一の安全を追い続けることである」 (Rather than competing for the world's fastest speed, the important thing is to continue pursuing the world's highest level of safety).
default.q.n2-26-q62-62.why.1: (b) Incorrect because the author explicitly says 「世界一の速度を競うより...」(rather than competing for the world’s fastest speed...), meaning that increasing speed is not regarded as the top priority for the future.
default.q.n2-26-q62-62.why.2: (c) Incorrect because accuracy in time ("正確注") is an achievement resulting from 40 years of effort, not a future goal emphasized by the author at the end of the passage.
default.q.n2-26-q62-62.why.3: (d) Incorrect because the increase in the number of services (「本数は増えた」) has already occurred and is causing overcrowding (「過密」), which needs to be considered carefully; it is not a goal that should be increased further.
default.q.n2-26-q63-63.verdict: The correct answer is 3: Elementary and junior high school reunions are more interesting because they include a greater variety of people, and the extent to which each person has changed over the years is substantial.
default.q.n2-26-q63-63.explanation:
- Main point: The author explains that elementary-school and junior-high reunions are much more interesting than high-school or university reunions because they bring together many different kinds of people (何種類ものタイプの人間が混ざっていて), and because the degree of change in each person’s life after a long period since graduation is substantial (人間の変化の度合いが大きい).
- Question translation: When the author says, "Many people believe that elementary-school or junior-high reunions are much more interesting than university or high-school reunions," why does the author say this is so?
- Answer choices:
  1. Because people who once had poor academic records have now become successful.
  2. Because it is fun to have both top students and delinquents together.
  3. Because many diverse types of people gather, and the changes in them are also substantial.
  4. Because a long time has passed since graduation, making the reunions nostalgic.
default.q.n2-26-q63-63.why.0: (a) Incorrect. The example of someone who once performed poorly and later succeeded is merely a specific illustration of change, not the author’s broad underlying reason.
default.q.n2-26-q63-63.why.1: (b) Incorrect. Having high-achieving students and mischievous leaders are merely examples illustrating changes after entering school; they do not cover the underlying reason.
default.q.n2-26-q63-63.why.2: (c) Correct. The author provides clear evidence: 「それは、後者のほうが何種類ものタイプの人間が混ざっていて、かつ、卒業後長い時間が経過しているために、人間の変化の度合いが大きいということに依存しているのでしょう。」 This depends on the latter group including many different types of people and on the degree of human change being greater because a long time has passed since graduation.
default.q.n2-26-q63-63.why.3: (d) Incorrect. The author mentions the passage of a long period of time as the reason people change so greatly (人間の変化の度合いが大きい), not because they feel nostalgic (なつかしい).
default.q.n2-26-q64-64.verdict: The correct answer is 4: The idea that once people enter society, their academic performance at school is almost no longer relevant.
default.q.n2-26-q64-64.explanation:
- Summary of the main point: The demonstrative phrase 「このように考えれば」 (“If we think of it this way”) follows a series of real-life examples: an academically excellent student may become useless, a bottom-ranked or rebellious student may succeed in business, a hardworking person may suffer misfortune, and someone who often receives failing grades may still become a respectable worker. From this, the passage concludes that once people enter society, school performance has little relevance.
- Translation of the question: There is a statement saying “If we think of it this way.” What kind of way of thinking does “this way” refer to?
- Translation of the answer choices:
  1. People who perform well at school will also grow up to be respectable and talented.
  2. People who perform poorly at school will also have an unsuccessful life later on.
  3. Whether someone succeeds is determined by their academic performance.
  4. Once people enter society, school performance is largely irrelevant.
default.q.n2-26-q64-64.why.0: (a) Incorrect. The article points to the opposite: a student who once had perfect grades (オール5の優等生) has now become a useless father (ダメ親父).
default.q.n2-26-q64-64.why.1: (b) Incorrect. The article gives examples of people who ranked last in their class (ビリ) or consistently received failing grades (赤点の連続), yet later became successful or worked very respectably.
default.q.n2-26-q64-64.why.2: (c) Incorrect. The series of supporting examples shows that success or failure in life does not depend on one's academic achievements at school.
default.q.n2-26-q64-64.why.3: (d) Correct. The preceding sentence provides clear evidence: 「世間に出れば学業成績などはほとんど関係ないらしく、立派に仕事をやっている人もたくさんいます。」 (Once people enter society, academic performance apparently has little relevance, and many people still do their jobs very well.)
default.q.n2-26-q65-65.verdict: The correct answer is 1: The author concludes that if you do not like studying something, it is better not to study it at all.
default.q.n2-26-q65-65.explanation:
- Main idea: The author wonders whether education-obsessed mothers (教育ママゴン) will all strongly oppose them. Since academic achievement does not determine success in real life, the author suggests that "it may be more beneficial to decisively avoid studying subjects one does not like" (好きでもない勉強はいっそのことやらないほうが得).
- Question translation: Why does the author think that "education-obsessed mothers everywhere might launch a massive vote of no confidence against the author"?
- Answer choices:
  1. Because the author thinks it is better not to study subjects one dislikes.
  2. Because the author thinks that no matter how much one studies, one’s academic performance will not improve.
  3. Because the author thinks children who do not study will be more successful.
  4. Because the author thinks that people with poor academic performance cannot get respectable jobs.
default.q.n2-26-q65-65.why.0: (a) Correct because the author states: 「『好きでもない勉強はいっそのことやらないほうが得』という結論を下すとしたら、世の教育ママゴンたちは大挙して筆者に不信任を突きつけるのでしょうか。」 (If one were to conclude that “it is better not to study subjects one does not like at all,” would education-obsessed mothers everywhere descend in force to express their lack of confidence in the author?) This exactly matches the idea that “it is better not to study subjects one dislikes.”
default.q.n2-26-q65-65.why.1: (b) Incorrect. The author does not claim that performance will not improve no matter how much one studies.
default.q.n2-26-q65-65.why.2: (c) Incorrect. The author does not claim that children who do not study will be more successful, but only states that grades do not determine everything.
default.q.n2-26-q65-65.why.3: (d) Incorrect. The article demonstrates the opposite by noting that many people who performed poorly at school nevertheless went on to work properly and succeed in life.
default.q.n2-26-q66-66.verdict: The correct answer is 1 (先生になるための受験勉強).
default.q.n2-26-q66-66.explanation:
The author shares that they took the teacher recruitment exam three times but failed each time. Looking back on those three years of exam preparation, the author realized that this kind of studying was extremely boring and brought nothing good («ああいうつまらない勉強してるとろくなことはない»).
- Question translation: The passage contains the phrase "that kind of boring studying." What kind of studying is boring?
- Answer choices:
1. Studying to prepare for the teacher recruitment exam.
2. Studying at elementary school, junior high school, and preschool.
3. Studying during lessons/classes.
4. Studying in education for older adults.
default.q.n2-26-q66-66.why.0: (a) Correct because the passage states directly: 「考えてみれば、先生になろうと思ったその 3 年間というのは、非常に勉強になったなあとおもうんですよね。ああいうつまらない勉強してるとろくなことはないぞということだけは、身についたんじゃないかなあという気がします。」 The phrase refers to studying for the teacher certification examination for 3 years.
default.q.n2-26-q66-66.why.1: (b) Incorrect because teaching classes at elementary schools, middle schools, or kindergartens (「小中学校や幼稚園のクラスで授業ができるようになってきて」) is the author's current teaching work, not the boring study mentioned in the passage.
default.q.n2-26-q66-66.why.2: (c) Incorrect because this refers to the author’s current classroom teaching activity («クラスで授業»), not the boring studying that the author criticizes.
default.q.n2-26-q66-66.why.3: (d) Incorrect because the classes for older adults («高齢者の教室») helped the author overcome the regret of failing to become a teacher; they were not boring exam-preparation classes.
default.q.n2-26-q67-67.verdict: The correct answer is 4 (わかるように教えてくれるなら、だれにでもお願いする。).
default.q.n2-26-q67-67.explanation:
The expression "bowing even to a cat" is a vivid metaphor: although an academically weak student («劣等生») has a strong sense of pride and does not want to bow easily before people of high status, if they encounter teaching that helps them understand and find something extremely interesting, they are willing to humble themselves and seek instruction from anyone—even a cat.
- Question translation: What does the expression "bowing even to a cat" mean?
- Answer choices:
1. Greeting everyone, not only great or high-ranking people.
2. A weak student respecting not only great people but anyone at all.
3. Easily bowing before beings inferior to oneself, such as cats.
4. Being willing to rely on anyone if they can teach you something you can understand.
default.q.n2-26-q67-67.why.0: (a) Incorrect because the author writes: 「どんな偉い人にも簡単には頭を下げたくはない」 (“I do not want to bow easily to anyone, no matter how important they are”), which has nothing to do with greeting everyone.
default.q.n2-26-q67-67.why.1: (b) Incorrect because the author does not say that the students lack respect for anyone; rather, they are not quick to bow to people with fame or power.
default.q.n2-26-q67-67.why.2: (c) Incorrect because «ネコにだって» (even to a cat) is an exaggerated expression emphasizing the speaker's willingness to humble themself before anyone if it helps that person understand the lesson. It does not mean looking down on others as inferior like cats and bowing to them.
default.q.n2-26-q67-67.why.3: (d) Correct because the passage states: 「自分にもわかってすごく面白いということがあると、もう ネコにだって頭を下げる ― そういうふうに思っているのが劣等生なんですよね。」 (If there is something that they can understand themselves and find extremely interesting, they will even bow their heads to a cat.) This means that once they are helped to understand something, they are willing to seek help from anyone.
default.q.n2-26-q68-68.verdict: The correct answer is 4 (わかりやすく、興味が持てる授業).
default.q.n2-26-q68-68.explanation:
The author criticizes rote, boring study («つまらない勉強») and, drawing on the perspective of a struggling student («劣等生»), understands that lessons need to be easy to understand and engaging («自分にもわかってすごく面白い»). It can therefore be inferred that, in the classes they currently teach, the author always conducts lessons that are engaging and easy for students to follow.
- Question translation: What kind of lessons can be inferred that the author conducts in the classes they currently teach?
- Answer choices:
1. Lessons that soothe the desire to become a teacher.
2. Lessons resembling years of studying for entrance exams.
3. Lessons that may be boring but enable students to acquire knowledge.
4. Lessons that are easy to understand and spark interest.
default.q.n2-26-q68-68.why.0: (a) Incorrect because the easing of the author's regret («未練も和らいでいる») is a psychological feeling experienced by the author while teaching, not a characteristic or aspect of the lesson taught to the students.
default.q.n2-26-q68-68.why.1: (b) Incorrect because the author criticizes exam-oriented study as pointless and boring (「ああいうつまらない勉強してるとろくなことはない」), so the author clearly would not teach a class like that.
default.q.n2-26-q68-68.why.2: (c) Incorrect because the author strongly opposes boring study («つまらない勉強») and argues that studying in that way will not produce good results.
default.q.n2-26-q68-68.why.3: (d) Correct. From the perspective of a struggling student («劣等生»), the author understood that lessons should be 「自分にもわかってすごく面白い」—easy for the student to understand and extremely interesting. This implies that the author’s current lessons are easy to follow and engaging («わかりやすく、興味が持てる授業»).
default.q.n2-26-q69-69.verdict: The correct answer is 4: In the passage, 「何か」 refers to dangers or unexpected accidents that may happen to children.
default.q.n2-26-q69-69.explanation:
- Main point: Both passages A and B discuss how to respond to dangerous, risky, and unforeseen situations that may occur in children’s lives or in nature. Passage A emphasizes preventing risks to children, while Passage B emphasizes allowing children to learn how to deal with risks when they encounter them.
- Question translation: What does 「何か」 (“something”) in the passage refer to?
- Answer choices:
  1. Violating rules of etiquette / being impolite
  2. A water-related accident
  3. A fire or fire-related accident
  4. Dangerous or risky situations
default.q.n2-26-q69-69.why.0: (a) Choice 1 is incorrect because “breaking rules or etiquette” (マナー違反) is merely one aspect of social behavior mentioned in passage A (周囲に対するマナー); it does not encompass the general meaning of 「何か」, referring to something unexpected or dangerous, in both texts.
default.q.n2-26-q69-69.why.1: (b) Choice 2 is incorrect because water-related accidents (水の事故) are only one specific example given by Author A (子供の水での事故などのニュース), and do not represent the entire concept of 「何か」 in both passages.
default.q.n2-26-q69-69.why.2: (c) Choice 3 is incorrect because the reference to fire is only a specific example of not letting children use fire alone (子供に火を使わせない); it does not encompass the meaning of '何か'.
default.q.n2-26-q69-69.why.3: (d) Choice 4 is correct because paragraph A says 「子供に何かあってからでは遅いのである」 (it would be too late if something happened to the child), while paragraph B says 「自然は楽しいこともあるが、危険なこともたくさんある... 何かが起こる可能性があるから、どうしたらいいか考えさせるべきである」 (nature can be enjoyable, but it also contains many dangers... Since something could happen, children should be made to think about what to do). Therefore, 「何か」 refers to dangerous or risky situations (危険なこと).
default.q.n2-26-q70-70.verdict: The correct answer is 2: A’s view is that children should be protected from danger, while B believes that children should experience those risks so they can learn and mature on their own.
default.q.n2-26-q70-70.explanation:
- Main idea: Author A argues that safety and good manners are most important, and that adults must set boundaries and protect children from dangers before it is too late. In contrast, Author B argues that children learn nothing if they are merely kept safe; they need real-world experiences, even when facing danger, so that they can recognize their own limits and learn to solve problems themselves.
- Translation of the question: “Which of the following correctly describes the views of A and B?”
- Translation of the choices:
  1. A believes that safety and avoiding inconvenience must be given top priority, whereas B believes that safety is hardly...
  2. A's view is that children should be protected from dangerous things, whereas B believes that such things should also... (so that children can experience and learn from them).
  3. A believes that safety and good manners are most important, whereas B believes that there is no need to think about safety and that children's learning is all that matters.
  4. A teaches children about dangerous things, whereas B gives them many experiences so that they can learn what is safe.
default.q.n2-26-q70-70.why.0: (a) Choice 1 is incorrect because its latter part says that B 'was not very concerned about safety' (安全などはあまり...), whereas B acknowledges that prohibition is safe ('安全だが子供の学びにはならない') and emphasizes helping children learn through their own experiences how far is safe ('どこまでなら大丈夫だということを... 子供自身の体験の中で学んでいく').
default.q.n2-26-q70-70.why.1: (b) Choice 2 is correct because Passage A emphasizes protecting children from danger by restricting their actions: 「子供を危険から守るため... 制限された中で遊ばざるを得ない」 and 「一人でしてはいけないことをちゃんと考え... 子供に何かあってからでは遅い」. Passage B, on the other hand, argues that children should be allowed to have experiences even when danger is involved: 「時には危ない目にもあうだろうが、そこでの学びはとても大きく、子供が成長する過程の真の学びと言える」.
default.q.n2-26-q70-70.why.2: (c) Answer choice 3 is incorrect because passage B does not mean 'not thinking about safety at all' (安全は考えずに); rather, it says that children should think about how to respond when they face a possible danger ('何かが起こる可能性があるから、どうしたらいいか考えさせるべきである').
default.q.n2-26-q70-70.why.3: (d) Choice 4 is incorrect because author A advocates preventing children from doing dangerous things—「子供だけで川などに行かせないとか、子供に火を使わせないとか」—rather than “teaching dangerous things” (危険なことを教え). In addition, part B does not accurately reflect the main point of B: allowing children to learn and think through problem-solving based on their own experiences.
default.q.n2-26-q71-71.verdict: The correct answer is 2: Illiteracy is not innate; the problem lies in the society that created the condition of illiteracy.
default.q.n2-26-q71-71.explanation:
- **Main idea**: The author asserts that illiteracy (文盲) is not caused by an innate disposition or an individual's fault, but is a "social disease" (社会的病状) arising from the environment and social conditions. The public's abnormal reaction—being sensitive to and rejecting the term "illiteracy" as discriminatory while refusing to face the underlying social problem honestly—is also criticized.
- **Question translation**: What does the author mean by the statement, "Illiteracy is absolutely not a result of a person's innate qualities. Rather, it is a disease of society"?
- **Answer choices**:
  1. Illiteracy is neither something people are born with nor the individual's responsibility, so...
  2. Illiteracy is not something people are born with; rather, the problem lies in the society that created this condition.
  3. Illiteracy is not something people are born with, so it is strange to regard the term as discriminatory...
  4. Illiteracy is not something people are born with, so the term illiteracy should be used more normally...
default.q.n2-26-q71-71.why.0: (a) Incorrect because the author does not discuss disregarding individual responsibility, but emphasizes that the fundamental source of illiteracy is society.
default.q.n2-26-q71-71.why.1: (b) Correct. The author clearly states: 「文盲も決してその人の素質ではない。むしろ社会的病状である。」 (Illiteracy is by no means an inherent quality of the individual; rather, it is a social illness.) In other words, its cause lies in society's lack of educational opportunities, not in the individual.
default.q.n2-26-q71-71.why.2: (c) Incorrect because the author does not say that treating the word for illiteracy as a discriminatory term is strange. Rather, the author criticizes people's excessive reaction to the wording instead of confronting the underlying social reality.
default.q.n2-26-q71-71.why.3: (d) Incorrect because the passage does not mention encouraging the ordinary or more widespread use of illiterate vocabulary.
default.q.n2-26-q72-72.verdict: The correct answer is 4: Although the mother heard the explanation, she could not understand how much medicine to give her child.
default.q.n2-26-q72-72.explanation:
- **Main point**: A mother brought her child to a nun's clinic. Although the nun explained in the local tribal language that she only needed to give the child half the medicine (2 tablets), the mother was illiterate and did not understand the concept of "half" (半分という概念を持てない). Afraid of giving the wrong dosage, she asked not to take the medicine home and said she would return to the clinic the following week to have the nun give it to the child.
- **Question translation**: Why did she say, "I will not take the medicine home; instead, I will come here again next week and ask you to give it to the child"?
- **Answer choices**:
  1. Although her home was far away, she thought the route was familiar and would not be difficult.
  2. Because the medicine was taken once a week, she thought there was no need to take it home.
  3. Although walking from her distant home would be difficult, she had shoes, so she thought walking would not be a problem.
  4. Even though the mother had heard the explanation, she still did not clearly understand how much medicine to give the child.
default.q.n2-26-q72-72.why.0: (a) This is incorrect because the passage clearly states that walking 20 km is extremely difficult (「大変なことだ」「楽な仕事ではない」); the mother does not think it is easy.
default.q.n2-26-q72-72.why.1: (b) Incorrect because the reason the mother left the medicine was that she did not understand the concept of taking half a dose, not because the medicine only needed to be taken once a week.
default.q.n2-26-q72-72.why.2: (c) Incorrect because the passage says that people walked barefoot with thick, callused soles like elephant feet, not that the mother had shoes and could walk without difficulty.
default.q.n2-26-q72-72.why.3: (d) Correct. When the nun explained how to divide the two pills, 「その母はどうにも理解できないような曖昧な表情で、あげくの果てに弱々しい声で言った。『薬はもらって帰らずに、また次の週にここで飲ませてもらいます』」. The passage further explains: 「この土地では、多くの人が半分という概念を持てないのだという。」 The mother could not understand how much medicine to give because she had no concept of “half.”
default.q.n2-26-q73-73.verdict: The correct answer is 4: The author feels regret and thinks that if the mother had received an education, she would not have had to endure such hardship and inconvenience.
default.q.n2-26-q73-73.explanation:
- Main idea: The author feels heartbroken upon seeing a thin, malnourished mother walk 20 km round-trip simply because she is illiterate and does not understand the concept of "half," so she cannot divide the medicine for her child at home. This detail highlights the author's belief that a lack of education forces people to endure great hardship and inconvenience in their daily lives.
- Translation of the question: In the sentence, "If they had been able to bring the medicine home, they would not have had to suffer such hardship, but they were unable to do so," which statement best expresses the author's feelings at that moment?
- Translation of the answer choices:
  1. I think not having enough money to buy medicine is truly difficult.
  2. I think if a hospital had been built closer, they would not have had to go to a distant hospital.
  3. I feel sorry that no one taught them the word "half."
  4. I think if they had received an education, they would not have had to endure such hardship and inconvenience.
default.q.n2-26-q73-73.why.0: (a) Incorrect because the passage does not mention lacking money to buy medicine; it says that the person lacks the ability to understand the dosage and use the medicine independently at home.
default.q.n2-26-q73-73.why.1: (b) Incorrect because the author does not discuss building a hospital closer; the focus is the lack of education/illiteracy.
default.q.n2-26-q73-73.why.2: (c) Incorrect because the author is not discussing a shortage of specific vocabulary teachers, but recognizes it as a general educational issue in society.
default.q.n2-26-q73-73.why.3: (d) Correct. The story of a mother who had to walk 20 km simply because she could not read or understand the concept of “one half” illustrates the point made at the beginning of the passage: illiteracy is a social disease. The sentence 「薬を持って帰ればそんな思いをしなくてすむのに、それができないのである」 expresses the author’s sorrow that, if people had access to basic education, they would not have to endure such hardship and great inconvenience.
default.q.n2-26-q74-74.verdict: The correct answer is 2 (a computer class for people who have just started using computers, a cookbook written in English used as teaching material).
default.q.n2-26-q74-74.explanation:
**Main point and basis:**
The notice introduces courses for practical skills and hobbies:
- Computer class (パソコン教室): Intended for people who have only recently started learning to use a computer (パソコンを始めたばかりの人), not an advanced web-page creation class (ホームページを作る教室).
- English class (英語教室): Uses a cookbook written in English as the learning material (教材に英語で書かれた料理の本を使う), rather than being a cooking class conducted in English (英語を使って料理を作る教室).
- Therefore, choice 2 most accurately reflects the content of the notice.

**Question and answer choice translations:**
- **Question:** Which of the following matches the content of the notice?
- **Choice 1:** A computer class for people who are not very familiar with computers, an English cooking class, a beginner class…
- **Choice 2:** A computer class for people who have just started, using an English-language cookbook as the textbook…
- **Choice 3:** A computer class for creating web pages, and an English class using an English-language cookbook as the textbook…
- **Choice 4:** A computer class for creating web pages, an English cooking class, and a basic calligraphy class…
default.q.n2-26-q74-74.why.0: (a) Choice 1 is inaccurate because the English class is not a cooking class conducted in English (英語を使って料理を作る教室); it is an English class that uses cookbook materials.
default.q.n2-26-q74-74.why.1: (b) Correct because it accurately states the contents of the announcement: a computer class for beginners (パソコンを始めたばかりの人) and an English class that uses an English-language cookbook as its textbook.
default.q.n2-26-q74-74.why.2: (c) Choice 3 is incorrect because the computer class is intended for beginners, not a class for creating webpages (ホームページを作る教室).
default.q.n2-26-q74-74.why.3: (d) Choice 4 is incorrect because it confuses both the purpose of the computer class, which is not to create websites, and the English class, which is not an English cooking class.
default.q.n2-26-q75-75.verdict: The correct answer is 3 (授業料は書道教室が 2500 円で、それ以外は 1500 円、教材費は英語教室が 1000).
default.q.n2-26-q75-75.explanation:
**Summary and supporting evidence:**
Details about tuition (授業料) and textbook fees (教材費) in the notice:
- Tuition (授業料): The calligraphy class (書道教室) costs 2,500 yen; all other classes (それ以外) cost 1,500 yen.
- Textbook/materials fee (教材費): The English class (英語教室) has a textbook fee of 1,000 yen.
- Comparing the answer choices, choice 3 accurately and completely states all the listed costs.

**Translation of the question and answer choices:**
- **Question:** How much are the tuition and textbook fees?
- **Choice 1:** Tuition for all classes is 1,500 yen, the English class textbook fee is 1,000 yen, and the calligraphy class fee is 500 yen.
- **Choice 2:** Tuition for the calligraphy class is 2,500 yen, tuition for the other classes is 1,500 yen, and there is no textbook fee.
- **Choice 3:** Tuition for the calligraphy class is 2,500 yen, tuition for the other classes is 1,500 yen, and the English class textbook fee is 1,000 yen.
- **Choice 4:** Tuition for the calligraphy class is 1,800 yen, the other classes are free, and the textbook fee for all classes is 1,500 yen.
default.q.n2-26-q75-75.why.0: (a) Choice 1 is incorrect because the tuition is not a uniform 1,500 yen for every class—the calligraphy class costs 2,500 yen—and the stated textbook fee for the calligraphy class is also wrong.
default.q.n2-26-q75-75.why.1: (b) Answer choice 2 is incorrect because the English class charges 1,000 yen for teaching materials, rather than having no teaching-material fee (教材費はなし).
default.q.n2-26-q75-75.why.2: (c) Answer choice 3 is correct because it matches the fee table exactly: the calligraphy class costs 2,500 yen, the other classes cost 1,500 yen, and the English-class textbook costs 1,000 yen.
default.q.n2-26-q75-75.why.3: (d) Choice 4 is incorrect because it gives the wrong calligraphy-class fee (1,800 yen), incorrectly states that the other classes are free, and gives the wrong textbook fee.
default.q.n2-26-q11-11.verdict: The correct answer is 1. 性, forming the noun 自主性 (independence, self-motivation).
default.q.n2-26-q11-11.explanation:
Sentence meaning: This school respects the students’ independence.
- Kanji note: 自主性 means independence or a spirit of self-motivation.
- Example: 子どもの自主性を育てることが大切だ。(It is important to foster children’s independence.)
default.q.n2-26-q11-11.why.0: (a) Correct: The suffix 「〜性」 (性) is attached to nouns/adjectives to indicate a quality or characteristic, forming the noun 「自主性」, meaning "independence, self-motivation".
default.q.n2-26-q11-11.why.1: (b) Incorrect: 「流」 is an erroneous character, not a suffix used to form words in Japanese.
default.q.n2-26-q11-11.why.2: (c) Incorrect: The suffix 「〜的」 forms a na-adjective, as in 「自主的な行動」; it cannot directly precede the particle を as an object (自主的を尊重する is not possible).
default.q.n2-26-q11-11.why.3: (d) Incorrect. The suffix 「〜式」 indicates a method or style (such as 「日本式」 — Japanese style, and 「卒業式」 — graduation ceremony) and does not combine with 自主.
default.q.n2-26-q12-12.verdict: The correct answer is 2. つける, forming the compound verb 言いつける (to tell or report something to someone).
default.q.n2-26-q12-12.explanation:
Meaning: If you do something like that, I will tell the teacher on you.
- Common expression: 「先生に言いつける」 (to tell/report someone to the teacher).
- Example: 弟は母に僕のいたずらを言いつけた。(My younger brother told my mother about my prank.)
default.q.n2-26-q12-12.why.0: (a) Incorrect. 「言いかける」means “to be about to say something” or “to start saying something but stop,” which does not fit the context of having something reported to a teacher.
default.q.n2-26-q12-12.why.1: (b) Correct: 「言いつける」 (言い付ける) means “to tell a superior, teacher, or parent about someone’s wrongdoing.”
default.q.n2-26-q12-12.why.2: (c) Incorrect: 「言い出す」 means “to start saying something,” “to blurt out,” or “to propose something,” not to report someone's wrongdoing.
default.q.n2-26-q12-12.why.3: (d) Incorrect: 「言い残す」 means to leave words or a message before departing or dying, so it does not fit the context.
default.q.n2-26-q13-13.verdict: The correct answer is 2. 和, as in 和菓子 (traditional Japanese sweets).
default.q.n2-26-q13-13.explanation:
Sentence meaning: I prefer traditional Japanese sweets to cakes or ice cream.
- Vocabulary: 和菓子 (traditional Japanese sweets), contrasted with 洋菓子 (Western-style sweets).
- Example: お茶と一緒に和菓子をいただく。(I enjoy wagashi with tea.)
default.q.n2-26-q13-13.why.0: (a) Incorrect: 「洋菓子」means Western-style sweets, such as cakes and chocolate, whereas the preceding clause compares preferences with cake and ice cream. Therefore, 洋菓子 does not fit in the following clause.
default.q.n2-26-q13-13.why.1: (b) Correct: The prefix 「和〜」 means Japanese; 「和菓子」 refers to traditional Japanese sweets such as dango, mochi, and manju, clearly contrasting with Western sweets such as ケーキ and アイスクリーム.
default.q.n2-26-q13-13.why.2: (c) Incorrect: The prefix「西」(west) does not combine with 菓子 to form a word for confectionery; Japanese uses the prefix 洋 in 洋菓子.
default.q.n2-26-q13-13.why.3: (d) Incorrect: The prefix「東」is not used to create vocabulary classifying confectionery.
default.q.n2-26-q14-14.verdict: The correct answer is 3. 始めた, forming the compound verb 書き始めた (started writing).
default.q.n2-26-q14-14.explanation:
Meaning: I decided on a topic and started writing a report.
- Grammar: V-masu stem (remove ます) + 始める: to start carrying out an action.
- Example: 桜の花が咲き始めた。(The cherry blossoms have begun to bloom.)
default.q.n2-26-q14-14.why.0: (a) Incorrect: 「書き止める」 (かきとめる) means “to write down” or “to note for later,” not “to begin writing a report after choosing a topic.”
default.q.n2-26-q14-14.why.1: (b) Incorrect: 「止む」 (やむ) is an intransitive verb used for natural phenomena coming to an end (such as 雨が止む, “the rain stops”), and it cannot be placed directly after the V-masu form to express a human action.
default.q.n2-26-q14-14.why.2: (c) Correct: V-masu stem (ます removed) + 「始める」 (a transitive verb) forms a compound verb meaning “begin doing V.” Here, 「書き始めた」 means that the speaker began writing the report.
default.q.n2-26-q14-14.why.3: (d) Incorrect: 「始まる」 is an intransitive verb and cannot follow the ます-stem of a transitive verb to express the subject actively beginning an action; 「始める」 must be used.
default.q.n2-26-q15-15.verdict: The correct answer is 4. 方, forming 明け方 (early morning, dawn).
default.q.n2-26-q15-15.explanation:
- Meaning: At dawn, I heard birds singing.
- Kanji meaning: 明け方 (literally, “becoming light” - dawn, daybreak).
- Similar time expressions: 夕方 (ゆうがた - evening), 昼頃 (ひるごろ - around noon).
- Example: 明け方に強い雨が降った。(There was heavy rain at dawn.)
default.q.n2-26-q15-15.why.0: (a) Incorrect: 「前」does not follow 明け- to form *明け前. The correct expression for “before dawn” is「夜明け前」(よあけまえ).
default.q.n2-26-q15-15.why.1: (b) Incorrect: 「ころ」 (頃) is a supplementary noun that normally follows a complete time expression, such as 明け方のころ, and cannot be attached directly to form *明けころ.
default.q.n2-26-q15-15.why.2: (c) Incorrect: 「時」does not combine directly with 明け- to form a fixed vocabulary word.
default.q.n2-26-q15-15.why.3: (d) Correct: The suffix 「〜方」 combines with the verb stem of 明ける (for the sky to become light) to form the fixed noun 「明け方」 (あけがた), meaning “dawn” or “early morning.”
default.q.n2-26-q16-16.explanation:
- Meaning: Because the electricity bill is high, I am careful not to waste electricity.
- Vocabulary: 無駄 (wasteful, waste), 無料 (free of charge), 無理 (unreasonable, beyond one's capacity).
- Example: 部屋を出るときは電気を消して、むだな電気を使わないようにしましょう。(Turn off the lights when leaving the room so that you do not waste electricity.)
default.q.n2-26-q16-16.why.0: (a) 無料 means “free of charge” and is a noun; it does not combine as 「無料な」 to modify electricity in this context.
default.q.n2-26-q16-16.why.1: (b) 無理 (too much, unreasonable, forced): a na-adjective commonly used for something excessive or beyond one's ability; it does not fit the meaning of wasting electricity.
default.q.n2-26-q16-16.why.2: (c) むだ (wasteful, useless): A na-adjective written with the kanji 無駄. むだな電気 means “wasteful/useless use of electricity,” which fits perfectly with the context of high electricity bills and the need to conserve power.
default.q.n2-26-q16-16.why.3: (d) むれ (a flock, herd, group): A noun (kanji: 群れ) referring to a group of animals or people; it does not fit the context.
default.q.n2-26-q17-17.verdict: The correct answer is 2 (恵まれた).
default.q.n2-26-q17-17.explanation:
- Meaning: Gifted with talent, Mr./Ms. Sato became a famous pianist at the age of ten.
- Vocabulary and grammar: 恵まれる (to be blessed or gifted; the pattern 〜に恵まれる means to be blessed with or favored with...), 才能 (talent).
- Example: 彼女は音楽の才能に恵まれている。(She is blessed with musical talent.)
default.q.n2-26-q17-17.why.0: (a) 豊富な (“abundant,” “ample”): a na-adjective that commonly takes が, as in 「才能が豊富な佐藤さん」, rather than 「〜に豊富な」.
default.q.n2-26-q17-17.why.1: (b) 恵まれた (blessed with, gifted with): The verb 恵まれる (めぐまれる) is used with the pattern 〜に恵まれる; 才能に恵まれた means “gifted with talent,” and is completely accurate both grammatically and semantically.
default.q.n2-26-q17-17.why.2: (c) 与えられた (given, assigned): the passive form of 与える, commonly used when something is given or entrusted to someone; it does not combine naturally with 才能に.
default.q.n2-26-q17-17.why.3: (d) あった (there was/possessed): It normally takes が (“才能があった”). If used with “才能にあった,” it would mean “suited to one’s talent,” which does not fit the context.
default.q.n2-26-q18-18.verdict: The correct answer is 2 (みっともない).
default.q.n2-26-q18-18.explanation:
- Translation: Wearing old shoes like that to a wedding is very shabby and embarrassing.
- Related vocabulary: みっともない (unsightly, embarrassing, sloppy), 見苦しい (unpleasant to look at, unsightly).
- Example: 人前でそんなみっともない格好をしないでください。(Please don't dress so sloppily in front of other people.)
default.q.n2-26-q18-18.why.0: (a) みにくい (ugly / difficult to see): It is written as 醜い when meaning physically unattractive, or 見にくい when meaning difficult to see. It is not used to describe an appearance or outfit that causes embarrassment at a formal event.
default.q.n2-26-q18-18.why.1: (b) みっともない (unseemly, shabby, embarrassing): Used for behavior, clothing, or appearance that is inappropriate and causes embarrassment or loss of face in a particular situation, such as wearing badly worn shoes to a wedding. This is completely accurate.
default.q.n2-26-q18-18.why.2: (c) ものすごい means tremendous, extraordinary, or intense; it does not fit the context.
default.q.n2-26-q18-18.why.3: (d) めんどうくさい: An adjective describing reluctance to do something because it is complicated or troublesome; it does not fit the context.
default.q.n2-26-q19-19.explanation:
- Meaning: Some fragrances have a calming or relaxing effect.
- Kanji meaning: 香り (fragrance), 落ち着く (calm down, become relaxed).
- Example: ラベンダーの香りには、心を落ち着かせる効果がある。(The scent of lavender has a calming effect on the mind.)
default.q.n2-26-q19-19.why.0: (a) かざり (decoration): A noun written 飾り, referring to an object used for decoration; it does not have the effect of soothing one's mood like a fragrance.
default.q.n2-26-q19-19.why.1: (b) こおり (ice, ice block): a noun (kanji: 氷), and does not mean to soothe someone’s mood in this context.
default.q.n2-26-q19-19.why.2: (c) かおり (fragrance, scent): a noun, written with the kanji 香り or 芳り. In aromatherapy, fragrance has a soothing effect on the mind, so this is completely correct.
default.q.n2-26-q19-19.why.3: (d) か山り: This is not a Japanese word (a typing error).
default.q.n2-26-q20-20.verdict: The correct answer is 4 (イメージ).
default.q.n2-26-q20-20.explanation:
- Meaning: These clothes do not suit your image or style.
- Katakana vocabulary: イメージ (image: image, style, impression), エチケット (etiquette: etiquette), シーズン (season: season).
- Example: その髪型は彼女のイメージにぴったり合っている。(That hairstyle suits her image perfectly.)
default.q.n2-26-q20-20.why.0: (a) シーズン (season): This usually refers to a season of the year or a sports season, and does not naturally combine with “君のシーズン.”
default.q.n2-26-q20-20.why.1: (b) エチケット (etiquette, rules of politeness): It refers to manners in public settings and is not used in 「君のエチケットに合わない」 to comment on clothing.
default.q.n2-26-q20-20.why.2: (c) イコール (equal, an equals sign, equivalent): Used in mathematics or to express an equivalence relationship such as A = B; it does not fit the context.
default.q.n2-26-q20-20.why.3: (d) イメージ (image, impression, style): 「君のイメージに合わない」 means “does not suit your image or style,” which is natural and accurate.
default.q.n2-26-q21-21.verdict: The correct answer is 1 (もぐると).
default.q.n2-26-q21-21.explanation:
- Meaning: When you dive into the warm sea, many beautiful fish are swimming around.
- Kanji and verbs: 潜る (もぐる) means to dive, 浮かぶ (うかぶ) means to float, and 沈む (しずむ) means to sink.
- Example: 彼は海に潜ってきれいな魚の写真を撮った。(He dived into the sea to photograph beautiful fish.)
default.q.n2-26-q21-21.why.0: (a) もぐると (when diving down): The verb 潜る (もぐる), as in 「海の中に潜る」, means to dive deep into the sea to observe marine life, which fits perfectly with the context of seeing many beautiful fish.
default.q.n2-26-q21-21.why.1: (b) うかぶと (when it floats up): The verb 浮かぶ (うかぶ) means “to float on the surface of the water” (often used with 海に浮かぶ), so it does not fit entering the sea to look at fish ('海の中に').
default.q.n2-26-q21-21.why.2: (c) しずむと (when it sinks): The verb 沈む (しずむ) means to sink or become submerged, as with a sinking ship. It does not describe actively diving to explore.
default.q.n2-26-q21-21.why.3: (d) はいると (when entering): 入る (はいる) and 海に入る generally mean entering or going into the sea, but with 海の中に〜 to describe seeing fish underwater, もぐる is much more precise and natural.
default.q.n2-26-q22-22.verdict: The correct answer is 1 (サークル).
default.q.n2-26-q22-22.explanation:
- Translation: I am participating in a tennis club.
- Katakana vocabulary: サークル (circle - an interest club or extracurricular group), クラブ (club), コンクール (competition in the arts), コンサート (concert).
- Example: 大学に入ったら、写真のサークルに入りたい。(When I enter university, I want to join a photography club.)
default.q.n2-26-q22-22.why.0: (a) サークル (circle: a club or extracurricular group): Used for sports and hobby clubs at universities or in the community. The phrase 'サークルに入る' means to join a club, so this is entirely correct.
default.q.n2-26-q22-22.why.1: (b) コンクール (concours; a music or art competition): a French-derived word referring to competitions in music, painting, or the arts. It is not used to mean regularly participating in a club.
default.q.n2-26-q22-22.why.2: (c) サービス (service, complimentary offer): Used for service or a free extra; it does not fit the context.
default.q.n2-26-q22-22.why.3: (d) コンサート (concert): A musical performance; it cannot combine with テニス to mean “a tennis concert.”
default.q.n2-26-q23-23.verdict: The correct answer is 1: 不安だ.
default.q.n2-26-q23-23.explanation:
- Sentence translation: Living alone for the first time feels very unsettling and frightening.
- Vocabulary: 「心細い」（こころぼそい）: feeling anxious and vulnerable because of being alone and having no one to rely on; 「一人暮らし」（ひとりぐらし）: living alone.
- Example: 見知らぬ土地で一人で夜道を歩くのは心細い。(Walking alone at night in an unfamiliar place feels very unsettling.)
default.q.n2-26-q23-23.why.0: (a) Correct because 「心細い」describes an uneasy, anxious, fearful feeling caused by loneliness or a lack of support, and is synonymous with 「不安だ」 (“anxious” or “uneasy”).
default.q.n2-26-q23-23.why.1: (b) Incorrect because 「さびしい」(寂しい) describes ordinary feelings of loneliness or sadness, without the nuance of fear or insecurity caused by lacking support, as in 「心細い」.
default.q.n2-26-q23-23.why.2: (c) Incorrect because 「つらい」（辛い） means bitter, painful, or difficult, describing physical or emotional suffering under pressure.
default.q.n2-26-q23-23.why.3: (d) Incorrect because 「不要心」 does not mean psychological anxiety. The commonly used correct spelling is 「不用心」, meaning careless, heedless, or off guard.
default.q.n2-26-q24-24.verdict: The correct answer is 3: 静かに.
default.q.n2-26-q24-24.explanation:
- Sentence translation: I gently closed the door.
- Vocabulary: 「そっと」: gently, softly, quietly (so as not to make a sound or disturb someone).
- Example: 赤ちゃんを起こさないように、そっと部屋を出た。(I quietly left the room so as not to wake the baby.)
default.q.n2-26-q24-24.why.0: (a) Incorrect because 「きちんと」 means properly, neatly, or tidily (e.g., closing a door securely without leaving it ajar).
default.q.n2-26-q24-24.why.1: (b) Incorrect because 「しっかりと」means firmly, securely, or reliably.
default.q.n2-26-q24-24.why.2: (c) Correct because 「そっと」describes closing a door gently and quietly so as not to make noise, synonymous with 「静かに」(quietly, softly).
default.q.n2-26-q24-24.why.3: (d) Incorrect. 「素早く」 means quickly or swiftly and has nothing to do with reducing noise or acting gently.
default.q.n2-26-q25-25.verdict: The correct answer is 2: つめたい.
default.q.n2-26-q25-25.explanation:
- Sentence translation: I received only a cold / curt reply from him.
- Vocabulary and kanji: 「そっけない」（素っ気ない - cold, curt, indifferent）, 「返事」（へんじ - reply, response）.
- Example: 彼女に相談したが、そっけない態度を取られた。（I consulted her, but she responded with a very cold attitude.）
default.q.n2-26-q25-25.why.0: (a) Incorrect because 「あじけない」（味気ない） means dull, bland, or tedious, often describing an uninteresting life or stretch of days.
default.q.n2-26-q25-25.why.1: (b) Correct because 「そっけない」 describes a cold, indifferent attitude or manner of speaking that lacks warmth or goodwill, and is synonymous with 「つめたい」（冷たい - cold, unfeeling）.
default.q.n2-26-q25-25.why.2: (c) Incorrect because 「やるせない」（遣る瀬ない）means deeply melancholy or sorrowful, with no one to confide in or seek comfort from.
default.q.n2-26-q25-25.why.3: (d) Incorrect because 「きどらない」 (気取らない) means natural, unpretentious, and not affected or pretentious.
default.q.n2-26-q26-26.verdict: The correct answer is 4: まじめに.
default.q.n2-26-q26-26.explanation:
- Sentence translation: I am thinking seriously about the future.
- Vocabulary and kanji: 「真剣」（しんけん: serious, earnest; originally meaning a real sword), 「将来」（しょうらい: future).
- Example: 彼は真剣な目つきで話を聞いていた。(He listened attentively with a very serious look in his eyes.)
default.q.n2-26-q26-26.why.0: (a) Incorrect because 「熱心に」 means enthusiastically, diligently, or devotedly putting effort into a specific activity, such as studying or research.
default.q.n2-26-q26-26.why.1: (b) Incorrect because「重要に」is not a natural adverbial expression modifying the verb「考える」.
default.q.n2-26-q26-26.why.2: (c) Incorrect because 「ていねいに」 (丁寧) means politely, courteously, carefully, or attentively.
default.q.n2-26-q26-26.why.3: (d) Correct because 「真剣に」 means seriously and earnestly, without joking, and is synonymous with 「まじめに」(真面目).
default.q.n2-26-q27-27.verdict: The correct answer is 2: 意図的に.
default.q.n2-26-q27-27.explanation:
- Translation: I was scolded for intentionally throwing the ball at someone.
- Vocabulary: 「わざと」(intentionally, deliberately), 「意図的」(いとてき, intentional, deliberate), 「ぶつける」(to hit or throw something at), 「叱られる」(しかられる, to be scolded).
- Example: わざと負けて相手に花を持たせた。(I deliberately lost to let my opponent have the glory.)
default.q.n2-26-q27-27.why.0: (a) Incorrect because 「わざわざ」means taking the trouble to do something, emphasizing the effort spent on an action that was not required.
default.q.n2-26-q27-27.why.1: (b) Correct because 「わざと」means intentionally or deliberately doing something, often something negative or undesirable, and is synonymous with 「意図的に」(deliberately, with intent).
default.q.n2-26-q27-27.why.3: (d) Incorrect because 「積極的に」 means actively, proactively, or enthusiastically participating.
default.q.n2-26-q28-28.verdict: The correct answer is sentence 4: 就職できなかったことが自分で事業を始める 契機 になった。
default.q.n2-26-q28-28.explanation:
「契機」（けいき）means an opportunity, motivation, or turning point that drives a major change or initiates a new event. It is often used in written or formal contexts in forms such as 「〜を契機に（して）」 and 「〜が契機となって／契機になる」.
Example: オリンピック開催を契機に、街の再開発が一気に進んだ。(The redevelopment of the city advanced rapidly בעקבות the hosting of the Olympics.)
default.q.n2-26-q28-28.why.0: Incorrect because the sentence describes a company rule or regulation (not being allowed to work overtime), so a word such as 「決まり」 or 「規則」 should be used instead of 「契機」.
default.q.n2-26-q28-28.why.1: Incorrect because the sentence describes a physical event that happened unexpectedly at the same time as the plane landed. 「拍子に」(just as...) or 「瞬間に」should be used, whereas 「契機」is not used for a random moment like this.
default.q.n2-26-q28-28.why.2: Incorrect because the sentence describes an ordinary occasion, whenever one goes out, so「際は」or「時は」should be used instead of「契機」, which refers to a major turning point.
default.q.n2-26-q28-28.why.3: Correct because 「契機になる」is a standard structure meaning that an event becomes an opportunity or turning point that prompts a new action—in this case, being unable to find a job becomes the turning point for starting a business.
default.q.n2-26-q29-29.verdict: The correct answer is sentence 1: 当社では経験や年齢を 考慮 して給料を計算します。
default.q.n2-26-q29-29.explanation:
「考慮」（こうりょ）means to consider, take into account, or weigh various aspects and factors before making a decision or solving a problem. It is commonly used in 「〜を考慮する」 and 「〜を考慮に入れる」.
Example: 周囲の状況を十分に考慮した上で、計画を変更した。(After carefully taking the surrounding circumstances into account, we changed the plan.)
default.q.n2-26-q29-29.why.0: Correct because 「〜を考慮して」is the standard expression meaning to consider or take factors into account (such as experience and age) when making a decision or calculation.
default.q.n2-26-q29-29.why.1: Incorrect because to say “please don’t be shy” when offering food or drink, use 「遠慮」（遠慮しないで）, not 「考慮」.
default.q.n2-26-q29-29.why.2: Incorrect because consideration and understanding of another person's feelings are expressed with 「配慮」（はいりょ）or「気遣い」, whereas 「考慮」is used when weighing or calculating objective factors.
default.q.n2-26-q29-29.why.3: Incorrect. The compound meaning thoughtful and careful is 「思慮深い」(しりょぶかい); Japanese does not use 「考慮深い」.
default.q.n2-26-q30-30.verdict: The correct answer is 2: その法律は日本以外の国では 効力 がない。
default.q.n2-26-q30-30.explanation:
「効力」（こうりょく）means legal force, validity, or the practical effect of a law, regulation, treaty, or contract. Common expressions include: 「効力がある／ない」「効力を失う（失効）」「効力が発生する（発効）」.
Example: 契約書に署名捺印した時点で、その契約は効力を持つ。（The contract becomes legally valid once it has been signed and sealed.）
default.q.n2-26-q30-30.why.0: Incorrect because when referring to the period during which a document remains valid (five years), the correct term is 「有効期間」 (or 「有効期限」), not 「効力」.
default.q.n2-26-q30-30.why.1: Correct because 「効力」 means legal force or effect and is used with 「効力がある／効力がない」 to express whether a law is legally effective.
default.q.n2-26-q30-30.why.2: Incorrect. To refer to work efficiency/productivity, use 「効率」(こうりつ) or 「能率」, not 「効力」.
default.q.n2-26-q30-30.why.3: Incorrect because 「適性」（てきせい）or 「能力」 should be used to express suitability or aptitude for a job, not 「効力」.
default.q.n2-26-q31-31.verdict: The correct answer is 3: 人種による 差別 は今もどこの国でも残っている。
default.q.n2-26-q31-31.explanation:
「差別」（さべつ）means discrimination or unfair prejudice based on assumptions about gender, race, background, status, and so on (such as 「人種差別」「性差別」「差別待遇」). It can also mean distinguishing clear differences, as in 「差別化」 in business.
Example: 性別や国籍による差別は決して許されない。(Discrimination based on gender or nationality is absolutely unacceptable.)
default.q.n2-26-q31-31.why.0: Incorrect because expressing the differences or individual traits that each person has requires「違い」「個性」or「差異」, not「差別」.
default.q.n2-26-q31-31.why.1: Incorrect because waste sorting according to regulations uses 「分別」 (ゴミの分別), not 「差別」.
default.q.n2-26-q31-31.why.2: Correct because 「差別」describes discriminatory or unfair treatment based on social prejudice, and 「人種による差別」(racial discrimination) is a standard usage.
default.q.n2-26-q31-31.why.3: Incorrect because identifying or distinguishing things by their features, such as birdsong, requires 「識別」（しきべつ）or 「区別」, not 「差別」.
default.q.n2-26-q32-32.verdict: The correct answer is sentence 4: 報告書を ざっと 見たけど、特に問題はなさそうだね。
default.q.n2-26-q32-32.explanation:
「ざっと」is an adverb with two main meanings:
1. To look at, read, or do something roughly or quickly, without examining it carefully: 「ざっと目を通す」「ざっと見る」「ざっと説明する」.
2. Approximately or roughly, used with an estimated quantity: 「ざっと100人」「ざっと見積もる」.
Example: 書類にざっと目を通してから、会議に出席した。(I skimmed the documents before attending the meeting.)
default.q.n2-26-q32-32.why.0: Incorrect because 「ざっと」 is used to estimate an approximate figure (around 5,000 yen), so it cannot be used with an exact amount such as 「4981 円」.
default.q.n2-26-q32-32.why.1: Incorrect. To describe the startled, frightened feeling of suddenly being called from behind, use 「ぞっとした」('it sent a shiver down my spine'), 「ぎょっとした」, or 「びくっとした」, not 「ざっとした」.
default.q.n2-26-q32-32.why.2: The usage is incorrect: eating quickly and efficiently to make it on time is expressed with 「さっと」 (or 「手早く」「急いで」), whereas 「ざっと」 does not combine with eating or drinking actions.
default.q.n2-26-q32-32.why.3: Correct because 「ざっと見る／ざっと目を通す」 are standard expressions meaning to skim or give a document a preliminary check without examining the details closely.
default.q.n2-26-q1-1.verdict: The correct answer is 3 (きょだいな).
default.q.n2-26-q1-1.explanation:
Meaning of the sentence: "I hear that a gigantic creature lives in this lake."
- Example: 巨大な船が港に入ってきた。(A gigantic ship entered the harbor.)
default.q.n2-26-q1-1.why.0: (a) Incorrect because the Sino-Japanese reading of 巨 is きょ, without a long vowel; きょうだい is the reading of 兄弟.
default.q.n2-26-q1-1.why.1: (b) Incorrect because 巨 does not have the reading ぐ (ぐ is the on-reading of 具 in 具体 - ぐたい).
