default.q.n2-37-q32-32.why.3: Incorrect because an attitude toward work requires enthusiasm and a sense of responsibility, so use「情熱 / やる気 / 責任感 (を持っている)」, not「ユーモアを持っている」.
default.q.n2-37-q1-1.verdict: The correct answer is 1. いはん.
default.q.n2-37-q1-1.explanation:
Meaning: "Throwing garbage into the river is against the law."
Sino-Japanese reading: 違反 (violation, infringement of regulations).
The kanji 「違」 has the on-reading イ (as in 違反 - いはん and 相違 - そうい) and the kun-reading ちが・う. The kanji 「反」 has the on-reading ハン (as in 反対 - はんたい).
Example: スピード違反で警察に捕まった。(I was arrested by the police for speeding.)
default.q.n2-37-q1-1.why.0: (a) Correct. 「違反」 is correctly read as 「いはん」 (violation).
default.q.n2-37-q1-1.why.1: (b) Incorrect. The on-reading of 「違」 is 「い」; it does not have the long-vowel reading 「いい」.
default.q.n2-37-q1-1.why.2: (c) Incorrect. 「反」(はん) does not undergo sound change to the semi-voiced 「ぱん」 in this word.
default.q.n2-37-q1-1.why.3: (d) Incorrect. 「いっぱん」 is the reading of 「一般」(ordinary, common), not the reading of 「違反」.
default.q.n2-37-q2-2.verdict: The correct answer is 1. しゅのう.
default.q.n2-37-q2-2.explanation:
Meaning of the sentence: "It is rumored that the leaders of the two countries will hold talks soon."
Sino-Japanese reading: 首脳 (THỦ NÃO — head, leader, national leader).
The kanji 「首」(THỦ) has the on-reading シュ (as in 首相 - しゅしょう, 首都 - しゅと) and the kun-reading くび. The kanji 「脳」(NÃO) has the on-reading ノウ (as in 頭脳 - ずのう, 洗脳 - せんのう).
Example: 主要国の首脳が集まるサミットが開かれた。(A summit attended by the leaders of major countries was held.)
default.q.n2-37-q2-2.why.0: (a) Correct. 「首脳」is correctly read as 「しゅのう」(head of state, leader).
default.q.n2-37-q2-2.why.1: (b) Incorrect. The On-reading of 「首」 is 「しゅ」; it is not lengthened to the long vowel 「しゅう」.
default.q.n2-37-q2-2.why.2: (c) Incorrect. 「しゅしょう」 is the reading of 「首相」(prime minister); 「脳」(のう) has been confused with 「相」(しょう).
default.q.n2-37-q2-2.why.3: (d) Incorrect. Both kanji are misread: the long vowel in 「首」 is changed to しゅう, and 「脳」 is read as しょう.
default.q.n2-37-q3-3.verdict: The correct answer is 2. かんづめ.
default.q.n2-37-q3-3.explanation:
Meaning of the sentence: “If you eat nothing but canned food and frozen foods, it isn’t good for your health.”
Kanji compound: 缶詰 (canned food).
The kanji 「缶」 has the on-reading カン (as in 空き缶 - あきかん and 缶ビール - かんびーる). The kanji 「詰」 has the kun-reading つ・める; when it appears at the end of a compound, the sound often becomes voiced as 「づめ」.
Example: 非常用にマグロの缶詰を買い置きしている。(I keep canned tuna stocked for emergencies.)
default.q.n2-37-q3-3.why.0: (a) Incorrect. In the compound noun 「缶詰」, 「詰」(つめ) undergoes rendaku and becomes 「づめ」.
default.q.n2-37-q3-3.why.1: (b) Correct. 「缶詰」 is correctly read 「かんづめ」 (canned food).
default.q.n2-37-q3-3.why.2: (c) Incorrect. It confuses 「缶」(かん, can/tin) with 「瓶」(びん, bottle) and has not applied the voiced sound change in 「つめ」.
default.q.n2-37-q3-3.why.3: (d) Incorrect. 「びんづめ」 is the reading of 「瓶詰」 (food bottled or packed in glass jars), not 「缶詰」.
default.q.n2-37-q4-4.verdict: The correct answer is 1. ばくはつ.
default.q.n2-37-q4-4.explanation:
Meaning: “Materials were distributed about the possibility of a gas explosion in the event of an earthquake.”
Kanji readings: 爆発 (BẠO PHÁT - explosion, detonation).
The character 「爆」(BẠO/BỘC) has the on-reading バク (as in 爆破 - ばくは, 爆弾 - ばくだん). The character 「発」(PHÁT) has the on-reading ハツ (as in 発生 - はっせい, 発見 - はっけん).
Example: 工場で爆発事故が起き、多くのけが人が出た。(An explosion occurred at the factory, injuring many people.)
default.q.n2-37-q4-4.why.0: (a) Correct. 「爆発」is correctly read 「ばくはつ」 and means “explosion” or “to explode.”
default.q.n2-37-q4-4.why.1: (b) Incorrect. The on-reading of 「爆」is 「ばく」, not 「ぼく」.
default.q.n2-37-q4-4.why.2: (c) Incorrect. The 「発」 in this word uses the Kan-on reading 「はつ」, not the Go-on reading 「ほつ」, as in 発作 - ほっさ and 発起 - ほっき.
default.q.n2-37-q4-4.why.3: (d) Incorrect. The on-readings of both kanji are wrong: 「爆」 is changed to ぼく and 「発」 to ほつ.
default.q.n2-37-q5-5.verdict: The correct answer is 4. ねつえん.
default.q.n2-37-q5-5.explanation:
Meaning of the sentence: "The pianist with the most passionate performance won first place in the competition."
Sino-Japanese vocabulary: 熱演 (ねつえん — passionate, wholehearted performance).
The kanji 「熱」(ねつ) has the on-reading ネツ (as in 熱心 — ねっしん, 情熱 — じょうねつ) and the kun-reading あつ・い. The kanji 「演」(えん) has the on-reading エン (as in 演技 — えんぎ, 演奏 — えんそう).
Example: 彼の熱演に観客から惜しみない拍手が送られた。(The audience gave his wholehearted performance a tremendous round of applause.)
default.q.n2-37-q5-5.why.0: (a) Incorrect. 「めいえん」 is the reading of 「名演」(an outstanding performance); the first kanji is 「名」, not 「熱」.
default.q.n2-37-q5-5.why.1: (b) 「きょうえん」is the reading of 「共演」(performing together) or 「競演」(competing performances).
default.q.n2-37-q5-5.why.2: (c) Incorrect. 「こうえん」 is the reading of 「公演」(public performance) or 「講演」(lecture).
default.q.n2-37-q5-5.why.3: (d) Correct. 「熱演」 is correctly read as 「ねつえん」 and means a passionate performance.
default.q.n2-37-q6-6.verdict: The correct answer is 3. 県庁 (the prefectural government office).
default.q.n2-37-q6-6.explanation:
- Meaning: People going to the prefectural government office are having trouble because the parking lot is too small.
- Kanji-derived meaning: 県庁 (kenchō) = prefectural government office / prefectural government building.
- Example: 彼は県庁に勤める公務員です。(He is a civil servant who works at the prefectural government office.)
default.q.n2-37-q6-6.why.0: (a) 「見庁」: The first kanji is incorrect. 「見」 (KIẾN) has the on-reading 「けん」 and means seeing or looking, so it does not form this word.
default.q.n2-37-q6-6.why.1: (b) 「原庁」: The first kanji is incorrect. 「原」has the on-reading 「げん」, not 「けん」, and does not form this word.
default.q.n2-37-q6-6.why.2: (c) 「県庁」: Correct. 「県」 is read as 「けん」 and 「庁」 as 「ちょう」, forming 「県庁」 (けんちょう), meaning a prefectural government or prefectural administrative office.
default.q.n2-37-q6-6.why.3: (d) 「厚庁」: The first kanji is incorrect. 「厚」 has a component visually similar to 「県」, which can cause confusion, but its on-reading is 「こう」.
default.q.n2-37-q7-7.verdict: The correct answer is 2. 偶然 (by chance, accidental).
default.q.n2-37-q7-7.explanation:
- Meaning: Yesterday, I happened to run into an old friend at the ticket gate.
- Kanji-derived meaning: 偶然 (gūzen) = by chance, accidentally. The antonym is 必然 (ひつぜん, inevitable).
- Example: 旅先で偶然、昔の同僚に出会った。(I happened to run into a former colleague while traveling.)
default.q.n2-37-q7-7.why.0: (a) 「寓然」: the first kanji is incorrect. 「寓」 has the same on-reading 「ぐう」, but means lodging or allegory, as in 寓話 (ぐうわ); it is not used in the word meaning “accidental” or “random.”
default.q.n2-37-q7-7.why.1: (b) 「偶然」: Correct. 「偶」 is read as 「ぐう」 and 「然」 as 「ぜん」, forming 「偶然」(ぐうぜん: by chance, accidentally).
default.q.n2-37-q7-7.why.2: (c) 「隅然」: The first kanji is incorrect. 「隅」(corner, nook) has the on-reading 「ぐう」and kun-reading 「すみ」, and is not used to form this word.
default.q.n2-37-q7-7.why.3: (d) 「伝然」: The first kanji is incorrect. 「伝」 has the on-reading 「でん」, not 「ぐう」.
default.q.n2-37-q8-8.verdict: The correct answer is 3. 招待 (to invite, invitation).
default.q.n2-37-q8-8.explanation:
- Meaning: When I was invited to a celebration party, drinks were served.
- Kanji note: 招待 means invitation, inviting, or entertaining guests.
- Example: 誕生パーティーに親しい友人を招待した。(I invited close friends to my birthday party.)
default.q.n2-37-q8-8.why.0: (a) 「紹待」: Incorrect first kanji. 「紹」, as in 紹介, has been mistakenly combined with「待」.
default.q.n2-37-q8-8.why.1: (b) 「紹介」: Incorrect word. 「紹介」is read as 「しょうかい」and means “introduction,” not 「しょうたい」.
default.q.n2-37-q8-8.why.2: (c) 「招待」: Correct. 「招」 (to invite) is read as 「しょう」 and 「待」 (to receive or entertain) as 「たい」, forming 「招待」 (しょうたい: to invite, entertain).
default.q.n2-37-q8-8.why.3: (d) 「招介」: Incorrect kanji in the second position. 「介」 does not combine with 「招」 to form a word with this meaning.
default.q.n2-37-q9-9.verdict: The correct answer is 1. 岸 (riverbank, seashore, bank).
default.q.n2-37-q9-9.explanation:
- Translation: The bank is covered entirely with rocks, and flowers are in full bloom.
- Sino-Japanese note: 岸 (がん) = a riverbank, seashore, or waterside. Common compounds include 海岸 (かいがん: seashore) and 対岸 (たいがん: the opposite bank).
- Example: 川の岸に腰を下ろして、流れる水を見ていた。(I sat down on the riverbank and watched the flowing water.)
default.q.n2-37-q9-9.why.0: (a) 「岸」: Correct. The kun-reading of 「岸」 is 「きし」, meaning a riverbank, seashore, or strip of land along the water’s edge.
default.q.n2-37-q9-9.why.1: (b) 「崖」: Incorrect. 「崖」 means a steep cliff and has the kun-reading 「がけ」, not 「きし」.
default.q.n2-37-q9-9.why.2: (c) 「砂」: Incorrect. The kanji 「砂」 (sand) has the Kun-reading 「すな」, not 「きし」.
default.q.n2-37-q9-9.why.3: (d) 「炭」: Incorrect. 「炭」 means charcoal or coal and has the kun-reading 「すみ」, not 「きし」.
default.q.n2-37-q10-10.explanation:
- Meaning: There are many slopes on the outskirts of this town, as well as lakes and ponds, so the scenery is beautiful.
- Kanji note: 湖 means a large lake. Common compounds include 湖畔 (こはん — lakeside) and 琵琶湖 (びわこ — Lake Biwa).
- Example: 家族と一緒に湖の周りをサイクリングした。(I cycled around the lake with my family.)
default.q.n2-37-q10-10.why.0: (a) 「池」: Incorrect. 「池」 (pond) has the kun-reading 「いけ」, which is the 「いけ」 appearing later in the question.
default.q.n2-37-q10-10.why.1: (b) 「湖」: Correct. 「湖」 has the kun-reading 「みずうみ」 (large lake) and the on-reading 「こ」.
default.q.n2-37-q10-10.why.2: (c) 「泉」: Incorrect. The kanji 「泉」 means a spring or water source and has the kun-reading 「いずみ」; it is not read 「みずうみ」.
default.q.n2-37-q10-10.why.3: (d) 「潮」 is incorrect. The kanji 「潮」 means tide or seawater and has the kun-reading 「しお」, not 「みずうみ」.
default.q.n2-38-q33-33.verdict: The correct answer is 3. ほど.
default.q.n2-38-q33-33.explanation:
- Meaning: “It is probably because it is inexpensive yet good quality. This product sells surprisingly well.”
- Expression: 「おもしろいほど（よく売れる／釣れる…）」: to sell or catch fish in strangely or unexpectedly large quantities.
- Example: 練習した成果が出て、おもしろいほど点が取れるようになった。(My practice paid off, and I began getting surprisingly high scores.)
default.q.n2-38-q33-33.why.0: (a) 「だけ」 means “only” and does not combine with an adjective to create an expression indicating the degree of surprise shown in the sentence.
default.q.n2-38-q33-33.why.1: (b) 「こそ」 is used for emphasis (“precisely because...”); it does not create a degree expression with 「おもしろい」.
default.q.n2-38-q33-33.why.2: (c) 「ほど」 combines to form the idiomatic expression 「おもしろいほど」, meaning “to an astonishing or unbelievable extent,” which is very suitable for describing how unexpectedly fast the products sold.
default.q.n2-38-q33-33.why.3: (d) 「たび」 means “each time...,” and does not combine with the adjective 「おもしろい」 to express degree.
default.q.n2-38-q34-34.verdict: The correct answer is 2. のみならず.
default.q.n2-38-q34-34.explanation:
- Meaning: “His research is highly valued not only by specialists but also by ordinary people.”
- Pattern: `N / plain form + のみならず、～も` (not only... but also...).
- Sino-Japanese readings: 専門家 (せんもんか: specialist, expert), 評価 (ひょうか: evaluation, appreciation).
- Example: この映画は日本のみならず、世界中で大ヒットしている。(This film is a huge hit not only in Japan but throughout the world.)
default.q.n2-38-q34-34.why.0: (a) 「にかかわらず」(printed incorrectly in the question as にかか山らず) means "regardless of..." and does not combine with the following 「...にも」structure to express an added point.
default.q.n2-38-q34-34.why.1: (b) 「～のみならず（～も）」means “not only... but also...,” expressing that the research was highly regarded by both specialists and the general public.
default.q.n2-38-q34-34.why.2: (c) 「～をぬきにして」means “excluding / leaving aside...,” so it does not fit a context involving a positive evaluation of both objects.
default.q.n2-38-q34-34.why.3: (d) 「～にかぎって」 means “only,” and does not fit a context listing additional items such as “A and also B.”
default.q.n2-38-q35-35.verdict: The correct answer is 3. 反面.
default.q.n2-38-q35-35.explanation:
- Meaning: “The Internet provides us with a great deal of information, but on the other hand, it can also have a harmful effect on society.”
- Pattern: `Plain form (Na な/である, N である) + 反面` (“on the other hand,” “whereas” — expresses two contrasting sides of the same issue).
- Vocabulary: 反面 (opposite side, downside), 影響 (influence, effect).
- Example: 一人暮らしは自由な反面、寂しさを感じることもある。(Living alone is liberating, but on the other hand, it can sometimes feel lonely.)
default.q.n2-38-q35-35.why.0: (a) 「～といっても」 means “although one says..., in reality...” and is not used to present two parallel contrasting aspects of something.
default.q.n2-38-q35-35.why.1: (b) 「～につれて」 means “as A changes, B changes along with it”; it does not express two opposing sides such as good and bad.
default.q.n2-38-q35-35.why.2: (c) 「～反面（はんめん）」 means “on the other hand” or “in contrast,” and is used to indicate the two opposing sides—positive and negative—of the Internet.
default.q.n2-38-q35-35.why.3: (d) 「したがって」 is a conjunction expressing a cause-and-effect relationship (“therefore,” “as a result”), and does not directly follow a relative clause.
default.q.n2-38-q36-36.verdict: The correct answer is 1. ものなら.
default.q.n2-38-q36-36.explanation:
- Meaning: "If possible, I would like to return to my home country right now. But that is impossible."
- Structure: V-potential form + ものなら (If only I could... / If it were possible, I would really like to...—used for a supposition that is difficult or impossible to realize).
- Kanji-derived meaning: 不可能 (impossible).
- Example: 戻れるものなら、高校時代に戻りたい。(If I could go back, I would like to return to my high school days.)
default.q.n2-38-q36-36.why.0: (a) 「V可能形＋ものなら」 means “if it were possible to..., I would really like to...,” expressing a wish to do something that is nearly impossible. The following clause is 「不可能だ」.
default.q.n2-38-q36-36.why.1: (b) 「～からには」 means “now that...” or “once...,” expressing determination based on something certain to happen.
default.q.n2-38-q36-36.why.2: (c) 「～ことだから」 means “given someone’s character, they are sure to...” and is used to make a prediction about another person.
default.q.n2-38-q36-36.why.3: (d) 「はずなら」 is not a grammatically correct structure in Japanese.
default.q.n2-38-q37-37.verdict: The correct answer is 4. ものの.
default.q.n2-38-q37-37.explanation:
- Sentence translation: “Although spring has arrived, it is still cold in the mornings and evenings.”
- Pattern: `Plain form + とはいうものの` (although it is said that..., in reality...).
- Kanji: 朝晩 (CHŌBAN: mornings and evenings).
- Example: 免許は取ったものの、車を持っていないので運転していない。(Although I got my driver's license, I do not drive because I do not own a car.)
default.q.n2-38-q37-37.why.0: (a) 「～にもかかわらず」(printed incorrectly in the test as にもかか山らず) means “although...”; it cannot form the phrase 「とはいうにもかかわらず」.
default.q.n2-38-q37-37.why.1: (b) 「～にしては」 means “considering...” or “for..., unusually,” and does not follow 「とはいう」.
default.q.n2-38-q37-37.why.2: (c) 「～ながら（も）」 means “although,” and is attached directly to a noun, adjective, or Masu-stem; it does not follow 「とはいう」.
default.q.n2-38-q37-37.why.3: (d) 「～とはいうものの」is a standard grammar expression meaning “although one says... / even so, in reality...,” presenting a fact contrary to the statement in the preceding clause.
default.q.n2-38-q38-38.verdict: The correct answer is 2. わりに.
default.q.n2-38-q38-38.explanation:
- Meaning: "That child is remarkably perceptive about other people's feelings for their age."
- Structure: `Nの / plain form + わりに(は)` (for..., comparatively / relatively..., compared with the usual standard).
- Example: この料理は値段のわりに量が多くておいしい。(This dish is filling and delicious for its price.)
default.q.n2-38-q38-38.why.0: (a) 「～ほどに」 means “to the extent that...,” and does not combine with 「年の」 to express a relative comparison involving age.
default.q.n2-38-q38-38.why.1: (b) 「Nの＋わりに（は）」 means “considering...” or “compared with...,” contrasting a characteristic with what is normally expected of that person or thing (although the child is young, the child is very mature for their age).
default.q.n2-38-q38-38.why.2: (c) 「～くせに」 means “even though / despite the fact that,” with a sarcastic or reproachful nuance, so it does not fit the complimentary clause 「よくわかる」.
default.q.n2-38-q38-38.why.3: (d) 「～だけに」means “precisely because..., all the more...,” expressing a corresponding relationship; it is not used for something that goes against the usual standard.
default.q.n2-38-q39-39.verdict: The correct answer is 3. 考えようではありませんか.
default.q.n2-38-q39-39.explanation:
- Meaning: "To create a society that is easy to live in, why don't we all think about what we ourselves can do now!"
- Structure: `volitional form + ではありませんか / ではないか` ('Let's...together!' — a formal call to collective action).
- Vocabulary: 暮らす (to live), 社会 (society).
- Example: 地球環境を守るために、今できることから始めようではありませんか。(To protect the global environment, why don't we start with what we can do right now!)
default.q.n2-38-q39-39.why.0: (a) 「～とはかぎらない」means “it is not necessarily the case that...”; combining it with a negative question makes the meaning unnecessarily complicated and does not suit the intended appeal.
default.q.n2-38-q39-39.why.1: (b) 「～さえできる」 means “even ... can,” and cannot be combined with 「いっしょに」 to make a joint call to action.
default.q.n2-38-q39-39.why.2: (c) 「V-よう ＋ ではありませんか」 is a formal sentence pattern used to call on or encourage a group: "Let's all do ... together!"
default.q.n2-38-q39-39.why.3: (d) 「～わけではない」 means “it is not necessarily the case that...”; it is not used to express a call or invitation to take action.
default.q.n2-38-q40-40.verdict: The correct answer is 1. 得る.
default.q.n2-38-q40-40.explanation:
- Meaning: "It was an accident that could have been completely predicted to happen."
- Structure: `V (ます-stem) + 得る（うる／える）` (can / be capable of... — the negative form is `得ない (えない)`).
- The kanji 予測 means prediction, and 事故 means accident.
- Example: 考え得るすべての方法を試してみた。(I tried every method I could think of.)
default.q.n2-38-q40-40.why.0: (a) 「Vます (remove ます) ＋ 得る（うる／える）」 means “can” or “be capable of happening.” Combined with 「十分に」, it forms the phrase “an accident can quite possibly be predicted in advance.”
default.q.n2-38-q40-40.why.1: (b) 「～かねる」means “to find it difficult to...” or “be unable to...,” which directly conflicts with the adverb 「十分に」(fully/completely).
default.q.n2-38-q40-40.why.2: (c) 「～ながら」 means “while” or “although,” and cannot directly form an attributive phrase modifying the noun 事故.
default.q.n2-38-q40-40.why.3: (d) 「～つつある」 means “be gradually...,” describing an ongoing change, so it does not suit a context modifying the nature of an accident.
default.q.n2-38-q41-41.verdict: The correct answer is 3. やめかねない.
default.q.n2-38-q41-41.explanation:
- Translation: “If we make Mr. Mori do even more difficult work, there is a strong possibility that he will quit.”
- Structure: `V (ます-stem) + かねない` (there is a risk that... / may well... — used to warn that a bad or negative result may occur).
- Sino-Japanese reading: 辛い (difficult, painful, bitter).

default.q.n2-38-q41-41.why.1: (b) 「Vる ＋ ことだ」is used to give advice about what someone should do, so it is unsuitable for predicting a third party’s action.
default.q.n2-38-q41-41.why.2: (c) 「Vます (remove ます) + かねない」means “may very well” or “there is a risk of,” expressing concern that Mr. Mori may quit if he is forced to work excessive hours.
default.q.n2-38-q41-41.why.3: (d) 「Vます (remove ます) + がたい」 means “difficult to do” in a psychological or emotional sense, so it does not fit a context involving a predicted action.

default.q.n2-38-q42-42.explanation:

- Related kanji reading: 賛成 (さんせい—agreement).

default.q.n2-38-q42-42.why.0: (a) 「Vない ＋ ずにはいられない」means “cannot help but...” or “cannot suppress the feeling to...,” which does not fit a context of politely expressing disagreement.
default.q.n2-38-q42-42.why.1: (b) 「Vます（bỏ ます）＋ かねる」means “find it difficult to/cannot,” and is a polite expression showing reluctance or difficulty in agreeing (“I find it difficult to agree”).
default.q.n2-38-q42-42.why.2: (c) 「Vる ＋ しかない」 means “there is no choice but to…,” and does not express the idea of “there is still a point of disagreement.”

- Meaning: “How beautiful Mount Fuji looks when viewed at sunset!”

default.q.n2-38-q43-43.why.1: (b) 「～ことに（は）」means “to one's...,” or “how...,” and is usually placed at the beginning of a sentence to introduce an emotion, as in 嬉しいことに. It does not appear at the end of an exclamatory sentence with 「なんと」.
default.q.n2-38-q43-43.why.2: (c) 「～せいか」means “perhaps because...,” and does not fit the exclamatory sentence pattern.
default.q.n2-38-q43-43.why.3: (d) 「なんと ＋ [adjective/verb] ＋ ことか」 is the correct exclamatory sentence pattern, expressing deep emotion (“How beautiful!”).

default.q.n2-38-q44-44.why.2: (c) 「～かねない」 means “there is a risk that...”; it is not used to give advice after the condition 「～たければ」.

default.q.n2-38-q50-50.explanation: Question 50 requires a connective structure expressing concession or simultaneous action that fits the context. 「〜ながら」 is the most accurate answer because it can express a mild contrast ("although...,") as well as simultaneous action, fitting naturally with the grammar of the sentence.

default.q.n2-38-q58-58.verdict: The correct answer is 1: It is unfortunate that few young people have great hopes for their own future.

Which of the following is consistent with the content of the passage?

1. It is regrettable that few young people have great hopes for their own futures.
2. When trying something new, if you lack courage, it is better not to begin.
3. No matter how hard older people try to appear healthy, they cannot overcome declining physical strength.
4. It is unavoidable for young people to criticize older people who push themselves too hard.

This means that too few young people hold ambitious hopes for the future.
default.q.n2-38-q58-58.why.1: (b) Incorrect. The author criticizes the attitude of giving up before even trying (「手をつける前から、自分なんかにできるわけがないとあきらめる態度ほどじれったいものはない」) and states that nothing can begin unless one tries (「やってみなければ何も始まらない」). The author does not advise people not to start if they lack courage.
default.q.n2-38-q58-58.why.2: (c) Incorrect. The author praises and admires the enthusiasm of the older generation, who are eager to try something even while confronting declines in physical strength and memory (「体力や記憶力の衰えと闘っても何かやってみたくてしかたないというシルバー世代の元気なこと！」). The passage is not negatively suggesting that older people cannot overcome such decline.
default.q.n2-38-q58-58.why.3: (d) Incorrect. The author says that elderly people do not lose heart in the face of hurtful remarks made behind their backs (「『年寄りの冷や水』なんて陰口にもめげることなく」). The author does not agree that young people speaking ill of the elderly is natural or unavoidable (しかたがない).
default.q.n2-38-q59-59.verdict: The correct answer is 2 (なぜ廃止しなくてはならないのか。), because the question 「なぜなのか」 appears immediately after the author states that the exchange program is about to be abolished, expressing a question about why it must be abolished.
default.q.n2-38-q59-59.explanation:
- Summary of the main point: The passage discusses information that the city’s student exchange program is scheduled to be abolished next year. The author questions and expresses skepticism about this decision through the phrase 「なぜなのか」 (“Why is that?”), then explains that abolishing the program to save money would not produce much economic benefit but would cause significant damage by eliminating the city’s distinctive cultural and musical exchange. The author also suggests an alternative: having individuals pay part of the cost themselves.
- Translation of the question: In this context, which of the following is closest in meaning to 「なぜなのか」 (“Why is that?”) when expressed differently?
- Translation of the answer choices:
  1. Why did this program exist in the first place?
  2. Why does this program have to be abolished?
  3. Why did it not become a distinctive feature of the city?
  4. Why not have individuals pay part of the cost themselves?
default.q.n2-38-q59-59.why.0: (a) Incorrect because the author is not questioning why this system existed in the past. The passage clearly states that it began 20 years ago and became a distinctive feature of the city; the author is concerned about the decision to abolish it.
default.q.n2-38-q59-59.why.1: (b) Correct. The text states that the exchange-study program, which began 20 years ago, is apparently going to be abolished next year (「来年度より、交換留学制度が廃止されるらしい。... この制度は、この市の特色でもあった」). The author immediately asks 「なぜなのか」 (Why?), and the following sentences repeatedly argue against abolishing it for financial reasons. Therefore, 「なぜなのか」 is equivalent to 「なぜ廃止しなくてはならないのか」 (Why must it be abolished?).
default.q.n2-38-q59-59.why.2: (c) Incorrect. The author states that this system was itself a distinctive feature of the city (「この制度は、この市の特色でもあった」), not that the author wonders why it did not become one.
default.q.n2-38-q59-59.why.3: (d) Incorrect because having individuals pay part of the cost (「それならそれで、費用の一部を個人負担にすればいいではないか」) is a solution proposed later to avoid abolishing the system; it is not the meaning of the question 「なぜなのか」 at the beginning of the passage.
default.q.n2-38-q60-60.verdict: The correct answer is choice 3: The baby has to look at the mother’s face and then control its facial muscles to move in a similar way and imitate her.
default.q.n2-38-q60-60.explanation:
- Main point: The passage clearly states that imitating a mother’s facial expressions is not simple. A newborn must look at the mother’s face and then convert that visual information into movements of its own facial muscles, while a baby only a few months old cannot yet look in a mirror to see how its own face changes.
- Question: Why does the passage say 「この能力はそう簡単なものとは思えない」(This ability does not seem to be that simple)?
- Answer choices:
1. Because understanding the meaning of facial expressions while the mother is talking is very difficult.
2. Because after looking at the mother, the baby must immediately decide which direction to turn.
3. Because the baby must look at the mother and move its own facial muscles in a similar way.
4. Because understanding the content of what the mother is saying is very difficult.
default.q.n2-38-q60-60.why.0: (a) Incorrect because the passage is not about difficulty understanding the meaning of facial expressions (表情の意味); its focus is on children imitating facial movements without understanding anything.
default.q.n2-38-q60-60.why.1: (b) Incorrect because “deciding which direction to turn” is a reaction in the sound experiment described later, not an explanation for the complexity of the ability to imitate facial expressions.
default.q.n2-38-q60-60.why.2: (c) Correct. The passage says: 「赤ちゃんは目でお母注んの顔を見て、それを自分の顔の形を変える➽肉の活動に訳注なければならない。」 (A baby looks at its mother’s face and must convert what it sees into muscle activity that changes the shape of its own face.)
default.q.n2-38-q60-60.why.3: (d) Incorrect. The passage says 「赤ん均は何も理解しているはずはない」(The baby could not possibly understand anything), but not understanding the content of speech is not the reason why the ability to imitate facial expressions is far from simple.
default.q.n2-38-q61-61.verdict: The correct answer is choice 1: The baby will look at the screen showing the mother’s face when pronouncing “I.”
default.q.n2-38-q61-61.explanation:
- Main point: Kuhl's research demonstrated that infants can identify which sound corresponds to a particular mouth shape simply by looking at the speaker's mouth. When the sound 'A' was played through a speaker while screens showed the mother's face saying 'A' and 'I', the baby looked at the screen showing the face saying 'A'. Therefore, if the sound 'I' is played, the baby will look at the screen showing the face saying 'I'.
- Question translation: Based on the results of Kuhl's "recent study," what will the baby do if it hears its mother say 'I'?
- Choice translations:
1. Look at the screen showing the mother's face saying 'I'.
2. Look at the screen showing the mother's face saying 'A'.
3. Try to find where the real mother is.
4. Turn its head toward the source of the mother's voice.
default.q.n2-38-q61-61.why.0: (a) Correct. The quotation states: 「スピーカーから「ア」という音を出す。... 赤ん均は「ア」といっている顔の方に目や顔を向けることがわかる。」 (When the sound “A” is played, the baby turns its eyes and face toward the screen showing the mother saying “A.” By the same principle, when the sound “I” is played, the baby will look at the screen showing the mother saying “I.”)
default.q.n2-38-q61-61.why.1: (b) Incorrect because, according to the experimental results, the baby turns toward the screen whose mouth shape matches the sound heard. For the sound "I," the baby turns toward the "I" face rather than the "A" face.
default.q.n2-38-q61-61.why.2: (c) Incorrect because the passage does not mention the baby searching for its real mother (本物の母親).
default.q.n2-38-q61-61.why.3: (d) Incorrect because the experiment examined whether infants directed their gaze toward the screen corresponding to the mouth movements for the sound being pronounced; it did not concern turning toward the direction from which the sound came.
default.q.n2-38-q62-62.verdict: The correct answer is choice 4: People learn the relationship between faces and voices very soon after birth.
default.q.n2-38-q62-62.explanation:
- Main point: The passage concludes that voices and facial expressions are important signals in human society. Therefore, people are born with the ability to learn the relationship between faces and voices from a very early stage, and this connection becomes deeply ingrained in the mind during infancy.
- Question: Which of the following is consistent with the passage?
- Answer choices:
1. People can imitate their mother’s facial expressions as soon as they are born.
2. As people grow up, they separate and understand faces and voices independently.
3. Infants prefer their mother’s “A” face to her “I” face.
4. People learn the relationship between faces and voices very early after birth.
default.q.n2-38-q62-62.why.0: (a) Incorrect because the passage clearly states 「しばらくして次目の↔点が合わせられるようになると、赤ん均がそれを真似る」 (only after some time, when the two eyes can focus together, does the baby imitate it), not that this happens immediately after birth (生まれてすぐ).
default.q.n2-38-q62-62.why.1: (b) Incorrect because the passage does not mention adults separating faces and voices when perceiving them.
default.q.n2-38-q62-62.why.2: (c) Incorrect because the passage does not say that the baby preferred (好む) one face over another. It says that the baby looked at the face whose mouth movements matched the sound heard.
default.q.n2-38-q62-62.why.3: (d) Correct. The passage states: 「赤ん均が声と顔の関係を早く習う能力を持って、生まれてくれる のであろう。このように、口の形と声との関連性は、赤ん均の頃から顔に焼き付けられる」 (Humans are born with the ability to quickly learn the relationship between voices and faces; the connection between mouth shape and voice is imprinted from infancy.)
default.q.n2-38-q63-63.verdict: The correct answer is 1: 25 歳で結婚している男性.
default.q.n2-38-q63-63.explanation:
- Question translation: Which of the following part-time workers is called a "freeter"?
- Answer choices:
  1. A married 25-year-old man
  2. A married 25-year-old woman
  3. An unmarried 40-year-old man
  4. An unmarried 40-year-old woman
- Main point and basis: According to the definition given by the Ministry of Labor in the passage, a "freeter" is a man or woman aged 15 to 34 who works part-time. People over 34 are no longer called freeters; they are simply ordinary part-time workers. For women, only unmarried women are called freeters, while married women or homemakers with part-time jobs are classified differently. Therefore, a 25-year-old married man fits the definition of a freeter.
default.q.n2-38-q63-63.why.0: (a) Correct. The passage states: 「労働省の定義によれ消、「フリーター」とは、 15 歳から 34 歳までのパートやアルバイトをしている男女次ということになる」. Since the restriction to unmarried people applies only to women, a 25-year-old man within the 15–34 age range is still considered a freeter even if he is married.
default.q.n2-38-q63-63.why.1: (b) Incorrect. The passage clearly states: 「女性の場合、フリーターといわれるのは、独身者のことで、主婦になると、パートのお消注んである」, meaning that married women or housewives are not called freeters.
default.q.n2-38-q63-63.why.2: (c) Incorrect. The passage clearly states: 「34 歳をすぎると、もうフリーターとは呼ばれない」. Since the man is 40, he is over 34 and is no longer called a freeter.
default.q.n2-38-q63-63.why.3: (d) Incorrect. Similarly, a 40-year-old exceeds the age range of 15–34; according to the definition, 「34 歳をすぎると、もうフリーターとは呼ばれない」.
default.q.n2-38-q64-64.verdict: The correct answer is 1: フリーターが失業者だと思われていないから.
default.q.n2-38-q64-64.explanation:
- Translation of the question: The article says, "It does not become a major social problem." Why is that?
- Translation of the choices:
  1. Because freeters are not considered unemployed.
  2. Because freeters make up a small proportion of the overall workforce.
  3. Because the term "freeter" is not yet widely known.
  4. Because freeters enjoy freedom according to their own wishes.
- Main point and evidence: The author explains that although the number of freeters has increased, they are not considered a serious social problem because the term "freeter" conceals the reality that they are unemployed; society never calls them unemployed, so it does not regard this as a serious issue.
default.q.n2-38-q64-64.why.0: (a) Correct. The passage gives the direct reason immediately after the question: 「たいした社会問題にならないのは、フリーターという呼び名だからである。けっして失業者と呼ばれない」, meaning that because they are called “freeters,” they are never called or regarded as unemployed people.
default.q.n2-38-q64-64.why.1: (b) Incorrect. The opening passage says that the number of freeters is increasing to nearly 2 million («フリーターがふえている。 200 万人に活かい次ともいわれる»), not that the number is small.
default.q.n2-38-q64-64.why.2: (c) Incorrect. The passage does not say that this name is unknown. Rather, because they are called “freeters,” the issue is not regarded as serious.
default.q.n2-38-q64-64.why.3: (d) Incorrect. The passage points out that doing whatever one wants is only an outward appearance («自由を楽しんでいるようにみえるが、実際のところは...»); this is not the reason explaining why it does not become a social problem.
default.q.n2-38-q65-65.verdict: The correct answer is 2: 正社員になりたいのに採用されないフリーター.
default.q.n2-38-q65-65.explanation:
- Question translation: In the passage, what does the word "これ" refer to?
- Answer choices:
  1. A freeter living an unstable, unemployed life while enjoying freedom
  2. A freeter who wants to become a regular employee but is not hired
  3. A freeter who refuses to work despite having a job
  4. A freeter who works hard and has been made a regular employee
- Main point and evidence: The demonstrative "これ" appears in the final sentence and directly refers to the group mentioned in the immediately preceding sentence: freeters who work hard hoping to be promoted to regular employees but ultimately are not hired; the author states that this group genuinely falls under the category of unemployed people.
default.q.n2-38-q65-65.why.0: (a) Incorrect. «自由を楽しんでいる...» appears earlier in the passage and describes an apparent state; it is not the direct referent of «これ».
default.q.n2-38-q65-65.why.1: (b) Correct. 「これ」replaces the content of the immediately preceding sentence: 「正社員に登用される かもしれない次と思って、一生懸命働いたが、採用されな かった 次というフリーターも多い」 (many freeters hoped to become regular employees and worked hard, but were not hired).
default.q.n2-38-q65-65.why.2: (c) Incorrect. The passage says that they wanted to be formally hired but were not hired («採用されなかった»), not that they had jobs but chose not to go to work.
default.q.n2-38-q65-65.why.3: (d) Incorrect. The passage clearly states that the person was not hired («採用されな かった»), which is completely opposite to being officially promoted.
default.q.n2-38-q66-66.verdict: The correct answer is 3: Even when you see someone in difficulty, you should not help them, because they will become dependent on others and grow lazy.
default.q.n2-38-q66-66.explanation:
**Relevant summary:**
The author discusses the proverb 「情けは人のためならず」. Its traditional meaning is that showing compassion and treating others kindly ultimately benefits oneself as well. However, its interpretation today has changed to mean that helping someone too much will make that person dependent and lazy, so one should not take pity on or help them.

**Question and answer choices:**
- **Question:** Which statement matches the current interpretation of the proverb 「情けは人のためならず」?
- **Choice 1:** When you are in trouble, you should rely on others. Everyone has problems, and people should help one another...
- **Choice 2:** If you see someone in trouble, help them. When you are in trouble, someone will help you in return...
- **Choice 3:** Even if you see someone in trouble, you should not help them, because they will become dependent on others and lazy...
- **Choice 4:** If you see someone in trouble, help them. That person will definitely treat you well in return later...
default.q.n2-38-q66-66.why.0: (a) Incorrect because the passage does not advise relying on others when facing difficulties; it criticizes a dependent and lazy mentality.
default.q.n2-38-q66-66.why.1: (b) Incorrect because the idea “help people in trouble, and they will help you when you are in trouble” is the traditional interpretation from the past (今までの解釈), not the current interpretation (現在の解釈).
default.q.n2-38-q66-66.why.2: (c) Correct. The passage states: 『あんまり情けをかけると、それを当てにして 怠け者になってしまう。だから情けはかけるな次ということなのだそうだ。』 (If you help someone too much, they will come to rely on it and become lazy, so do not show them too much compassion.) Choice 3 accurately expresses this content.
default.q.n2-38-q66-66.why.3: (d) Incorrect because this is a traditional cause-and-effect interpretation, and the passage never says that the person will definitely treat us well in return later.
default.q.n2-38-q67-67.verdict: The correct answer is 4: Because there are no longer people in urgent need of help like there were in the past.
default.q.n2-38-q67-67.explanation:
**Relevant summary:**
The author explains how the meaning of the proverb has changed with the times. Nowadays, hardly anyone becomes so destitute and hungry that they urgently need the kind of help people needed in the past. If someone is unemployed, it is often because of personal issues such as laziness or being too selective about jobs. Since society no longer has people who must be helped in the same way as before, attitudes toward helping others have changed.

**Translation of the question and answer choices:**
- **Question:** Why has the interpretation of the proverb 「情けは人のためならず」 changed?
- **Choice 1:** Because the number of lazy people who refuse to work has decreased.
- **Choice 2:** Because the number of kind people who help others has increased compared with the past.
- **Choice 3:** Because the number of people who are Japanese but cannot understand one another's Japanese has increased.
- **Choice 4:** Because there are no longer people who need help as they did in the past.
default.q.n2-38-q67-67.why.0: (a) Incorrect because the passage does not say that lazy people work less. It clearly states that people who do not work nowadays are mainly lazy or choosy (『怠けて働かなかったり、選り好み をしていて仕事をしていなかったり』).
default.q.n2-38-q67-67.why.1: (b) Incorrect because the passage does not mention that the number of kind people helping others has increased compared with the past.
default.q.n2-38-q67-67.why.2: (c) Incorrect because the opening statement—that Japanese speakers may not understand one another—is merely an introduction to the phenomenon of interpreting words. It is not the reason the proverb’s meaning has changed.
default.q.n2-38-q67-67.why.3: (d) Correct. The passage provides this evidence: 『現答は食べるのに困るというような人がいなくなってしまった。どうしても助けなければならないような人がいない。』 (Nowadays, there are no longer people struggling even to obtain food. There is no one who absolutely must be helped.)
default.q.n2-38-q68-68.verdict: The correct answer is 1: The explanations and meanings of words seem to change along with the times.
default.q.n2-38-q68-68.explanation:
**Relevant summary:** Through the example of how the meaning of the proverb 「情けは人のためならず」 has changed as economic and social conditions have changed, the author reaches a general conclusion: The meanings and interpretations of words always reflect and change with the times (『言葉の意味は時答（時代）を反映する』).

**Question and answer choices:**
- **Question:** What does the author most want to say?
- **Choice 1:** The way words are interpreted seems to change along with the times.
- **Choice 2:** The interpretation of words inherently differs depending on the person using them.
- **Choice 3:** It is unfortunate that the meanings of words from the past have not been accurately passed down to the present.
- **Choice 4:** People today have become more affluent and therefore no longer understand the meaning of compassion.
default.q.n2-38-q68-68.why.0: (a) Correct. The author concludes: 『この解釈があながち間違っているとは言えない のが、時答性というものだ。… 言葉の意味は時答を反映する。』 (The fact that this interpretation cannot necessarily be called wrong is what it means to be shaped by the times... The meanings of words reflect their era). Choice 1 accurately expresses this point.
default.q.n2-38-q68-68.why.1: (b) Incorrect because the author emphasizes that the meaning of words changes with the times and social circumstances (『時答性』, 『言葉の意味は時答を反映する』), not because of individual users.
default.q.n2-38-q68-68.why.2: (c) Incorrect because the author states that the new interpretation is not necessarily wrong (『この解釈があながち間違っているとは言えない』) because it reflects the times. The author does not express regret (『残念だ』).
default.q.n2-38-q68-68.why.3: (d) Incorrect because this is merely an example analyzing the state of society to clarify the cause of a shift in meaning, not the author’s central message.
default.q.n2-38-q69-69.verdict: The correct answer is 1 (3,600 people) because both passages state that approximately 3,600 people die from exposure to secondhand smoke at the workplace.
default.q.n2-38-q69-69.explanation:
- Main point: Both passages A and B provide estimates of the number of deaths caused by passive smoking. When categorized by exposure location—workplaces and homes—the number of deaths caused by passive smoking in workplaces is approximately 3,600.
- Question translation: Which of the following is the correct number of people affected by passive smoking in workplaces?
- Answer choices:
  1. 3,600 people
  2. 4,600 people
  3. 4,914 people
  4. 6,800 people
default.q.n2-38-q69-69.why.0: (a) Passage A states: 「煙にさらされる場所を職場と家庭で分けると、職場が約 3,600 人で多かった」, and passage B states: 「全体のうち半数以上の約 3,600 人は職場での受動喫煙とみられる」. Both confirm that approximately 3,600 deaths from passive smoking occurred in the workplace.
default.q.n2-38-q69-69.why.1: (b) 4,600 people refers to the number of women who died from passive smoking (Article A: 「女性が約 4,600 人」; Article B: 「女性が約 4,600 人と被害が大きく」), not the number of people affected in the workplace.
default.q.n2-38-q69-69.why.2: (c) The 4,914 people were those who died in traffic accidents in 2009, as stated in Passage A (「2009 年の交通事故による死者 4,914 人」), for comparison—not the number of people at the workplace.
default.q.n2-38-q69-69.why.3: (d) 6,800 people is the estimated total number of annual deaths nationwide caused by passive smoking (Article A:「少なくとも年間約 6800 人」, Article B:「毎年約 6,800 人」), not the number occurring only in workplaces.
default.q.n2-38-q70-70.verdict: The correct answer is 3 (受動喫煙による死亡者推計値を発表した機関) because both passages A and B clearly state that the estimates were published by a research team from Japan’s Ministry of Health, Labour and Welfare (厚生労働省の研究班).
default.q.n2-38-q70-70.explanation:
- Main-point summary: Articles A and B both report on the same report, released on the 28th, containing estimates of deaths caused by secondhand smoke from a research team at Japan's Ministry of Health, Labour and Welfare (厚生労働省の研究班). Other information, such as the definition of the term and places where women are likely to encounter secondhand smoke, appears only in article A, while detailed figures by disease type and gender appear only in article B.
- Question translation: Which of the following is mentioned in both articles A and B?
- Answer choices:
  1. The meaning of the term "secondhand smoking"
  2. Places where women are likely to experience secondhand smoke
  3. The organization that released estimates of deaths caused by secondhand smoke
  4. A detailed table analyzing estimated deaths caused by secondhand smoke
default.q.n2-38-q70-70.why.0: (a) The definition of “passive smoking” appears only in Passage A (「他人のたばこの煙を吸わされる「受動喫煙」」); Passage B does not explain this definition.
default.q.n2-38-q70-70.why.1: (b) The place where women are likely to experience secondhand smoke, namely the home, is mentioned only in Passage A (「家庭での受動喫煙にあいやすい女性」); Passage B only says that women suffer greater harm and does not mention this location.
default.q.n2-38-q70-70.why.2: (c) Article A states:「...との推計を、厚生労働省の研究班が 28 日発表した」, while Article B states:「...との推計値を厚生労働省研究班が 28 日、発表した」. These quotations show that both articles identify the announcing body as the research group of Japan's Ministry of Health, Labour and Welfare (厚生労働省の研究班).
default.q.n2-38-q70-70.why.3: (d) The detailed analysis of estimated deaths, including percentages and case numbers for lung cancer and cardiovascular disease by gender, appears only in the final paragraph of Passage B (「その結果、肺がんで死亡した女性...」). Passage A contains no such detailed analysis.
default.q.n2-38-q71-71.verdict: The correct answer is 4 (親に食べ物を与える点 - providing food for or feeding one's parents).
default.q.n2-38-q71-71.explanation:
- Question translation: In what decisive way does the author say humans differ from other animals?
- Answer choices:
  1. Walking on two legs.
  2. Speaking a language.
  3. Using tools.
  4. Providing food for their parents.
- Main point: The author explains that many animals also live in groups and know how to use things around them as tools. Humans differ because they can invent and improve tools themselves, enabling them to support not only themselves and their children but also elderly parents who can no longer obtain food independently. The author argues that caring for and supporting one’s parents is the most decisive difference.
default.q.n2-38-q71-71.why.0: (a) Choice 1 is incorrect because walking on two legs (ニ足歩行) is mentioned only as a premise that freed the hands to create tools, not as the decisive difference emphasized by the author.
default.q.n2-38-q71-71.why.1: (b) Choice 2 is incorrect because the passage does not mention speaking a language (言葉を話す) anywhere.
default.q.n2-38-q71-71.why.2: (c) Choice 3 is incorrect because the passage clearly states that monkeys can also use things around them as tools, 「サルは身のまわりにあるものを道具として使うことができますが」. What distinguishes humans is that they create tools (作り出す), and most importantly, use them to support their elderly parents.

default.q.n2-38-q28-28.explanation:
「それとも」 is a conjunction meaning "or" or "or else." It is specifically used to connect two alternatives in a question, usually in the pattern 「Aですか、それともBですか」, asking the listener to choose one of the two options. It is not used to connect nouns in declarative or affirmative sentences; in that case, use 「または」 or 「あるいは」.
Example: コーヒーにしますか、それとも紅茶にしますか。(Would you like coffee or tea?)

default.q.n2-38-q28-28.why.1: Incorrect because this sentence states an ordinary rule or condition rather than presenting a choice. To link the two nouns, use 「または」 or 「もしくは」.
default.q.n2-38-q28-28.why.2: Incorrect because the following clause is a declarative supposition, not a choice question; 「あるいは」 or 「または」 should be used here.
default.q.n2-38-q28-28.why.3: Correct because 「それとも」is a conjunction used to connect two alternatives in a question (Aですか、それともBですか).
default.q.n2-38-q29-29.explanation:
「夢中（むちゅう）」means “absorbed, engrossed, or completely immersed.” It describes a state in which someone is so focused on or enthusiastic about something they enjoy that they lose awareness of their surroundings. Common patterns include: 「〜に夢中だ」「〜に夢中になる」「夢中で〜する」.
Example: 彼は時間を忘れて読書に夢中になっている。(He is so engrossed in reading that he has forgotten the time.)
default.q.n2-38-q29-29.why.0: Incorrect because 「夢中」is a noun / na-adjective and cannot combine directly with 「〜している」to form a verb; if this meaning is intended, 「夢中になっている」must be used.

default.q.n2-38-q29-29.why.2: The context is inappropriate because 「夢中」 means being absorbed in or fascinated by something one likes. It is not used with a negative mental state such as 「悩む」; 「深刻に」, 「真剣に」, or 「深く」 would be appropriate here.
default.q.n2-38-q29-29.why.3: Incorrect because 「夢中」 describes a person's psychological state or behavior (being absorbed in something); it is not used to ask about things or phenomena that are popular among young people. For a trend, use 「流行（はやり）」 or 「人気」.
default.q.n2-38-q30-30.explanation:
「作法（さほう）」 means “etiquette, proper conduct, or formal manners,” especially in traditional practices such as the tea ceremony, flower arranging, greetings, dining manners, and social etiquette. Common expressions include: 「礼儀作法」「お茶の作法」「食事の作法」.
Example: 日本の伝統的な食事の作法を学ぶ。(Learn the proper manners for a traditional Japanese meal.)
default.q.n2-38-q30-30.why.0: This is a vocabulary error: for the use of machines or electronic devices, use 「使い方」 or 「操作方法」, not 「作法」.
default.q.n2-38-q30-30.why.1: This is a vocabulary error. For the method or process of making a dish or bread, use 「作り方」 or 「製法」, not 「作法」.

default.q.n2-38-q30-30.why.3: Incorrect vocabulary. For a Japanese teaching method, use 「教え方」, 「教授法」, or 「指導法」, not 「作法」.
default.q.n2-38-q31-31.explanation:
「たまたま」 is an adverb meaning “by chance, accidentally” (= 偶然), describing something that happens randomly and was not planned or anticipated. Do not confuse it with 「たまに」 (occasionally), which refers to low frequency.
Example: 駅でたまたま高校時代の友人に出会った。(I happened to run into a friend from high school at the station.)
default.q.n2-38-q31-31.why.0: Incorrect because the sentence describes a repeated habit whenever the person has free time, so an adverb of frequency such as 「たまに」 (“occasionally”) or 「よく」 (“often”) is required, not 「たまたま」 (“by chance”).
default.q.n2-38-q31-31.why.1: Incorrect because this is an invitation asking someone to drop by from time to time, so 「たまには / ぜひ」 should be used, not 「たまたま」, an adverb meaning “by chance.”

default.q.n2-38-q32-32.explanation:
「せめて」is an adverb meaning “at least” or “at a minimum.” It expresses the minimum level that the speaker hopes for or is willing to accept when the ideal outcome cannot be achieved. It commonly appears with sentence endings expressing wishes, commands, or requests, such as 「〜たい」「〜てほしい」「〜てください」「〜だけでも」「〜ばいい」. It is not used for completed events or with the structure 「〜しか...ない」.
Example: 一緒に行けなくても、せめて電話だけでもかけてほしい。(Even if you cannot go with me, I would at least like you to call me.)

default.q.n2-38-q32-32.why.2: Incorrect because 「せめて」is used to express an unfulfilled wish or hope, typically with 〜たい, 〜てほしい, or 〜てください. It is not used for an event or result already completed in the past; 「なんとか / 少なくとも」would be appropriate here.

Sino-Japanese reading: 整 (CHỈNH).
