default.q.n2-5-q28-28.explanation:
「こなす」means to handle or smoothly complete a large amount of assigned work or tasks (仕事をこなす, ノルマをこなす), or to master a skill or tool (使いこなす).
Example: 彼女は毎日多くのノルマを見事にこなしている。(She skillfully completes many work quotas every day.)
default.q.n2-5-q28-28.why.0: Incorrect for both context and vocabulary; 「こなす」 does not combine with this meaningless phrase. For a routine, use ルーティンワークをこなす.
default.q.n2-5-q28-28.why.1: Incorrect because when saying that someone finished lunch or ate early, use「昼食を済ませた」or「昼食をとった」, not「こなす」.
default.q.n2-5-q28-28.why.2: Incorrect because when putting a phone call on hold, Japanese uses 「電話を保留にした」, not 「保留をこなす」.
default.q.n2-5-q28-28.why.3: Correct because 「仕事をこなす」 is a natural expression meaning to complete or handle work smoothly and on schedule.
default.q.n2-5-q29-29.verdict: The correct answer is 3 because 「ゴマをする」 means to flatter one's superior in order to gain favor or advance.
default.q.n2-5-q29-29.explanation: 「ゴマをする（胡麻を擂る）」is a set expression meaning to flatter or curry favor with someone powerful, such as a superior, in order to gain personal benefits. Example: 上司にゴマをするのが上手な人ばかりが出世するわけではない。(It is not the case that everyone who is good at flattering their superiors gets promoted.)
default.q.n2-5-q29-29.why.0: Incorrect because the adverb 「正直に」 (honestly, frankly) directly contradicts the flattering, ingratiating behavior expressed by 「ゴマをする」.
default.q.n2-5-q29-29.why.1: The context is inappropriate because listening and offering advice (相談にのる) does not combine with the purpose of flattering a superior.
default.q.n2-5-q29-29.why.2: Correct because the sentence accurately describes flattering and currying favor with one's superiors to advance one's career.
default.q.n2-5-q29-29.why.3: Incorrect because resting when tired requires 「ひと休みする」 or 「休憩する」, not 「ゴマをする」.
default.q.n2-5-q30-30.verdict: The correct answer is 2 because 「添付」 precisely expresses attaching a photo to an application or résumé.
default.q.n2-5-q30-30.explanation:
「添付（てんぷ）」means attaching documents, images, files, and so on to the main text, an email, or an application.
Example: 詳細な資料をメールに添付して送信いたしました。(I attached the detailed materials to the email and sent it.)
default.q.n2-5-q30-30.why.0: Incorrect because moving the mouse cursor to the right requires 「移動させた」 or 「合わせた」, not 「添付した」.
default.q.n2-5-q30-30.why.1: Correct because 「写真を添付する」 is the standard expression for attaching a photograph to a résumé (履歴書).
default.q.n2-5-q30-30.why.2: Incorrect because deleting unnecessary images from a computer requires 「削除した」 or 「消去した」.
default.q.n2-5-q30-30.why.3: This is incorrect because for a printer’s ink status (running out of ink or refilling it), use 「切れた」 or 「補充した」, not 「添付した」.
default.q.n2-5-q31-31.verdict: The correct answer is 3 because 「つまらないものですが」is the standard humble expression used by someone giving a gift.
default.q.n2-5-q31-31.explanation: 「つまらないものですが」 ("It’s only a small gift, but...") is a classic humble expression (謙譲表現) used by the giver when presenting a gift to someone. Example: これ、旅先で見つけたつまらないものですが、どうぞお受け取りください。(This is just a small gift I found on my trip; please accept it.)
default.q.n2-5-q31-31.why.0: This is incorrect because the context is welcoming a guest and asking about their health, not giving a gift.
default.q.n2-5-q31-31.why.1: Incorrect because this sentence invites guests to relax and take their time (どうぞごゆっくり...), and has nothing to do with giving a gift.
default.q.n2-5-q31-31.why.2: Correct because the sentence expresses the standard humble wording used when presenting or giving a gift to someone.
default.q.n2-5-q31-31.why.3: Incorrect because 「つまらないものですが」 is said by the person giving a gift. The recipient does not use this expression, but simply thanks the giver and says 「いただきます」.
default.q.n2-5-q32-32.verdict: The correct answer is 3 because 「ける」 means to kick with one's foot and is correctly used in the reminder not to kick the seat in front.
default.q.n2-5-q32-32.explanation: 「蹴る（ける）」literally means to kick with one’s foot (ボールを蹴る, 座席を蹴る); figuratively, it means to reject or turn down a request/proposal (要求を蹴る). Example: 映画館では前の座席を蹴らないように気をつけましょう。(At the movie theater, be careful not to kick the seat in front of you.)
default.q.n2-5-q32-32.why.0: Incorrect because an action performed with the hands (手で) requires 「殴られた」(was punched) or 「叩かれた」(was slapped or hit), not 「蹴る」(to kick, using the foot).
default.q.n2-5-q32-32.why.1: Incorrect because being scolded loudly (大声で) requires 「怒鳴られた」 or 「叱られた」, not 「蹴られた」.
default.q.n2-5-q32-32.why.2: Correct because「ける」describes using one's foot to kick or push the back of the seat in front, as commonly happens on buses or in movie theaters.
default.q.n2-5-q32-32.why.3: Grammatically and contextually incorrect because the ball cannot perform the action of kicking itself. Use the passive form or the verb 「入らなかった」 instead.
default.q.n2-5-q1-1.verdict: The correct answer is 2. きろく.
default.q.n2-5-q1-1.explanation:
- Meaning: Record the matters decided during the discussion.
- Kanji note: 記 means to remember or record, and 録 means to copy or record; together, 記録 means to record or keep a record.
- Example: 会議の内容を細かく記録しておく。(Record the details of the meeting.)
default.q.n2-5-q1-1.why.0: (a) Incorrect: 「きえん」, as in 奇縁 (a remarkable connection) or 気炎 (spirited enthusiasm), is not the reading of 「記録」.
default.q.n2-5-q1-1.why.1: (b) Correct, because 「記録」 has the on-reading 「きろく」 and means a record or to record something.
default.q.n2-5-q1-1.why.2: (c) Incorrect because 「きそく」is the reading of 「規則」(rules, regulations).
default.q.n2-5-q1-1.why.3: (d) Incorrect because 「きりょく」 is the reading of 「気力」 (mental energy, physical strength).
default.q.n2-5-q2-2.verdict: The correct answer is 2. ちえ.
default.q.n2-5-q2-2.explanation:
- Meaning: The more children grow, the more knowledge and wisdom they gain.
- Kanji etymology: 知 (knowledge) + 恵 (wisdom) = 知恵 (wisdom, intelligence).
- Common expressions: 知恵がつく (to grow wiser, become more knowledgeable), 知恵を絞る (to rack one's brain).
- Example: みんなで知恵を出し合って問題を解決した。(We pooled our ideas and solved the problem together.)
default.q.n2-5-q2-2.why.0: (a) Incorrect because 「知」 in this compound uses the on-reading 「ち」, not 「し」.
default.q.n2-5-q2-2.why.1: (b) Correct because 「知恵」 is read as 「ちえ」 and means “wisdom,” “cleverness,” or “knowledge.”
default.q.n2-5-q2-2.why.2: (c) Incorrect because「しけい」is the reading of「死刑」(death penalty).
default.q.n2-5-q2-2.why.3: (d) Incorrect because 「ちけい」is the reading of 「地形」(terrain) or 「知己」(a close acquaintance).
default.q.n2-5-q3-3.verdict: The correct answer is 3. れいがい.
default.q.n2-5-q3-3.explanation:
- Meaning: We do not allow exceptions in this matter.
- Kanji: 例 (example, rule) + 外 (outside) = 例外 (exception, exceptional case).
- Common expressions: 例外を認める (allow an exception), 例外なく (without exception).
- Example: 規則にはどんな例外もあってはならない。(There must not be any exceptions to the rules.)
default.q.n2-5-q3-3.why.0: (a) Incorrect because the long vowel 「い」 is missing from the reading of 「例」 (the standard on-reading is 「れい」).
default.q.n2-5-q3-3.why.1: (b) Incorrect because the reading of 「例」 was confused with 「れつ」, the reading of 「列」.
default.q.n2-5-q3-3.why.2: (c) Correct because 「例外」 is correctly read 「れいがい」 and means “exception.”
default.q.n2-5-q3-3.why.3: (d) Incorrect because「例」is not read with the nasal sound or sokuon「ん」(confused with「連」- れん).
default.q.n2-5-q4-4.verdict: The correct answer is 1. いじょう.
default.q.n2-5-q4-4.explanation:
- Sentence meaning: We received a message reporting that there was an abnormality in the engine.
- Kanji components: 異 (い: different, unusual) + 常 (じょう: normal) = 異常 (いじょう: abnormality, something unusual).
- Common expressions: 異常気象 (abnormal weather), 異常が見つかる (an abnormality is found).
- Example: 体調に異常を感じたら、すぐに病院へ行ってください。(If you notice anything unusual about your health, go to the hospital immediately.)
default.q.n2-5-q4-4.why.0: (a) Correct because 「異常」 is read as 「いじょう」 and means that something is abnormal or malfunctioning.
default.q.n2-5-q4-4.why.1: (b) Incorrect because 「こしょう」 is the reading of 「故障」(breakdown, malfunction).
default.q.n2-5-q4-4.why.2: (c) Incorrect because 「ししょう」is the reading of 「支障」(obstacle) or 「師匠」(master or teacher).
default.q.n2-5-q4-4.why.3: (d) Incorrect because 「ひじょう」is the reading of 「非常」(emergency, unusual, extremely).
default.q.n2-5-q5-5.verdict: The correct answer is 3. ひかくてき.
default.q.n2-5-q5-5.explanation:
- Sentence meaning: This machine is relatively easy to operate.
- Kanji breakdown: 比 (comparison) + 較 (comparison) + 的 (characteristic) = 比較的 (relatively, comparatively).
- Related compounds: 比較 (comparison), 比較する (to compare).
- Example: 今年の冬は例年に比べて比較的暖かい。(This winter is relatively warm compared with previous years.)
default.q.n2-5-q5-5.why.0: (a) Incorrect because the reading of「較」was mistaken for「こう」(confused with「非行」or「飛行」).
default.q.n2-5-q5-5.why.1: (b) Incorrect because it is confused with 「ひごうてき」, as in 「非合理的」(illogical, unreasonable).
default.q.n2-5-q5-5.why.2: (c) Correct because 「比較的」 is read 「ひかくてき」 and means “relatively” or “fairly.”
default.q.n2-5-q5-5.why.3: (d) Incorrect because 「較」 is incorrectly voiced as 「がく」; its standard on-reading is 「かく」.
default.q.n2-5-q6-6.verdict: The correct answer is 1. 申し込み.
default.q.n2-5-q6-6.explanation:
- Sentence meaning: The application form has been redesigned.
- Sino-Japanese readings: 申 (しん) + 込 (こ) → 申し込み (もうしこみ: application, registration).
- Example: セミナーの申し込みは明日までです。(Applications to attend the seminar are due by tomorrow.)
default.q.n2-5-q6-6.why.0: (a) Correct. 「もうしこみ」is written in kanji as「申し込み」, combining「申す」(もうす) and「込む」(こむ), and means an application or registration.
default.q.n2-5-q6-6.why.1: (b) Incorrect. 「甲」 has a vertical stroke that does not extend downward, making it easy to confuse with 「申」. It does not have the kun-readings もう・す.
default.q.n2-5-q6-6.why.2: (c) Incorrect. The kanji 「混」(as in 混ぜる/混雑) means to mix or be crowded; it is not used to form a compound verb or noun meaning registration.
default.q.n2-5-q6-6.why.3: (d) Incorrect. Both kanji are mistaken: 「申」 is confused with 「甲」, and 「込」 with 「混」.
default.q.n2-5-q7-7.verdict: The correct answer is 4. 積極的.
default.q.n2-5-q7-7.explanation:
- Sentence translation: Everyone, please take an active part in the discussion.
- Sino-Japanese readings: 積 (accumulate) + 極 (extreme) + 的 → 積極的 (active, proactive).
- Antonym: 消極的 (しょうきょくてき — passive, unassertive).
- Example: 彼女は何事にも積極的な態度で取り組んでいる。(She approaches everything with a very positive and proactive attitude.)
default.q.n2-5-q7-7.why.0: (a) Incorrect. Both kanji are wrong: 「責」(as in 責任) and 「局」(as in 薬局/局面), creating a nonexistent word.
default.q.n2-5-q7-7.why.1: (b) Incorrect. It confuses 「責」, meaning blame or responsibility and read せき in its on-reading, with 「積」, as in 積極的 and 積もる.
default.q.n2-5-q7-7.why.2: (c) Incorrect. It confuses 「局」 (on-reading きょく) with 「極」, as in 極める/積極的.
default.q.n2-5-q7-7.why.3: (d) Correct. 「せっきょくてき」 is written with the kanji 「積極的」 and means “positive,” “active,” or “proactive.”
default.q.n2-5-q8-8.verdict: The correct answer is 2. 珍しい.
default.q.n2-5-q8-8.explanation:
- Translation: The mineral discovered at the bottom of the valley is extremely rare.
- Kanji: 珍 (precious, rare, unusual).
- Distinction: 珍しい (めずらしい - rare, unusual, seldom seen) vs 稀な (まれな - rare in frequency or quantity).
- Example: この鳥は日本では非常に珍しい。(This bird is extremely rare in Japan.)
default.q.n2-5-q8-8.why.0: (a) Incorrect. 「妙」 is a na-adjective, 「妙な」(みょうな: strange or unusual); it does not have the i-adjective form 「妙しい」.
default.q.n2-5-q8-8.why.1: (b) Correct. 「めずらしい」 is written with the kanji 「珍しい」, meaning rare, unusual, or seldom seen.
default.q.n2-5-q8-8.why.2: (c) Incorrect. The kanji 「貴」 has the kun-reading 「貴い」(とうとい / たっとい: noble, precious), not めずらしい.
default.q.n2-5-q8-8.why.3: (d) Incorrect. The character 「稀」 (rare) is generally used in forms such as 「稀な」(まれな) or 「稀に」(まれに); the form 「稀しい」 does not exist.
default.q.n2-5-q9-9.verdict: The correct answer is 4. 願う.
default.q.n2-5-q9-9.explanation:
- Translation: I hope war will never happen again.
- Sino-Japanese character meaning: 願 (NGUYỆN - wish, request).
- Similar expressions: 願う (ねがう - to wish, hope, or request), 祈る (いのる - to pray to a deity or offer blessings), 望む (のぞむ - to hope for, desire, or aspire to).
- Example: 世界の平和を心から願っています。(I sincerely hope for world peace.)
default.q.n2-5-q9-9.why.0: (a) Incorrect. 「求」 has the kun-reading 「求める」(もとめる: to seek or request), not ねがう.
default.q.n2-5-q9-9.why.1: (b) Incorrect. 「祈」 has the kun-reading 「祈る」(いのる: to pray), not ねがう.
default.q.n2-5-q9-9.why.2: (c) Incorrect. The kanji 「望」 has the kun-reading 「望む」(のぞむ: to hope for, expect), not ねがう.
default.q.n2-5-q9-9.why.3: (d) Correct. 「ねがう」 is written with the kanji 「願う」 and means to hope, wish, or pray for something.
default.q.n2-5-q10-10.verdict: The correct answer is 3. 自信.
default.q.n2-5-q10-10.explanation:
- Sentence translation: No matter how confident you are in your physical health, you will still catch a cold if you become careless and let your guard down.
- Kanji: 自 (self) + 信 (belief) → 自信 (self-confidence).
- Homophones: 自信 (じしん - self-confidence), 自身 (じしん - oneself), 地震 (じしん - earthquake).
- Common expression: 〜に自信がある (be confident in something).
- Example: 彼は日本語の会話力に自信を持っている。 (He is confident in his Japanese conversational ability.)
default.q.n2-5-q10-10.why.0: (a) Incorrect in context. 「自身」 is also pronounced じしん, but means oneself or one's own self, as in 自分自身 or 首相自身, and does not fit the confidence pattern 「〜に自信がある」.
default.q.n2-5-q10-10.why.1: (b) Incorrect. 「真」, as in 写真/真実, has the on-reading しん, but the word 「自真」 does not exist.
default.q.n2-5-q10-10.why.2: (c) Correct. 「じしん」 is written 「自信」 in this context and appears in the phrase 「健康に自信がある」(to be confident about one’s health).
default.q.n2-5-q10-10.why.3: (d) Incorrect. 「伸」 (as in 伸びる and 伸縮) has the on-reading しん, but the word 「自伸」 does not exist.
default.q.n2-6-q33-33.verdict: The correct answer is 4. だけあって (just as expected of, true to its reputation).
default.q.n2-6-q33-33.explanation:
Meaning: It is indeed a place visited by many tourists, so the scenery is truly wonderful.
- Structure: V/A/N + だけあって: as expected of, befitting, indeed because.
- Example: さすが高級ホテルだけあって、サービスが素晴らしい。(As expected of a luxury hotel, the service is excellent.)
default.q.n2-6-q33-33.why.0: (a) 「以上（は）」 means “once...,” implying that one must or naturally will do something. It commonly accompanies volition, obligation, or determination, and is not used to praise a result that matches one's reputation.
default.q.n2-6-q33-33.why.1: (b) 「反面」 means "on the other hand" or "in contrast" and is used to present two opposing aspects of the same matter, so it does not fit a following clause asserting an excellent result.
default.q.n2-6-q33-33.why.2: (c) 「ことなら」 is commonly used in the structure 「～（できる）ことなら」 (“if it is possible…”), so it does not fit the context of the sentence.
default.q.n2-6-q33-33.why.3: (d) 「だけあって」means “as one would expect from...” or “true to its reputation.” It is used when an actual result fully matches the reputation or expectations, as in the scenery being truly beautiful because many visitors come to see it.
default.q.n2-6-q34-34.verdict: The correct answer is 3. 行ったついでに (while you are there, taking the opportunity to go...).
default.q.n2-6-q34-34.explanation:
Sentence meaning: While going to see an exhibition, I took the opportunity to stroll leisurely around a nearby park.
- Kanji compounds: 展覧会 (exhibition), 散歩 (stroll, walk).
- Pattern: V-た / V-る / N-の + ついでに: while doing something, taking the opportunity to do something else.
- Example: 買い物のついでに、郵便局に寄ってきた。(While shopping, I stopped by the post office.)
default.q.n2-6-q34-34.why.0: (a) 「からには」 means "once... then one must / will definitely..." and expresses determination or obligation. It is not used to recount an additional action done casually along the way.
default.q.n2-6-q34-34.why.1: (b) 「うちに」means “while/during the time that…,” indicating that a change occurs, and does not combine with「行くうちに散歩してきた」to express an intentional stopover.
default.q.n2-6-q34-34.why.2: (c) 「ついでに」 means “while you are at it” or “incidentally.” It is used when taking advantage of the opportunity created by the main action (going to an exhibition) to do an additional action (taking a walk in the park).
default.q.n2-6-q34-34.why.3: (d) 「上は（うえは）」 is synonymous with 「からには」 (“now that…,” implying that one must or will…), expressing determination or obligation. It does not fit here.
default.q.n2-6-q35-35.verdict: The correct answer is 3. からといって (just because... does not mean...).
default.q.n2-6-q35-35.explanation:
Meaning: Just because you were rejected once, please do not give up so easily.
- Pattern: Plain form + からといって: Just because ... (the following clause is often negative or expresses advice).
- Example: 忙しいからといって、朝ご飯を食べないのはよくない。(It is not good to skip breakfast just because you are busy.)
default.q.n2-6-q35-35.why.0: (a) 「ものの」 means “although...,” and the following clause usually states a fact contrary to expectations; it is not used with a negative request or instruction such as 「～ないでください」.
default.q.n2-6-q35-35.why.1: (b) 「わりに（は）」 means “although...,” or “considering the degree, ...,” and expresses a mismatch between the two clauses. It does not fit the logic of the sentence.
default.q.n2-6-q35-35.why.2: (c) 「からといって」means "just because/even if one says that..." and is usually followed by a negative clause such as「～ないでください」or「～わけではない」, advising someone not to give up merely because they were refused once.
default.q.n2-6-q35-35.why.3: (d) 「のみではなく」means “not only... but also...,” and does not fit the grammatical meaning required by the sentence.
default.q.n2-6-q36-36.verdict: The correct answer is 4. のように (like, as if...).
default.q.n2-6-q36-36.explanation:
Meaning: Her smile is as radiant as sunlight.
- Comparison pattern: N + のように + V/A: do something / be a certain way like N.
- Example: 彼は風のように速く走った。(He ran as fast as the wind.)
default.q.n2-6-q36-36.why.0: (a) 「気味（ぎみ）」means “having a slight feeling of” or “showing symptoms of,” and is used for negative conditions such as 風邪気味 (“slightly feverish”); it is not used for figurative comparisons.
default.q.n2-6-q36-36.why.1: (b) 「っぽい」means “seems” or “has the characteristics of.” To modify an adverb, it must become 「っぽく」. Moreover, it is not used with a specific noun in a comparison such as the sun.
default.q.n2-6-q36-36.why.2: (c) To modify the following verb/adjective phrase 「明るく輝いている」, 「みたい」 must be changed to 「みたいに」. Leaving it as 「みたい」 is grammatically incorrect.
default.q.n2-6-q36-36.why.3: (d) 「のように」is used after a noun (N + のように) to make a simile meaning “like N,” directly modifying the adverb/verb「明るく輝いている」that follows.
default.q.n2-6-q37-37.verdict: The correct answer is 2. ながら (Unfortunately...).
default.q.n2-6-q37-37.explanation:
Sentence meaning: Although I gave it my all, unfortunately I was unable to win the championship.
- Fixed expression: 残念ながら (unfortunately, regrettably).
- On-readings: 全力 (one's full effort), 残念 (regret, disappointment), 優勝 (championship).
- Example: 残念ながら、明日のイベントは中止となりました。(Unfortunately, tomorrow's event has been canceled.)
default.q.n2-6-q37-37.why.0: (a) 「だけに」means “precisely because…, all the more…” and cannot directly be used with the adjective「残念」in this structure.
default.q.n2-6-q37-37.why.1: (b) 「ながら（も）」 combines with certain nouns and adjectives, such as 「残念ながら」「いつもながら」「勝手ながら」, to form fixed expressions meaning “although it is very unfortunate...”.

default.q.n2-6-q38-38.why.1: (b) 「につれ（て）」 means “as...” or “along with...,” describing a change that accompanies the passage of time; it does not fit here.

default.q.n2-6-q39-39.why.2: (c) 「をこめては」(an OCR error for を込めて) means "putting or devoting all of one's feelings or emotions into something"; it is not used to compare or evaluate quality.

Meaning: Before the meeting began, the new member was introduced.

Meaning: The wind is blowing the papers away, so please put a book or something heavy on top of them.

default.q.n2-6-q44-44.explanation:
Meaning: If the product is not completed by the promised date, our company's reputation will be completely lost.
- OCR note: 「山が社」is actually「我が社（わがしゃ — our company）」.
- Sino-Japanese roots: 約束 (yakusoku: promise), 製品 (seihin: product), 完成 (kansei: completion), 信用 (shin'yō: reputation, trust).
- Structure: Plain form + としたら: “Supposing that ...” or “If ...”
- Example: 明日雨が降るとしたら、試合は延期になります。(If it rains tomorrow, the game will be postponed.)
default.q.n2-6-q44-44.why.0: (a) 「ように」 means "so that" or "in the hope that," and is used to express a purpose or wish; it is not used to set a hypothetical condition leading to a negative consequence.
default.q.n2-6-q44-44.why.1: (b) 「としたら」means “assuming that” or “if that were the case.” It introduces a hypothesis—if the product is not completed on time—and reasons about the inevitable consequence in the following clause: the company would lose credibility.
default.q.n2-6-q44-44.why.2: (c) 「につけても」 means “whenever...” or “even if...”. It is commonly used with 「何事につけても」 or repeated as 「〜につけても〜につけても」, so it does not fit this hypothetical context.

default.q.n2-6-q50-50.verdict: The correct answer is 4. かいもなく.
default.q.n2-6-q50-50.explanation:
The N2 pattern 「〜かいもなく／〜たかいもなく」 (or 「N + のかいもなく」) expresses that despite considerable effort, the result is not as expected and the effort proves fruitless.

In this context, the preceding clause clearly states the efforts of various countries and regions (様々な国や地域の努力), while the following clause says that the situation only continues to worsen (その状況は悪化するばかりだ). The contrast between the effort made and the worsening result makes 「かいもなく」 the only correct choice.
default.q.n2-6-q50-50.why.0: (a) 1. さえあれば: Used with a noun to mean “as long as there is... / all that is needed is...,” expressing a minimum condition. It does not fit with 「努力の」to express a negative result occurring despite one’s efforts.
default.q.n2-6-q50-50.why.1: (b) 2. かいがあって: means “worth the effort” or “rewarding,” implying a good result. This is completely opposite to the following clause, which says that the situation is getting worse ("悪化").
default.q.n2-6-q50-50.why.2: (c) 3. 限り: It means “within the limit/as long as...,” but does not form a natural grammar structure with「努力の...」in this context.
default.q.n2-6-q50-50.why.3: (d) 4. かいもなく: The pattern "N + のかいもなく" means that despite making considerable effort, it was all in vain and produced no result. This fits perfectly with the following clause "悪化するばかりだ" (the situation only keeps getting worse).
default.q.n2-6-q51-51.verdict: The correct answer is 1. するばかりだ.
default.q.n2-6-q51-51.explanation:
The N2 grammar pattern 「V-る + ばかりだ」 follows verbs expressing change, such as 悪化する, 増える, 減る, and 悪くなる. It indicates a continuously worsening or changing trend with no sign of stopping, translated as “keep becoming...” or “only continue to...”.

The full sentence emphasizes that, despite the efforts made by countries and regions, the situation has only continued to worsen (悪化するばかりだ), with no benefit from those efforts (努力のかいもなく).
default.q.n2-6-q51-51.why.0: (a) 1. するばかりだ: The structure “V-る + ばかりだ” expresses a negative trend that continues without stopping (“keep becoming increasingly...”); combined with 「悪化する」, it forms 「悪化するばかりだ」 (“it only keeps getting worse”).
default.q.n2-6-q51-51.why.1: (b) 2. しないことはない: This double negative means “it is not that one does not do it” or “one can also do it,” so it does not fit the context describing an objective negative change in the environment.
default.q.n2-6-q51-51.why.2: (c) 3. してはならない: This prohibition pattern means “must never do ...” and cannot describe an objective phenomenon or state such as 「悪化する」.
default.q.n2-6-q51-51.why.3: (d) 4. してはいられない: Means “cannot keep doing something” because one lacks the time or mental capacity. It is semantically unsuitable with the verb indicating deterioration, 「悪化する」.
default.q.n2-6-q52-52.verdict: The correct answer is 4. ありうる.
default.q.n2-6-q52-52.explanation:
The N2 pattern 「V-ます (without ます) + 得る（うる／える）」 means “to be possible” or “to have the potential to happen” (the negative form is ありえない).

According to the passage, because global warming is continuing to worsen, the author warns that if things continue this way (このままでは), it is “entirely possible” (ありうる) that all the ice in Antarctica will melt, creating the risk that rising sea levels will submerge low-lying areas and islands.
default.q.n2-6-q52-52.why.0: (a) 1. あるかいもない: The structure「かいもない」does not naturally combine with「ある」in this way and would mean “not worth existing,” which is completely inappropriate here.
default.q.n2-6-q52-52.why.1: (b) 2. ありえない means "impossible" or "not likely to happen," which contradicts the argument warning about the real risk of the Antarctic ice sheet melting due to global warming.
default.q.n2-6-q52-52.why.2: (c) 3. ある限りだ: 限りだ usually follows an adjective expressing emotion (うれしい限りだ, 残念な限りだ) to indicate an extreme degree of feeling; it is not used to state the possibility that something will happen.
default.q.n2-6-q52-52.why.3: (d) 4. ありうる: The structure "V-ます stem + 得る (うる)" expresses the possibility that something may happen ('entirely possible / could happen'). Combined with "ということも," it indicates that the complete melting of the Antarctic ice sheet is a real possibility.
default.q.n2-6-q53-53.verdict: The correct answer is 2. 保護してまで.
default.q.n2-6-q53-53.explanation:
The N2 grammar pattern 「V-てまで / Nまでして」expresses accepting an expensive, extreme, or unusual action in order to achieve a goal (“even going so far as to...”, “going to the extent of...” ).

The passage discusses a country losing land as sea levels rise, forcing some areas to “even resort to the costly or extreme measure of protecting the coast with concrete” (コンクリートなどで海岸を保護してまで) in an effort to prevent (食い止めようとしている) the danger of being submerged by the sea.
default.q.n2-6-q53-53.why.0: (a) 1. 保護さえすれば: This pattern expresses a minimum condition, "as long as one protects..."; the following clause usually describes a favorable result, so it does not directly fit 「それを食い止めようとしている」 (is trying to prevent it).
default.q.n2-6-q53-53.why.1: (b) 2. 保護してまで: The structure "V-て + まで" expresses accepting an extreme, costly, or unusual measure ('going so far as to ... in order to ...'). It is precisely appropriate for pouring concrete to protect the coastline and prevent land loss.
default.q.n2-6-q53-53.why.2: (c) 3. 保護したからこそ: This pattern means “precisely because [someone] protected [it], ...,” emphasizing that a past action produced a present result. It does not fit the following clause, which describes preventive efforts in the present or future.
default.q.n2-6-q53-53.why.3: (d) 4. 保護したかいがあって: Means "it was worth protecting it / thanks to protecting it, a good result was achieved" and does not fit the sentence's purpose of describing a forceful countermeasure.
default.q.n2-6-q54-54.verdict: The correct answer is 1. 限り.
default.q.n2-6-q54-54.explanation:
The N2 grammar pattern 「V-る／V-ている／V-ない + 限り（は）」expresses an ongoing prerequisite or condition: “as long as...,” “for as long as...”.

The sentence summarizes an idea and calls for responsibility in protecting the environment: “As long as we are alive (生きている限り), we must continue living on this Earth (この地球に住み続けなければならない),” so we must change our way of life while there is still time to make a difference.
default.q.n2-6-q54-54.why.0: (a) 1. 限り: The pattern "V-ている + 限り" means "as long as... / for as long as...". Here, it means "as long as we are alive, we must continue living on this Earth," which is completely correct in meaning and logic.
default.q.n2-6-q54-54.why.1: (b) 2. ばかり: 「生きているばかり」 cannot mean a time condition or scope of survival; 「V-ているばかり」 means doing only one particular thing.
default.q.n2-6-q54-54.why.2: (c) 3. としても: This means “even if” or “even supposing that ...” and would destroy the logical assertion of responsibility for survival in the sentence.
default.q.n2-6-q54-54.why.3: (d) 4. うちに: “while doing V, another unexpected change occurs.” It cannot express the necessary prerequisite meaning “as long as one is alive, one must...” conveyed by 「限り」.
default.q.n2-6-q55-55.verdict: The correct answer is 3 because 「それ」 refers to reconsidering the things taken for granted that were mentioned in the immediately preceding sentence.
default.q.n2-6-q55-55.explanation:
- Main point: The passage explains that the true starting point of scientific research is not studying distant or difficult subjects, but learning to question, think about, and reevaluate things that we normally take for granted in everyday life.
- Question translation: What does 「それ」 (“that”) refer to?
- Answer choices:
  1. Studying only difficult subjects
  2. Having specialized knowledge
  3. Rethinking things that seem obvious
  4. Things that ordinary people think about in everyday life
default.q.n2-6-q55-55.why.0: (a) Choice 1 is incorrect because “researching only difficult subjects” is merely the common stereotype people have when they think of scientists (「普通の人ではとても考えられないような難しいことばかり研究している人だと思ってしまいます」), not the action replaced by 「それ」.
default.q.n2-6-q55-55.why.1: (b) Choice 2 is incorrect because “specialized knowledge” is a necessary condition for scientific research (sentence 2: 「専門的な知識がなければ科学の研究は出来ないでしょう」), not the starting point or action mentioned in the preceding sentence.
default.q.n2-6-q55-55.why.2: (c) Choice 3 is correct, based on the preceding sentence: 「しかし、科学の研究の出発点は、私たちがふだん当たり前に思っていることがらについて、それが当たり前かどうか考え直すことにあるのです。それができたら、その人は科学者になる第一歩を踏み出したといえるかもしれません。」 「それ」 directly refers back to 「それが当たり前かどうか考え直すこと」—reconsidering whether something really is self-evident.
default.q.n2-6-q55-55.why.3: (d) Choice 4 is incorrect because the passage refers to things we take for granted (当たり前に思っていることがら), not “things ordinary people usually think about every day.”
default.q.n2-6-q56-56.verdict: The correct answer is 2: The writer wants the other person to understand that the mistaken abusive phone call in the middle of the night was rude and bothersome.
default.q.n2-6-q56-56.explanation:
**Main idea summary:**
At 3 a.m., the person「私」is angrily called by a woman who mistakenly believes that「私」is making noise by practicing the piano. Although「私」feels that the woman is extremely rude for calling at 3 a.m. without identifying herself,「私」calmly asks her name and hangs up. At exactly 3 a.m. the following day,「私」calls back, politely gives their own name, and then informs her that they do not own a piano or know how to play one. By deliberately calling back at 3 a.m.,「私」protests politely, allowing the woman to understand what it feels like to be disturbed and realize that her own action was rude and bothersome.

**Question and choice translations:**
- **Question:** What does「私」want to convey to the「女性」when calling her home?
- **Choice 1:** That「私」was very happy to receive her call the previous day.
- **Choice 2:** That her phone call was bothersome and rude.
- **Choice 3:** That「私」has stopped practicing the piano.
- **Choice 4:** That「私」caused a great deal of trouble with the sound of the piano.
default.q.n2-6-q56-56.why.0: (a) Choice 1 is incorrect because the character「私」was awakened at 3 a.m. and felt that the other person was rude (「朝の 3 時に、しかも名前を言わないのは失礼だと思った」). There is no feeling of happiness (「うれしかった」).
default.q.n2-6-q56-56.why.1: (b) Choice 2 is correct. When 「私」 was scolded over the phone in the middle of the night, he thought that 「朝の 3 時に、しかも名前を言わないのは失礼だと思った」. He then deliberately called back at exactly 「翌日の午前 3 時活ょうど」, introduced himself by name, and said 「私はピアノを持っていませんし、弾くこともできません」, making the other person experience being disturbed at 3 a.m. and realize that their behavior was unreasonable, bothersome, and rude.
default.q.n2-6-q56-56.why.2: (c) Choice 3 is incorrect because 「私」states that the speaker does not own a piano and cannot play one (「私はピアノを持っていませんし、弾くこともできません」), not that they have stopped practicing.
default.q.n2-6-q56-56.why.3: (d) Choice 4 is incorrect because 私 did not play the piano and affect anyone; the previous day’s phone call was entirely the woman’s misunderstanding.
default.q.n2-6-q57-57.verdict: The correct answer is 4 (The station-name sign on the Shinkansen platform is almost useless).
default.q.n2-6-q57-57.explanation:
- Main point: The author analyzes how the station-name signs on Shinkansen platforms are unnecessary for passengers boarding the train (because they already know which station they are departing from) and for passengers getting off (because there are announcements and onboard displays). They could only be useful to passengers on trains that pass through the station without stopping, but the trains travel too fast or the letters are too small for the passengers to read them at all. The author therefore raises a sarcastic, rhetorical question: “So what on earth is the point of displaying the station name on a Shinkansen platform?” This implies that the signs are of almost no practical use.

- Translation of the question: What does the author want to say?
- Translation of the answer choices:
1. Passengers boarding and leaving Shinkansen trains should pay more attention to station names.
2. Announcements on Shinkansen trains should pronounce station names more clearly.
3. Shinkansen trains travel too fast and are dangerous for passengers.
4. The station-name signs on Shinkansen platforms are almost completely useless.
default.q.n2-6-q57-57.why.0: (a) This does not match the passage because the author says that passengers boarding already know where they are going, while passengers getting off receive announcements on the bus and therefore do not need to check the station name. The author does not advise them to pay more attention to station names.
default.q.n2-6-q57-57.why.1: (b) Does not match the passage because the author only mentions that passengers getting off the train had some kind of announcement on board (車内でのアナウンスなりなんなりがある) as a reason they do not need to check the station-name sign; the author does not demand clearer announcements.
default.q.n2-6-q57-57.why.2: (c) This does not match the passage because the author only says that the train was moving too fast for passing passengers to read the signs, not that its speed endangered the passengers.
default.q.n2-6-q57-57.why.3: (d) This matches the content of the passage. The author shows that the station name is unnecessary for people boarding or getting off at that station (「その駅から乗る人やその駅で降りる人には必要ない」), and cannot be read by passengers passing through (「とても読めたものではない」). The author concludes with a rhetorical question highlighting its uselessness: 「つまり、何のために新幹線のプラットホームに駅名が書いてあるのだろうか」 In short, what is the point of writing the station name on a Shinkansen platform?
default.q.n2-6-q58-58.verdict: The correct answer is 1: Katou was surprised that Yang's wife's Japanese had become very good.
default.q.n2-6-q58-58.explanation:
**Main point of the passage:**
The dialogue records a conversation between Katou (加藤) and Yang (ヤン). Katou says that he recently met Yang's wife, who was with a neighbor named Chin, and praises her greatly improved Japanese. He also expresses genuine surprise: 「いや、本当にび流くり（びっくり）しましたよ。とてもお上手なんで」("I was really surprised. She is very good."). Although Yang modestly says that his wife still has many difficulties when she is not accompanied by her husband, and that only their children have almost no problems, Katou reiterates his surprise at how much Yang's wife has improved her Japanese.

**Translation of the question:**
加藤注んは、なぜび流くりしたのか。
(Why was Katou surprised?)

**Translation of the answer choices:**
1. ヤン注んの奥注んが日本語が上手になったから。 (Because Yang's wife had become good at Japanese.)
2. ヤン注んがが日本語が上手になったから。 (Because Yang had become good at Japanese.)
3. ヤン注んの子供たちが日本語が上手になったから。 (Because Yang's children had become good at Japanese.)
4. チン注んが日本語が上手になったから。 (Because Chin had become good at Japanese.)
default.q.n2-6-q58-58.why.0: (a) Correct. The passage says that Kato begins by mentioning the person he has just met: 「おとなりのチン注んもいっしょでしたよ」, then praises them: 「日本語がとても上手になりましたね」, and reiterates his surprise: 「いや、本当にび流くりしましたよ。とてもお上手なんで」. From Mr. Yang's modest reply about his wife, 「まだ私といっしょでなければ 困ることが 多くて・・・」, it can be determined that the person being praised is Mr. Yang's wife.
default.q.n2-6-q58-58.why.1: (b) Incorrect. The person directly speaking with 加藤さん is Yang, and 加藤さん is praising the person he had just met—Yang’s wife—not Yang himself.
default.q.n2-6-q58-58.why.2: (c) Incorrect. The detail 「子供たちは毎日勉強してますから、今はもうほとんど問題ないんですが」 is additional information told by Mr. Yang, not the reason Ms. Kato was surprised.
default.q.n2-6-q58-58.why.3: (d) Incorrect. チン注ん is mentioned only as the neighbor who was accompanying them at the time (「おとなりのチン注んもいっしょでしたよ」), not as the person who surprised 加藤さん with his Japanese ability.
default.q.n2-6-q59-59.verdict: The correct answer is 4 (a: 25%, b: 37%, c: 40%, d: 32%).
default.q.n2-6-q59-59.explanation:
The passage presents the results of an NHK survey on the trend toward shorter sleep among Japanese people: the proportion of people who slept 7 hours or less on weekdays increased from 25% in 1970 to 37% in 1990, while the proportion who slept 8 hours or more fell from 40% to 32%.

- Question translation: Which combination of numbers is appropriate for filling in a–d?
- Answer choices:
  1. a: 18%, b: 25%, c: 35%, d: 32%
  2. a: 25%, b: 34%, c: 40%, d: 32%
  3. a: 25%, b: 37%, c: 15%, d: 12%
  4. a: 25(%), b: 37(%), c: 40(%), d: (32%)
default.q.n2-6-q59-59.why.0: Choice 1 is incorrect because the figures a = 18%, b = 25%, c = 35%, and d = 32% do not match the survey results.
default.q.n2-6-q59-59.why.1: Choice 2 is incorrect because b = 34% does not reflect the actual percentage of people who slept for seven hours or less in 1990; the correct figure was 37%.
default.q.n2-6-q59-59.why.2: Choice 3 is incorrect because c = 15% and d = 12% are far too low for the group sleeping eight hours or more; the actual figure decreases from 40% to 32%.
default.q.n2-6-q59-59.why.3: Answer choice 4 is correct based on the passage: 「平日の睡眠時間が 7 時間以下の人は、 ’ 70年には（ a: 25% ）だったが ’ 90 年 には（ b: 37% ）に増えている。一方、 8 時間以上の睡眠をよる人は（ c: 40% ）（ d: 32% ）に減っている。」 The figures a = 25%, b = 37%, c = 40%, and d = 32% accurately reflect the NHK survey results.
default.q.n2-6-q60-60.verdict: The correct answer is 4: Failing in one's new life by being unable to become independent, overcome difficulties, and mature.
default.q.n2-6-q60-60.explanation:
• Summary: The author is about to begin an independent life in Tokyo to attend a vocational school. Although excited, the author is also anxious because it is their first time living away from home. The author sees attending school and meeting many people as a precious opportunity and resolves to move forward steadily and grow rather than waste it.
• Question translation: In the sentence 「Tôi không muốn làm lãng phí nó」, what does “waste it” mean here?
• Answer choices:
1. Feeling that the expectations of people around them are a source of anxiety.
2. Taking a long time before achieving their dream.
3. Being unable to attend the school they had planned to attend.
4. Failing in their new life.
default.q.n2-6-q60-60.why.0: (a) Incorrect because the passage only mentions the author's own anxiety when leaving home for the first time («親元を始めて離れる私にとっては、とても怖いことでもあります»). It does not say that the author feels pressured or uneasy about the expectations of others.
default.q.n2-6-q60-60.why.1: (b) Choice 2 is incorrect because the passage does not discuss how much time it takes to fulfill a dream. It focuses on making use of educational opportunities and living independently.
default.q.n2-6-q60-60.why.2: (c) Choice 3 is incorrect because the author has definitely decided to attend a vocational school in Tokyo starting in the spring (「この春から東京の専門学校に行くことが決まっており」), not that attending school is impossible.
default.q.n2-6-q60-60.why.3: (d) Choice 4 is correct because the passage states that the author is about to begin a challenging and frightening life alone in Tokyo: 「東京という大都会でのたった一人の生活なので...とても怖いことでもあります」. However, the author also regards it as an opportunity for personal growth: 「自分が成長するための第一歩として、し流かり歩んでいきたいです」. Therefore, wasting this opportunity means failing to overcome the difficulties and failing in the new life.
default.q.n2-6-q61-61.verdict: The correct answer is 1: Starting an independent life in Tokyo in the spring.
default.q.n2-6-q61-61.explanation:
• Summary: The author says that, in order to have the opportunity to move to Tokyo and live alone while attending a vocational school to pursue a dream, they received help and support from many people and resolved never to forget their gratitude.
• Translation of the question: What does 「this opportunity」 (in 告/②) refer to?
• Translation of the choices:
1. Starting an independent life in Tokyo in the spring.
2. Being able to meet many different people.
3. Making an effort to achieve a future dream.
4. Feeling anxious so that one can mature.
default.q.n2-6-q61-61.why.0: (a) Choice 1 is correct. The passage states: 「私はこの春から東京の専門学校に行くことが決まっており、一人暮らしをする予定だからです」 and emphasizes that many people supported the author in obtaining this opportunity: 「この機会を得るにあたって、たくさんのひとから支援があったことを忘れず」. “This opportunity” refers to going to Tokyo to study and live independently.
default.q.n2-6-q61-61.why.1: (b) Choice 2 is incorrect because “meeting many people” was only one opportunity that came with studying in Tokyo (「たくさんの人と出会える機会を得ることができた」); it does not encompass the entire new life that others helped the author experience.
default.q.n2-6-q61-61.why.2: (c) Choice 3 is incorrect because "making an effort to achieve one's dreams" is an action the author must carry out personally, not something or an opportunity received through support from people around the author.
default.q.n2-6-q61-61.why.3: (d) Choice 4 is incorrect because “feeling anxious” is the author’s personal psychological state, not an “opportunity” gained through someone else’s help.
default.q.n2-6-q62-62.verdict: The correct answer is 3: To express one's determination when beginning a new life.
default.q.n2-6-q62-62.explanation:
• Summary: Throughout the passage, the author shares feelings ranging from a New Year’s dream to the reality of preparing to live alone in Tokyo. Although the author feels fear and anxiety, they affirm their determination not to waste the opportunity or be defeated by any difficulty, and to become a strong, steadfast adult.
• Question translation: What is the purpose for which the author is thought to have written this passage?
• Translation of the choices:
1. To express gratitude to the people who helped them.
2. To announce that they will attend a vocational school in Tokyo.
3. To express their determination as they begin a new life.
4. To discuss or share their feelings of anxiety with someone.
default.q.n2-6-q62-62.why.0: (a) Choice 1 is incorrect because continuing to feel grateful («感謝の気持ちを持ち続けようと思います») is merely a thought reminding the author to be thankful; the main purpose is not to write a thank-you letter to those who helped.
default.q.n2-6-q62-62.why.1: (b) Choice 2 is incorrect because attending a vocational school in Tokyo is merely the real-life setting; the article is not intended to send a news announcement to others.
default.q.n2-6-q62-62.why.2: (c) Choice 3 is correct. The passage quotes the author’s strong determination to overcome challenges and grow at the conclusion: «自分が成長するための第一歩として、し流かり歩んでいきたいです» and «これから先どんな困難にも負けない強くて立派な大人になるために、大きな一歩を踏み出します». The passage as a whole focuses on her will and determination as she begins a new independent life.
default.q.n2-6-q62-62.why.3: (d) Choice 4 is incorrect because the author is encouraging and strengthening their own resolve, not seeking advice or confiding in someone else to relieve their feelings.
default.q.n2-6-q63-63.verdict: The correct answer is choice 2: Enabling foreigners to work in Japan using only English.
default.q.n2-6-q63-63.explanation:
- Main point: The author feels annoyed that foreigners come to Japan, refuse to learn or speak Japanese, and still make a great deal of money (荒稼ぎ), while the author uses their own English to help them, allowing them to work smoothly in Japan using only English.
- Question translation: The passage says that the author "uses their English to help them." What does this mean?
- Answer choices:
  1. Taking care of their daily lives in a foreign country.
  2. Helping them work using only English, without having to learn Japanese.
  3. Frequently working in teams with Americans at headquarters.
  4. Providing free interpreting as a form of financial support.
default.q.n2-6-q63-63.why.0: (a) Choice 1 is incorrect because the text only discusses the work context and does not mention taking care of foreigners’ daily lives (生活の世話).
default.q.n2-6-q63-63.why.1: (b) Choice 2 is correct because the passage states: 「日本にきている外国人が日本語を話注ず、荒稼ぎしている... そういう外国人を、自分の英語で助けてしまっている」. The author is frustrated that by translating and helping in English, they are indirectly enabling foreigners to work and make money in Japan without needing to speak Japanese.
default.q.n2-6-q63-63.why.2: (c) Choice 3 is incorrect because the text mentions only one occasion when the author went to meet clients with Americans at the headquarters. It does not say that the expression refers to regularly working as a team.
default.q.n2-6-q63-63.why.3: (d) Choice 4 is incorrect because the passage does not consider free interpreting to be financial support; it is talking about helping them communicate and work.
default.q.n2-6-q64-64.verdict: The correct answer is choice 2: To show foreigners that anyone who wants to work in Japan needs to know Japanese.
default.q.n2-6-q64-64.explanation:
- Main idea: To make his American colleague understand that knowing Japanese is necessary when working in Japan, the author deliberately did not interpret during the entire two-hour meeting with Japanese clients, leaving the American completely bewildered and unable to understand anything.
- Question translation: The passage says that he “played a little mean trick.” Why did the author do this?
- Answer choices:
  1. Because he felt unhappy that foreigners were paid such high salaries.
  2. To teach that person that Japanese is necessary when working in Japan.
  3. Because his colleague Kawakami enjoyed playing practical jokes.
  4. Because he found it troublesome to use English when working with Japanese people.
default.q.n2-6-q64-64.why.0: (a) Option 1 is incorrect because although the passage mentions a foreigner making a great deal of money (荒稼ぎ), the author plays a prank on him to make him experience the inconvenience of not knowing Japanese, not simply out of jealousy over his salary.
default.q.n2-6-q64-64.why.1: (b) Choice 2 is correct because the passage states that the author took an American to meet a client but 「彼には一切通訳しませんでした」, so the man 「二時間ほど、私達の議論のうずの中で、ぽかんとすわっていました」. This was intended to show him that without knowing Japanese, he could not participate in work in Japan.
default.q.n2-6-q64-64.why.2: (c) Choice 3 is incorrect because the passage only says that the author discussed it with colleague Kawakami (同僚の川上さんと話して); it does not say that Kawakami liked playing tricks or teasing people.
default.q.n2-6-q64-64.why.3: (d) Choice 4 is incorrect because the author deliberately did not translate it so that Americans would not understand the practical lesson, not because the author personally found speaking English troublesome.
default.q.n2-6-q65-65.verdict: The correct answer is choice 4: It is the Japanese people themselves who take the trouble to provide benefits or assistance to foreigners who do not know Japanese.
default.q.n2-6-q65-65.explanation:
- Main idea: The author believes that when Japanese people speak English, they should adopt the mindset that "we are the ones making the effort to speak English because the other person does not know Japanese"—in other words, Japanese speakers are the ones providing support and benefits to the other person. With this justifiable sense of superiority, Japanese people can speak English confidently and naturally, without feeling inferior or afraid.
- Question translation: The passage says that "it is only natural." Why does the author think so?
- Answer choices:
  1. Because it would be strange to let foreigners relax and do nothing.
  2. Because Japanese people are superior to Americans.
  3. Because being able to speak English is valuable.
  4. Because we are the ones providing the benefit or convenience to the other person.
default.q.n2-6-q65-65.why.0: (a) Choice 1 is incorrect because it does not explain why maintaining confidence when speaking English would be considered “natural.”
default.q.n2-6-q65-65.why.1: (b) Choice 2 is incorrect because the author only discusses the legitimate sense of superiority one may feel when helping someone in a foreign language; the author does not claim that Japanese people are more capable or superior to Americans.
default.q.n2-6-q65-65.why.2: (c) Choice 3 is incorrect because the passage does not discuss the general value of English-speaking ability; it emphasizes the speaker’s position when helping the listener.
default.q.n2-6-q65-65.why.3: (d) Choice 4 is correct because the passage says: 「私達が、英語を話すときに、『日本語のできない人のために、こちらがわざわざ英語を話してやっているのだ』という気持ちをどこかでもっておくことは、当然だと考えるからです」. This shows that the Japanese side is taking the trouble to speak English for the other person's benefit, meaning that the Japanese are the party providing the benefit (利益を与える側).
default.q.n2-6-q66-66.verdict: The correct answer is 4: Sushi and desserts are not traditionally considered ordinary Japanese dishes, so the author felt confused when customers asked about them.
default.q.n2-6-q66-66.explanation:
- Main point: While working in Paris, the author had difficulty because French customers asked why a Japanese restaurant did not serve sushi or dessert. In traditional Japanese cuisine, training to make sushi and training to cook Japanese dishes are completely separate fields, and European-style desserts are not normally included on a Japanese cuisine menu.
- Question translation: The author says, “What put me in a difficult position was...”; why did the author say they were in a difficult position?
- Answer choices:
1. Because there are no restaurants in Europe that do not serve dessert.
2. Because it was not permitted to serve dishes that were not on the menu.
3. Because they were still an apprentice and had not yet mastered sushi.
4. Because sushi and dessert are not part of ordinary Japanese cuisine.
default.q.n2-6-q66-66.why.0: (a) Incorrect because the fact that there are no restaurants in Europe without desserts only explains why customers demand them; it is not the fundamental reason Japanese-cuisine chefs face difficulties.
default.q.n2-6-q66-66.why.1: (b) Incorrect because the passage does not mention that serving items outside the menu is prohibited.
default.q.n2-6-q66-66.why.2: (c) Incorrect. The author does not say that they cannot yet handle sushi because they are still learning the trade. Rather, the author explains that learning to make sushi is completely different from learning to cook Japanese cuisine in general.
default.q.n2-6-q66-66.why.3: (d) Correct, as shown by: 「お寿司は、日本料理とは修業（注2）が全然違うのですが、フランス人にとってみれば『日本レストランなのに寿司がないのはどうしてだ？』となるわけです」 and 「デザートのないレストランなんてヨーロッパにはあり得ませんから」. The customers demanded sushi and dessert, even though sushi requires a separate training process and European-style desserts are not part of a traditional Japanese menu.
default.q.n2-6-q67-67.verdict: The correct answer is 1: "それ" refers to the belief that pizza is a representative dish of Italian cuisine, leading Japanese people to expect an Italian restaurant to serve pizza.
default.q.n2-6-q67-67.explanation:
- Main point: The author compares French diners who assume that a Japanese restaurant must have sushi with people in Japan in the past who would enter an Italian restaurant and become angry if there was no pizza, mistakenly believing that pizza had to be the representative Italian dish.
- Translation of the question: In the phrase "The feeling is similar to that," what does "that" (それ) refer to?
- Translation of the choice:
1. The mistaken belief among Japanese people that pizza is a representative dish of Italian cuisine.
2. French people wanting to eat sushi at a Japanese restaurant.
3. Being able to eat pizza at Italian restaurants in Japan.
4. Sushi being very popular at restaurants in Europe.
default.q.n2-6-q67-67.why.0: (a) Correct, as shown by the passage: 「フランス人にとってみれば『日本レストランなのに寿司がないのはどうしてだ？』となるわけです。日本のイタリアンレストランにピザがなくて叱られた時代もあったのでしょうが、それと同じような感じでしょう」. \"それ\" refers to the time when Japanese people mistakenly assumed that an Italian restaurant had to serve pizza and criticized it when it did not, similar to French people assuming that a Japanese restaurant must serve sushi.
default.q.n2-6-q67-67.why.1: (b) Incorrect because the fact that a French person wants to eat sushi at a Japanese restaurant is the point the author compares with "それ"; it is not what "それ" itself refers to.
default.q.n2-6-q67-67.why.2: (c) Incorrect because the passage says that the Italian restaurant in Japan “does not have pizza” (ピザがなくて), not that “pizza can be eaten.”
default.q.n2-6-q67-67.why.3: (d) Incorrect because the passage does not mention sushi being popular at European restaurants, and that is not what 「それ」 refers to.
default.q.n2-6-q68-68.verdict: The correct answer is 4: ご飯 (rice) is the dish that concludes a traditional Japanese meal.
default.q.n2-6-q68-68.explanation:
- Main point: At the author's restaurant, after the soup (お椀), guests are served a few small pieces of sushi called "oshisogi" (a small snack to tide them over). Although the meal ends with rice (ご飯), serving sushi in the middle of the meal temporarily fills the guests' stomachs so they can continue drinking.
- Question: Which vocabulary item is most appropriate for [ A ]?
- Translation of the choices:
1. Alcohol
2. Mood / feeling
3. Bowl of soup
4. Rice
default.q.n2-6-q68-68.why.0: (a) Incorrect because お酒 is consumed throughout the meal and continues to be served after the sushi appetizer (「ここからまたお酒を飲みましょう」); it is not the dish that ends the meal.
default.q.n2-6-q68-68.why.1: (b) Incorrect because a mood (気分) is an abstract noun, not a dish served at the end of a meal.
default.q.n2-6-q68-68.why.2: (c) Incorrect because the soup (お椀) was served before the sushi appetizer (「お椀の次は、『お凌ぎ』といって…」).

default.q.n2-6-q73-73.why.1: (b) Incorrect. This contradicts the author’s advice: books should be used only as references, and one should not expect everything to be solved simply by following them exactly («本は、...あくまで参考程度にして、その通りにやったらなんでも解決と期待し過ぎないほうがいい»).

default.q.n2-6-q11-11.verdict: The provided answer is 4 (ながめる), but the correct answer is 1 (景色).
default.q.n2-6-q11-11.explanation:
- Meaning: The view outside from the balcony is absolutely spectacular.
- Related vocabulary: 景色 (scenery), 眺める (look at, gaze into the distance).
- Common expression: 外の景色 (the view outside).

default.q.n2-6-q11-11.why.0: (a) 1. 景色 (けしき): A noun meaning scenery or landscape, naturally forming 「外の景色」(the scenery outside), and fitting both grammatically and semantically.
default.q.n2-6-q11-11.why.1: (b) 2. 日当たり (ひあたり): the amount or direction of sunlight, commonly used in 「日当たりがいい/悪い」. It does not fit the context of enjoying a view from a balcony.
default.q.n2-6-q11-11.why.2: (c) 3. 住まい (すまい): a noun meaning home or place of residence; it does not fit after “外の” in this sentence.
default.q.n2-6-q11-11.why.3: (d) 4. ながめる (眺める): This dictionary-form verb means 'to gaze at' or 'to look out over.' After "外の" (noun + の), a noun must follow, so placing the verb in its basic form here is grammatically incorrect.
default.q.n2-6-q12-12.explanation:
- Meaning: In class, I always sit directly behind Rin.
- Related kanji: 真後ろ (directly behind), 直後 (immediately afterward in time).
- Prefix rule: The prefix 真- (ま/しん) emphasizes exactness or being directly in a position or state (e.g., 真後ろ - directly behind, 真前 - directly in front, 真上 - directly above, 真下 - directly below, 真ん中 - right in the middle).
- Example: 映画館で彼の真後ろの席に座った。(I sat in the seat directly behind him at the movie theater.)
default.q.n2-6-q12-12.why.0: (a) 1. 直後 (ちょくご): Refers to the point in time immediately after an event or action (e.g., 食事の直後). It is not used for a spatial position behind a person.
default.q.n2-6-q12-12.why.1: (b) 2. 直後ろ: This combination violates Japanese word-formation rules; the word does not exist in Japanese.
default.q.n2-6-q12-12.why.2: (c) 3. 真後ろ (まうしろ): the prefix 真- combines with a noun indicating direction or position to mean “directly behind,” so this is completely correct.
default.q.n2-6-q12-12.why.3: (d) 4. 真ん後ろ: Incorrect combination. The prefix 真ん- forms words such as 真ん中 (right in the middle), but it does not combine with 後ろ.
default.q.n2-6-q13-13.verdict: The correct answer is 4 (いたずら).
default.q.n2-6-q13-13.explanation:
- Meaning: My five-year-old son is always getting into mischief.
- Related on'yomi: 悪戯 (いたずら: mischief, teasing), 躾 (しつけ: discipline, upbringing).
- Grammar: [Noun] + ばかりしている (to do nothing but..., with a complaining or admonishing nuance).
- Example: 弟は勉強もしないで、ゲームばかりしている。(My younger brother does not study at all and does nothing but play games.)
default.q.n2-6-q13-13.why.0: (a) 1. しつけ (躾): a noun meaning the discipline and upbringing provided by parents or adults; it is not used for the five-year-old child’s own behavior.
default.q.n2-6-q13-13.why.1: (b) 2. いじめ (苛め): A noun referring to malicious bullying or harassment of others, which does not fit the context of mischievous, energetic children.
default.q.n2-6-q13-13.why.2: (c) 3. おじめ: A meaningless word in Japanese.
default.q.n2-6-q13-13.why.3: (d) 4. いたずら (悪戯): a noun meaning children’s mischief or pranks. Combined with する, it forms 「いたずらをする」, which fits perfectly with 「いたずらばかりしている」.
default.q.n2-6-q14-14.explanation:
- Meaning: Eating out is expensive, so let’s try to cook for ourselves next time.
- Related kanji compounds: 外食 (eating out), 自炊 (cooking for oneself).
- Common fixed expressions:
  + 高くつく (たかくつく): to be expensive, cost more than expected.
  + 安くつく (やすくつく): to be inexpensive, save money.
- Example: 自炊を始めると、食費がかなり安くつく。(When you start cooking for yourself, your food expenses become much lower.)
default.q.n2-6-q14-14.why.0: (a) 1. する: 「高くする」 means actively “to make something more expensive” or “to raise the price”; it does not express the idea that the cost of something rises on its own.
default.q.n2-6-q14-14.why.1: (b) 2. とる:「高くとる」usually means “charge a high price” or “charge a high fee,” and does not combine with an action as the subject to indicate how costly it is.
default.q.n2-6-q14-14.why.2: (c) 3. でる: The idiomatic expression "高くでる" does not exist in this context.
default.q.n2-6-q14-14.why.3: (d) 4. つく: It combines with an -i adjective in its adverbial form to create the idiom 「高くつく」 (turn out to be expensive), so it is completely correct.
default.q.n2-6-q15-15.verdict: The correct answer is 2 (あまやか注ない).
default.q.n2-6-q15-15.explanation:
- Translation: Raising children without spoiling them is truly difficult.
- Related vocabulary: 甘やかす (あまやかす: to spoil), 育てる (そだてる: to raise, bring up, educate).
- Grammar: V-ないで (do the following action without doing the preceding action).

default.q.n2-6-q15-15.why.0: (a) 1. なぐらない (殴る): Although 「なぐらないで」 is grammatically correct, the meaning “raising children without hitting them is difficult” is inconsistent with common educational standards and thinking.
default.q.n2-6-q15-15.why.1: (b) 2. あまやか注ない (甘やかさない — do not spoil): The verb 甘やかす combines with the negative form + で to produce “甘やかさないで育てる” (to raise someone without spoiling or indulging them), which is grammatically accurate and practical.
default.q.n2-6-q15-15.why.2: (c) 3. いじめない (苛める): Means “not bully”; bullying others does not fit the context of parents raising their children.
default.q.n2-6-q15-15.why.3: (d) 4. しつけない (躾ける - to discipline, teach proper behavior): "Not disciplining one's child" is permissive behavior and easy to do, not something "difficult to carry out" (難しい).
default.q.n2-6-q16-16.verdict: The correct answer is 1 (かついで) because the verb 「担ぐ（かつぐ）」means to carry or shoulder something and naturally combines with 「肩に…」.

default.q.n2-6-q18-18.verdict: The correct answer is 2 (すべって) because 「滑る（すべる）」means “to slip” or “to skid,” describing tires sliding on a wet road because of rain.

• Example: 道が凍っていて足が滑りそうになった。(The road was icy, and I almost slipped.)
default.q.n2-6-q18-18.why.0: (a) つまづいて (躓く): To trip or stumble, commonly used when a person’s foot catches on something or when someone encounters failure in a task; it is not used for a car tire.
default.q.n2-6-q18-18.why.1: (b) すべって (滑る): to slip or skid (as in a tire skidding on a wet road: タイヤが滑る), completely correct in both meaning and grammar.
default.q.n2-6-q18-18.why.2: (c) ねじれて (捩れる): “to become twisted,” as with a cable or joint. It does not fit the context of a tire driving on a rainy road.
default.q.n2-6-q18-18.why.3: (d) またいで (跨ぐ): to step over or cross (a ditch, barrier); it is not appropriate when the subject is a tire.
default.q.n2-6-q19-19.verdict: The correct answer is 4 (たよりにしては), because 「〜を頼りにする（たよりにする）」means “to rely on” or “to depend on someone.”
default.q.n2-6-q19-19.explanation:
Translation: You can't keep depending on your parents forever.
• Vocabulary: 頼 means to rely on, depend on, or count on.
• Fixed expression: 「～を頼りにする」 (to rely on someone or something).
• Example: 彼は自立して、もう誰をも頼りにせずに生きている。(He has become independent and now lives without relying on anyone.)
default.q.n2-6-q19-19.why.0: (a) 楽にしては (楽にする): To make something easy or comfortable; in this sentence, it would mean “must not make the parents comfortable,” which is completely wrong in meaning.
default.q.n2-6-q19-19.why.1: (b) 改めては (改める): to revise, renew, or improve; it does not combine naturally in this sentence pattern.
default.q.n2-6-q19-19.why.2: (c) 恵まれては (恵まれる): to be blessed or endowed, usually used with the particle に, as in 才能に恵まれる; it is not used with を in 「親を恵まれる」.
default.q.n2-6-q19-19.why.3: (d) たよりにしては (頼りにする): to rely on, depend on. Combined with 「～てはいけない」, it forms advice or a warning: “you must not keep relying on your parents.”
default.q.n2-6-q20-20.verdict: The correct answer is 1 (うらぎられて), because 「裏切る（うらぎる）」 means “to betray,” and the passive form 「裏切られて」 describes losing trust after being betrayed by someone close and trusted.
default.q.n2-6-q20-20.explanation:
Translation: Betrayed even by my best friend, I can no longer trust anyone.
• Vocabulary: 裏切 (betrayal), 信用 (trust, confidence).
• Expression: 「〜に裏切られる」(to be betrayed by someone).
• Example: 仲間に裏切られたショックからなかなか立ち直れない。(I cannot recover easily from the shock of being betrayed by my friends.)
default.q.n2-6-q20-20.why.0: (a) うらぎられて (裏切られる): To be betrayed. It fits the context perfectly: being betrayed by a close friend (親友に裏切られる) causes the speaker to lose all trust in people.
default.q.n2-6-q20-20.why.1: (b) なぐ注められて (慰められる - to be comforted): It has a positive meaning (to be comforted or encouraged), which completely contradicts the negative result, "no longer being able to trust anyone."
default.q.n2-6-q20-20.why.2: (c) や流つけられて (やっつけられる - to be defeated, beaten, or dealt with): It does not fit the relationship of trust between friends in the sentence.
default.q.n2-6-q20-20.why.3: (d) さからわれて (逆らわれる — to be opposed or talked back to): commonly used when someone of lower status disobeys someone of higher status. It does not fit the result of losing trust in people.
default.q.n2-6-q21-21.verdict: The correct answer is 2 (あいまいな) because 「曖昧（あいまい）」means vague or evasive, directly contrasting with 「はっきり言う」 (to speak clearly/directly) in the following clause.
default.q.n2-6-q21-21.explanation:
Sentence translation: Don't give such an evasive answer; if you don't like it, just say clearly that you don't.
• Sino-Japanese term: 曖昧 (ÁI MUỘI - vague, ambiguous, unclear).
• Phrase: 「あいまいな返事をする」(give an evasive or noncommittal answer).
• Example: 曖昧な態度をとらずに、自分の意見をはっきり言いなさい。(Stop being so vague and state your opinion clearly.)
default.q.n2-6-q21-21.why.0: (a) みにくい (醜い/見難い): Means ugly or difficult to look at, and does not modify 返事 (reply) appropriately in this context.
default.q.n2-6-q21-21.why.1: (b) あいまいな (曖昧な): vague, ambiguous, noncommittal, indecisive. 「あいまいな返事」fits perfectly with the preceding reminder, “If you do not like it, say so clearly (はっきり言って).”
default.q.n2-6-q21-21.why.2: (c) ふ注山しい (ふさわしい - 相応しい): suitable, appropriate, fitting; it does not fit the meaning of urging someone to speak frankly.
default.q.n2-6-q21-21.why.3: (d) ありふれた (有り触れた): Ordinary, commonplace, familiar everywhere; it is not used for an evasive answer.
default.q.n2-6-q22-22.verdict: The correct answer is 4 (く山えて—くわえて), because 「咥える／くわえる」means to hold something in one’s mouth and is characteristically used with a cigarette: 「たばこをくわえる」.
default.q.n2-6-q22-22.explanation:
Translation: He is always reading the newspaper with a cigarette between his lips.
• Vocabulary: 咥える／銜える (くわえる: to hold in one's mouth), 挟む (はさむ: to place or hold between).
• Fixed expression: 「たばこをくわえる」 (to hold a cigarette between one's lips).
• Example: 彼はパイプをくわえながら考え事をしていた。(He was deep in thought with a pipe between his lips.)
default.q.n2-6-q22-22.why.0: (a) かじって (齧る): to bite or gnaw (hard food such as an apple or bread), or to dabble in learning; it is not used for holding a cigarette between one's lips.
default.q.n2-6-q22-22.why.1: (b) かかえて (抱える): to hold something against one’s chest or take on a heavy responsibility; it is not used with cigarettes.
default.q.n2-6-q22-22.why.2: (c) は注んで (挟んで - はさんで): Means “to place between” or “to pinch.” If holding a cigarette between one’s fingers, 「指に挟む」 is used, whereas holding a cigarette in one’s mouth while reading the newspaper is くわえる.
default.q.n2-6-q22-22.why.3: (d) く山えて (くわえて - 咥える): to hold something in one’s mouth. The expression 「たばこをくわえる」 specifically describes holding a cigarette between one’s lips.
default.q.n2-6-q23-23.verdict: The correct answer is 2. ことわった.
default.q.n2-6-q23-23.explanation:
Translation: I turned down that part-time job.
- Kanji meaning: The kanji 断 in the verb 断る (ことわる) means to refuse or decline.
- Example: 誘いを断る (Decline an invitation).
default.q.n2-6-q23-23.why.0: (a) 「やめた」 means quit or stopped doing something; it is not synonymous with 「断った」, which means refused from the outset.
default.q.n2-6-q23-23.why.1: (b) 「ことわった」 is the correct reading and synonymous expression for 「断った」 (to refuse an offer or job).
default.q.n2-6-q23-23.why.2: (c) 「ことづけた」 (to send a message or regards—言付ける) has a completely different meaning.
default.q.n2-6-q23-23.why.3: (d) 「ことなった」 (different - 異なる) has a completely different meaning.
default.q.n2-6-q24-24.verdict: The correct answer is 1. 接続した (connected, accessed).
default.q.n2-6-q24-24.explanation:
Sentence meaning: I accessed that company's homepage.
- Vocabulary: 接続 (connection, linking to a network/system).
- IT vocabulary: アクセスする (access) is synonymous with 接続する (connect to/access a network or website).
- Example: サーバーにアクセスする／接続する (access/connect to a server).
default.q.n2-6-q24-24.why.0: (a) 「接続した」 means connected or accessed a network/website, and is synonymous with 「アクセスした」.
default.q.n2-6-q24-24.why.1: (b) 「登録した」 means to register an account or information; it is not synonymous with accessing something.
default.q.n2-6-q24-24.why.2: (c) 「検索した」means searched or looked up; it is not synonymous with accessed.
default.q.n2-6-q24-24.why.3: (d) 「保存した」 means stored or saved, and is not synonymous with accessing something.
default.q.n2-6-q25-25.verdict: The correct answer is 3. ペーストした (pasted).
default.q.n2-6-q25-25.explanation:
Meaning: I pasted an image obtained from the internet into the document.
- 貼り付ける (はりつける, to paste) in computer operations is equivalent to the loanword ペーストする (paste).
- Common expression: コピー＆ペースト (copy & paste) is equivalent to コピー＆貼り付け.
default.q.n2-6-q25-25.why.0: (a) 「添付した」 means “attached,” as when attaching a file to an email; it does not mean pasting a picture into a document.
default.q.n2-6-q25-25.why.1: (b) 「挿入した」means “inserted”; the action of directly pasting an image corresponds precisely to ペーストする.
default.q.n2-6-q25-25.why.2: (c) 「ペーストした」 (paste) is a computer-operation term meaning to paste an image or content into a document, equivalent to 「貼り付けた」.
default.q.n2-6-q25-25.why.3: (d) 「コピーした」 means “copied,” which is the opposite of the action “pasted.”
default.q.n2-6-q26-26.verdict: The correct answer is 1. 手応えがある (to feel worthwhile, to feel that one's efforts have paid off).
default.q.n2-6-q26-26.explanation:
Sentence meaning: This work is well worth doing; it gives a sense of satisfaction and purpose.
- やりがい (the value or fulfillment found in making an effort to do something; verb stem + 甲斐).
- 手応え (a positive response or the feeling that one's efforts have produced worthwhile results).
- Example: 手応えを感じる (to feel that one's efforts are paying off).
default.q.n2-6-q26-26.why.0: (a) 「手応えがある」 expresses the feeling that one's work has produced good results and was worth the effort, making it closest in meaning to 「やりがいがある」.
default.q.n2-6-q26-26.why.1: (b) 「簡単だ」 means simple or easy and does not express the value of the work or effort involved.
default.q.n2-6-q26-26.why.2: (c) 「利益が出る」 means to generate profit or money and does not fully convey the spiritual meaning of やりがい.
default.q.n2-6-q26-26.why.3: (d) 「楽しい」 simply means enjoyable; it does not express the sense of achievement and fulfillment that comes from making an effort, as やりがい/手応え do.
default.q.n2-6-q27-27.verdict: The correct answer is 2. 出向いてください (please go there in person).
default.q.n2-6-q27-27.explanation:
Meaning: Please go to the director's office.
- Sino-Japanese roots: 出向く: to go personally to a particular place to handle business.
- Example: 現場に出向く (go personally to the scene).
default.q.n2-6-q27-27.why.0: (a) 「伺ってください」 is the humble form of 行く/聞く/訪ねる for the speaker’s own action; it is not used as a request directed at the other person with 「〜てください」.
default.q.n2-6-q27-27.why.1: (b) 「出向いてください」means to go somewhere in person for work. It is a polite expression equivalent to 「行ってください」in a business context.
default.q.n2-6-q27-27.why.2: (c) 「向かってください」 means “please head toward that direction,” emphasizing the direction of movement; 出向く is more natural here.
default.q.n2-6-q27-27.why.3: (d) 「訪ねてください」means “please visit” or “please call on” a house or acquaintance, and does not fit the context of moving internally to the director’s office.
default.q.n2-6-q28-28.verdict: The correct answer is 2: 「高くつく」 is used correctly to mean that the actual cost ends up being higher and more expensive than originally expected.
default.q.n2-6-q28-28.explanation:
「高くつく」means to cost more than expected, usually because additional costs arise or an option that seemed inexpensive turns out to be costly.
Example: 自炊するつもりが、材料を買いすぎて外食より高くついてしまった。(I intended to cook for myself to save money, but I bought too many ingredients, so it ended up costing more than eating out.)
default.q.n2-6-q28-28.why.0: Incorrect because the physical height of a 36-story building must be described with the i-adjective 「高い」, not 「高くつく」, which means that something costs a lot.
default.q.n2-6-q28-28.why.1: Correct because 「高くつく」 is used appropriately to describe going to a distant supermarket because it seemed cheaper, but spending extra on transportation ultimately makes it more expensive than expected.
default.q.n2-6-q28-28.why.2: It is incorrect because describing a mountain as the highest geographically or in natural elevation requires the adjective 「高い」(一番高い山), not 「高くつく」.
default.q.n2-6-q28-28.why.3: Incorrect because when something is sold at a high auction price, use 「高く売れた」, not 「高くついて売れた」. 高くつく means that something costs more than expected.
default.q.n2-6-q29-29.verdict: The correct answer is 4: 「できたて」is the standard expression meaning food that has just been cooked.
default.q.n2-6-q29-29.explanation:
The suffix 「〜たて」（〜立て）is attached to the verb stem (the ます-form without ます) and means “freshly made,” “just finished,” or “still hot/fresh.” It is commonly used for food, drinks, and other newly completed states, such as 焼きたて (freshly baked), 炊きたて (freshly cooked rice), できたて (freshly made), and 淹れたて (freshly brewed).
Example: 焼きたてのパンはとても香りがいい。(Freshly baked bread smells wonderful.)
default.q.n2-6-q29-29.why.0: Incorrect because to express a way of speaking or tone of voice resembling one's father's, use 「話し方」or 「話しぶり」; 「話したて」is not a valid combination.
default.q.n2-6-q29-29.why.1: Incorrect because describing leaving a meal unfinished requires the suffix 「〜かけ」 (食べかけ), not 「食べたて」.
default.q.n2-6-q29-29.why.2: Incorrect because expressing becoming familiar with or mastering the use of a computer requires expressions such as 「使い始め」 or 「使いこなす」. 「使いたてにする」 is grammatically incorrect.
default.q.n2-6-q29-29.why.3: Correct because the suffix 「〜たて」combines with the verb stem of the ます-form to create 「できたて」, precisely meaning food that has just been made or cooked and is still hot.
default.q.n2-6-q30-30.verdict: The correct answer is 2: 「まさか」 combined with the structure 「〜とは」 expresses surprise at something completely unexpected.
default.q.n2-6-q30-30.explanation: 「まさか」 is an adverb meaning “that can't be true,” “no way,” or “surely not,” used when something unbelievable happens or to express a strong negative prediction. It often occurs with patterns such as 〜とは（思わなかった/信じられない）, 〜ないだろう, and 〜まい. Example: まさか彼が犯人だったとは夢にも思わなかった。(I never dreamed that he could be the culprit.)
default.q.n2-6-q30-30.why.0: Incorrect because a simile meaning “just as if it were a monkey or a person” requires the comparative adverb 「まるで」 or 「あたかも」, not 「まさか」.
default.q.n2-6-q30-30.why.1: Correct because 「まさか」 used with the sentence ending 「〜とは、信じられない」 expresses shock and disbelief at an unimaginable fact.
default.q.n2-6-q30-30.why.2: Incorrect because the adverb 「まさに」 must be used to emphasize “exactly” or “that is precisely what I mean,” not 「まさか」.
default.q.n2-6-q30-30.why.3: Incorrect because expressing regret when declining—“Unfortunately, I have something to do today”—requires 「あいにく」 or 「残念ながら」, not 「まさか」.
default.q.n2-6-q31-31.verdict: The correct answer is 1: The pattern 「にわかには〜できない」means that something cannot be decided immediately or in an instant.
default.q.n2-6-q31-31.explanation: 「にわかに」（俄かに） is an adverb with two main uses: (1) to describe a sudden change in an event or state, as in にわか雨 (a sudden shower) and にわかに空が暗くなった (the sky suddenly grew dark); (2) with the negative form 「にわかには〜ない/できない」, meaning “cannot immediately / cannot do something in an instant” (for example: にわかには信じがたい, difficult to believe right away). Example: その提案にはにわかには賛成しかねる。(I cannot readily agree to that proposal.)
default.q.n2-6-q31-31.why.0: Correct because the negative expression 「にわかには〜できない」 is a standard idiomatic expression meaning that something cannot be done immediately.
default.q.n2-6-q31-31.why.1: Incorrect because an event beginning at a specific time (7:00) requires 「ちょうど」 or 「きっかり」, not 「にわかに」.
default.q.n2-6-q31-31.why.2: It is incorrect because an approximate quantity such as “about” or “at least 100 people” requires 「およそ」「少なくとも」, or 「約」, not 「にわかに」.
default.q.n2-6-q31-31.why.3: Incorrect because a strong request meaning “please come immediately” requires 「すぐに」, 「大至急」, or 「至急」. 「にわかに」 is not used in an imperative request.
default.q.n2-6-q32-32.verdict: The correct answer is 2: 「いっそ」is correctly used in the structure 「〜より、いっそ…」to express the decision to choose a more decisive or drastic solution.
default.q.n2-6-q32-32.explanation: 「いっそ」（often used as 「いっそのこと」）means "rather, might as well, decisively," and is used when the speaker chooses a more drastic or definite option instead of continuing an inconvenient halfway situation. Distinguish it from 「いっそう/一層」, which means "even more" or "further." Example: こんなに毎月修理代がかかるなら、いっそ新車に買い替えたほうがいい。(If repairs cost this much every month, we might as well replace the car with a new one.)
default.q.n2-6-q32-32.why.0: Incorrect because saying that the ordered pizza has still not arrived requires the adverb 「まだ」, not 「いっそ」.
default.q.n2-6-q32-32.why.1: Correct because the structure「〜より、いっそ…」expresses a firm decision to choose a more radical solution (building a new house) instead of continuing with time-consuming minor repairs.
default.q.n2-6-q32-32.why.2: Incorrect because expressing an additional increase in degree—“the food becomes even tastier”—requires the adverb 「一層（いっそう）」, not 「いっそ」.
default.q.n2-6-q32-32.why.3: Incorrect because describing drinking water and finishing it in one go due to thirst requires 「一気に」, not 「いっそ」.
default.q.n2-6-q1-1.verdict: The correct answer is 4. きゅうそく.
default.q.n2-6-q1-1.explanation:
Meaning: Halfway up the mountain, I rested in a mountain hut.

- Common expression: 休息をとる (to rest, take a break).
- Example: 激しい運動の後は、十分な休息をとることが大切だ。(It is important to get enough rest after strenuous exercise.)
default.q.n2-6-q1-1.why.0: (a) Incorrect because 「きゅうけい」is the reading of 「休憩」(a short break).
default.q.n2-6-q1-1.why.1: (b) Incorrect: 「きゅうか」 is the reading of 「休暇」, meaning a vacation or day off.
default.q.n2-6-q1-1.why.2: (c) Incorrect because 「きゅうよう」 is the reading of 「休養」, meaning to rest and recuperate.
default.q.n2-6-q1-1.why.3: (d) Correct because 「休息」consists of 休 (HŪ: きゅう) and 息 (SOKU: そく), read together as 「きゅうそく」, meaning rest.
default.q.n2-6-q2-2.verdict: The correct answer is 1. しんぞう.
default.q.n2-6-q2-2.explanation:
Sentence meaning: “Fortunately, my father’s heart surgery went smoothly.”

- Related body parts: 腎臓 (kidney), 肝臓 (liver), 肺 (lung).

default.q.n2-6-q2-2.why.0: (a) Correct because 「心臓」 consists of 心 (しん) and 臓 (ぞう), and is correctly read as 「しんぞう」.
default.q.n2-6-q2-2.why.1: (b) Incorrect because 「臓」 has the on-reading 「ぞう」, with voicing, not the unvoiced sound in 「そう」.
default.q.n2-6-q2-2.why.2: (c) Incorrect because the on-reading of 「心」is 「しん」, not 「じん」; 「じんぞう」is the reading of 「腎臓」(kidney) or 「人造」(artificial/man-made).
default.q.n2-6-q2-2.why.3: (d) Incorrect because the readings of both kanji are wrong: 「心」 is read as 「しん」 and 「臓」 as 「ぞう」.
default.q.n2-6-q3-3.verdict: The correct answer is 2. こうそう.
default.q.n2-6-q3-3.explanation:
Sentence meaning: "The residents are protesting the construction of a high-rise apartment building."
- Kanji reading: 高層 (こうそう: high-rise).
- Related vocabulary: 高層ビル (high-rise/skyscraper), 低層 (ていそう: low-rise), 構造 (こうぞう: structure, construction).

default.q.n2-6-q3-3.why.1: (b) Correct because 「高層」 consists of 高 (こう) and 層 (そう), forming the reading 「こうそう」.
default.q.n2-6-q3-3.why.2: (c) Incorrect because 「層」has the on-reading 「そう」and does not undergo voicing to become 「ぞう」, as in the 造 of 「構造」(こうぞう).
default.q.n2-6-q3-3.why.3: (d) Incorrect because 「層」 is read as 「そう」 (unvoiced, with a long vowel), not 「ぞ」.
default.q.n2-6-q4-4.verdict: The correct answer is 2. むかえた.
default.q.n2-6-q4-4.explanation:
Meaning: "We warmly welcomed our friend home after 20 years."
Sino-Japanese reading: 迎 (to welcome, receive).
Common expressions: 暖かく迎える / 温かく迎える (welcome warmly), 新年を迎える (welcome the New Year), 出迎える (go out to meet someone).
