default.q.n2-8-q49-49.why.1: (b)「もとより」occupies the second position after the noun phrase marked by「形は」to form the grammar pattern「〜はもとより」("let alone... / of course...").
default.q.n2-8-q49-49.why.2: (c) 「形は」 occupies the first position immediately after 「この家具、」 and is the first element marked by 「は」 in the structure 「〜はもとより」.
default.q.n2-8-q49-49.why.3: (d) 「いい」 occupies position 4, the final slot, and functions as the predicate adjective ending the sentence and expressing praise (good/nice).
default.q.n2-8-q50-50.verdict: The correct answer is 2. にかけて.
default.q.n2-8-q50-50.explanation: Based on the structure 「4月の上旬から中旬＿＿」, the N2 grammar pattern 「N1 から N2 にかけて」 indicates an approximate span of time or area extending from N1 to N2 (“from around early to mid-April”). Therefore, choice 2 is the most accurate answer. Complete sentence: 「この町では4月の上旬から中旬にかけて、チューリップ祭りが開かれます。」(In this town, a tulip festival is held from around early to mid-April.)
default.q.n2-8-q50-50.why.0: (a) Incorrect because 「に山ったて」(possibly a typing error for にわたって) is misspelled. In addition, 「～から～にわたって」usually emphasizes continuous coverage of an entire period or area, rather than an approximate span as in 「～から～にかけて」.
default.q.n2-8-q50-50.why.1: (b) Correct because the structure 「N1 から N2 にかけて」 indicates a span of time or space from N1 to N2 (from the beginning to the middle of April).
default.q.n2-8-q50-50.why.2: (c) Incorrect because 「～にあたって」 means “on the occasion of...” or “when beginning...,” and is used before an important event. It is not used to connect two points in time.
default.q.n2-8-q50-50.why.3: (d) Incorrect because 「～につれて」 means that as A changes, B changes along with it; it does not follow a time expression to indicate a duration.
default.q.n2-8-q51-51.verdict: The correct answer is 4. からといって.
default.q.n2-8-q51-51.explanation: Based on the pattern that is followed by the partial negative ending 「～わけではない」 (“it is not necessarily the case that” / “it does not mean that”): The N2 grammar pattern 「V/A/N (plain form) + からといって... わけではない / とは限らない」 means “just because one says that..., it does not necessarily mean that...” The sentence means: “However, just because there is a festival, it does not necessarily mean that many people in the town grow tulips.” Therefore, choice 4 is correct.
default.q.n2-8-q51-51.why.0: (a) Incorrect because 「～からすると」 means “from the perspective of...” and is used to make an assessment or inference based on a viewpoint or position. It does not combine with the negative ending 「～わけではない」 here.
default.q.n2-8-q51-51.why.1: (b) Incorrect. 「～からには」 means “now that…,” and the following clause usually expresses intention, obligation, or determination.
default.q.n2-8-q51-51.why.2: (c) Incorrect because 「～からして」means “judging from... alone,” giving a representative example from which to make an overall judgment.
default.q.n2-8-q51-51.why.3: (d) Correct. The grammar pattern「～からといって」combined with「～わけではない」expresses the familiar meaning "just because... does not mean that...".
default.q.n2-8-q52-52.verdict: The correct answer is 3. 植えてからでないと.
default.q.n2-8-q52-52.explanation: The following clause contains 「祭りはできない」(the festival cannot be held). The JLPT N2 pattern 「V-てからでないと / V-てからでなければ + negative clause」 expresses a prerequisite: “Unless A has been done, B cannot be done.” Since the townspeople do not grow enough flowers themselves, the festival cannot be held until flowers have been brought in from elsewhere and planted. Therefore, 3 is the correct answer.
default.q.n2-8-q52-52.why.0: (a) Incorrect because 「～折には」 means “on the occasion of / when...,” and is used for the time an action takes place. It does not combine with the following negative possibility clause 「祭りはできない」.
default.q.n2-8-q52-52.why.1: (b) Incorrect because 「～以来」 normally follows a noun or V-て form and means “since...”; 「植え以来」 is grammatically incorrect and does not fit the meaning.
default.q.n2-8-q52-52.why.2: (c) Correct because 「V-てからでないと...ない」 expresses a necessary condition: “The festival cannot be held unless the flowers are brought back and planted first.”
default.q.n2-8-q52-52.why.3: (d) Incorrect because 「～以上（は）」 means “once...” or “now that...,” and the following clause generally expresses intention or obligation; it does not combine with a negative statement of ability.
default.q.n2-8-q53-53.verdict: The correct answer is 4. をはじめ.
default.q.n2-8-q53-53.explanation: Based on the noun phrase 「日本一の生産量を誇る富山」(Toyama, which boasts Japan’s highest tulip production) and the following phrase 「全国各地のチューリップ産地」(tulip-producing regions throughout the country), this context presents the most representative example of a larger group. The N2 grammar pattern 「N + をはじめ（として）」means “with N as the most notable example” or “beginning with N.” Therefore, choice 4 is correct.
default.q.n2-8-q53-53.why.0: (a) Incorrect because 「～にて」 is a formal expression meaning “at/in” a place or “by” a means of transportation; it does not express the relationship of presenting a representative example.
default.q.n2-8-q53-53.why.1: (b) Incorrect because 「～をめぐって」 means “concerning” or “over” something, such as a dispute or discussion, and is completely unsuitable here.
default.q.n2-8-q53-53.why.2: (c) Incorrect because 「～において」 means “at / in,” referring to a field or place; it is not used to introduce a typical example before a large group.
default.q.n2-8-q53-53.why.3: (d) Correct because 「N + をはじめ」 introduces a representative leading example (Toyama) before a group of similar items (flower-producing regions throughout the country).
default.q.n2-8-q54-54.verdict: The correct answer is 1. あるのだとか.
default.q.n2-8-q54-54.explanation: The sentence begins with 「そういえば」(come to think of it / that reminds me), used when recalling information one has heard or suddenly remembered. The pattern 「～のだとか」(plain form + のだとか) is a hearsay expression meaning “I hear that...” or “apparently...”. 「姉妹関係にある」means “to have a sister-city relationship.” Therefore, the sentence means: “Come to think of it, I hear that the town also has a sister-city relationship with a city in the Netherlands famous for its tulips.” Answer choice 1 is correct.
default.q.n2-8-q54-54.why.0: (a) Correct because 「姉妹関係にあるのだとか」 naturally conveys reported information after the conjunction 「そういえば」.
default.q.n2-8-q54-54.why.1: (b) Incorrect because 「～まい」 expresses a negative conjecture or intention (“probably will not...” or “will never...”), which conflicts with the positive flow of the passage.
default.q.n2-8-q54-54.why.2: (c) Incorrect because 「～ものだ」 expresses a general truth, an inherent nature, or recollection; it is not used to present specific factual information.
default.q.n2-8-q54-54.why.3: (d) Incorrect because「～てこそ」means “only when...,” and requires the following clause to express a result; it cannot be left hanging at the end of the sentence.
default.q.n2-8-q55-55.verdict: The correct answer is 1. 自分の気持ちを口に出すことができなくなったこと (The fact that the person could no longer express their own feelings and thoughts).
default.q.n2-8-q55-55.explanation:
**Main point of the passage:**
The passage discusses the biggest change in children today compared with the past. In the past, when asked why they had done something wrong, children tried their best to think through the question and give an answer. Today, however, although children engage in a great deal of casual conversation, they are awkward and struggle to use words to express their inner thoughts, and they can no longer talk about themselves. The main reason is that they lack the environment and experiences needed to reveal and share who they are.

**Question and answer choices:**
- **Question:** Compared with children in the past, what has changed about children today?
- **1.** They can no longer express their own feelings and thoughts.
- **2.** They have become skilled at expressing their inner world in words.
- **3.** They have more opportunities to talk about themselves and have become more talkative.
- **4.** When asked why they did something wrong, they cannot answer unless they think carefully.
default.q.n2-8-q55-55.why.0: (a) Correct. The passage states: 「いまの子どもたちが一番変わったところは、自分を語れなくなったこと。」 and 「自分の心を言葉にするのは苦手で、自分を理解してもらおうという努力がないのである。」 The biggest change in children today is that they no longer know how, or are reluctant, to express themselves and have difficulty putting their feelings and inner thoughts into words (equivalent to 自分の気持ちを口に出すことができなくなったこと).
default.q.n2-8-q55-55.why.1: (b) Incorrect. The passage states that children today are very poor at putting their inner feelings into words (「自分の心を言葉にするのは苦手で」), which is the complete opposite of becoming good at expressing themselves (じょうずになった).
default.q.n2-8-q55-55.why.2: (c) Incorrect. The passage clearly states that the reason is that children today lack places and opportunities to express themselves (「これは、自分を語るという場が少なく、経験もないからに違いない」), not that their opportunities have increased (機会が増えて).
default.q.n2-8-q55-55.why.3: (d) Incorrect. In the past, when asked why they had done something wrong, children tried hard to think and come up with an answer (「一生懸命考えて答えを出してよこしたものだが」). Nowadays, even when asked, they can no longer answer (「いま、そう問いかけても答えられなくなっている」). It does not mean that they cannot answer unless they think carefully.
default.q.n2-8-q56-56.verdict: The correct answer is 4. 留学生が日本語で発表することをうれしく思っている (They are pleased that the international students will give presentations in Japanese).
default.q.n2-8-q56-56.explanation:
**Summary of the passage:**
The letter is from Tanaka Yoshiko to Ian, an international student who stayed with her family in a homestay two years earlier when he had just arrived in Japan. She thanks him for his letter and invitation to attend his graduation commemorative presentation (卒業記念発表会). She recalls that she was worried two years earlier because Ian could hardly speak Japanese when he first arrived, but she is now surprised and delighted to hear that he will give a presentation in Japanese in front of many people. Her whole family plans to attend and is eagerly looking forward to Ian's presentation.

**Translation of the question:**
Which choice best describes the writer's feelings expressed in this letter?

**Translation of the choices:**
1. Worried that the international student could not speak Japanese.
2. Anxious about the international student giving a presentation in Japanese.
3. Eagerly looking forward to the international student coming to stay with her family.
4. Feeling happy that the international student will give a presentation in Japanese.
default.q.n2-8-q56-56.why.0: (a) Choice 1 is incorrect because concern about an international student being unable to speak Japanese refers only to the past, when Ian had just arrived in Japan two years earlier (あの時はほとんど日本語が話せなかったので心配でしたが). It is not the writer's current feeling.
default.q.n2-8-q56-56.why.1: (b) Choice 2 is incorrect because the writer does not feel anxious (不安). Instead, the writer is surprised, impressed, and eagerly looking forward to Ian’s presentation (本当に驚きました / イアンさんの発表をお聞きするのが今からとても楽しみです).
default.q.n2-8-q56-56.why.2: (c) Choice 3 is incorrect because the international student's homestay at the writer's home took place two years ago (ホームステイでわが家にいらっしゃった時は、まだ来日なさったばかりでしたのに、もう 2 年にもなるのですね), not as an upcoming event to look forward to.
default.q.n2-8-q56-56.why.3: (d) Answer choice 4 is correct because the writer clearly expresses joy and anticipation about Ian speaking Japanese before a large audience, as shown by: 「発表会では大勢の人の前で日本語で話されるのですね。本当に驚きました。発表会へは、家族そろって、うかがうつもりです。イアンさんの発表をお聞きするのが今からとても楽しみです。」
default.q.n2-8-q57-57.verdict: The correct answer is 3 (慣れてきた時 - when one has gradually become accustomed to it / familiar with it).
default.q.n2-8-q57-57.explanation:
- Main idea: In interpersonal communication, meeting several times and gradually becoming familiar with each other (慣れが生じます) is a turning point (分岐点) that determines whether the relationship will develop smoothly. Precisely because the two people are becoming closer, it is even more important to maintain a certain distance, observe the other person carefully again, and choose an appropriate way to interact based on an understanding of their personality.

- Question translation:
  筆者は人づきあいにおいて、どんな時に注意することが必要だと言っているか。
  (When does the author say it is necessary to be careful in interpersonal relationships?)

- Answer choices:
  1. 初対面の時: When meeting for the first time
  2. 緊張した時: When feeling tense
  3. 慣れてきた時: When one has gradually become familiar with the other person
  4. 距離をおいた時: When keeping one’s distance
default.q.n2-8-q57-57.why.0: (a) Incorrect. The passage indicates that after the first meeting, the decisive turning point is when people meet two or three more times and begin to feel familiar with each other, determining whether the relationship will proceed smoothly. It does not say that the time to pay attention to adjusting one's behavior is at the very first meeting.
default.q.n2-8-q57-57.why.1: (b) Incorrect. Tension usually appears when people first meet, but the reading does not say that this is a turning point requiring attention in order to maintain a good relationship.
default.q.n2-8-q57-57.why.2: (c) Correct. The passage states: 「2回、3回と顔を合わせるうち、次第に慣れが生じます。その時が、人づきあいがスムーズになるかどうかの分岐点ではないかと思うのです。」 (As people meet two or three times, they gradually become accustomed to one another. That is the turning point that determines whether the relationship will proceed smoothly.) It is precisely when familiarity begins to develop that one must pay attention to maintaining an appropriate distance and understanding the other person.
default.q.n2-8-q57-57.why.3: (d) Incorrect. 「距離をおく」 (to keep one’s distance) is the solution or action the author recommends once the people have gradually become close; it is not the point in time when the situation in question arises.
default.q.n2-8-q58-58.verdict: The correct answer is 2: The author believes that not doing well at first is only natural, so there is no reason to feel ashamed even if one cannot succeed.
default.q.n2-8-q58-58.explanation:
**1. Summary of the relevant passage:**
Even as people grow older, they continue to want to experience new things. The author emphasizes that when starting a new challenge, it is perfectly normal not to succeed immediately—for example, making a crooked bowl or baking an unsuccessful cake—and there is no reason to feel ashamed. If everyone could do something well from the very beginning, society would have no need for schools or apprenticeships and training. Therefore, when people try something new, the understanding and support of those around them are very important.

**2. Translation of the question:**
When the phrase “a new challenge” appears, what does the author think about it?

**3. Translation of the answer choices:**
1. If the people around me do not understand me, I think it is best not to try it in the first place.
2. Since it is natural for things not to go smoothly at first, there is no reason to feel ashamed even if one cannot do them. (Correct answer)
3. If someone tries something new after growing older, they will certainly succeed thanks to encouragement from those around them.
4. When trying something for the first time, one should first go to school...
default.q.n2-8-q58-58.why.0: (a) Incorrect because the author does not advise that one should never try something in the first place if others do not understand. The author only states that understanding and encouragement from family are essential when trying something for the first time, so that one does not lose heart.
default.q.n2-8-q58-58.why.1: (b) Correct because the passage states: 「だが、それを恥ずかしく思う必要はないのだ。最初からうまくできるなら、世の中のさまざまな学校や修業は必要ないことになる。初めはうまくいかないのが当たり前なのだ。」 There is no need to feel ashamed of it. If people could do things well from the beginning, schools and training would be unnecessary. It is natural not to succeed at first. This completely matches choice 2.
default.q.n2-8-q58-58.why.2: (c) Incorrect, because the passage points out that success is initially unlikely (「それがうまくいくことは少ない」) and that family members may even make discouraging remarks. It does not claim that having someone’s support guarantees a smooth outcome (「うまくいくはずだ」).
default.q.n2-8-q58-58.why.3: (d) Incorrect because the passage mentions schools and vocational training (「学校や修業」) only as examples supporting the idea that beginners naturally perform poorly. It does not advise people to attend school first when trying something new.
default.q.n2-8-q59-59.verdict: The correct answer is 1 (ア :B イ :D ウ :C エ :A).
default.q.n2-8-q59-59.explanation:
**Summary of the passage:**
The passage tells of a six-year-old boy named Susumu who often visits the library even though he does not particularly like books. At first, whenever he visited, he made noise and ran around, but instead of scolding him, a library staff member read picture books to him. From then on, every time he came, he begged to have a story read to him. However, after observing him closely, the staff member realized that he was not actually interested in the contents of the books; he switched to another book as soon as he neared the last page. In the end, what made him happy about having books read to him was the feeling of being cared for by an adult.

**Translation of the question and answer choices:**
*Question:* Which of the following is the most appropriate choice to fill [ ア ], [ イ ], [ ウ ], and [ エ ]?
*Sentences A–D:*
- A: For Susumu, having stories read to him must have been very enjoyable because it meant that someone was caring for him.
- B: As soon as he arrived, he skimmed through several magazines, began making strange sounds, ran between the rows of tables, and made a commotion.
- C: I realized that the boy was not very interested in the important book that was being read to him.
- D: Every time he came, he begged to have a story read to him.

*Sentence-order choices:*
1. ア: B, イ: D, ウ: C, エ: A
2. ア: D, イ: B, ウ: C, エ: A
3. ア: D, イ: B, ウ: A, エ: C
4. ア: B, イ: D, ウ: A, エ: C
default.q.n2-8-q59-59.why.0: (a) It fits the flow and context perfectly: [ ア ] is B (describing the child making a disturbance), which provides the basis for the following sentence, 「それをしかるかわりに、絵本を読んでやった」 (instead of scolding him, I read him a picture book); [ イ ] is D (「それからは、来るたんびに、読め読めとせがむようになりました」 - after that, every time he came, he began begging me to read to him); [ ウ ] is C (「でも、見ていますと、肝心の読んでもらっている本には、それほど興味を持っていないことが分かるのです」 - it follows 「でも」 and sets up the contrast with 「それでいて...」); [ エ ] is A (「結局、進くんにとっては... かまってもらえるという意味でうれしかったのでしょう」 - after 「結局」, it summarizes the child’s underlying feelings).
default.q.n2-8-q59-59.why.1: (b) This choice is incorrect because it places D in [ ア ] and B in [ イ ]. The sentence immediately following [ ア ] contains 「それをしかる」 (“scold that”), so [ ア ] must be an act of mischief deserving scolding (B), not asking to have a story read (D).
default.q.n2-8-q59-59.why.2: (c) This choice is incorrect because all four positions are assigned incorrectly: D is placed in [ア], B in [イ], A is moved to [ウ], and C to [エ], disrupting the passage’s semantic connections and chronological flow.
default.q.n2-8-q59-59.why.3: (d) This choice is incorrect because it reverses the positions of [ ウ ] and [ エ ]. After 「でも、見ていますと」 should come an observation of what actually happened (C—the child was not interested in the book’s content), while after 「結局」 should come the concluding explanation (A—the child was happy to receive attention).
default.q.n2-8-q60-60.verdict: The correct answer is 1. 「そういうこと」 refers to whether there might be a better or more effective method that people have failed to consider.
default.q.n2-8-q60-60.explanation:
• Main point: The author points out that people tend to choose familiar methods because they are easy, without considering whether those methods are truly optimal or whether another, better and more effective approach exists.
• Question translation: What does “that” (そういうこと) refer to?
• Answer choices:
1. The possibility that there may be a better method.
2. The fact that most people choose the method they have always used.
3. The fact that the current method is the best approach.
4. The fact that trying an unfamiliar new method would be difficult.
default.q.n2-8-q60-60.why.0: (a) QUOTATION: 「それがベスト（注 1 ）の方ぐかどうか、あるいはほかにもっと能率的にできる方ぐがあるかもしれないのに、 ① そういうこと は考えもせず...」. 「そういうこと」 directly replaces the preceding clause: whether that method is the best or whether there might be a more efficient way to do the work. Therefore, choice 1 is completely correct.
default.q.n2-8-q60-60.why.1: (b) Incorrect because “most people choose the method they have always used” is an actual action or habit mentioned in paragraph 1, not something people “do not even bother thinking about” (考えもせず).
default.q.n2-8-q60-60.why.2: (c) Incorrect because the author asks whether that might be the best approach (それがベストの方ぐかどうか), rather than asserting that the current approach is the best.
default.q.n2-8-q60-60.why.3: (d) Incorrect because being reluctant to take on the difficulty of trying a new method is the reason people choose the old method in paragraph 1; it is not the content referred to by 「そういうこと」.
default.q.n2-8-q61-61.verdict: The correct answer is 4. 「従来どおりのやり方」 means a method of doing things the same way as before (以前と同じやり方).
default.q.n2-8-q61-61.explanation:
• Main point: "従来どおりのやり方" (the conventional way of doing things) means the way things have been done up to now (いままでどおり / 以前と同じやり方), which people tend to follow out of habit because it is the easiest option.
• Question translation: What kind of method is "the easiest conventional way of doing things"?
• Choice translations:
1. A method that produces results.
2. A method that can be carried out most efficiently.
3. A method suited to the times.
4. A method that is the same as before.
default.q.n2-8-q61-61.why.0: (a) Incorrect because the passage only says that following the old method produces “fairly satisfactory results” (そこそこの成果があがる). That is not the essential definition of “the old-fashioned method.”
default.q.n2-8-q61-61.why.1: (b) Incorrect because the passage shows that people follow the old method without looking for a more efficient way to do things ("ほかにもっと能率的にできる方ぐがあるかもしれないのに"), so this is not the most efficient method.
default.q.n2-8-q61-61.why.2: (c) Incorrect because the passage warns that if the old method is maintained, it will gradually become unsuitable for the times (「そのやり方が時代に合わなくなってきても」).
default.q.n2-8-q61-61.why.3: (d) QUOTATION: 「その中に『いままでどおりやる』というのがあると... ひたすら 告 一番楽な従来どおりのやり方 を続けていこうとする。」 「従来どおり」 is synonymous with 「いままでどおり」, meaning a way of doing things that is the same as before (以前と同じやり方). Therefore, choice 4 is correct.
default.q.n2-8-q62-62.verdict: The correct answer is 3. The author advises that even when a method has worked in the past, we must always consider whether it is still appropriate to leave it unchanged.
default.q.n2-8-q62-62.explanation:
• Main point: The author emphasizes that, regardless of the type of work, managers should continually question whether the current way of doing things is still appropriate for the times and optimal, rather than becoming complacent about familiar methods from the past and causing the organization to become rigid and stagnant.
• Question translation: (What is the best way to approach one’s work, according to the author?)
• Answer choices:
1. Even if other organizations use methods suited to the times, do not worry about it as long as your methods are effective and improve results...
2. Continue using the methods used so far while also applying simple methods suited to human nature that anyone can use...
3. Even when a method has succeeded in the past, always consider whether it is still acceptable to leave it unchanged, and if it is not good...
4. Do not repeat methods that succeeded in the past; instead, always try new methods so that, even if only slightly...
default.q.n2-8-q62-62.why.0: (a) Incorrect because the author emphasizes that failing to keep up with the times will turn an organization into an outdated one and cause it to lose in competition (“時答遅れの組織になって、競争に負けてしまう”), not that it should disregard other organizations.
default.q.n2-8-q62-62.why.1: (b) Incorrect because the author criticizes the tendency to continue following old habits ("従来どおりのやり方を続けていこうとする"), which causes an organization to stagnate, become rigid, and lose progress.
default.q.n2-8-q62-62.why.2: (c) QUOTE: 「特に管理者は、今のやり方でいいのか、時答に合っているか、もっと能率的な方ぐがあるのではないか・・・・いかなる種類の仕事であっても、そのことを常に考えていかなければなりません。」 The author advises people to continually consider whether their current methods are effective and adjust them in a timely manner. Choice 3 expresses this idea accurately.
default.q.n2-8-q62-62.why.3: (d) Incorrect because the author recommends regularly questioning and evaluating whether the current method is appropriate and effective ("今のやり方でいいのか...常に考えていかなければなりません"), not completely rejecting old methods and always trying something new.
default.q.n2-8-q63-63.verdict: The correct answer is 3: Just like one's youth, middle age and old age are also important stages of life.
default.q.n2-8-q63-63.explanation:
The passage explains that each person experiences youth only once, but middle age and old age also occur only once. Therefore, middle age and old age are just as important as youth, and there is no reason to regard youth alone as special.

- Question: Why does the passage say, “There is no need to regard youth alone as special”?
- Answer choices:
1. Because youth occurs only once.
2. Because the author is a sarcastic person.
3. Because, just like youth, middle age and old age are also very important.
4. Because old age has its own advantages.
default.q.n2-8-q63-63.why.0: (a) Incorrect. “You are young only once” is a common argument used to emphasize youth, but the author stresses that middle age and old age also occur only once.
default.q.n2-8-q63-63.why.1: (b) Incorrect because "I am a sarcastic person" is merely the author's self-deprecating way of presenting a counterargument, not an objective reason why youth need not be treated specially.
default.q.n2-8-q63-63.why.2: (c) Correct. The passage states: 「われわれは若い時答を大中にすべきであるが、同様に中年を大中にすべきであるし、老年を大中にしなければならない。①若い時答だけを特別視する必要はないのである。」(We should value youth, but we should likewise value middle age and old age.)
default.q.n2-8-q63-63.why.3: (d) Incorrect because the idea that "old age has its own appeal" is the author's thought when discussing being 53; it is not the reason why youth should not be regarded as special compared with other stages of life.
default.q.n2-8-q64-64.verdict: The correct answer is 2: “The flavor of life” here refers to the joys and sorrows of life.
default.q.n2-8-q64-64.explanation:
The author states that each stage of life has its own “flavor of life” (人生のこく), and clarifies in the following sentence that this refers to “the distinctive joys and sorrows of life” (特有な人生の喜びと悲しみ), which should be felt and experienced at each stage.

- Question translation: What does the phrase “the flavor of life” refer to here?
- Answer choices:
1. The uniqueness of human life.
2. The joys and sorrows of life.
3. The importance of life.
4. The preparatory stage of life.
default.q.n2-8-q64-64.why.0: (a) Incorrect because “the uniqueness of human life” is not the specific meaning of “the flavor of life” in this context.
default.q.n2-8-q64-64.why.1: (b) Correct. The immediately following explanation states: 「人生のそれぞれの段階には、それぞれに違った 告 人生のこく がある。私はそう思っている。私達はそれぞれの段階に特有な人生の喜びと悲しみを味山いながら生きたい。」 (Each stage of life has its own distinctive flavor. I believe that. We want to live while experiencing the joys and sorrows of life unique to each stage).
default.q.n2-8-q64-64.why.2: (c) Incorrect because “the importance of human life” is a vague general idea and does not closely match “the flavor of life,” which the author explains specifically in the following sentence.
default.q.n2-8-q64-64.why.3: (d) Incorrect because “a preparatory stage in a person’s life” is society’s view of youth, which is completely contrary to the author’s meaning of enjoying both the joys and sorrows of life.
default.q.n2-8-q65-65.verdict: The correct answer is 4: The mistake the author is referring to is calling on young people to exercise self-restraint and abstain from sex.
default.q.n2-8-q65-65.explanation:
People commonly regard youth as merely a period of preparation: instead of enjoying themselves, young people are expected to focus on studying and building up their knowledge and experience. In the end, this imposes "self-restraint and abstinence" (自制と禁欲) on young people. The demonstrative expression "that" (それ) in the sentence "I think that is a mistake" directly refers to this call for self-restraint and abstinence.

- Translation of the question: In the sentence "I think that is a mistake," what does the author consider a mistake?
- Translation of the choices:
1. Spending one's youth absorbed in having fun.
2. Building a solid foundation of knowledge and experience while young.
3. Not regarding it as something special.
4. Calling on young people to practice self-restraint and abstinence.
default.q.n2-8-q65-65.why.0: (a) Incorrect because “spending one’s youth absorbed in playing around” is something people advise against, not the object replaced by the pronoun それ.
default.q.n2-8-q65-65.why.1: (b) Incorrect because “building a solid foundation of education and experience while young” is merely the rationale people give for forcing young people to restrain themselves; it is not the mistaken action criticized by the author.
default.q.n2-8-q65-65.why.2: (c) is incorrect because this choice lacks the necessary meaning and does not correctly express what the demonstrative “that” (それ) refers to.
default.q.n2-8-q65-65.why.3: (d) Correct. The preceding sentence says: 「と、結局は、若者に自制と禁欲を呼びかけているのである。でも、私は、③ それは間違いだと思う。」 (Ultimately, they are calling on young people to exercise self-restraint and abstinence. But I think that is wrong).
default.q.n2-8-q66-66.verdict: The correct answer is 3: 努力は、かけた時間によって測定できる (Effort can be measured by the time spent on it).
default.q.n2-8-q66-66.explanation:
- Main point: The author shares a maxim they formulated at age 38 that helped them stop being afraid of making an effort and live more easily: measuring effort objectively using “time” as the standard.
- Question: Fill in ( ① ) with the statement that influenced the author’s life. Which one is it?
- Answer choices:
  1. The value of making an effort lies in concealing the appearance of effort.
  2. If you make an effort, other people’s evaluations will change.
  3. Effort can be measured by the amount of time invested.
  4. If you make an effort, you will also become better at managing time.
default.q.n2-8-q66-66.why.0: (a) Incorrect because the author describes concealing one’s efforts (謙遜して努力を隠す対応) as “very dangerous” (とても危険), not as valuable.
default.q.n2-8-q66-66.why.1: (b) Incorrect because the author does not claim that effort will change other people's evaluations. Rather, the author wants to free themself from worrying about and fearing others' evaluations (他者の評価を気にし始めると...).
default.q.n2-8-q66-66.why.2: (c) Correct because it matches the author's explanation in the following paragraphs: 「そして、努力を客観視するための規定方法が「時間」なのです。努力をする、しないはあくまで主観ですが、その分量を時間換算する仕組みを取り入れれば、自分がどこまで努力をしたのがわかりやすく管理できるようになり... 努力を時間で測定すれば... という気持ちになれる魔法の言葉なのです」 (Defining effort in terms of time is a way to make it objective and manage it.)
default.q.n2-8-q66-66.why.3: (d) Incorrect because the author says only that time is used to measure and manage one's level of effort, not that making an effort automatically leads to better time-management skills.
default.q.n2-8-q67-67.verdict: The provided answer is 3; however, based on the passage, the correct answer should be 2 (自分の努力の結果に対し、他人にいろいろ言われたり思われたりしたくないから), because the author identifies the cause as fearing that others will judge the results of one’s efforts.
default.q.n2-8-q67-67.explanation:
- Main point: The author analyzes why people tend to deny or conceal their own efforts because they are overly concerned with other people's opinions and judgments (afraid of being ridiculed if they fail, or having their efforts diminished if they succeed).
- Question translation: Why does the author say that people often deliberately deny their own efforts?
- Answer choices:
  1. They feel that their effort is merely subjective and that others cannot understand it.
  2. They do not want others to gossip about or speculate on the results of their efforts.
  3. They feel that their efforts are insufficient compared with those of others and think they need to work harder.
  4. By showing themselves making an effort, they want others to think they are humble.
default.q.n2-8-q67-67.why.0: (a) Incorrect because the passage does not mention that denying the effort is caused by other people being unable to understand its subjective nature.
default.q.n2-8-q67-67.why.1: (b) Correct. According to the passage, the tendency to deny or hide one's efforts comes from fear of being judged by the outcome: "まず結果が出なかったとき「あいつ、あれだけやってダメだった」とバカにされるのを恐れます。結果が出ても「あれだけ準備すれば当然だ」と評価が下がるのを恐れます。他者の評価を気にし始めると、いずれにせよ努力を隠すに越したことはないわけです。それは社会人になっても同じです" (People fear being mocked if they fail and being rated less highly if they succeed).
default.q.n2-8-q67-67.why.2: (c) The provided answer (3) is incorrect because the passage does not mention feeling that one’s efforts are insufficient compared with others or needing to try harder.
default.q.n2-8-q67-67.why.3: (d) Incorrect because concealing one’s efforts stems from fear of other people’s views or judgments, not from a desire to be seen as modest.
default.q.n2-8-q68-68.verdict: The given answer is 1; however, based on the passage, the correct answer should be 4 (何をどれだけ努力したかを確認しながら、努力自体を楽しむことが大切だ), because the author emphasizes measuring one's efforts and enjoying the process of making them.
default.q.n2-8-q68-68.explanation:
- Main idea: The author believes that people should not avoid or hide their efforts out of fear of being judged. Instead, they should incorporate effort into their lives, enjoy the process, and use time as a measure to confirm and manage what they have been and are striving toward.
- Question: What view of “effort” does the author express?
- Choices:
  1. Since effort is subjective, it is enough to decide for yourself how far you should go.
  2. Once you start working, it is better not to let others see you making an effort.
  3. To achieve good results, it is important to let others see you making an effort.
  4. It is important both to confirm what and how much you have worked toward and to enjoy the effort itself.
default.q.n2-8-q68-68.why.0: (a) Choice (1) is incorrect. The author says that whether one makes an effort is subjective ("努力をする、しないはあくまで主観ですが"), but that it must be converted into time for clear management and that one must think for oneself and decide what to make an effort toward ("何を努力するのか自分で考え、決めなければいけません"). It does not mean “deciding for oneself how much effort is enough.”
default.q.n2-8-q68-68.why.1: (b) Incorrect because the author warns that concealing one's efforts is very dangerous (“この「謙遜して努力を隠す対応」はとても危険です”), rather than recommending that one hide them.
default.q.n2-8-q68-68.why.2: (c) Incorrect because the passage does not advise that one must show others one’s efforts in order to achieve good results.
default.q.n2-8-q68-68.why.3: (d) Correct according to the passage: The author emphasizes the need to create a system for enjoying the process of making an effort ("そのプロセスを楽しむ仕組みをつくらなければなりません") and to convert the amount of effort into time so that it can be managed and clearly measured ("その分量を時間換算する仕組みを取り入れれば、自分がどこまで努力をしたのがわかりやすく管理できるようになり", "何を努力するのか自分で考え、決めなければいけません").
default.q.n2-8-q69-69.verdict: The precise answer is 2: The person seeking advice (相談者) understands「いただきます」as an expression of gratitude for things given by others.
default.q.n2-8-q69-69.explanation:
Main point: The person seeking advice believes that because they paid the school lunch fee (給食費), they are not “receiving food from the school” (食べ物を学校からもらっているわけではない), and therefore do not understand why they should say 「いただきます」. This shows that they understand 「いただきます」 in its ordinary sense as an expression of thanks for something received from another person.

Question and answer choices:
Question: How does the person seeking advice understand the meaning of 「いただきます」?
1. A greeting said before eating lunch at school.
2. An expression of thanks for things received from other people.
3. A greeting said when one has not paid the school lunch fee.
4. An expression of thanks to the person who cooked the food.
default.q.n2-8-q69-69.why.0: (a) Incorrect because this is B's explanation of greeting before meals at school, not the interpretation of the person seeking advice, who is dissatisfied that their child is forced to say it at school.
default.q.n2-8-q69-69.why.1: (b) Correct. The adviser says: 「いただきます」だなんて、食べ物を学校からもらっているわけではありません。活ゃんと給食費を払っているのに... This shows that the person understands the expression as meaning receiving something from someone else. Respondent A also explicitly distinguishes this interpretation: 確かに、人から何かをもらったときに「ありがとうございます。いただきます。」というふうにも言いますが、それとは違います。
default.q.n2-8-q69-69.why.2: (c) Incorrect because the adviser suggested saying this only to families who did not pay for meals, since they were receiving free food. It was not regarded as a conventional greeting (挨拶) specifically for people who did not pay.
default.q.n2-8-q69-69.why.3: (d) Incorrect because thanking the person who cooked or prepared the meal is the view expressed by respondent B (「どちらかというと料理を作ってくれた人や食べ物を用意してくれた人への感謝の気持ちが自然に山[わ]いてくることが多い」), not by the advisor.
default.q.n2-8-q70-70.verdict: The correct answer is 3: Both A and B believe that the counselor has misunderstood the meaning of 「いただきます」 before a meal.
default.q.n2-8-q70-70.explanation:
Related main point: The questioner thinks that, having paid for the meal, there is no need to say 「いただきます」 and intends to complain to the school. In response:
- Person A is surprised that the questioner does not understand the true meaning of 「いただきます」 before a meal: expressing gratitude for the lives of the plants and animals that sustain us. It has nothing to do with whether one has paid, and A advises the questioner to understand its meaning correctly before complaining.
- Person B considers it a greeting (挨拶) and an expression of gratitude toward the person who prepared the food. It has nothing to do with the meal fee; although it is acceptable not to say it at home, treating it as a greeting at school is normal.
=> Both A and B believe that the questioner has misunderstood the meaning of 「いただきます」 and that saying it has nothing to do with paying for a school meal.

Translation of the question and answer choices:
Question: Which of the following correctly describes A and B’s responses to the adviser’s question?
1. A is surprised that the adviser does not understand the meaning of 「いただきます」, whereas B ...
2. A believes the adviser should complain to the school for forcing students to say 「いただきます」, whereas B ...
3. Both A and B believe that the adviser [has not correctly understood] the meaning of the expression 「いただきます」 before a meal.
4. Both A and B believe that the greeting 「いただきます」 before a meal [should be said both at home and at school].
default.q.n2-8-q70-70.why.0: (a) This is incorrect because the sentence is incomplete and does not accurately reflect the similarity between the two respondents. B does not agree with the questioner's indignation; B explains that it is an ordinary greeting unrelated to paying for the meal.
default.q.n2-8-q70-70.why.1: (b) Incorrect because A says that the people making the complaint are the ones in the wrong: 「学校が強制的に『いただきます』と言わなければ絶対にいけないと言わない限り、抗議するほうが間違っていると思います」 (Unless the school absolutely forces students to say “itadakimasu,” I think the person making the complaint is in the wrong.)
default.q.n2-8-q70-70.why.2: (c) Correct, because both A and B assert that saying 「いただきます」 does not depend on whether the school lunch fee (給食費) has been paid, contrary to the consultant's assumption. A explains that its true meaning is gratitude for the lives of plants and animals (「まずは、あなたが『いただきます』の本当の意味を理解すべきでしょう」), while B explains that it is a greeting or expression of gratitude toward the person who prepared the meal (「給食費を払っているかどうかとは関係ないのです」). Both show that the consultant has misunderstood the essence of this expression.
default.q.n2-8-q70-70.why.3: (d) Incorrect because B explicitly says that it is also fine not to say anything at home: 「あなたの家では食べるときに何も言わないのですね。それはそれで構山[わ]ないと思いますが」.
default.q.n2-8-q71-71.verdict: The correct answer is choice 3: It requires the user to handle and operate it carefully and gently.
default.q.n2-8-q71-71.explanation:
■ Main point:
The author points out that when objects are extremely sturdy, people tend to use them carelessly and roughly. In contrast, shoji paper screens are thin and easily torn, so users must handle them carefully and gently in every movement, such as when opening and closing a traditional door. This helps cultivate people's character and manner.

■ Question translation:
What does 「もののあり方の非常によい面」 (a very good aspect of the way things are) mean here?

■ Answer choices:
1. Being sturdy and not breaking.
2. It does not matter if users handle it roughly.
3. Requiring users to handle it carefully and gently.
4. There is no need to increase its durability.
default.q.n2-8-q71-71.why.0: (a) Incorrect because the author argues that objects being excessively durable and not breaking unintentionally fostered rough habits and attitudes in users, rather than representing a positive aspect of shoji screens.
default.q.n2-8-q71-71.why.1: (b) Incorrect because feeling that it would not matter if one became rough or uncivilized is a negative expression (「粗暴な気持ち」) associated with using excessively durable objects, contrary to the objects’ educational value for human beings.
default.q.n2-8-q71-71.why.2: (c) Correct, as shown in the passage: 「だが障子は、弱いがゆえにこそ、取り扱う者に丁寧な扱いを要求する。それによって、扱う者が育つ。」 (Precisely because shoji screens are fragile, they require the people who handle them to treat them carefully; through this, those people are trained and mature.)
default.q.n2-8-q71-71.why.3: (d) Incorrect because the fact that no one demanded greater durability is merely an actual situation presented at the beginning of the passage; it is not the meaning of “the very good aspect of the existence of objects.”
default.q.n2-8-q72-72.verdict: The correct answer is choice 4: After the shoji door was damaged and repaired, it became even more beautiful than before.
default.q.n2-8-q72-72.explanation:
■ Main-point summary:
From the perspective of repairing objects, the author praises shoji screens because, when one is torn, people do not replace the entire screen. Instead, they carefully attach colored pieces of paper shaped like maple leaves and cherry blossoms over the tear. Thanks to this artistic approach, the shoji screen becomes even more beautiful after being repaired than it was originally, with its score rising from 100 to 130.

■ Question translation:
The passage says 「実にすばらしいものだ」 (It is truly wonderful). According to the author, why is that?

■ Answer choices:
1. Because advanced technology made it possible to repair the shoji screen one section at a time.
2. Because a shoji screen does not need to be repaired when it has only one tear.
3. Because repairing a shoji screen does not require much effort and is practical.
4. Because the shoji screen becomes more beautiful after being damaged and repaired.
default.q.n2-8-q72-72.why.0: (a) Incorrect because advanced modern technology replaces the entire group of components instead of repairing each part, which is completely opposite to the meticulous hand repair of shoji screens.
default.q.n2-8-q72-72.why.1: (b) Incorrect because when one part is torn, people repair it by joining the pieces and attaching decorative patterned paper; it does not mean that no repair is needed.
default.q.n2-8-q72-72.why.2: (c) Incorrect because “saving effort and being rational” is the repair philosophy of modern technology, which replaces both defective and nondefective component units. It is not the method used for shoji screens.
default.q.n2-8-q72-72.why.3: (d) Correct, as shown in the passage: 「すると、その障子は、修理する以前よりも美しくなる。... 障子は破れる前が 100 で、直せば 130 にもなる。壊れて修理したほうがより美しくなる。」 (The shoji then becomes more beautiful than it was before being repaired... If it was worth 100 before tearing, it can be worth 130 after being repaired. Once damaged and repaired, it becomes even more beautiful.)
default.q.n2-8-q73-73.verdict: The correct answer is choice 2: Repairing objects nurtures an attitude of appreciating and valuing them.
default.q.n2-8-q73-73.explanation:
■ Main idea:
Using the image of the traditional Japanese shoji screen, the article conveys the message that objects and people have a deep, mutually influential relationship. Rather than discarding belongings in accordance with the modern disposable lifestyle, personally caring for, preserving, and repairing them helps people cultivate affection, a sense of connection, and appreciation for the objects around them.

■ Translation of the question:
What does the author want to say through this passage?

■ Translation of the answer choices:
1. Repairing things as a nonprofessional is just as necessary as having them repaired by a specialist.
2. Repairing objects cultivates feelings of appreciation and care for them.
3. Repairing objects is actually progressive and rational.
4. When repairing an object, it should be repaired so that it becomes better than before.
default.q.n2-8-q73-73.why.0: (a) Incorrect because the passage does not mention or compare repairs done by amateurs (素人) with those done by professional specialists (専門家).
default.q.n2-8-q73-73.why.1: (b) Correct because the passage concludes: 「ものを直すということは人間にとって非常にだいじなことであり、道具というものにほんとうの愛情を感じる源でもある。修理は機械と人間とが一体となることなのだ。」(Repairing things is extremely important for human beings, and it is also the source of genuine affection for tools. Repair is the process through which machines and people become one.)
default.q.n2-8-q73-73.why.2: (c) Incorrect because the passage opposes modern society’s mechanical “rationalization,” which causes people to lose affection for objects; it does not claim that repairing things is progressive and rational in that sense.
default.q.n2-8-q73-73.why.3: (d) Incorrect because the detail that the shoji screen looked better after being repaired is given as a distinctive example. The author does not present it as a standard or requirement for repairing all objects.
default.q.n2-8-q74-74.verdict: The correct answer is 3: Both a document confirming her current address and a document confirming her employment in the city are required.
default.q.n2-8-q74-74.explanation:
- Main point and evidence: According to Kasumi City's library-card application guide, a person who does not live in the city but commutes to work or school there (かすみ市に通勤または通学していますか -> はい) must bring proof of their current address, such as a driver's license or health-insurance card, together with proof that they work or study in the city, such as an employee ID or student ID: 「上記の現住所が確認できるものに加えて、学生証、社員証など通勤・通学が確認できるものをお持ちください。」
- Translation of the question: What does someone who does not live in Kasumi City but works there need when applying for a library card?
- Translation of the answer choices:
  1. Documents that can verify their current address.
  2. Documents that can verify that they commute to work or school.
  3. Documents that can verify both their current address and their employment.
  4. Documents that can verify their current address and an alien registration card.
default.q.n2-8-q74-74.why.0: (a) Incorrect because merely carrying documents confirming one’s current address is insufficient for someone who does not live in the city but works there.
default.q.n2-8-q74-74.why.1: (b) Incorrect because carrying only documentation confirming employment or school attendance is insufficient; the rules also require documentation confirming the current address.
default.q.n2-8-q74-74.why.2: (c) Correct. The passage states: 「上記の現住所が確認できるものに加えて、学生証、社員証など通勤・通学が確認できるものをお持ちください」 (In addition to the documents listed above confirming your current address, please bring something such as a student ID or employee ID confirming your commute to school or work.) Therefore, both proof of current address and proof of commuting to work are required.
default.q.n2-8-q74-74.why.3: (d) Incorrect because this person works in the city; the passage does not say that the person is a foreign national. Moreover, the job requires documentation proving employment, not a foreign resident registration card (外国人登録証).
default.q.n2-8-q75-75.verdict: The correct answer is 4: Except for the latest issue, which cannot be checked out, one person may borrow up to 5 magazines.
default.q.n2-8-q75-75.explanation:
- Main point: Under 貸し出し冊数 (number of items that may be borrowed), the library states that up to five books and magazines 「図書（本・雑誌）」 may be borrowed per person (1人5冊まで), with the clear exception: 「ただし、雑誌の最新号は貸し出しできません」 (However, the latest issue of a magazine cannot be borrowed). Therefore, excluding the latest issue, each person may borrow up to five magazines.
- Question: How may magazines be borrowed when a library card is presented?
- Choices:
  1. They may be borrowed as long as the total is no more than eight.
  2. They may be read in the library but cannot be taken home.
  3. Any issue may be borrowed, up to five per person.
  4. Except for the latest issue, each person may borrow up to five.
default.q.n2-8-q75-75.why.0: (a) Incorrect because the limit of 8 items (点) is the total for books/magazines and audiovisual materials such as CDs/DVDs; books and magazines alone may be borrowed up to 5 items.
default.q.n2-8-q75-75.why.1: (b) Incorrect because magazines may still be borrowed and taken home (up to 5 issues); only the latest issue cannot be borrowed.
default.q.n2-8-q75-75.why.2: (c) Incorrect because 「どれでも」(any book) is unsuitable: the newest issue is excluded and cannot be borrowed.
default.q.n2-8-q75-75.why.3: (d) Correct. The passage states:「図書（本・雑誌） 1 人 5 冊まで」 (each person may borrow up to 5 books or magazines) and「ただし、雑誌の最新号は貸し出しできません」 (however, the latest issue of a magazine cannot be borrowed). Therefore, excluding the latest issue, each person may borrow up to 5 items.
default.q.n2-8-q11-11.verdict: The correct answer is 2 (ノック): 「ドアをノックする」 means “to knock on the door.”
default.q.n2-8-q11-11.explanation:
Meaning: When you enter the room, please knock.
• Vocabulary: ノックする (to knock), ドアをノックする (to knock on the door).
• Example: ノックしてから部屋に入ってください。(Please knock before entering the room.)
default.q.n2-8-q11-11.why.0: (a) プラス (plus): an addition, a positive point, an advantage; it does not combine with 「ドアを～する」 to mean entering a room.
default.q.n2-8-q11-11.why.1: (b) ノック (knock): to knock; 「ドアをノックする」means knocking before entering a room, which fits the context perfectly.
default.q.n2-8-q11-11.why.2: (c) サイン (sign): a signature, signing, or gesture; it is not used with a room door in this context.
default.q.n2-8-q11-11.why.3: (d) カープ means a carp or is a misspelling of “curve” (a bend or curved section, usually カーブ); neither meaning fits the context.
default.q.n2-8-q12-12.verdict: The correct answer is 1 (しつこい): persistent, insistent, bothersome (continuing to ask for help despite being refused several times).
default.q.n2-8-q12-12.explanation:
Sentence meaning: No matter how many times we refuse, that person keeps coming back to ask us for favors. They really are persistent and annoying.
• Vocabulary: しつこい (persistent, obstinate, bothersome; also rich or overpowering in taste or smell).
• Example: しつこく電話をかけてこないでください。(Please stop calling me repeatedly.)
default.q.n2-8-q12-12.why.0: (a) しつこい: Persistent, annoying, troublesome; accurately describes someone who continues asking for favors even after being refused many times.
default.q.n2-8-q12-12.why.1: (b) こまかい (small, detailed, meticulous): It is used for trivial details or someone who is overly particular, so it does not fit the context.
default.q.n2-8-q12-12.why.2: (c) すまない (feeling sorry, guilty) expresses remorse; it is not an adjective modifying「人」to describe someone who persistently imposes on others.
default.q.n2-8-q12-12.why.3: (d) おもたい (heavy, oppressive): Describes physical weight or a heavy atmosphere, not a persistent, demanding personality.
default.q.n2-8-q13-13.verdict: The correct answer is 4 (あふれ): The verb 「あふれる」(溢れる) means to overflow or flood (as when a river overflows and causes damage).
default.q.n2-8-q13-13.explanation:
Meaning: Because of yesterday's heavy rain, the river overflowed and houses in the surrounding area suffered damage.
• Vocabulary: あふれる (溢れる: overflow; be flooded), 被害に遭う (suffer damage), 付近 (surrounding area), 家屋 (houses; buildings).
• Example: 大雨で池の水があふれ出た。(The heavy rain caused the pond to overflow.)
default.q.n2-8-q13-13.why.0: (a) うなり (うなる - to growl, roar, or moan): used for the sound of howling wind, an engine, or a growling animal. It is not used to describe a river rising and causing flooding.
default.q.n2-8-q13-13.why.1: (b) つもり (つもる— accumulate, pile up): used for snow (雪が積もる) and dust, but not for river water.
default.q.n2-8-q13-13.why.2: (c) 手入れ (ていれ): maintenance, care, or grooming. It refers to maintaining or tending objects, gardens, or one’s skin (e.g., 庭の手入れ), and does not mean cooking in this context.
default.q.n2-8-q13-13.why.3: (d) あふれ (あふれる - to overflow, be filled to overflowing): Combines with「川の水」to describe river water rising and overflowing its banks, causing flooding; it is completely accurate.
default.q.n2-8-q14-14.verdict: The correct answer is 3 (比較): the pattern 「AをBと比較する」 means “to compare A with B.”
default.q.n2-8-q14-14.explanation:
Meaning: Let's try comparing the shape of the coastline around this area with that of 50 years ago.
• Vocabulary: 比較（ひかく: comparison), 海岸線（かいがんせん: coastline), 測定（そくてい: measurement), 一致（いっち: agreement, match), 統一（とういつ: unification, standardization).
• Pattern: AをBと比較する (compare A with B).
• Example: 現在の売上を昨年のデータと比較する。(Compare current sales with last year's data.)
default.q.n2-8-q14-14.why.0: (a) 測定 (そくてい — measuring size, weight, or dimensions): It is not used in a structure comparing appearance with that of 50 years ago.
default.q.n2-8-q14-14.why.1: (b) 一致 (いっち): means “to match” or “to coincide completely” and is used intransitively. It cannot be used in the transitive pattern 「～を…と一致してみましょう」 to mean “compare.”
default.q.n2-8-q14-14.why.2: (c) 比較 (ひかく): The structure 「AをBと比較する」 means “compare A with B.” Comparing the current coastline with its shape 50 years ago is exactly correct.
default.q.n2-8-q14-14.why.3: (d) 統一 (とういつ: making things uniform or bringing them together) does not fit a comparison of shapes over time.
default.q.n2-8-q15-15.verdict: The correct answer is 2 (おかまいなく): The phrase 「（どうぞ）おかまいなく」 (“please do not worry about me” or “please do not trouble yourself”) is used to politely decline an offer of tea or other hospitality.
default.q.n2-8-q15-15.explanation:
Meaning: 「Would you like another cup of tea?」 - 「Oh, no thank you. Please don't go to any trouble. I have to leave soon anyway.」
• Vocabulary: お構いなく（おかまいなく - a polite expression used to decline an offer: please don't trouble yourself / no need to fuss), おかわり (a refill, an additional serving).
• Example: 「コーヒーをもう一杯いかがですか」「どうぞおかまいなく」(「Would you like another cup of coffee?」 - 「No, thank you. Please don't go to any trouble.」)
default.q.n2-8-q15-15.why.0: (a) おまたせしました (“I’m sorry to have kept you waiting”): used when someone has been made to wait, so it is completely inappropriate in this context.
default.q.n2-8-q15-15.why.1: (b) おかまいなく (お構いなく - “Please do not worry about it” / “Please do not trouble yourself”) is a polite expression used to decline when the host offers to make more tea or serve more food because the speaker is about to leave.
default.q.n2-8-q15-15.why.2: (c) かしこまりました (I understand clearly / Certainly): a response used by a subordinate or service employee when accepting a request from a customer or superior, not a phrase for refusing an invitation.
default.q.n2-8-q15-15.why.3: (d) ごえんりょなく (ご遠慮なく - “Please don’t hesitate”): this is something an inviter says to a guest so the guest can enjoy themselves freely; it is not used to describe one’s own behavior when declining.
default.q.n2-8-q16-16.verdict: The correct answer is 2. 手間 (time and effort).
default.q.n2-8-q16-16.explanation:
- Meaning: It takes both effort and time to make this soup.
- Vocabulary:
  + 手間 (てま): time and effort spent on a task. Common expressions: 手間がかかる (to take time and effort), 手間を省く (to save effort).
  + 手段 (しゅだん): means, method.
  + 手入れ (ていれ): maintenance, care, repair.
  + 手続き (てつづき): paperwork, administrative procedure.
- Example: 手間を惜しまずに作った料理は格別に美味しい。(Food prepared without sparing any effort tastes exceptionally good.)
default.q.n2-8-q16-16.why.0: (a) 手段 (しゅだん — means, method): It refers to a method or means of achieving a goal and does not combine with the pattern 「～も時間もかかる」.
default.q.n2-8-q16-16.why.1: (b) 手間 (てま): The effort and time required to complete a task. The expression 「手間（も時間）がかかる」means that something takes considerable effort (and time), which fits the context of preparing the soup perfectly.
default.q.n2-8-q16-16.why.2: (c) こぼれ (こぼれる): to spill, overflow, or fall out. It is used when liquid spills from a cup or bowl, or when tears fall. For a river overflowing its banks and causing widespread flooding,「あふれる」must be used.
default.q.n2-8-q16-16.why.3: (d) 手続き (てつづき - procedure): Refers to regulated administrative or paperwork procedures; it is not used in a cooking context.
default.q.n2-8-q17-17.verdict: The correct answer is 3. と流くに (the original form is とっくに: long ago, already).
default.q.n2-8-q17-17.explanation:
- Translation: 「Hey, where is Kobayashi?」 「Kobayashi? He went home a long time ago.」
- Note: 「と流くに」 in the question is an OCR/display error for the adverb 「とっくに」 (a long time ago).
- Related vocabulary:
  + とっくに: a long time ago, already.
  + いまに (今に): before long, sooner or later.
  + さらに (更に): furthermore, additionally.
- Example: そんなことはとっくに知っていたよ。(I knew that a long time ago.)
default.q.n2-8-q17-17.why.0: (a) いまに (before long; sooner or later): used to predict something that will happen in the near future. It does not fit a completed past event such as 「帰りましたよ」.
default.q.n2-8-q17-17.why.1: (b) さらに (furthermore, in addition): It expresses an increase in degree or an added amount, and is not used to indicate the point at which an action is completed.
default.q.n2-8-q17-17.why.2: (c) と流くに (an OCR error for とっくに): An adverb meaning “long ago” or “already,” referring to an action that happened and ended quite some time earlier. It fits naturally in the context of replying to someone who had already left.
default.q.n2-8-q17-17.why.3: (d) どこかに (somewhere): an indefinite location pronoun. With it, the sentence would mean "has gone back somewhere," which is unnatural when confirming that someone has left this place.
default.q.n2-8-q18-18.verdict: The correct answer is 2. ただし (however / provided that).
default.q.n2-8-q18-18.explanation:
- Meaning: Handwritten reports are also accepted. However, they must be written very neatly. (Note: 「式ポート」 in the question is an OCR error for 「レポート」.)
- Vocabulary & grammar:
  + ただし (但し): a conjunction introducing an additional condition, restriction, or exception to the preceding statement.
  + 手書き (てがき): handwritten.
  + 可 (か): permitted, acceptable.
  + ～こと: a pattern expressing an order or mandatory rule.
- Example: 入場は無料です。ただし、整理券が必要です。(Admission is free. However, an admission ticket is required.)
default.q.n2-8-q18-18.why.0: (a) うそれに (a typographical error for それに, “moreover / in addition”): This adds further information in the same direction and is not used to introduce a condition or constraint.
default.q.n2-8-q18-18.why.1: (b) ただし (however, provided that): a conjunction that adds a condition or limitation to the preceding clause (handwriting is allowed, provided that it is neat and legible).
default.q.n2-8-q18-18.why.2: (c) だって (because, the thing is): This is used in informal spoken language to explain or make excuses for a reason, so it is not used in official rules or announcements.
default.q.n2-8-q18-18.why.3: (d) そのうえ (moreover/in addition): Used to add information that reinforces or supplements what was just stated; it does not express a limiting condition.
default.q.n2-8-q19-19.verdict: The correct answer is 4. 平和な (peaceful, tranquil).
default.q.n2-8-q19-19.explanation:
- Translation: The international conference was held with the goal of realizing a peaceful society without war.
- Vocabulary and related kanji-based terms:
  + 平和 (へいわ): peace.
  + 安易 (あんい): easygoing, careless, superficial.
  + 簡易 (かんい): simple, simplified.
  + 平気 (へいき): calm, unbothered, fine.
  + 実現を目指す (じつげんをめざす): aim to realize.
- Example: 私たちは平和な世界を築くために努力しなければならない。 (We must work to build a peaceful world.)
default.q.n2-8-q19-19.why.0: (a) 安易な (あんいな - facile, careless, thoughtless): usually has a negative meaning, describing immature thinking or a careless approach, as in 安易な考え. It does not combine with 社会.
default.q.n2-8-q19-19.why.1: (b) 簡易な (かんいな): simplified and convenient; used for objects or procedures made simpler for convenience (such as 簡易トイレ or 簡易宿泊所), not to modify “society.”
default.q.n2-8-q19-19.why.2: (c) 平気な (へいきな - calm, unconcerned): Describes a person's calm, fearless attitude or emotions, and is not used for society.
default.q.n2-8-q19-19.why.3: (d) 平和な (へいわな — peaceful): It means peaceful, without war or conflict, and correctly forms 「戦争のない平和な社会」.
default.q.n2-8-q20-20.verdict: The correct answer is 4. 覚悟 (being mentally prepared / resolving to face the risks).
default.q.n2-8-q20-20.explanation:
- Meaning: I opposed the director’s order, prepared to resign.
- Vocabulary & kanji:
  + 覚悟 (かくご): preparedness, readiness to face a difficult situation. Pattern: ～覚悟で (with the resolve/readiness to accept...).
  + 逆らう (さからう): to oppose, go against.
  + 不満 (ふまん): dissatisfaction, discontent.
  + 我慢 (がまん): patience, endurance.
  + 承知 (しょうち): knowledge, consent, acceptance.
- Example: 批判される覚悟で、自分の意見を正直に述べた。(I stated my opinion honestly, prepared to be criticized.)
default.q.n2-8-q20-20.why.0: (a) 不満 (ふまん: dissatisfaction, frustration) does not combine with 「～不満で」 to express a mindset of preparing to face the consequences.
default.q.n2-8-q20-20.why.1: (b) 我慢 (がまん — endurance, patience): It expresses restrained forbearance and does not fit a structure used with 「逆らった」 (resisted, went against).
default.q.n2-8-q20-20.why.2: (c) 承知 (しょうち - understanding, acknowledgment): Although the expression 「承知の上で」 means “knowing this but doing it anyway,” the correct word in the structure 「～で」 expressing an attitude of accepting a possible bad outcome is 覚悟.
default.q.n2-8-q20-20.why.3: (d) 覚悟 (かくご): 「～覚悟で」 means “with the readiness to accept” a possible negative outcome, expressing a willingness to risk losing one’s job by disobeying the director’s orders.
default.q.n2-8-q21-21.verdict: The correct answer is 3. い流せいに (the original form is 一斉に / いっせいに: all at once, simultaneously).
default.q.n2-8-q21-21.explanation:
- Translation: The cherry blossoms all came into full bloom at once.
- Note: The 「い流せいに」 in the question is a display/OCR error for the adverb 「いっせいに」 (kanji: 一斉に — all at once, simultaneously).
- Vocabulary & kanji readings:
  + 一斉に (いっせいに): all at once, simultaneously.
  + 開花 (かいか): flowering, coming into bloom.
  + ひとりでに: naturally, by itself.
  + めいめい (銘々): each person, individually.
  + ずらりと: in a long row, in a line.
- Example: ベルが鳴ると、生徒たちは一斉に教室から駆け出した。(When the bell rang, the students all rushed out of the classroom at once.)
default.q.n2-8-q21-21.why.0: (a) ひとりでに (naturally, spontaneously): Describes something changing automatically without an external force (e.g., ドアがひとりでに開いた); it is not used to describe flowers blooming all at once.
default.q.n2-8-q21-21.why.1: (b) めいめい (each person, individually): It refers to each individual doing something, as in めいめい意見を言う; it is not used for flowers.
default.q.n2-8-q21-21.why.2: (c) い流せいに (a typing/OCR error for いっせいに - 一斉に - “all at once”): It describes multiple subjects carrying out an action or undergoing a change at the same time, and naturally combines with 「開花した」 to mean “the cherry blossoms bloomed all at once.”
default.q.n2-8-q21-21.why.3: (d) ずらりと (in a long row, lined up in succession) usually modifies verbs describing things being lined up or displayed, such as 並ぶ, and does not go with 開花する.
default.q.n2-8-q22-22.verdict: The correct answer is 2. こ流そり (the original form is こっそり: secretly, stealthily).
default.q.n2-8-q22-22.explanation:
- Meaning: Because I was hungry, I secretly sneaked a snack in the middle of the night.
- Note: 「こ流そり」 in the question is an OCR/display error for the adverb 「こっそり」 (secretly, stealthily).
- Related vocabulary:
  + こっそり: secretly, stealthily.
  + 夜中 (よなか - DẠ TRUNG): midnight, middle of the night.
  + ぴったり: exactly fitting, perfectly suited.
  + ぎっしり: tightly packed, crammed full.
- Example: 家族が寝静まったあと、こっそり部屋を抜け出した。(After my family had fallen asleep, I secretly slipped out of the room.)
default.q.n2-8-q22-22.why.0: (a) 消ったり is a misspelling and does not exist as an adverb; it cannot describe behavior in this context.
default.q.n2-8-q22-22.why.1: (b) こ流そり (a typing/OCR error for こっそり—secretly, surreptitiously): it describes doing something quietly to avoid being noticed by others, exactly matching secretly sneaking a snack because one is hungry in the middle of the night.
default.q.n2-8-q22-22.why.2: (c) ぴったり (a perfect fit, exactly) describes a match in size, timing, or personality, so it is not appropriate for secretly eating something.
default.q.n2-8-q22-22.why.3: (d) ぎっしり: packed tightly or crammed full; it describes a space filled with objects (such as 箱にぎっしり詰める), and is not used to modify the act of eating sweets in this way.
default.q.n2-8-q23-23.verdict: The correct answer is 2. ちからづよく because 「勢いよく」 means strongly, decisively, and is synonymous with 「力強く」.
default.q.n2-8-q23-23.explanation:
Meaning: When the signal appears, you are required to raise your right hand decisively and forcefully.
- Sino-Japanese readings: 勢 (THẾ - force, momentum), 力 (LỰC - strength).
- Example: 彼は勢いよくドアを開けて部屋に入ってきた。(He flung the door open and entered the room.)
default.q.n2-8-q23-23.why.0: (a) 「すばやく」（素早く） means “quickly” or “swiftly,” emphasizing speed of movement. It is not synonymous with the forceful, decisive manner expressed by 「勢いよく」.
default.q.n2-8-q23-23.why.1: (b) 「ちからづよく」（力強く）means “strongly, with power,” and is the closest in meaning to 「勢いよく」 (energetically, decisively, with force).
default.q.n2-8-q23-23.why.2: (c) 「まっすぐに」（真っ直ぐに）means “straight” or “directly,” describing direction or a straight shape; it does not express force or vigor.
default.q.n2-8-q23-23.why.3: (d) 「たかく」（高く）means “high,” referring to position or spatial height; it does not convey the strength or decisiveness of the action.
default.q.n2-8-q24-24.verdict: The correct answer is 3. 合計に含まれない because 「勘定に入れない」 means not to count something or include it in the total.
default.q.n2-8-q24-24.explanation:
Sentence translation: Not counting children, each room can accommodate up to four people.
- Expression: 「勘定に入れる」（かんじょうにいれる）means “to count” or “to include in the calculation”; the negative forms 「勘定に入れない / 勘定に入れず」mean 合計に含めない (not to include in the total).
- Example: 今回の旅行の人数には、まだ子どもは勘定に入れていない。(The number of people for this trip does not yet include the children.)
default.q.n2-8-q24-24.why.0: (a) 「料金が不要である」means "free of charge / no payment is required". It refers only to cost and does not match the meaning of "not count someone in the total" expressed by「勘定に入れない」in this sentence.
default.q.n2-8-q24-24.why.1: (b) 「使用を禁止する」 means “to prohibit use,” which is completely wrong and opposite to the context permitting use.
default.q.n2-8-q24-24.why.2: (c) 「合計に含まれない」 means “not included in the total,” which is exactly equivalent to 「勘定に入れない / 勘定に入れず」 (“not count toward the list or total number of people”).
default.q.n2-8-q24-24.why.3: (d) 「計算ができない」means “cannot calculate,” describing an inability to do arithmetic and being completely inappropriate for the context.
default.q.n2-8-q25-25.verdict: The correct answer is 4. 考慮する because, in the context of “being aware of and understanding one’s position,” 「心得る」 is synonymous with paying attention to, considering, and understanding something (考慮する/理解して自覚する).
default.q.n2-8-q25-25.explanation:
Sentence translation: If you are a minister, I think you should be more aware of and attentive to your own position.
- Kanji vocabulary: 心得 (understanding, awareness, principles to remember), 考慮 (consideration, deliberation).
- Example: 自分の役割をよく心得て行動してください。(Please understand your role well and act accordingly.)
default.q.n2-8-q25-25.why.0: (a) 「承認する」（しょうにんする）means "to acknowledge, approve, or consent to" and is not used to mean being conscious of or concerned about one's own status.
default.q.n2-8-q25-25.why.1: (b) 「同意する」（どういする） means to agree with or endorse an opinion or viewpoint, so it does not match the meaning of 「心得る」.
default.q.n2-8-q25-25.why.2: (c) 「経験する」 (けいけんする) means “to experience” or “to go through” and does not express consciously understanding one’s responsibility or position.
default.q.n2-8-q25-25.why.3: (d) 「考慮する」（こうりょする）means “to consider,” “to take into account,” or “to give consideration to.” In the context of being aware of and understanding one’s duties and position, it is the closest match.
default.q.n2-8-q26-26.verdict: The correct answer is 2. 覚悟 because 「観念する」 means to accept one’s fate and mentally prepare for a bad outcome, making it synonymous with 「覚悟する」.
default.q.n2-8-q26-26.explanation:
Sentence translation: Now that things have come this far, I suppose all I can do is prepare myself to accept it and face the consequences.
- Sino-Japanese readings: 観念 (QUAN NIỆM: in colloquial speech, to accept one’s fate, resign oneself, or give up), 覚悟 (GIÁC NGỘ: to prepare oneself mentally for risks or difficulties).
- Example: 逃げ切れないと分かって、犯人は観念した。(Realizing that he could not escape, the criminal resigned himself to his fate.)
default.q.n2-8-q26-26.why.0: (a) 「決心」（けっしん）means “to resolve to do something.” It expresses an active, positive intention toward a goal and does not carry the nuance of resigned acceptance of an outcome, as 「観念する」 does.
default.q.n2-8-q26-26.why.1: (b) 「覚悟」（かくご）means 'to mentally prepare oneself, to be ready to face something bad' and is synonymous with 「観念する」(to resign oneself to or accept a difficult fate or reality).
default.q.n2-8-q26-26.why.2: (c) 「決意」(けつい) means “determination” or “a firm decision,” similar to 決心. It does not convey the nuance of giving up and accepting a bad reality.
default.q.n2-8-q26-26.why.3: (d) 「断念」（だんねん）means “to give up” a plan or dream. Although it is semantically close to giving up, 「観念する」 emphasizes realizing and mentally preparing oneself (覚悟) to face an unavoidable situation.
default.q.n2-8-q27-27.verdict: The correct answer is 2. 検討して because 「十分に考える」 means to think over or consider something carefully, synonymous with 「検討する」.
default.q.n2-8-q27-27.explanation:
Meaning: This issue must be carefully considered while being resolved step by step.
- Kanji note: 検討 means to study, discuss, and consider carefully.
- Example: その提案については、現在社内で検討しています。(We are currently considering that proposal within the company.)
default.q.n2-8-q27-27.why.0: (a) 「工夫して」（くふうして）means “to devise creatively” or “to put effort into finding a new way”; it is not equivalent to carefully considering something (十分に考える).
default.q.n2-8-q27-27.why.1: (b) 「検討して」（けんとうして）means “considering, examining, or carefully weighing,” and is fully equivalent in meaning to 「十分に考えながら」.
default.q.n2-8-q27-27.why.2: (c) 「理解して」（りかいして） means “understand” or “comprehend,” referring to the result of taking in information. It is not synonymous with the process of thinking something through carefully.
default.q.n2-8-q27-27.why.3: (d) 「反省して」（はんせいして）means “reflect on one’s mistakes” or “repent,” and is used when looking back on wrongdoing in the past.
default.q.n2-8-q28-28.verdict: The correct answer is 4 because 「実に」 combines naturally with the adjective 「残念」 to emphasize the degree (“extremely, truly regrettable”).
default.q.n2-8-q28-28.explanation:
「実に」(じつに) is an adverb with an exclamatory tone used to emphasize the high degree of a quality or state ("truly, indeed, extremely"). It commonly modifies an adjective or adverb, as in 実にすばらしい, 実に残念, and 実に面白い. Do not confuse it with 「実は」("actually...") or 「実際に」("in reality, actually").
Example: 昨日のコンサートは実に素晴らしかった。(Yesterday's concert was truly wonderful.)
default.q.n2-8-q28-28.why.0: Incorrect because expressing “actually” or “with one’s own eyes” to confirm the authenticity of an event requires 「実際に」 (or 「確かに」), not 「実に」.
default.q.n2-8-q28-28.why.1: To acknowledge or reveal the fact that “actually, I was the one who did it,” use 「実は」 or 「本当に」, not 「実に」.
default.q.n2-8-q28-28.why.2: Incorrect because the fixed expression used to discreetly state a fact or reason is 「実を言いますと」(or 「実は」); 「実に言いますと」is not used.
default.q.n2-8-q28-28.why.3: Correct because 「実に」is an exclamatory adverb meaning "truly, extremely". It modifies the adjective「残念」to form the natural phrase「実に残念な～」(extremely regrettable～).
default.q.n2-8-q29-29.verdict: The correct answer is 2 because 「ふもと」 (the foot of a mountain) is the appropriate word used with 「山」 (山のふもと).
default.q.n2-8-q29-29.explanation:
「ふもと」（麓） is a noun meaning “the foot of a mountain”—the flat or gently sloping area directly below a mountain (山のふもと). It is used specifically for mountains or hilly areas, not for people, trees, or buildings.
Example: 富士山のふもとには美しい湖がいくつかあります。(There are several beautiful lakes at the foot of Mount Fuji.)
default.q.n2-8-q29-29.why.0: Incorrect because for a high-rise building, the area at its base is expressed as 「ビルの足元」 or 「ビルの下」, not 「ふもと」.
default.q.n2-8-q29-29.why.1: Correct because 「ふもと」 (麓) means the area at or below the foot of a mountain and correctly forms the phrase 「山のふもと」.
default.q.n2-8-q29-29.why.2: Incorrect because the area directly below a person's feet is called 「足元」（あしもと）, not 「ふもと」.
default.q.n2-8-q29-29.why.3: Incorrect because the base of a tree or the part near ground level is expressed as 「木の根元」（ねもと） or 「木の下」, not 「ふもと」.
default.q.n2-8-q30-30.verdict: The correct answer is 1 because「がっかりする」expresses the disappointment and letdown felt when a long-awaited trip is canceled.
default.q.n2-8-q30-30.explanation:
「がっかり」is an onomatopoeic adverb, often used with する, that describes disappointment, discouragement, or feeling let down when the result does not meet expectations or when something hoped for does not happen.
Example: 試験に落ちてしまい、ひどくがっかりした。(I failed the exam and was extremely disappointed.)
default.q.n2-8-q30-30.why.0: Correct. 「がっかりする」 expresses disappointment or letdown when something expected, such as a trip, cannot take place.
default.q.n2-8-q30-30.why.1: Incorrect because a company one founded doing well is a positive outcome, so 「安心した」 (felt relieved) or 「嬉しかった」 (was happy) should be used, not 「がっかりした」 (was disappointed).
default.q.n2-8-q30-30.why.2: Incorrect because unexpectedly meeting someone one thought one could never meet is a positive, surprising experience, so 「嬉しかった」 or 「びっくりした」 should be used, not 「がっかりした」.
default.q.n2-8-q30-30.why.3: Incorrect because when someone becomes nervous before speaking and their heart beats rapidly from tension, use 「ドキドキする」 or 「緊張する」, not 「がっかりする」.
default.q.n2-8-q31-31.verdict: The correct answer is 4 because 「スピードを増す」 is a natural expression for a vehicle, such as a truck, accelerating.
default.q.n2-8-q31-31.explanation:
「スピード」 (speed) is a loanword from English meaning “speed,” referring to the movement of vehicles, people, or machines, or the pace of work. It commonly appears in expressions such as 「スピードを出す」 (to speed up), 「スピードを上げる / スピードを増す」 (to increase speed), and 「スピードを落とす」 (to slow down).
Example: コーナーの手前で車のスピードを落とした。(I slowed the car down before the corner.)
default.q.n2-8-q31-31.why.0: Incorrect because the word for the strength or resistance of glass that keeps it from breaking when hit by a ball is 「強度」, not 「スピード」.
default.q.n2-8-q31-31.why.1: As the volcano's energy or force increases, use 「勢い」 (force, momentum) or 「強さ」, not 「スピード」, which does not describe volcanic energy.
default.q.n2-8-q31-31.why.2: It is incorrect because when temperatures rise with the season, expressions such as 「上昇する」or 「勢いを増す」are used; temperature does not combine with 「スピードを増す」.
default.q.n2-8-q31-31.why.3: Correct because 「スピードを増す」 is a standard collocation describing a vehicle, such as a truck, gradually increasing its speed.
default.q.n2-8-q32-32.verdict: The correct answer is 1 because 「人を差別する」 means to discriminate against or unfairly treat people differently.
default.q.n2-8-q32-32.explanation:
「差別」（さべつ） means “discrimination, prejudice” (treating someone unfairly or with bias based on gender, race, social status, and so on). It should be distinguished from 「区別」（くべつ: distinguishing the differences between two or more things) and 「分ける」（to divide/separate).
Example: 人種や性別によって差別することは許されない。(Discrimination based on race or gender is not allowed.)
default.q.n2-8-q32-32.why.0: Correct because 「差別する」 describes unfairly discriminating against or stigmatizing people (人を差別する).
default.q.n2-8-q32-32.why.1: Incorrect because separating an egg yolk and white into two parts requires 「分ける」 (わける) or 「分離する」, not 「差別」.
default.q.n2-8-q32-32.why.2: Incorrect because dividing people into groups of ten in order of arrival is expressed with 「区切って」 or 「グループに分けて」, not 「差別」.
default.q.n2-8-q32-32.why.3: Incorrect because clearly distinguishing between two sounds, pronouncing “hi” and “shi” distinctly, requires 「区別する」 or 「発音し分ける」, not 「差別」.
default.q.n2-8-q1-1.verdict: The correct answer is 2. いいがたい.

default.q.n2-8-q1-1.why.1: (b) Correct because the verb 言う combines with the suffix 〜難い, undergoing sound change to become 「いいがたい」, meaning “difficult to say” or “hard to claim.”
default.q.n2-8-q1-1.why.2: (c) The reading is incorrect: 「難」is not read as つらい (the kanji 「辛」in 辛い is read as つらい). Moreover, after a verb, the combined form is 〜づらい.

default.q.n2-9-q33-33.verdict: The correct answer is 4. 注意するようになった.
default.q.n2-9-q33-33.explanation:
Sentence translation: "The stomach surgery I underwent three years ago prompted me to start paying more attention to my health."
• Kanji readings: 胃 (stomach); 手術 (surgery); 健康 (health); 注意 (attention).
• Grammar: 「N / V-たの + をきっかけに(して) / を契機に」 means "taking something as an opportunity or turning point," leading to a change, habit, or new action. It is often used with expressions indicating change, such as 「〜ようになる」 and 「〜始める」.
